Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How much does an extra year of education raise wages, once experience, tenure, ability and demographics are held fixed? This is the Mincer wage regression. The model is with \(x_i\) containing education, experience, tenure, IQ and dummies for marriage, race, region and city. OLS gives one number per coefficient and a standard error. A Bayesian regression gives a whole posterior distribution for each coefficient: you can read off the probability that the return to schooling exceeds 5%, combine the data with the results of earlier studies, and compare specifications without a p-value threshold. The OES engine uses a conjugate Normal-inverse-gamma prior. Everything is exact: no simulation, no convergence to check, and the log marginal likelihood is available in closed form. Two priors are offered for the slopes:
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Prior What it says When to use it Zellner's g-prior \(\beta \sim N(\beta_0, g\,\sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1})\) : the prior is as informative as \(1/g\) of an observation's worth of the sample, scaled to the regressors Default. Unit-free, so it needs no judgement about the scale of each variable. \(g = n\) is the "unit-information prior" Normal \(\beta_j \sim N(\beta_{0j}, s^2)\) , the same standard deviation for every slope When the variables are in comparable units, or when you have a prior from earlier work The constant has a flat prior and \(\sigma^2\) an inverse-gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior in both cases. A large \(g\) (or large \(s\) ) lets the data speak; a small one pulls the slopes towards the prior mean \(\beta_0\) .
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Frequentist or Bayesian? With 663 observations and a weak prior, the two give almost the same numbers, and that is the point: a Bayesian regression is a way of reporting the answer (probabilities, intervals that mean what people think they mean) and of using extra information, not a different estimate. Use it when the sample is small, when you have genuine prior information, or when model comparison is part of the question. How to write it: the model We estimate the log-wage equation by Bayesian linear regression with a Zellner g-prior on the slopes ( \(g = n\) , the unit-information prior), a flat prior on the constant and an inverse-gamma(0.01, 0.01) prior on the error variance (Zellner 1986; Liang et al. 2008). With this conjugate prior the marginal posterior of each coefficient is a Student- \(t\) distribution, available in closed form, and we report its mean, standard deviation, 95% credible interval and the posterior probability that the coefficient is positive.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it 663 men, with log wages averaging 6.81 (about $900 a month) and a standard deviation of 0.41. Education averages 13.7 years. Nine in ten are married, 8% are Black, 32% live in the South and 72% in a city. Dummy variables like these have a standard deviation below 0.5, while IQ has 14.7: the g-prior is useful here because it scales the prior for each coefficient by the spread of its regressor, so you do not have to choose a different prior standard deviation for IQ and for a dummy.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it Each row is a posterior distribution. Take education: the posterior mean is 0.055 with a standard deviation of 0.008, so a year of schooling raises wages by about 5.5%, and there is a 95% probability that the effect lies between 3.9% and 7.1%. That is a direct statement about the parameter; a frequentist confidence interval cannot be read that way. The last column, \(P(>0)\) , is the posterior probability that the effect is positive: 1.000 for education, experience, marriage and city; 0.999 for tenure and IQ; and 0.012 and 0.019 for Black and South, whose effects are negative with high probability. Compare with OLS: coefficients agree to the third decimal place. The g-prior with \(g = n\) carries the weight of a single observation, so with 663 observations it moves nothing. This is the expected result with a weak prior and a decent sample; Step 6 shows what happens with a stronger prior.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

The log marginal likelihood is the probability of the data under the model with the coefficients integrated out. It rewards fit and automatically penalises a model for having parameters it does not need. The difference between two models is the log Bayes factor . How to read it A log Bayes factor above about 1 is "some evidence" for the full model, above 2.3 is "strong" and above 4.6 "decisive" (Jeffreys' scale). Dropping urban costs almost 17 log points: the city dummy is decisive. Dropping IQ costs 2.0 and tenure 1.3: moderate evidence for both. Dropping south or black raises the marginal likelihood by 1.1 and 0.7: the data, after the penalty for extra parameters, slightly prefer the model without them. This does not mean the coefficients are zero (both have \(P(>0)\) below 0.02); it means they are not worth their cost in predictive terms.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Report the table if the specification is a topic in the paper, and describe the scale you use. Do not use the Bayes factor as a mechanical rule; use it with the posterior intervals and with economic reasoning.

If earlier studies find a return to education of about 7%, you can say so. prior_mean sets the prior mean of each slope: one number for all, or a list in the order of the regressors. How to read it The posterior mean of the education coefficient barely moves (0.0551 against 0.0550), because this prior carries the weight of one observation. To let earlier work matter, use a small g or a Normal prior with a small standard deviation, and report the sensitivity table below. In a small sample the prior would matter much more, and writing it down becomes part of the paper's identification of the result.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior
Robustness: how much does the prior matter?

How to read it Each row re-estimates the slopes under a different prior. For \(g \ge 663\) and for the Normal priors with standard deviation 1 or 10, the slopes are the same as OLS: the data dominate. With \(g = 10\) the coefficients shrink by about 9% (education 0.050), and with \(g = 1\) by half (education 0.028; marriage 0.10 against 0.20). The tight Normal prior (standard deviation 0.1) pulls every slope towards zero, with the largest effect on marriage (0.075) and race ( \(-0.037\) ), which have the largest coefficients. What to say: the signs and ranking of the effects do not depend on the prior unless it is much more informative than the data. If a result flips only for a prior that acts like a handful of observations, it is not robust. The table is cheap evidence to show a referee.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior
Robustness: how much does the prior matter?

For a non-conjugate prior (a Normal prior with the same standard deviation for each slope and independent of \(\sigma^2\) ), the posterior is obtained by a Gibbs sampler, which needs a convergence check: How to read it The effective sample size equals the number of draws (3000) for every coefficient, because a Gibbs sampler for a linear model draws from two exact conditional distributions and the chain mixes immediately. Geweke's test compares the first 10% and the last 50% of the chain: a statistic with |z| above 2 would mean the chain had not settled. It is borderline for black (z = 2.0): with nine parameters one such value is expected by chance, and increasing the burn-in confirms nothing changes. Report effective sample sizes for any sampler you use.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to read it Residual autocorrelation is rejected by neither the portmanteau nor the Ljung-Box test, as expected in a cross-section. Residuals are not normal (Jarque-Bera rejects) and the variance is not constant (Breusch-Pagan, p = 0.003). The regression coefficients stay consistent, but the posterior standard deviations assume a constant variance and are too small if the variance is unevenly spread: the table compares the posterior standard deviations with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC3) OLS standard errors. The ratios run from 0.90 (Black) to 1.06 (South), so the robust errors are within about 10% of the posterior ones and the conclusions stand, with one qualification: with robust errors the South coefficient is borderline (t about 1.96). Report the robust errors next to the posterior as a check; the point estimates are the same.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

How to write it: results Table 1 reports posterior summaries. A year of education raises hourly wages by 5.5% (posterior standard deviation 0.8 percentage points; 95% credible interval 3.9% to 7.1%), with a posterior probability of one that the effect is positive. Experience, tenure, IQ, marriage and living in a city have positive effects (probability above 0.999), while the effects of being Black or living in the South are negative with probabilities of 0.988 and 0.981. The posterior means are almost identical to OLS because the g-prior carries the weight of one observation. The log Bayes factors indicate decisive support for the city dummy (16.8), and moderate support for IQ (2.0) and tenure (1.3); the data slightly prefer a model without the South and Black dummies, though their credible intervals exclude zero. The signs and ranking of the effects are unchanged for all priors except those that carry the weight of fewer than ten observations (Table 2). Residual diagnostics show heteroskedasticity, so we also compare with heteroskedasticity-robust OLS standard errors, which are within 10% of the posterior standard deviations; the South coefficient is then only borderline significant.
Bayesian Linear Regression with a g-Prior

Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

What happens to output and inflation after an unexpected rise in the short-term interest rate? This is the classic question of the monetary VAR. The model is a VAR( \(p\) ) in three variables, quarterly GDP growth, CPI inflation and the 3-month Treasury bill rate: With \(p = 4\) lags each equation has \(1 + 3 \times 4 = 13\) coefficients, 39 in all, plus 6 in \(\Sigma\) . Fifty years of quarterly data give about 200 observations: enough to estimate the coefficients, but not to estimate them precisely . Unrestricted OLS fits the noise, impulse responses come out jagged, and forecasts are poor. A Bayesian VAR adds a prior that pulls every coefficient towards a sensible benchmark. The Minnesota prior (Litterman 1986) says that each variable behaves like its own random walk or white noise, that recent lags matter more than distant ones, and that other variables' lags matter less than a variable's own. The data then move the coefficients away from this benchmark only as far as they have evidence for.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

Term Meaning Default here \(\delta_i\) prior mean of variable \(i\) 's own first lag 1 for an I(1) series in levels, 0 for a stationary one \(\lambda_1\) overall tightness: how strongly all coefficients are pulled to the prior 0.2, then chosen by the data \(\lambda_2\) extra tightness on the lags of other variables 0.5 \(\lambda_3\) how fast the prior tightens with the lag length ( \(1/l^{\lambda_3}\) ) 1 \(\lambda_4\) tightness on the constant 100 (essentially flat) Four priors, one idea The OES engine offers the four priors of the ECB's BEAR toolbox. They share the Minnesota means and scales and differ in how they treat \(\Sigma\) : Minnesota (Litterman): \(\Sigma\) is fixed at the residual variances of univariate AR models. Exact, fast, equation by equation. Good for forecasting.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

Normal-Wishart: \(\Sigma\) is estimated with an inverse-Wishart prior, and the posterior and the marginal likelihood are analytic, so lag length and tightness can be chosen by the data. It forces \(\lambda_2 = 1\) . Independent Normal-Wishart: frees \(\lambda_2\) and allows block exogeneity; estimated by Gibbs sampling. Normal-diffuse: Minnesota prior on the coefficients, no information on \(\Sigma\) ; Gibbs sampling. Start with Normal-Wishart to choose the lags and \(\lambda_1\) , then report the prior you prefer and show the others as robustness. How to write it: the model We estimate a Bayesian VAR in real GDP growth, CPI inflation and the 3-month Treasury bill rate, \(y_t = c + \sum_{l=1}^{p} A_l y_{t-l} + u_t\) , \(u_t \sim N(0,\Sigma)\) , on quarterly U.S. data for 1959Q3–2009Q3. Following Litterman (1986) and Kadiyala and Karlsson (1997), we use a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments: the prior mean of each variable's own first lag is one for the interest rate, which is persistent, and zero for growth and inflation; all other coefficients have prior mean zero, with prior standard deviations that shrink with the lag length.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Load the data and test for unit roots

The prior mean of the own first lag depends on whether a series is persistent. Test first. How to read it GDP growth and inflation reject a unit root in levels (ADF p-values below 0.05) and are treated as stationary: prior mean 0 on their own first lag. The T-bill rate does not reject; it is stationary only after differencing, so it gets a random-walk prior (prior mean 1). Notice that nothing is differenced: a Bayesian VAR is estimated in levels, and the prior handles the persistence. Sims, Stock and Watson (1990) show that inference on impulse responses remains valid in levels even with unit roots or cointegration.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Choose the lag length and the tightness

The Normal-Wishart prior gives the marginal likelihood , the probability of the data under the model with the coefficients integrated out. It rewards fit and penalises complexity automatically, so it can choose both the number of lags and \(\lambda_1\) (Giannone, Lenza and Primiceri 2015). How to read it Lags. The marginal likelihood rises quickly up to three or four lags and then flattens: extra lags add little once the prior has shrunk them. BIC, which has no prior to shrink with, prefers fewer lags. With quarterly data four lags is the convention, and the marginal likelihood supports it; more lags would be harmless under the prior. Tightness. The marginal likelihood peaks at \(\lambda_1 = 0.2\) : looser priors overfit, tighter ones ignore the data. This is the value used below. Always report how \(\lambda_1\) was chosen; a value picked to deliver a result is a red flag for referees.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to read it Each row is a posterior: its mean, standard deviation, 95% credible interval and the posterior probability that the coefficient is positive. The interest-rate equation is a monetary policy rule in reduced form: the T-bill rate is highly persistent (own first lag about 0.93) and rises after strong GDP growth and higher inflation, with posterior probabilities above 0.9 for several of these lags. "Distance from OLS" in the summary shows how much the prior moved the coefficients: about half, which is typical for a VAR of this size. A credible interval is read literally: given the model and the prior, there is a 95% probability that the coefficient lies in it. Bayesian results do not need p-values, but P(> 0) close to 0 or 1 plays the same role.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Impulse responses: a monetary policy shock

The policy shock is identified recursively (Cholesky), with the interest rate ordered last : the Fed reacts within the quarter to output and inflation, while output and prices respond to the interest rate only with a lag. This is the standard ordering of Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (1999). How to read it After a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, GDP growth falls, and the 68% credible band stays below zero for about two years. Inflation, however, rises before it falls back: the well-known price puzzle (Sims 1992). It usually means the VAR omits information the Fed uses to forecast inflation, such as commodity prices; the FAVAR guide shows how adding many indicators addresses it. Report the puzzle honestly rather than hiding it; it is a known limitation of small monetary VARs.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
Impulse responses: a monetary policy shock
Bayesian VAR papers report 68% bands (16th to 84th percentiles) by convention, as here; add 90% bands if referees ask.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors
How important is the shock? Variance decomposition

How to read it Monetary policy shocks explain only a few percent of the forecast-error variance of GDP growth and inflation, even after five years. Most movements in output and inflation are due to other shocks; the interest rate itself is driven increasingly by output and inflation, as the policy rule implies. This is the standard result: policy matters for how the economy responds, but surprises in policy are a small source of fluctuations.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to read it Stability. Almost every posterior draw has all roots inside the unit circle, and the largest root at the posterior mean is below one: the VAR is stationary and impulse responses die out. Autocorrelation. Ljung-Box does not reject for GDP growth and inflation but does for the T-bill rate, and the joint portmanteau test rejects. A fifth or sixth lag removes most of it; check that the responses do not change (they do not, in Step 7). Normality and ARCH. Strongly rejected for inflation and the interest rate. The 1970s oil shocks and the Volcker disinflation produce large residuals, and their variance changes over time. The coefficient estimates remain valid, but bands that assume constant variance are too narrow in volatile periods. The SV-VAR guide models this directly; mention it as a limitation.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

With the Normal-Wishart prior the posterior draws are independent, so there is nothing to converge. The Gibbs samplers (Independent Normal-Wishart, Normal-diffuse) need a check: How to read it Effective sample sizes are close to the number of draws and the Geweke statistics are small: the chain mixes well and has settled. If |z| were above 2 for several parameters, increase the burn-in.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

A result that depends on the prior is not a result. Three checks: How to read it Tightness. With tight and moderate priors ( \(\lambda_1 \le 0.2\) ) the output response is negative at every horizon. With very loose priors and with OLS, the response at four quarters turns positive : without shrinkage the VAR fits noise, and the sign is not robust. This is exactly why a Bayesian VAR is used, and the table is the evidence a referee needs. Prior family. All four priors give a fall in GDP growth of similar size. Report the Normal-Wishart results and these as robustness. How to read it Recursive one- and four-quarter-ahead forecasts over the last 20% of the sample. The BVAR beats the OLS VAR for inflation at both horizons and is close for the other variables; a random walk is hard to beat for the interest rate at short horizons, as usual. In a forecasting paper, test the differences formally with the Diebold-Mariano test and report several evaluation windows.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

When some variables cannot be affected by the others, such as world variables in a model of a small open economy, the Independent Normal-Wishart and Normal-diffuse priors can impose it: the coefficients of the other variables in the block's equations get (almost) zero prior variance. Here GDP growth is (for illustration) made block-exogenous: the lags of inflation and the interest rate in its equation are pushed to zero. In a real application use it for foreign variables, oil prices or anything determined outside the economy you model.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

How to write it: results The marginal likelihood selects four lags and an overall tightness of \(\lambda_1 = 0.2\) . Figure 1 shows the responses to a one-standard-deviation monetary policy shock, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last. GDP growth falls by about 0.1 percentage point within a year, and the 68% credible band excludes zero for two years. Inflation initially rises, the price puzzle familiar from small monetary VARs (Sims 1992), before returning to its baseline. Policy shocks account for less than 3% of the forecast-error variance of output growth at all horizons. The output response is negative under all four priors (Minnesota, Normal-Wishart, Independent Normal-Wishart and Normal-diffuse) and for any \(\lambda_1 \le 0.2\) ; with much looser priors, and with OLS, the response becomes erratic, which illustrates the value of shrinkage in a sample of this length.
Bayesian VAR with Minnesota and Normal-Wishart Priors

Factor-Augmented VAR (FAVAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does a small monetary VAR omit information that matters? A VAR in inflation, unemployment and the interest rate has the price puzzle: inflation rises after a tightening. One explanation is that the central bank sees far more than three series, and the VAR leaves that information in the residual. A factor-augmented VAR (Bernanke, Boivin and Eliasz 2005) adds a few unobserved factors \(F_t\) that summarise a large panel \(X_t\) of \(N\) informational series: where \(Y_t\) are the observed variables (here inflation, unemployment and the policy rate, ordered last). Two things follow from the first equation. The factors enter the VAR, so the policy shock is identified with more information in the system. And every series in \(X_t\) has an impulse response, \(\Lambda' \times\) the VAR response, so you can report the effect of the shock on dozens of series without estimating a dozen VARs.

OES implements the two-step estimator: the factors are the principal components of the standardised panel, and the VAR on \((F_t, Y_t)\) is a Bayesian VAR with the Minnesota-type priors of the BVAR guide, with prior mean zero on the factors. What this example is, and is not The example panel has only six series, all real-activity growth rates from the same national accounts. A real FAVAR uses 50 to 150 series (the McCracken-Ng FRED-QD data are the standard source) with prices, interest rates, employment, financial and monetary variables. With six series the factors can say little that the three observed variables do not already say, and the guide shows this honestly in Step 8. Use this guide for the mechanics and diagnostics, and bring a large panel to your own application. The OES page accepts any number of series.

How to write it: the model We estimate a factor-augmented VAR (Bernanke, Boivin and Eliasz 2005). The informational panel, \(N\) quarterly series standardised to mean zero and variance one, is summarised by \(K\) principal components. The factors, together with inflation, unemployment and the Treasury bill rate, enter a VAR( \(p\) ) estimated with a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments (Litterman 1986), with prior mean zero for the factors and for stationary variables and one for the variables with a unit root. The policy shock is the innovation to the Treasury bill rate, identified recursively with the rate ordered last. Responses of the panel series are obtained from their estimated loadings on the factors and the observed variables.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it The principal components do not need stationary data, but they behave well when the panel is stationary, which is why informational series are transformed to growth rates or differences. All six series reject a unit root. Of the observed variables, inflation rejects (ADF p = 0.03), but unemployment and the T-bill rate do not, so they get a random-walk prior ( delta = "0, 1, 1" ). The factors are standardised and stationary, so they get zero.

How to read it Two tools: the cumulative share of variance, and the Bai and Ng (2002) information criterion, which finds the number of factors in a large panel. It needs a large \(N\) and \(T\) ; with \(N = 6\) it is not informative (it keeps falling up to the maximum of five factors, which is nearly the whole panel). In a real application, \(N \ge 50\) and you would choose with the criterion and a scree plot, then check that the results do not depend on the choice (Step 8). Here two factors explain 61% of the variance of the six series, which is what the model uses.

How to read it The first factor explains 42% of the panel: the common real-activity cycle. The second adds 19%. The interest-rate equation is a policy rule: the rate is persistent and responds to inflation, unemployment and the real-activity factors; the question for a FAVAR is whether the factors add to the rule beyond the three observed variables.
The policy shock and the whole panel

How to read it Observed variables first. A one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate (about 0.6 percentage point) raises unemployment gradually, by 0.10 percentage point after two years and 0.14 after three, with the 68% band above zero from the second year. This is the expected sign and size. Inflation, however, rises on impact, by 0.28 percentage point, with a band that excludes zero for more than a year: the price puzzle is still there. This is a result, not an error: six real-activity series carry no information about prices that the VAR does not already have. Step 8 shows that the response is the same with and without the factors.
The policy shock and the whole panel

The advantage of a FAVAR shows in the table and the last two charts: the same shock traced through all six panel series, with no extra VARs. Output growth falls by about 0.15 percentage point after one year (68% band from \(-0.23\) to \(-0.09\) ) and returns to zero after about three years; consumption and income growth fall by 0.12 and 0.09; investment growth falls by 0.58, four times more than output, with a wide band, as in most monetary VARs. Government spending growth hardly moves. The \(R^2\) column tells you how well the factors and observed variables explain each series (0.91 for GDP growth, 0.44 for income growth): the response of a series with a low \(R^2\) is mostly about the common component, so treat it with care.

How to read it Rows are the variables, columns the shocks (Cholesky). The policy shock explains 9% of the forecast-error variance of inflation after five years, 14% of unemployment and 2% of the real-activity factor; the interest rate's own shock accounts for 53% of its variance. The first factor, the real cycle, is the main driver of unemployment (47% to 61%). The policy shock is a modest source of fluctuations, the standard result; policy matters through the rule, not through surprises.

How to read it The factors are fairly well behaved (Ljung-Box does not reject at 5% for either factor), but the observed variables have serial correlation in the residuals (Ljung-Box p below 0.002), non-normal residuals and ARCH. The interest rate is the extreme case (Jarque-Bera 1875): the largest quarterly changes in the T-bill rate, up to 5.9 percentage points, are all in 1980 to 1982, the Volcker disinflation. Adding more lags helps only a little (the portmanteau rejects with two, four and six lags, p = 0.0002 with six), and the joint test has 300 degrees of freedom with 198 observations, so it over-rejects in samples this short; rely on the individual tests. The practical answer is the stochastic-volatility VAR (see the SV-VAR guide), which allows the shock variance to change; in the paper, state the limitation and show that the main results do not depend on the lag length (Step 8).
Robustness: factors, lags and the plain VAR

How to read it The response of inflation to a policy shock, at 1, 4, 8 and 12 quarters, under different choices. It is stable across the number of factors (0.26 to 0.28 at one quarter, 0.16 to 0.17 at three years) and lags, and the same as the BVAR without factors (0.28, 0.29, 0.24, 0.18). Shorter or longer lag lengths move the response at one year by about 0.04, never the sign. Two conclusions for a paper: (1) the FAVAR results are robust to \(K\) and \(p\) ; (2) with this small information set the factors do not change the answer. When the factors do not matter, say so; in a real application with 100 series, this comparison is the main test that the FAVAR is worth the extra complexity.

How to write it: results Two factors, which explain 61% of the variance of the six informational series, are added to a VAR(4) in inflation, unemployment and the Treasury bill rate. A one-standard-deviation shock to the policy rate (about 0.6 percentage point) raises unemployment gradually, by 0.10 percentage point after two years, with a 68% credible band above zero from the second year. Output growth falls by 0.15 percentage point after one year and returns to its baseline after about three years; investment growth falls by 0.58, with a wide band. Inflation rises by 0.28 percentage point on impact and stays above zero for about three years, a price puzzle that is unchanged when the number of factors varies between one and four or the lags between two and six, and that is the same as in the VAR without factors. We conclude that the six real-activity series add no information about prices; a larger panel with price and commodity series is needed to test whether omitted information explains the puzzle. Policy shocks explain 9% of the forecast-error variance of inflation and 14% of that of unemployment after five years.

Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

What is GDP growth this quarter, before the statistical office has published it? Industrial production and interest rates are published monthly, within weeks, but GDP only quarterly, after a month or more. A mixed-frequency VAR estimates the monthly dynamics of all variables jointly, including a latent monthly GDP growth series \(y^*_t\) , and links it to the published quarterly figure \(y^Q\) : in the last month \(t\) of each quarter, and unobserved in the other months. The triangle weights \((1,2,3,2,1)/9\) of Mariano and Murasawa (2003) express the fact that quarterly growth is a weighted average of monthly growth rates; for variables in levels, the alternative is a three-month average. The VAR has a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota-type moments, and the posterior is simulated by a Gibbs sampler that alternates between the VAR parameters and the latent monthly path, which is drawn with the Carter-Kohn simulation smoother (Schorfheide and Song 2015).
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

What you get Three outputs: (1) a monthly estimate of GDP growth with credible bands, which the data never contain; (2) a nowcast of the current quarter, updated each month as new monthly data arrive (the "Nowcasts" table gives the implied quarterly value after each month of the quarter); (3) VAR coefficients and impulse responses at the monthly frequency. The latent monthly series is poorly identified from quarterly data alone: the bands are wide (Step 4). The model does not create information; it uses the monthly indicators to fill in the months between quarterly releases. How to write it: the model We estimate a mixed-frequency Bayesian VAR (Schorfheide and Song 2015) with industrial production growth, the federal funds rate and quarterly GDP growth, with five monthly lags. GDP growth is modelled as an unobserved monthly series whose triangle-weighted sum over five months (Mariano and Murasawa 2003) equals the published quarterly growth rate in the last month of each quarter. The VAR has a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments (overall tightness 0.2, prior mean of the first lags zero). The posterior is simulated with a Gibbs sampler, drawing the latent months with the Carter-Kohn algorithm; we use 3,000 draws after 2,000 burn-in.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

The file has one row per month. Put each quarterly value in the row of the quarter's last month and leave the other months of the quarter blank. How to read it 419 months from 1985-02 to 2019-12, 139 quarterly observations (GDP growth appears in March, June, September and December only). Industrial production growth is annualised monthly growth and very volatile (standard deviation 7.3, range \(-54\) to 24). Quarterly GDP growth averages 2.6% with a standard deviation of 2.3. Unit roots: IP growth and GDP growth reject (p < 0.001); the federal funds rate does not (p = 0.11). Use growth rates for I(1) variables such as GDP (triangle weights) and levels for stationary ones (three-month average). The rate enters in levels, which is common in monthly VARs; the prior mean of its own lag is zero by default, which pulls it towards a constant: consider delta close to one if the persistence of the rate matters for your question.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data
Estimate and the monthly path of GDP

How to read it The figure shows the posterior median of monthly GDP growth (annualised) and a 68% band. The monthly path is very uncertain : the band is typically 6 to 8 percentage points wide, and the median swings between about \(-5\) and 7 from month to month, because only the quarterly aggregate is observed and the model has to split it across three months using industrial production and the interest rate. Use the monthly path to see the direction and timing of movements (for example the dip in early 2014), not to read off precise monthly values. The published quarterly points are drawn as dots; the monthly path aggregates to them by construction.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

How to read it After the last published quarter, the model produces a monthly estimate for each month as industrial production and the federal funds rate arrive: \(-1.45\) for October 2019 (68% band \(-5.2\) to 2.4), 1.96 for November and 2.39 for December. The implied value for the quarter, which aggregates the monthly path with the triangle weights, moves from 3.83 after October to 2.51 after November and 1.42 after December. The December figure is the nowcast of the release, 1.4% annualised. The monthly bands are wide, so state the nowcast with its uncertainty, and the large change between months shows how much the nowcast depends on the first monthly data points: update it as each month arrives, rather than treating the first value as final.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

How to read it In the monthly GDP equation, only industrial production has a clear effect: the coefficient on its first lag is 0.14 (posterior probability of being positive 0.96); the interest-rate coefficients are very imprecise (the first-lag mean of 0.43 has a standard deviation of 1.4) and the lags of GDP are close to zero. The interest-rate equation is close to a random walk: its own first lag is 1.26, and it responds positively to industrial production and GDP growth (probabilities of being positive 0.98). The impulse responses to a one-standard-deviation GDP-growth shock show industrial production rising after two to three months and the interest rate rising slowly for about 14 months, with 68% bands that exclude zero after the first months. The responses are from a model with constant volatility (see the diagnostics below).
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

How to read it The convergence check is not clean. Effective sample sizes are between 135 and 3000 out of 3000 draws; the GDP-equation coefficient on the first lag of industrial production has only 135 (efficiency 4.5%), below the rule of thumb of 200, and three of the twelve reported parameters have Geweke statistics beyond 1.96 (p between 0.03 and 0.04). With twelve parameters, one such value is expected by chance, so three together with the low ESS means the chains need to be longer for a paper: use at least 10,000 draws. Residual tests reject: the monthly GDP residuals are autocorrelated (Ljung-Box p < 0.001), which is expected in part because the latent monthly series is constructed from overlapping quarterly aggregates, and industrial production and the interest rate show ARCH effects (p < 0.001) and non-normal residuals (the industrial production growth series has a minimum of \(-53.8\) ). A constant-volatility VAR is a rough description of 1985–2019, which includes the 2008–09 crisis; the SV-VAR guide shows how to allow for changing volatility.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data
Does it nowcast better than a simple rule? A pseudo real-time test

For each of the last eight quarters, we drop the quarter's GDP figure, re-estimate the model on the data available up to that quarter's last month, and compare the nowcast with the published value and with two benchmarks: the previous quarter's value, and the historical mean. How to read it For each of the last eight quarters the model is re-estimated on the data available at the end of that quarter, without the quarter's GDP figure, and its nowcast is compared with the published value and two benchmarks. The mixed-frequency BVAR does not beat the benchmarks over these eight quarters : its RMSE is 1.68, against 1.35 for repeating the previous quarter and 1.28 for the historical mean. Its error is smaller than that of the previous-quarter rule in five of the eight quarters, but it misses badly in the last three (errors of 1.9, 2.1 and 2.9 points in 2019, when published growth was 2.5, 3.3 and 4.65 and the nowcasts were 0.6, 1.2 and 1.8). With eight quarters, differences in RMSE of this size are not statistically meaningful, and we did not run a formal test; the honest conclusion is that this sample gives no evidence that the model improves on simple rules, so do not present a nowcast gain. The published quarterly figures are those in the example file shipped with OES.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data
Robustness: lags, tightness and the nowcast

How to read it The nowcast of the last quarter varies between 1.40 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.5\) ) and 1.59 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.1\) ); three lags give 1.55 and eight lags 1.44. These runs use 800 draws, so they differ slightly from the 1.42 of Step 4, which used 3000. The spread of 0.2 points across specifications is small next to the width of the monthly bands and next to the evaluation errors in Step 7, so specification choices are not what limits this nowcast; the uncertainty in the data is.
Mixed-Frequency BVAR: Nowcasting Quarterly GDP with Monthly Data

How to write it: results We estimate a mixed-frequency Bayesian VAR (Schorfheide and Song 2015) with industrial production growth, the federal funds rate and quarterly GDP growth, 1985–2019, with five monthly lags and a Minnesota-type prior (overall tightness 0.2). Monthly GDP growth is a latent series that aggregates, with triangle weights over five months (Mariano and Murasawa 2003), to the published quarterly growth rate. The posterior (3,000 draws after 2,000 burn-in) places the latent monthly path within a 68% band about 6 to 8 points wide, and the nowcast for 2019Q4 evolves from 3.8 after October to 2.5 after November and 1.4% annualised after December. The nowcast is robust to the number of lags and the prior tightness (1.4 to 1.6). In a pseudo real-time exercise over the last eight quarters, the model's RMSE of 1.68 is higher than that of the previous-quarter rule (1.35) and of the historical mean (1.28), so we do not claim a forecasting gain over simple benchmarks in this sample. Effective sample sizes are low for some coefficients (as low as 135 of 3,000) and the residuals show autocorrelation and ARCH; results should be confirmed with longer chains and stochastic volatility.

Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How do output growth and unemployment move together across rich countries, and are the dynamics the same everywhere? The data are 14 OECD countries observed for 25 years, 336 usable observations. Each country has the VAR With one lag each country has 6 coefficients and 25 observations per equation: estimable, but noisy. Pool all countries and the noise averages out, at the price of assuming that every country has the same dynamics. A panel VAR is a choice on the line between these two extremes: Estimator Idea Use it when OLS mean group (Pesaran-Smith) Estimate each country separately and average \(T\) is not too small, units differ, and you want the average effect with honest standard errors
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

Bayesian pooled One set of coefficients for all units, Minnesota prior Units are similar and you want the most precise estimate Zellner-Hong random effects Unit coefficients are drawn around a common mean, with a fixed amount of shrinkage \(\lambda_1\) You want partial pooling and can set the shrinkage yourself Hierarchical (Jarociński 2010) Same, but the amount of shrinkage is estimated You want the data to decide how alike the units are Static factor (Canova-Ciccarelli) Coefficients are sums of common, unit, variable and lag factors; all units' lags enter every equation Countries influence each other and you want spillovers Dynamic factor Same, with factors that change over time The relationships are unstable
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to choose Start with mean group and pooled: if they give similar answers, units are similar and the choice does not matter. If they differ, use the hierarchical model to let the data decide how much to pool (its shrinkage parameter is a measure of heterogeneity). Use the factor estimators when cross-country spillovers are the question, or the pre-tests show strong dependence between countries (Step 2). Report at least two estimators. How to write it: the model We estimate a panel VAR in GDP growth and unemployment for 14 OECD countries, 1966–1990, with one lag. To allow for heterogeneity across countries we use the mean-group estimator of Pesaran and Smith (1995), which averages country-specific VARs and computes standard errors from the dispersion of the coefficients across countries, and compare it with a Bayesian pooled estimator with a Minnesota prior, the Zellner-Hong (1989) random-effects estimator and the hierarchical prior of Jarociński (2010). Spillovers between countries are examined with the static and dynamic factor estimators of Canova and Ciccarelli (2009).
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it Two tests, one per variable. The Fisher ADF test combines the unit-root tests of the 14 countries: GDP growth rejects a unit root (p < 0.001), but unemployment does not (p = 0.76): it is persistent, and a VAR in levels is an approximation. The Pesaran CD test rejects cross-sectional independence for both variables (mean absolute correlation 0.45 for growth and 0.72 for unemployment): countries share common shocks, such as the oil crises. This matters in two ways: standard errors that assume independent countries are too small, and the factor estimators of Step 7 are designed for this. What to do about persistent unemployment: the VAR in levels with a persistent variable is common in the literature and consistent, but you should say so and check robustness with the variable in first differences, using a time-series transformation of your own data before loading it.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it BIC of the pooled VAR is lowest at two lags (0.739), against 0.849 for one lag and 0.750 for three. With 25 observations per country, one lag already costs six parameters per unit, so the guide uses one lag for the main results and two as a robustness check in Step 10. Report the BIC table, whichever lag length you choose.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it Each row is the average over the 14 country VARs, with the Pesaran-Smith standard error (the standard deviation across countries divided by \(\sqrt{14}\) ); the last two columns show the smallest and largest country coefficient. Unemployment equation: unemployment is persistent (0.81, every country between 0.69 and 0.94) and falls when growth is high: a one-point increase in growth lowers unemployment next year by 0.19 percentage point (z = −8.3), negative in every one of the 14 countries (range −0.36 to −0.04). Growth equation: growth has modest persistence (0.25) and is not affected by lagged unemployment (−0.01, z = −0.1), but the country values range from −0.62 to +0.73, so the average hides large differences between countries.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it Four estimators, three coefficients. All agree on the sign and the main picture: unemployment is persistent (0.81 to 0.89) and falls when growth rises ( \(-0.13\) to \(-0.19\) ), while lagged unemployment has little or a slightly negative effect on growth. They differ in size. The mean-group effect of growth on unemployment ( \(-0.19\) ) is about 50% larger than the pooled one ( \(-0.125\) ), and pooled persistence (0.88) is higher than mean-group (0.81). This is the pattern expected when slopes differ across units and a pooled estimator imposes a common value: dynamic coefficients are biased towards more persistence (Pesaran and Smith 1995). The hierarchical estimate sits between the two ( \(-0.15\) and 0.84), which is what partial pooling should do. For growth on lagged unemployment, mean group finds nothing ( \(-0.01\) , standard error 0.10), while the pooled and hierarchical estimates are small and negative ( \(-0.07\) and \(-0.09\) ): this relationship is weak and not robust to the estimator, and should not be a headline result.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries
In a paper: report the mean-group estimate as the main result if the aim is the average effect and the units differ, show the others as robustness, and describe how they differ.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it The response is to a one-standard-deviation growth shock (2.3 percentage points), with growth ordered first: unemployment may respond within the year, growth responds to unemployment only with a lag. The median country sees unemployment fall by 0.5 point on impact and by 0.9 point after one year (range across countries \(-1.1\) to \(-0.4\) ), 0.5 after four years and 0.3 after eight; it has not quite returned to baseline after twelve ( \(-0.17\) ). Growth itself fades in two years (2.3, 0.5, 0.2). The response of growth to an unemployment shock is zero on average ( \(-0.008\) ), with country values from \(-0.09\) to +0.17. The bands in this model are the 16th to 84th percentiles across countries , not estimation uncertainty: they measure heterogeneity. Say so under the figure.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

Variance decomposition: growth shocks explain 43% of the forecast-error variance of unemployment at one year, 76% at four and 79% at twelve, while unemployment shocks explain under 1% of the variance of growth: in this panel, growth drives unemployment and not the reverse.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries
Spillovers between countries: the factor estimators

How to read it The factor estimators let every country's equation include the lags of all countries and report the effect of a growth shock in one country on the same country and on the other countries (average per country). Convergence first: with 3000 draws after 2000 burn-in the effective sample size of the own-lag factor is 964 and all Geweke statistics are below 2 in absolute value (with the default 1000 draws and 500 burn-in it was 181 and the statistic was \(-4.6\) : do not use the defaults for the dynamic model). The responses: a shock to growth in one country lowers its own unemployment by 0.13 to 0.17 over the next two years, and moves other countries' growth by \(-0.04\) (3% of the domestic growth response of 1.2 after a year) and their unemployment by +0.04 (about a third of the domestic fall of 0.13, with the opposite sign). Spillovers are small and their sign is not stable across estimators: the static version gives \(-0.01\) to \(-0.02\) for the unemployment spillover. Two cautions. First, these estimators assume uncorrelated shocks, so there is no contemporaneous effect by construction, although the CD test in Step 2 shows strong correlation between countries. Second, the own-country response of unemployment is much smaller than in the mean-group model because the factor prior shrinks coefficients strongly in a short panel and there is no impact effect. Use these estimators to compare the size of domestic and foreign effects, not for the size of the domestic effect.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries
Hierarchical estimation: how alike are the countries?

How to read it The shrinkage parameter \(\lambda_1\) measures how different the countries are: it is 0.016 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.034), small, so the hierarchical model pools the countries strongly. The country-specific own-lag coefficients are accordingly close together: unemployment persistence from 0.73 (Japan) to 0.93 (United Kingdom), growth persistence from 0.07 (United Kingdom, Belgium) to 0.34 (Japan), a much narrower range than the unit-by-unit OLS estimates behind the mean-group table (growth: \(-0.14\) to 0.56). The reading is that most of the apparent difference between countries in Step 4 is noise from 25 observations, not real heterogeneity. That supports reporting the mean-group and pooled estimates together. Convergence: with 3000 draws after 1500 burn-in the effective sample sizes are 232 or more and every Geweke statistic is below 2 (the largest is 1.88, for \(\lambda_1\) ). With the default 1000 draws they were 85 to 124 for most parameters, too few: use at least 3000 for this estimator.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to read it Growth residuals have remaining autocorrelation (Ljung-Box p = 0.003) while unemployment residuals have none (p = 0.42), and the joint portmanteau test rejects (p = 0.003; with 336 observations and 48 degrees of freedom it is only approximate). Normality is rejected for both (Jarque-Bera 46 and 101): the residuals have heavy tails, as expected with recessions in the sample. There is no sign of ARCH at 5% (p = 0.54 and 0.07). Serial correlation in the growth equation suggests a second lag; Step 10 shows that the main result does not depend on it. Dependence between countries is not in this table: it is tested in Step 2 and motivates the factor estimators.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries
Robustness: lags, estimators and dropping one country at a time

How to read it Three checks of the effect of growth on unemployment (mean group, \(-0.19\) ). Lags: with one, two and three lags the coefficient is \(-0.19\) , \(-0.18\) and \(-0.20\) . Leave one country out: re-estimating without each country in turn gives values between \(-0.20\) (dropping Japan) and \(-0.18\) (dropping the United Kingdom): no single country drives the result. Estimators: Step 5 shows \(-0.13\) to \(-0.19\) . The conclusion that growth lowers unemployment next year is robust; the size depends on the estimator, by about a third.
Panel VAR: Six Estimators for Heterogeneous Countries

How to write it: results Table 1 reports the mean-group estimates. Unemployment is persistent (0.81) and responds negatively to lagged growth: a one-percentage-point increase in growth lowers unemployment by 0.19 percentage point in the following year (Pesaran-Smith standard error 0.023), and the coefficient is negative in all 14 countries. Lagged unemployment has no effect on growth on average ( \(-0.01\) , standard error 0.10) but the country estimates range widely. A one-standard-deviation growth shock lowers unemployment by 0.9 percentage point after one year (the 16th to 84th percentile across countries is \(-1.1\) to \(-0.4\) ); the effect halves after about four years. Growth shocks explain 76% of the forecast-error variance of unemployment at a four-year horizon. The pooled, Zellner-Hong and hierarchical estimators give the same signs and a smaller effect ( \(-0.13\) to \(-0.15\) ), consistent with the upward bias in the persistence of pooled dynamic estimators when slopes differ. The hierarchical model estimates a small degree of heterogeneity ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.016\) ). Spillovers estimated with the Canova-Ciccarelli factor model are small: a growth shock in one country moves other countries' growth by 3% of its domestic effect and their unemployment by about a third of the domestic effect, with the opposite sign, and the sign is not stable across the static and dynamic versions. Results are unchanged with two or three lags and when any one country is dropped ( \(-0.20\) to \(-0.18\) ). Unemployment fails the panel unit-root test, so we also note that the estimates relate to a persistent variable in levels.

Mean-Adjusted (Steady-State) Bayesian VAR: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Where will growth, inflation and the interest rate be in five years, given what we know about their long-run levels? In an ordinary VAR the long-run mean of the variables is a nonlinear function of all the coefficients, \(\mu = (I - A_1 - \dots - A_p)^{-1} c\) , so a prior on the constant says nothing sensible about it. Forecasts converge to a mean the researcher never chose. The mean-adjusted VAR of Villani (2009) moves the constant out of the way: Here \(\psi\) is the steady state , the unconditional mean of \(y_t\) , and it gets its own prior: \(\psi \sim N(\psi_0, \Omega)\) . Forecasts converge to \(\psi\) , so the prior disciplines the long horizon directly. The lag coefficients get a Minnesota prior with mean zero (the variables are deviations from the steady state, so they are stationary by construction). Estimation is by Gibbs sampling.

Where does \(\psi_0\) come from? From outside the sample: an inflation target, a long-run growth estimate from a growth model, an interest rate equal to the target plus the neutral real rate. State this in the paper; it is the main modelling choice. What the model assumes The VAR is stationary around \(\psi\) : the steady state exists only if the variables do not have a unit root. Growth rates and inflation are fine. Interest rates and unemployment are borderline in postwar U.S. data, as the unit-root table in Step 2 shows. If a series is better described by a random walk, use the ordinary BVAR with a random-walk prior instead, or transform it (differences, deviations from a trend).

How to write it: the model We estimate a mean-adjusted Bayesian VAR (Villani 2009) in GDP growth, inflation and the three-month Treasury bill rate, \(y_t - \psi = \sum_{l=1}^{p} A_l (y_{t-l} - \psi) + \varepsilon_t\) . The prior on the steady state \(\psi\) is normal with means of 3% (growth), 3.5% (inflation) and 5% (interest rate) and standard deviations of 0.5, 1 and 1 percentage point. The lag coefficients have a Minnesota prior with mean zero and overall tightness \(\lambda_1 = 0.1\) . The posterior is simulated by Gibbs sampling with 1,000 draws after a burn-in of 500.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Growth rejects a unit root clearly (p < 0.001) and inflation at 5% (p = 0.03). The T-bill rate does not reject (p = 0.28, KPSS p = 0.05): over 1959 to 2009 it has a long upward and downward swing, so a stationary model around a fixed mean is an approximation. The largest root of the system will be close to one (Step 7). This is the usual compromise for a steady-state VAR; the prior on \(\psi\) is what keeps the long-run forecast anchored, and Step 8 shows how much the answer depends on it.
Choose the prior for the steady state

The prior mean and standard deviation of \(\psi\) are the model's judgement. The sample means (3.1, 4.0, 5.3) are one data-based guide but a poor prior, since the data would then be used twice. A better guide: Variable Prior mean Prior s.d. Reason GDP growth 3 0.5 Trend growth of about 3% a year Inflation 3.5 1 Between the 1960s low and the 1970s peak, wide enough to leave room for the data T-bill rate 5 1 A real rate of about 1.5% plus inflation of 3.5% A tight prior (small standard deviation) fixes the steady state at your belief and makes the forecast an implication of it; a loose prior lets the data choose and approximately reproduces the sample mean. Step 8 compares them.

How to read it Each row shows the posterior of one steady state. Growth: 3.11% a year (95% interval 2.58 to 3.66); inflation: 3.83% (2.98 to 4.68); T-bill rate: 5.01% (3.72 to 6.15). Compare with the prior in the note: the posterior standard deviations (0.27, 0.44, 0.61) are about half the prior ones (0.5, 1, 1), so the data are informative about the long-run means, and they move the inflation mean from the prior 3.5 up to 3.83. Where the posterior is close to the prior and the standard deviation has not fallen, the data have said nothing and the prior is your result; say so. Convergence: the effective sample size equals the number of draws (1000) and Geweke's |z| is below 2 for all three steady states, so the chain has settled and the posterior means are reliable.

How to read it The interest-rate equation is a policy rule in deviations from the steady state: the rate is persistent (own lags 0.77 and 0.14, sum 0.91) and responds positively but weakly to growth and inflation (posterior probabilities of a positive sign 0.81 to 0.89; none of the intervals excludes zero). There is no constant to interpret: the constant of the ordinary VAR is replaced by \(\psi\) and the lag coefficients. The variance decomposition rows show the Cholesky shocks (growth, inflation, T-bill rate). The interest-rate shock explains only 1% of the forecast-error variance of GDP growth and 6% of inflation after five years: policy surprises are a small source of fluctuations, as in the BVAR guide.
Forecasts: what the steady state does

How to read it The charts show the median forecast and a 68% band 20 quarters ahead from 2009Q3, when the T-bill rate was close to zero. The forecast of the T-bill rate rises from 0.6% to 3.6% after five years: it is converging towards the steady state of 5.0%, and the speed is set by the persistence of the system (Step 7). Inflation and growth, already close to their steady states, hardly move on the long horizon. This is the purpose of the model: the long-run forecast is an explicit function of the prior and the data. The out-of-sample table is for the ordinary Normal-Wishart BVAR with the same tightness, not for the steady-state model, and it is a useful benchmark in a paper rather than a test of the steady-state prior. For inflation the BVAR has the lowest error at both horizons (3.01 and 3.15, against 3.25 and 3.38 for the OLS VAR and 3.51 and 4.17 for a random walk). For the interest rate a random walk is best, and for GDP growth the OLS VAR is best at one quarter and a random walk at four. In a forecasting paper, evaluate the steady-state model itself against these benchmarks, with Diebold-Mariano tests.

How to read it Residuals are not white noise: Ljung-Box rejects for inflation and the interest rate (p < 0.001) but not for GDP growth (p = 0.28); normality is rejected for all three, extremely for the interest rate (Jarque-Bera 1133, from the 1979 to 1982 period), and ARCH is present in inflation and the interest rate. These are the usual features of postwar U.S. data; the SV-VAR guide models the changing volatility. Note them as limitations and check that the main results do not change with four lags (Step 8). Stability: every posterior draw is stationary, and the largest root at the posterior mean is 0.93, which is high: deviations from the steady state take about nine quarters to halve ( \(\ln 0.5 / \ln 0.928\) ). The steady state is therefore a slow attractor, and a five-year forecast does not reach it. The coefficient chains mix well (efficiency of 0.80 or above); one Geweke statistic is above 1.96 in absolute value (the constant of the growth equation, \(-2.4\) ), which is expected by chance among many parameters; raise the burn-in to confirm that nothing changes.
Robustness: the prior on the steady state

How to read it The table re-estimates the model with four priors on the steady state and reports the posterior steady states and the five-year forecasts. Data-based or loose priors (sample means and standard deviations, the guide's prior, a nearly flat prior with standard deviation 10): the steady states are the same within 0.1 point (growth 3.1, inflation 3.8 to 3.9, T-bill 5.0 to 5.1) and so are the five-year forecasts (inflation 3.2 to 3.3, T-bill 3.6 to 3.7). The data decide. A tight prior with different beliefs (inflation 2 ± 0.25, T-bill 3.5 ± 0.5): the posterior inflation mean is 2.27 and the T-bill mean 3.22, although the sample averages are 4.0 and 5.3, and the five-year forecasts fall to 1.5% and 2.0%. A tight prior wins over 200 observations. That is its point: it is an assumption, and the table shows exactly how much the answer depends on it.
Robustness: the prior on the steady state

Ordinary BVAR , with no prior on the long-run mean: 2.9% and 3.1%, between the two. Its long-run mean is whatever the lags imply, which is why it is a poor tool for a long-horizon question. Lags (1, 2, 4): the steady states change by less than 0.1. The rule for a paper: report the posterior steady states under a data-based prior and under your preferred prior, and discuss any difference as a statement about beliefs, not as an empirical finding.

How to write it: results The posterior mean of the steady state is 3.1% for GDP growth (95% credible interval 2.6 to 3.7), 3.8% for inflation (3.0 to 4.7) and 5.0% for the Treasury bill rate (3.7 to 6.1); the posterior standard deviations are about half the prior ones, so the data are informative about the long-run means. Starting from the low interest rate of 2009Q3, the median forecast of the bill rate rises to 3.6% after five years, converging slowly towards its steady state because the largest root of the system is 0.93. These results hardly change when the sample-mean prior or a nearly flat prior replaces our prior, or when the lag length varies between one and four. They depend strongly on the prior when it is tight: a prior of 2 ± 0.25% for inflation and 3.5 ± 0.5% for the interest rate lowers the five-year forecasts to 1.5% and 2.0%. Residual tests show serial correlation, non-normality and conditional heteroskedasticity in inflation and the interest rate, so the credible bands should be read as approximate.

Stochastic-Volatility VAR (SV-VAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Were the shocks of the 1970s larger than those of the 1990s, and does it matter for inference? The model is a VAR with constant coefficients and time-varying shock variances: where \(H_t = \text{diag}(h_{1t}, h_{2t}, h_{3t})\) holds the variances of the three structural (Cholesky) shocks and \(A_0\) is a lower-triangular matrix of contemporaneous relations (Cogley and Sargent 2005). The log-variances follow random walks: volatility can rise or fall gradually, but cannot jump back. The coefficients get the Minnesota prior of the BVAR guide. The model is estimated by Gibbs sampling, drawing the log-variances with the mixture-of-normals approximation of Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998). The parameter \(s_i\) , the variance of the innovation to the log-volatility, controls how fast volatility moves.

Volatility or coefficients? Changing volatility and changing coefficients are hard to tell apart, and a model that allows only one of them will attribute all the instability to it. Sims and Zha (2006) found that most of the apparent change in U.S. monetary policy since the 1960s was a change in the size of the shocks. The TVP-VAR guide allows time-varying coefficients with constant variance; this guide allows time-varying variance with constant coefficients. Compare them, and if both matter, use a TVP-SV-VAR (not in OES). How to write it: the model We estimate a VAR with stochastic volatility (Cogley and Sargent 2005) in inflation, unemployment and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags. The VAR coefficients are constant, with a Minnesota prior with overall tightness 0.1; the structural shocks, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last, have volatilities that follow independent random walks in logs. The posterior is simulated with a Gibbs sampler in which the log-volatilities are drawn using the mixture approximation of Kim, Shephard and Chib (1998); we use 4,000 draws after 2,000 burn-in.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Inflation rejects a unit root (p = 0.03); unemployment and the T-bill rate do not (p = 0.11 and 0.28), so they get a random-walk prior on their own first lag ( delta = "0, 1, 1" ). The VAR is in levels, as in the BVAR guide.

How to read it The coefficients are constant, so the interest-rate equation is read as in the BVAR guide: the policy rate is persistent (own lags 1.03 and \(-0.10\) , sum 0.93) and responds to inflation with a positive sign (probability 0.88 for the first lag, with an interval that includes zero). The new objects are the \(s_i\) , the variances of the quarterly innovations in log volatility: 0.20 for inflation, 0.38 for unemployment and 0.23 for the interest rate, all clearly above zero (the 95% intervals start at 0.08, 0.17 and 0.11). A value of 0.2 means that the log-variance of a shock moves by about 0.45 per quarter, so its standard deviation by about 22%. Unemployment shocks have the most erratic volatility. If an \(s_i\) had been close to zero, that shock would have constant variance and the model would reduce to the ordinary BVAR for it.

How to read it The charts show the posterior median standard deviation of each structural shock. The table gives the minimum, the maximum and the last value. The interest-rate shock is largest in 1980Q3 (2.5 percentage points, the Volcker period) and smallest in 1997Q3 (0.15): a 17-fold range. Inflation shocks are smallest in 1993Q1 (0.6) and largest in 2008Q4 (5.3), the collapse of prices at the start of the financial crisis. Unemployment shocks range from 0.09 (1999Q2) to 0.93 (2009Q2). The period averages show the Great Moderation : from 1960–1983 to 1984–2006 the volatility of inflation fell by 42%, that of unemployment by 40% and that of the interest rate by 50%, and it rose again in 2007–2009 (inflation shocks 4.2, above the 1960–1983 average of 2.4). Say how you chose the break at 1984 (it is the convention, not an estimate), and note that the table shows posterior medians without bands.
Is the volatility model needed? Compare with constant variance

How to read it If the volatility model is right, the shocks divided by their estimated volatility should be white noise with no ARCH. They are: the ARCH test does not reject for any of the three standardised shocks (p = 0.72, 0.37 and 0.18), while in the constant-variance BVAR it rejects for all (p below 0.0001). The heavy tails also disappear: the Jarque-Bera statistic of the interest-rate residual falls from 1,652 to 6.3, and normality is not rejected for the inflation shock (p = 0.12). Volatility changes, not fat-tailed shocks, explain most of the non-normality. What the volatility model does not fix is serial correlation: the Ljung-Box test still rejects for the standardised inflation and unemployment shocks (statistics 59 and 46), as in the constant-variance VAR. That is a problem with the conditional mean, and the remedy is more lags (Step 8). Report both tables: the contrast is the argument for the SV-VAR.
Impulse responses in calm and volatile periods

How to read it The charts show the response of inflation and unemployment to an interest-rate shock at three dates: the volatile 1980Q3, the calm 1997Q3 and the last date. With constant coefficients the responses have the same shape at every date, and differ only in the size of a one-standard-deviation shock: after a year inflation rises by 0.87 in 1980Q3 and by 0.05 in 1997Q3, a ratio of 17, which is the ratio of the shock sizes (2.5 and 0.15). Per percentage point of policy shock, both are about 0.35. Do not read the difference as a change in monetary transmission: it is a change in the size of the shock. Report responses to a shock of fixed size (such as 25 basis points) or normalise them, as the BVAR guide does. This is the key contrast with the TVP-VAR, where the responses change shape because the coefficients change. As in the BVAR guide, inflation rises after the shock (the price puzzle).

How to read it For the VAR coefficients the effective sample sizes are above 1,400 (efficiency of 35% to 100%) and the Geweke statistics are below 2 in absolute value except one (the second T-bill lag in the interest-rate equation, \(-2.1\) ), unremarkable among many parameters. The variances \(s_i\) of the volatility innovations mix more slowly: effective sample sizes of 125 to 187 (efficiency of 3% to 5%), below the guideline of 200, though their Geweke statistics are fine (up to 1.9). For a paper, use 10,000 draws or more and check that the volatility paths do not change.
Robustness: lags, tightness and the amount of volatility drift

How to read it Each row is a variant of the model, and each number the ratio of average volatility in 1984–2006 to that in 1960–1983 (below one means the Great Moderation). With one, two or four lags the ratios are 0.56 to 0.60 for inflation, 0.58 to 0.60 for unemployment and 0.48 to 0.51 for the interest rate. A tighter prior ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.05\) ) gives 0.48 for inflation, a looser one ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.3\) ) 0.68; the interest-rate ratio is stable at about 0.5. The conclusion that volatility fell by 30% to 50% is robust; the size of the fall for inflation depends on the prior by about 20 percentage points, so report a range.

How to write it: results Constant-variance residuals show strong conditional heteroskedasticity in all three variables (ARCH test p < 0.0001) and heavy tails (Jarque-Bera 1,652 for the interest rate). Allowing the variance of each structural shock to follow a random walk removes both: the standardised shocks show no ARCH (p between 0.18 and 0.72) and are close to normal. Estimated volatility fell sharply: between 1960–1983 and 1984–2006 the average standard deviation of inflation shocks fell by 42%, that of unemployment shocks by 40% and that of interest-rate shocks by 50%, and it rose again in the financial crisis. The interest-rate shock was 17 times larger in 1980Q3, at the height of the Volcker disinflation, than in 1997Q3. The ratios hardly change with one to four lags, and the fall in volatility ranges from 30% to 53% across lag lengths and prior tightness. Because the coefficients are constant, the impulse responses at different dates differ only in the size of the shock; for time-varying propagation we refer to the TVP-VAR. Standardised inflation and unemployment shocks remain serially correlated, which is a limitation of the model's conditional mean.
