Bayesian Threshold VAR: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does monetary policy work differently when inflation is high? A threshold VAR (Tsay 1998; Koop and Potter 2006) splits the sample into two regimes according to whether a threshold variable \(z_{t-d}\) lies above a threshold \(r\) : The coefficients and the covariance matrix differ between regimes. The threshold \(r\) and the delay \(d\) are unknown. In the Bayesian version used here, each regime has a Normal-Wishart prior (Minnesota-type moments), so its marginal likelihood is available in closed form and the posterior of \((r, d)\) is exact , computed over a grid of candidate thresholds. There is nothing to simulate for the threshold, so no convergence to check; coefficients are then drawn within each regime.

Two checks before you trust a threshold model Does the data prefer two regimes? The log Bayes factor of the threshold model against the linear VAR answers this directly. A threshold VAR can always fit better than a linear VAR; the Bayes factor penalises the extra parameters. If it is negative, use the linear VAR. Is the threshold variable the right one? Different candidates give very different Bayes factors (Step 3). Choose by the Bayes factor, and say that you did: the choice is part of the model. Also check that each regime has enough observations: with two lags of three variables, a regime has 21 coefficients per equation, so a regime of 30 quarters is thin. The prior helps but results for the small regime are imprecise.

How to write it: the model We estimate a Bayesian threshold VAR (Tsay 1998; Koop and Potter 2006) in GDP growth, inflation and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags. The regime is determined by whether inflation, \(d\) quarters earlier, exceeds a threshold \(r\) . Each regime has its own coefficients and covariance matrix, with a Normal-Wishart prior with Minnesota moments (overall tightness 0.2). Because the marginal likelihood is available analytically in each regime, the joint posterior of the threshold (over a 40-point grid between the 15th and 85th percentiles of the threshold variable) and the delay (one or two quarters) is computed exactly. We compare the threshold model with a linear VAR using the log Bayes factor, and report results for the posterior mode of the threshold.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it Inflation and GDP growth reject a unit root; the T-bill rate does not (p = 0.28). The regimes are defined by a stationary variable, which is what a threshold model needs: a trending threshold variable would spend the whole sample in one regime. Quarterly annualised inflation is volatile (it ranges widely), so the high regime also catches quarters of temporary price spikes, not only the high-inflation years.
Do you need a threshold, and on which variable?

Run the model with each candidate threshold variable and compare the log Bayes factor against the linear VAR. How to read it A positive log Bayes factor favours the threshold model; above 4.6 is "decisive" on Jeffreys' scale. Inflation (26.4) and the T-bill rate (16.8) are strongly supported; GDP growth ( \(-4.0\) ), consumption growth ( \(-3.7\) ), unemployment ( \(-8.4\) ) and investment growth ( \(-2.9\) ) are not (the linear VAR is preferred), and money growth is at zero (1.0). So the economy's dynamics depend on the level of inflation or interest rates, not on the stage of the business cycle measured by growth. Inflation is the natural choice for the question, and its Bayes factor is the largest; we use it below. This is a model choice made on the data: report the table.
Do you need a threshold, and on which variable?

Caution: a Bayes factor in favour of a regime split can also reflect different volatility in the two regimes (the 1970s were more volatile than the 1990s). Compare with the SV-VAR guide, which allows changing volatility without splitting the coefficients.

How to read it The data choose a threshold of 6.65% annualised quarterly inflation, with a delay of two quarters (the posterior probability of a delay of one quarter is below 0.0001): the economy is in the high regime when inflation two quarters earlier exceeded 6.65%. That regime holds 30 of the 200 quarters (15%) and the low regime 170. The log Bayes factor against a single linear VAR is 26.4 , overwhelming support for two regimes (on Jeffreys' scale, above 4.6 is decisive). The posterior mean of the threshold (6.646) equals the mode (6.647): with a finer grid of 100 points, 95% of the posterior mass sits on 6.65 and 3% on 6.58. Do not over-read this precision: it arises because moving a single quarter between regimes changes the marginal likelihood a great deal when the high regime has only 30 quarters. Step 9 shows how the threshold moves when the minimum regime size changes.

How to read it Because the regime is a function of an observed variable, regime membership is known once the threshold is fixed, so every probability is 1. The 30 high-inflation quarters fall into two real episodes and eight isolated quarters. The episodes are 1974Q1–1975Q2 (the first oil shock) and 1978Q2–1982Q1 (the second oil shock and the Volcker disinflation, 16 quarters). The single quarters are 1969Q3, 1973Q3, 1975Q4, 1977Q3, 1982Q4, 1991Q1, 2006Q1 and 2008Q4: spikes in the quarterly CPI, some from energy prices, not episodes of sustained inflation. In a paper, describe the high regime as largely the oil-shock years, and note that it is close to a period dummy for the 1970s, which limits what can be inferred about "high inflation" in general.

How to read it The policy-rate equation shows what changes. In the low regime the rate follows the economy: it responds to lagged GDP growth (0.046, 95% interval 0.016 to 0.072; probability of a positive sign 1.00) and is very persistent (own lag 0.91). In the high regime the response to growth is small and imprecise (0.015, interval \(-0.10\) to 0.14), the response to inflation is 0.059 ( \(-0.11\) to 0.22), and the own lag is lower (0.71, interval 0.38 to 1.02). With only 30 quarters, the intervals are wide: the data cannot say that the rule changed, only that the low-regime rule is estimated precisely and the high-regime rule is not. Report this limitation rather than reading the point estimates as a regime-dependent policy rule.

How to read it Responses to a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, within each regime (the chart shows posterior medians without credible bands). Output: in the low-inflation regime GDP growth does not respond (+0.01 after a year); in the high-inflation regime it falls by 0.40 percentage point after a year, 0.18 after two and 0.07 after three. Inflation: in the low regime it rises (0.15 after a year, 0.11 after two): the price puzzle of the BVAR guide; in the high regime there is no price puzzle ( \(-0.006\) after a year and \(-0.06\) after two). So the textbook sign of monetary transmission appears in the high regime, which is the regime of the oil-shock years, and the price puzzle in the low regime. Because the high regime has 30 observations, do not report these differences as significant without computing credible bands from the draws; the Bayes factor in Step 3 says that the regimes differ, not that each difference is large.

How to read it In the low regime (170 quarters) the joint portmanteau test does not reject (p = 0.10), but Ljung-Box rejects for inflation (p = 0.0001) and the interest rate (p = 0.034), normality is rejected for both, and the ARCH test rejects for GDP growth (p = 0.035). In the high regime (30 quarters) Ljung-Box rejects for inflation (p = 0.018) and nothing else does, but these tests have little power with 30 observations, so the absence of rejections says little. Remaining autocorrelation in inflation suggests more lags; Step 9 shows that the threshold and the Bayes factor survive three and four lags. Changing volatility between the regimes is not modelled beyond the regime-specific covariance matrix; if it matters to your question, see the SV-VAR guide.
Robustness: lags, trimming, grid and prior

How to read it Each row changes one thing. Lags: with one to four lags the threshold is 6.65 and the Bayes factor is 31.8, 26.4, 22.9 and 23.9. Minimum regime share: allowing 10% in each regime moves the threshold to 7.05 (29 high quarters); requiring 25% moves it to 5.0 (50 high quarters), with a Bayes factor of 16.7: the threshold is sensitive to how small the high regime may be, so report the trimming. Grid and delay: a grid of 100 points and a maximum delay of four quarters change nothing (the delay stays at two). Prior: the Bayes factor ranges from 5.4 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.1\) ) to 45.7 ( \(\lambda_1 = 0.5\) ). Marginal likelihoods depend on the prior, so the size of the Bayes factor is not robust, but it is positive and large in every variant, so the conclusion that two regimes beat one is. Report a range, not a single number.

How to write it: results We compare a Bayesian threshold VAR with a linear VAR using the log Bayes factor, for seven candidate threshold variables. The data support inflation (log Bayes factor 26.4) and the Treasury bill rate (16.8) as threshold variables; GDP growth, consumption growth, unemployment and investment growth are not supported (log Bayes factors between \(-8.4\) and \(-2.9\) ). With inflation as the threshold variable the posterior concentrates on a delay of two quarters and a threshold of 6.65%, which defines a high-inflation regime of 30 quarters, 22 of them in the oil-shock episodes of 1974–75 and 1978–82. In the low-inflation regime, a rise in the policy rate does not reduce output and raises inflation (the price puzzle); in the high-inflation regime output falls by 0.4 percentage point after a year and inflation does not rise. These regime differences are estimated with 30 observations and are imprecise. The threshold, the delay and the sign of the Bayes factor do not change with one to four lags, the grid, or the prior tightness; the threshold moves between 5.0 and 7.05 depending on the minimum regime size (10% to 25%), and the Bayes factor ranges from 5.4 to 45.7 with the prior.

Time-Varying Parameter VAR (TVP-VAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Has the effect of monetary policy on inflation changed since the 1960s? The model lets all VAR coefficients drift: where \(X_t\) holds a constant and \(p\) lags of the three variables. With three variables and two lags each date has 21 coefficients; the random walk lets them move a little each quarter. How much they move is governed by \(Q\) , whose prior is set from a training sample : the first 40 observations are used only to estimate a constant-parameter VAR, whose coefficients and covariance matrix centre the prior for \(\beta_0\) and \(Q\) (Primiceri 2005). The scale \(k_Q\) says how fast coefficients may drift: small values give nearly constant coefficients, large values a flexible but noisy path.

Be sceptical of time variation A TVP-VAR can always find movement in coefficients, even when the true model is constant, because the random walk is flexible and the data are noisy. Three habits keep a paper honest: (1) test whether coefficients really moved, using the posterior probability that they changed (Step 4); (2) show that the results do not depend on \(k_Q\) and the training sample (Step 8); (3) in a macroeconomic VAR, ask whether changing volatility (the SV-VAR guide) rather than changing coefficients explains the instability: much of the apparent time variation in the 1970s and 1980s turned out to be a change in shock variances (Sims and Zha 2006).

How to write it: the model We estimate a time-varying parameter VAR with random-walk coefficients and a constant error covariance matrix, in inflation, unemployment and the three-month Treasury bill rate, with two lags (Cogley and Sargent 2005; Primiceri 2005). The prior for the initial coefficients and the covariance of their innovations is calibrated on a training sample of the first 40 quarters (1959–1969), so estimation starts in 1969Q4 with 160 observations; the prior scale of the innovation variance is \(k_Q = 0.01\) . The posterior is simulated with a Gibbs sampler, drawing the coefficient paths with the Carter-Kohn (1994) simulation smoother, using 6,000 draws after 4,000 burn-in draws. Impulse responses at a date use the coefficients of that date, identified recursively with the interest rate ordered last.
Load the data and test for unit roots

How to read it A TVP-VAR is estimated in levels without a prior on unit roots: the training sample sets the prior mean of the coefficients, and the random walk lets the persistence change. Inflation rejects a unit root at 5% (p = 0.03), unemployment and the T-bill rate do not (p = 0.11 and 0.28). If you use differences, say so. Because coefficients can drift above one, the model can produce explosive paths in short stretches; the summary line "Iterations with no stable path" counts the draws where this could not be avoided (zero here).

How to read it 160 observations are used for estimation, 1969Q4 to 2009Q3, with the first 40 quarters kept for the prior. The covariance matrix of the residuals is constant here (stochastic volatility is the subject of the SV-VAR guide): inflation shocks have a variance of about 5, shocks to unemployment about 0.06, and interest-rate and inflation shocks are positively correlated (0.81 covariance), while unemployment shocks are negatively correlated with both.

The central table compares each coefficient at the start and the end of the estimation sample, with the posterior probability that it increased. How to read it Each row shows a coefficient at the start (1969Q4) and the end (2009Q3), and the posterior probability that it increased. Only 2 of 21 coefficients have a probability below 0.05 or above 0.95, which is what chance alone would give (about 2.1). So the evidence that the conditional means moved is thin. The exception is the second lag of inflation in the inflation equation: it falls from 0.36 to \(-0.19\) (probability of an increase 0.008), and the sum of the two own lags of inflation falls from about 0.5 to about zero, in line with the finding that U.S. inflation became less persistent (Cogley and Sargent 2005); a paper would test the sum directly, from the draws.

Look at the T-bill coefficients in the inflation equation to see why single coefficients mislead: the first lag falls by 0.88 and the second rises by 0.96, with probabilities of 0.17 and 0.87, because the two lags move in opposite directions and their sum barely changes (0.24 at the start, 0.32 at the end). Always judge time variation by sums of lags and by impulse responses, not by one coefficient.

How to read it The charts show the posterior median path of the T-bill rate's own first lag and of the constant of each equation. The own lag is about 0.98 in 1969, dips to 0.91 around 1979, and rises above one after 1990, reaching 1.19 by 2009. This should not be read as an explosive process: the second lag is about \(-0.27\) at the end, so the sum of the two lags is about 0.92. The constant in the interest-rate equation falls from about 1.0 to about 0.2, as inflation and rates came down. A path of this kind is a statement about the model's best description of each period, estimated with few effective observations at each date: treat its wiggles as noise, and its broad drift as the finding.

How to read it The charts show the response of inflation and unemployment to a one-standard-deviation rise in the T-bill rate, using the coefficients of 1969Q4, 1989Q4 and 2009Q3. (The date-specific responses here are posterior medians; compute bands from the draws if the paper relies on the comparison.) Inflation rises after the shock at all three dates: the price puzzle holds in every period. The response is 0.27 after two quarters in 1969 and 0.24 in 1989, and in 2009 it is delayed (0.02 after one quarter, 0.31 after two) and then more persistent, at 0.34 after eight quarters and 0.22 after twenty, against 0.19 and 0.03 in 1969. Unemployment falls by about 0.2 point after a year in 1969 and hardly moves in 1989 (0 after four quarters, +0.10 after eight, the expected sign). In 2009 it falls by 0.45 after eight quarters, the wrong sign for a tightening.

The 2009 responses are the least reliable: the policy rate was close to zero, its own lag exceeds one, and a shock to it is a very different object from a shock to the funds rate in 1969. A common remedy is to end the sample before the crisis or to treat it separately; if your sample ends in the crisis, say that the final responses reflect the zero lower bound.

How to read it Convergence of a TVP-VAR is demanding, because there are hundreds of states. With 6,000 draws after 4,000 burn-in, the effective sample sizes of the coefficients at the last date are 235 to 336 (efficiency of 4% to 6%, above 200 but low) and those of the covariance terms 1,600 to 3,700. Two covariance parameters fail Geweke's test : \(\Sigma_{\text{inflation, T-bill}}\) (z = 3.5) and \(\Sigma_{\text{T-bill, T-bill}}\) (z = 2.4): the chain for the covariance matrix is still drifting. With the default 1,000 draws the sample size for the T-bill coefficient was 26 and the statistic \(-4.5\) . In a paper, run at least 15,000 draws with a long burn-in, and report the convergence table, or the posterior means for the covariance matrix are suspect.

Residual diagnostics: serial correlation is rejected for all three variables (Ljung-Box p = 0.014, 0.003 and below 0.001), as is normality (Jarque-Bera 1,524 for the interest rate), and so is the absence of ARCH, in all three. The constant covariance matrix is therefore wrong, and the time variation in coefficients may be absorbing changes in volatility: the SV-VAR guide models these directly, and a paper that claims changing transmission should show that it survives stochastic volatility.
Robustness: the amount of drift, the training sample and the lags

How to read it The table follows the own first lag of the T-bill rate at the start, the middle and the end of the sample. \(k_Q\) (0.003, 0.01, 0.03): the path barely changes (end value 1.20 to 1.22), so the amount of drift permitted by the prior does not drive the result. Training sample of 30 or 50 quarters: the end value is 1.23 and 1.09; it is lower with the longer training sample, as the model has less time to drift. One lag: the own lag is flat at about 0.9 throughout. The comparison with the two-lag model shows that the rise above one is a feature of the two-lag specification (offset by the second lag), while the persistence of the rate (the sum of the lags) rises from about 0.75 to about 0.92 in the two-lag model and is roughly 0.9 throughout in the one-lag model. The honest summary is that the TVP-VAR finds modest changes in the persistence of the policy rate, and that their size depends on the specification.

How to write it: results We find limited evidence of time variation in the conditional means. Of the 21 coefficients, only two changed between 1969Q4 and 2009Q3 with posterior probability above 95%, no more than would be expected by chance; the main exception is the persistence of inflation, where the sum of the two own lags falls from about 0.5 to about zero. The policy-rate equation shows a decline in the constant from about 1.0 to 0.2 and a persistence that is higher at the end of the sample than at the start, with a size that depends on the lag length. Inflation rises after a monetary tightening at all three dates studied (1969Q4, 1989Q4, 2009Q3), so the price puzzle is not a feature of one regime. The responses at the end of the sample are affected by the near-zero policy rate and should be read with caution. These results do not depend on the prior scale of the coefficient innovations ( \(k_Q\) between 0.003 and 0.03). Residual tests reject a constant covariance matrix, so we cannot rule out that changing volatility, not changing coefficients, explains part of the variation; the stochastic-volatility VAR in the next section addresses this. Convergence statistics (Table A) show adequate effective sample sizes for the coefficients but not for two covariance parameters, for which longer chains are needed.

Report What Where Model Random-walk coefficients, training sample, \(k_Q\) , draws Step 1 Evidence Coefficients at two dates with \(P(\text{change} > 0)\) ; how many pass a threshold Step 4 Results Paths of key coefficients; impulse responses at selected dates Steps 5 and 6 Diagnostics Effective sample sizes and Geweke statistics; residual tests Step 7 Robustness \(k_Q\) , training sample, lags Step 8 Alternative Constant-parameter BVAR; SV-VAR BVAR and SV-VAR guides References. Cogley and Sargent (2005), Review of Economic Dynamics ; Primiceri (2005), Review of Economic Studies ; Carter and Kohn (1994), Biometrika ; Sims and Zha (2006), American Economic Review ; Koop and Korobilis (2010), Foundations and Trends in Econometrics ; Del Negro and Primiceri (2015), Review of Economic Studies .
Difference-in-Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Between 2005 and 2010 many U.S. states passed Castle Doctrine or “stand-your-ground” laws, which remove the duty to retreat before using lethal force in self-defence. Supporters argued they would deter crime; critics that they would escalate confrontations. Did the laws change homicide rates? This guide uses the 13 states that adopted a law in 2007 and the 29 states that never did, from the data of Cheng and Hoekstra (2013). States adopting in other years are left out, so every treated state shares one adoption date. (The staggered-DiD guide uses all of them.) The difference-in-differences estimate compares the change in homicide in adopting states with the change in non-adopting states over the same years:

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(\ln h_{st}\) l_homicide Log homicides per 100,000 population \(D_{st}\) castle_law 1 in a treated state from the year its law took effect \(\alpha_s\) , \(\lambda_t\) — State and year fixed effects \(\tau\) — The DiD estimate: the average effect on the treated (ATT) The identifying assumption \(\tau\) is causal under parallel trends : without the laws, homicide in the adopting states would have changed by the same amount as in the non-adopting states. The levels may differ (the state effects absorb that); the changes must not. The assumption cannot be tested after 2007, but its implication for the years before 2007 can, and the event study does so.

How to write it: design We compare homicide rates in the 13 states that enacted Castle Doctrine laws in 2007 with those in states that did not enact such laws between 2000 and 2010, using a difference-in-differences design with state and year fixed effects. The identifying assumption is that, absent the laws, homicide rates in adopting and non-adopting states would have followed parallel trends.
Load the data and look at the two groups

How to read it Adopting states have higher homicide rates throughout: that difference in levels is what the state fixed effects remove. What matters is whether the two lines move in parallel before 2007 . By eye they track each other reasonably closely, with year-to-year noise. The event study turns this impression into a test.

How to read it This table is the whole idea of DiD. Each group's change from before to after removes its permanent level; the difference between the two changes removes everything common to both groups in the later years (national crime trends, the recession). What remains is attributed to the law. With one adoption date and a balanced panel, this number is exactly the two-way fixed-effects estimate in the next step.

How to read it Estimate. The laws are associated with homicide rates about 6% higher, but the confidence interval is wide and includes zero: in this subsample the effect is not statistically significant. Clustered standard errors. The treatment varies at the state level and homicide is serially correlated within states, so standard errors must be clustered by state (Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan 2004). With 42 clusters this is fine; with fewer than about 30, use the wild cluster bootstrap.
Event study: test the pre-trends and trace the dynamics

How to read it Each point is the difference between adopting and non-adopting states in that year, relative to 2006 (year −1). Leads (before adoption). They fluctuate around zero, and the joint test does not reject that they are all zero. There is no evidence that adopting states were already on a different path before 2007. That is the implication of parallel trends that can be checked. Lags (after adoption). The estimated effects after 2007 are small and imprecise: no clear sign of a jump in homicide among this group of states. An insignificant pre-trend test is not proof of parallel trends: the test may simply lack power. A referee may ask for a sensitivity analysis (Rambachan and Roth 2023), which shows how large a violation of parallel trends would have to be to overturn the conclusion.
Robustness: placebo date and a different comparison

How to read it Placebo date. Pretending the law took effect in 2004 and using only pre-2007 data should give no effect. It does not, which supports the comparison. Different base period. The event-study average uses only 2006 as the base year, while the TWFE estimate uses the average of all pre-treatment years. The two answers differ because individual years are noisy, but both point estimates are small relative to their uncertainty. Report both and say so.

How to write it: results Table 1 reports the difference-in-differences estimates. Homicide rates in states that enacted Castle Doctrine laws in 2007 rose by about 6 percent relative to non-adopting states, but the estimate is imprecise and not statistically different from zero (standard errors clustered by state). Event-study estimates show no differential pre-trends: the coefficients for the years before adoption are jointly insignificant, and a placebo law dated to 2004 has no effect. Common mistakes Using this two-way fixed-effects regression when units adopt at different dates. The estimate can then be badly biased; see the staggered-DiD guide. Not clustering at the level of treatment assignment. Treating insignificant leads as proof of parallel trends. Show the event-study plot, and consider a sensitivity analysis.
Controlling for variables that the policy itself affects (bad controls). Ignoring anticipation: if behaviour changes when a law is announced, the base period must precede the announcement.
Generalized Synthetic Control: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why DiD fails here

The question: did stand-your-ground laws change the murder rate? The DiD guides used homicides from vital statistics; this guide uses the murder rate from police reports (FBI Uniform Crime Reports), in logs, for the same 50 states and the same laws. A second measure of the same outcome is a standard robustness check, and here it raises a problem the first measure did not. The difference-in-differences model assumes that, without treatment, every state's outcome would have moved by the same amount each year. Generalized synthetic control relaxes that: The \(f_t\) are a small number of unobserved common factors (for example, national trends in public-sector hiring or crime policy), and the loadings \(\lambda_i\) let each state respond to them differently. DiD is the special case with no factors. If treated states load more heavily on a rising factor, their outcome rises faster even without treatment, and DiD would wrongly attribute that to the law.
The question and why DiD fails here

How the method works Estimate the factors from the never-treated states, which are untouched by the policy. For each treated state, estimate its loadings from its pre-treatment years only. Predict its untreated outcome after adoption, \(\hat Y_{it}(0)\) , and take the gap \(Y_{it} - \hat Y_{it}(0)\) as the effect. Choose the number of factors by cross-validation: hold out each pre-treatment year in turn and see which number predicts it best. How to write it: design Because event-study estimates indicate that adopting and non-adopting states were on different trends before the laws took effect, we estimate the effect with the generalized synthetic control method of Xu (2017). It models untreated outcomes with state and year effects and a small number of latent factors with state-specific loadings, estimated from never-treated states, and imputes the counterfactual for each adopting state from its pre-adoption path. The number of factors is selected by cross-validation.
Load the data and test the pre-trends

How to read it The leads are not flat: the joint test rejects that they are zero at the 5% level. Before adopting a law, murder rates in the adopting states were already moving differently from those in the other states. Any DiD estimate here mixes that pre-existing difference in trends with the effect of the law, which is why the model selection tool sends this dataset to generalized synthetic control.

How to read it With zero factors the model is two-way fixed effects. Adding factors lets states follow different trends; too many factors overfit the short pre-treatment period. Cross-validation picks the number that best predicts held-out pre-treatment years of the treated states. A non-zero choice confirms that unit-specific trends matter, as the event study suggested.

How to read it Before adoption , the gaps between each treated state and its counterfactual should be close to zero: they measure how well the model fits. In the five years before adoption they stay within about ±0.07, against DiD leads of up to −0.13 in the first step: the factor has absorbed most of the difference in trends. The gaps 8 to 10 years before adoption rest on the one or two states that adopted last and are noisy; they inflate the overall pre-treatment RMSE. After adoption , the gaps are the estimated effects. The average effect on the murder rate is small and not significant. Standard errors come from bootstrapping states (both treated and control), re-estimating everything each time.

How to read it Two-way fixed effects suggests murder rose by about 9% (p ≈ 0.10). GSC and the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator, which handle the pre-trend in different ways, both put the effect near 2% and far from significance. The TWFE estimate is the outlier: it averages over all pre-adoption years and so attributes the adopting states' different pre-trend to the law. Because the pre-trend test rejected parallel trends, the GSC estimate, whose counterfactual fits the pre-treatment years, is the one to lead with. Report all three: the comparison shows how much the conclusion depends on the treatment of trends.

How to write it: results Event-study estimates reveal differential pre-trends in murder rates between adopting and non-adopting states (joint test of pre-adoption coefficients, p = 0.02), so difference-in-differences estimates are not credible for this outcome. Using the generalized synthetic control method with one latent factor selected by cross-validation, we find no significant effect of Castle Doctrine laws on the murder rate. The pre-adoption gaps between adopting states and their estimated counterfactuals are small, indicating a good fit. Common mistakes Using GSC with very few pre-treatment periods. The loadings of each treated unit are estimated from its pre-treatment years; with fewer than about five, the counterfactual is unreliable. Using GSC with very few control units. The factors are estimated from them.

Choosing the number of factors by looking at the post-treatment results. Fix it by cross-validation on pre-treatment data only. Forgetting to show the pre-treatment fit. It is the main evidence that the counterfactual is credible. In Stata or R, use gsynth (Xu) or fect (Liu, Wang and Xu) for the full method with covariates and parametric bootstrap.

Seven routes to a finished paper
Each guide takes one real dataset through estimation, diagnostic tests and writing, with Python code, real output and sample text for the paper.
Interrupted Time Series: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

On 31 January 1983 wearing a front seatbelt became compulsory in Great Britain. How many deaths and serious injuries of car drivers did the law prevent? The law applied to the whole country at once, so there is no untreated region to compare with. This is the classic dataset of Harvey and Durbin (1986). The interrupted time series (ITS) design uses the pre-law path of the series as the counterfactual, through a segmented regression: Term Meaning \(\beta_1\) Pre-law trend per month \(D_t\) 1 from February 1983 onwards \(\delta\) Level change : the immediate effect of the law \(\gamma\) Slope change : how the trend changed after the law \(\mu_m\) Month effects: road deaths are seasonal

The identifying assumption Without the law, the series would have continued along its pre-law trend and seasonal pattern. Nothing else that affects road deaths may change at the same time. This is a strong assumption, and the credibility of an ITS study rests on arguing it: listing other events (fuel prices, speed limits, recessions) and showing they did not coincide with the intervention. How to write it: design Because the seatbelt law applied nationwide from February 1983, no contemporaneous control group exists. We estimate its effect with an interrupted time series design: a segmented regression of monthly driver casualties on a linear trend, month effects, and a level and a slope change at the date the law took effect, with Newey–West standard errors to allow for serial correlation.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The series has a strong seasonal pattern (more casualties in winter), a gently falling trend, and a visible drop in early 1983. There is also a fall around 1974, the time of the first oil crisis, when fuel prices jumped and a national speed limit was introduced. Keep it in mind: it is exactly the kind of event that can masquerade as, or contaminate, a policy effect.

How to read it Level change ( post ). In the month the law took effect, driver casualties fell by about 300, roughly 17% of the pre-law monthly average. The effect is large and highly significant. Slope change ( t_post ). Positive: after the immediate drop, the series fell less steeply than before. With only 23 post-law months, this slope is estimated imprecisely, and it should not be extrapolated far. Standard errors are Newey–West with a few lags, which keeps inference valid when monthly errors are serially correlated.

How to read it The dashed line extends the pre-law trend and seasonal pattern into the post-law period: what the model says would have happened without the law. The observed series lies well below it after February 1983. Summed over the post-law months, this is several thousand fewer drivers killed or seriously injured, the number a policy reader wants.

How to read it The Durbin–Watson statistic below 2 and the Ljung–Box tests show positive serial correlation in the residuals: a bad month tends to be followed by another. The Newey–West errors already allow for this. Modelling the autocorrelation directly, with AR(1) errors, is the standard robustness check. The level change remains large and significant.

How to read it A placebo date is a date when nothing happened. Estimated on pre-law data only, it should show no effect. May 1978 : no significant effect, as it should be. January 1976 : a large negative “effect” of about −150, significant at the 10% level. This is not a failure of the method: it picks up the 1974–75 oil-crisis fall in the data, which a single linear trend cannot capture. It shows that this series has other breaks , and that the trend before 1983 is not as simple as the model assumes. Report both placebos. The case for the seatbelt effect rests on the size and sharpness of the 1983 drop, which no other event matches, and Harvey and Durbin strengthened it by modelling fuel prices and traffic volume and by comparing with rear-seat passengers, who were not covered by the law. When a comparison series exists, use it.

How to write it: results The segmented regression indicates an immediate reduction of about 300 drivers killed or seriously injured per month when the seatbelt law took effect, around 17 percent of the pre-law average (Newey–West standard errors). The estimate is robust to modelling the residual autocorrelation with AR(1) errors. A placebo intervention in 1978 shows no effect; a placebo in 1976 shows a sizeable decline, significant at the 10 percent level, reflecting the fall associated with the 1974 oil crisis, which underlines that the attribution of the 1983 drop to the law rests on the absence of other changes at that date. Common mistakes Ignoring seasonality: a policy that starts in a low season looks effective.

Using conventional standard errors with autocorrelated monthly data. Extrapolating the pre-trend far beyond the intervention, or over-interpreting a slope change estimated from few post-periods. Not checking for other events at the same date. ITS has no comparison group to absorb them. When a comparison series exists (an unaffected group, region or outcome), use it: that turns the ITS into a comparative ITS or a DiD.
Instrumental Variables: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. An instrument shifts the treatment.
The question and why OLS fails

What is the return to a year of schooling? A regression of log wages on years of education gives an answer, but not a causal one: people who study longer may also be more able or more motivated, and those traits raise wages on their own. Ability is not in the data, so OLS is biased (most likely upwards). Card (1995) proposed an instrument: whether a man grew up near a four-year college . Living near a college lowers the cost of attending, so it raises schooling; the argument is that, given region and urban residence, it affects wages only through schooling. Variable Role Definition lwage outcome Log hourly wage, 1976
The question and why OLS fails

educ endogenous treatment Years of schooling nearc4 instrument 1 if a four-year college was in the county at age 14 black , smsa , south , married , exper controls Race, urban residence, region, marital status, experience The three conditions Relevance: the instrument moves schooling. Testable: the first stage. Exclusion: proximity affects wages only through schooling. Not testable. Threat: families who live near colleges may differ in ways that also raise wages; that is why urban and regional controls matter. Independence: proximity is as good as random given the controls. Not testable. It must be argued. A paper's IV section stands or falls on the argument for exclusion and independence, not on the regression output.
The question and why OLS fails

How to write it: identification Because schooling is likely correlated with unobserved ability, we instrument years of education with an indicator for growing up near a four-year college, following Card (1995). Proximity lowers the cost of college attendance and so raises schooling; conditional on race, region, urban residence, marital status and experience, we assume it affects wages only through its effect on schooling.
Load the data and estimate OLS

How to read it OLS says each additional year of schooling is associated with wages about 7% higher, very precisely estimated. Precision is not the problem; bias is. The IV estimate will tell us how much of this association is causal.
The first stage: is the instrument relevant?

How to read it Men who grew up near a four-year college completed about a third of a year more schooling, holding the controls fixed. The robust F statistic is about 16.5, above the Staiger–Stock rule of thumb of 10, so the instrument is not weak in the traditional sense. It is not strong either: it explains only half a percent of the variation in schooling left after the controls. Lee, McCrary, Moreira and Porter (2022) show that conventional 2SLS t-tests have correct size only with F above about 105, which is why the Anderson–Rubin test below matters.

How to read it Reduced form. Men who grew up near a college earn about 4% more. Show this regression: it is the causal effect of the instrument itself, and if it is zero there is nothing to scale up. 2SLS. With one instrument, the 2SLS estimate is exactly the reduced form divided by the first stage: about 0.12, a return of 12% per year of schooling, larger than OLS. Precision. The 2SLS standard error is more than ten times the OLS one. The confidence interval is wide. Why would the IV estimate exceed OLS when ability bias pushes OLS up? Because the IV estimate is a local average treatment effect (LATE): the return for men whose schooling was changed by college proximity, typically from families for whom cost was a real barrier. Their return to schooling may be higher than average. Measurement error in schooling, which biases OLS towards zero, is another explanation.

How to read it The Anderson–Rubin test has the correct size however weak the instrument . It tests each candidate value of the return \(b_0\) by asking whether the instrument still predicts \(\ln w - b_0 \cdot educ\) ; the confidence set collects the values that are not rejected. Here it rejects a zero return, and the 95% set runs from about 0.03 to 0.25: wider than the conventional 2SLS interval, but excluding zero. This is the interval to report when the first stage is not overwhelmingly strong.

How to read it The test adds the first-stage residual to the OLS regression: if schooling were exogenous, the residual would add nothing. It does not reject. That does not prove schooling is exogenous: with an imprecise 2SLS estimate the test has little power, and the gap between 0.07 and 0.12 is economically large. With one instrument, the exclusion restriction cannot be tested at all (no overidentification test); Card's full dataset adds proximity to a two-year college, which allows a Hansen J test.

How to write it: results OLS estimates imply a return to schooling of about 7 percent per year. Instrumenting schooling with proximity to a four-year college, the 2SLS estimate is about 12 percent (robust standard error 0.05). The first stage is significant, with a robust F statistic of 16.5; because conventional 2SLS inference can be unreliable at this instrument strength, we also report the Anderson–Rubin 95 percent confidence set, which excludes zero. The 2SLS estimate is a local average treatment effect for men whose schooling was affected by college proximity, and its exceeding OLS is consistent with higher returns for individuals facing cost barriers to college, or with measurement error in schooling.

Common mistakes Treating the first-stage F above 10 as the end of the weak-instrument question. Report Anderson–Rubin intervals. Not reporting the first stage and the reduced form. Arguing exclusion with a statistical test. With one instrument there is none; even with several, the Hansen test only checks that instruments agree. Interpreting 2SLS as an average effect for everyone. It is local to the compliers. Computing the second stage by hand with OLS on fitted values: the standard errors are wrong. Use an IV routine.
Regression Discontinuity: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Treatment assigned by a cutoff.

Do voters choose policies, or only politicians? If candidates converge to the median voter, it should not matter much for how a district is represented which party narrowly wins. If they do not, a narrow Democratic win should produce a much more liberal representative than a narrow Republican win. Lee, Moretti and Butler (2004) answered this with a regression discontinuity. Whether a Democrat wins is determined by a cutoff: the Democratic vote share \(R_i\) crossing 0.5. Districts where the Democrat won 50.5% and those where she won 49.5% are, on average, alike in everything except who won. So the jump in the winner's liberal voting score at 0.5 measures the effect of electing a Democrat:

Symbol Variable in the file Definition \(Y\) score ADA score of the elected representative (0 = conservative, 100 = liberal) \(R\) demvoteshare Democratic share of the two-party vote \(D\) democrat 1 if the Democrat won (= 1 exactly when \(R \ge 0.5\) : a sharp design) — lagdemvoteshare Democratic vote share in the previous election (determined before the election) The identifying assumption The potential outcomes are continuous at the cutoff: nothing else jumps at 0.5. This fails if candidates can precisely control which side of 0.5 they land on (manipulation), which would make the winners of close races systematically different. It can be checked in two ways: the density of the running variable should not jump at the cutoff, and characteristics determined before the election should not jump either.

How to write it: design We exploit the discontinuity in party control created by the 50 percent threshold in two-party House elections. Comparing districts in which the Democratic candidate barely won with districts in which she barely lost identifies the effect of electing a Democrat on the representative's voting record, under the assumption that potential outcomes are continuous in the vote share at the threshold.
Load the data and plot the discontinuity

How to read it Always start with this plot: averages of the outcome in narrow bins of the running variable. The jump at 0.5 is unmistakable: districts that barely elect a Democrat are represented by someone with an ADA score roughly 45–50 points higher than districts that barely elect a Republican. On either side the relationship with the vote share is fairly flat. A plot like this, with the estimate overlaid, should be Figure 1 of an RD paper.
Local linear estimate with a data-driven bandwidth

How to read it The estimate fits a separate straight line on each side of the cutoff, using only elections within a vote-share distance \(h\) of 0.5 and giving more weight to those closest to it. The jump of about 47 points is the effect of a Democratic win on the winner's ADA score: party, not the median voter, determines roll-call voting. The WLS lines reproduce it exactly, which shows there is nothing hidden in the helper function. Local linear regression is the standard. Global high-order polynomials (fitting a fourth-degree curve to all the data) can produce misleading estimates and should not be used (Gelman and Imbens 2019).

How to read it The estimate barely moves between half and double the optimal bandwidth, and a local quadratic gives the same answer. That stability is what a referee wants to see. If the estimate changed sharply with the bandwidth, the effect would depend on functional-form assumptions away from the cutoff.

How to read it If candidates could precisely engineer narrow wins (through fraud or recounts, say), there would be too many elections just above 0.5 and too few just below. The histogram shows no such heaping, and the McCrary test finds no significant jump in the density. In settings like test scores or income eligibility, where people know the cutoff, this test often fails, and an RD with sorting is not credible.
Validity 2: covariate balance and placebo cutoffs

How to read it Covariate balance. The previous election's vote share was determined before this election, so it should not jump at 0.5. It shows a small jump of about 3 percentage points, statistically significant, and it does not disappear with half the bandwidth. This imbalance in close House elections is documented in the literature (Caughey and Sekhon 2011 discuss sorting in very close races). It must be reported. Re-running the main estimate with the covariate as a control leaves it essentially unchanged (47.2 against 46.7), so the imbalance does not drive the result. Placebo cutoffs. At vote shares of 0.4 and 0.6, where nothing changes, the estimated jumps are small compared with the 47-point effect at 0.5.

How to write it: results Figure 1 shows a sharp discontinuity in the ADA score of the elected representative at the 50 percent vote-share threshold. Local linear estimates with the Imbens–Kalyanaraman bandwidth imply that a Democratic victory raises the representative's ADA score by about 47 points (robust standard error 1.3). The estimate is stable across bandwidths from half to twice the optimal one and under a local quadratic specification. A McCrary test shows no discontinuity in the density of the vote share at the threshold. The previous election's Democratic vote share displays a small discontinuity of about 3 percentage points, consistent with incumbency effects; controlling for it does not change the results.

Common mistakes Using global high-order polynomials instead of local linear regression. Reporting one bandwidth only. Skipping the density test and covariate balance: they are the evidence that the design is valid. Forgetting that the RD effect is local : it applies to units at the cutoff (close elections), not to all districts. Treating a fuzzy design as sharp. If crossing the cutoff only raises the probability of treatment, divide the outcome jump by the treatment jump (a local IV estimate). For inference, the bias-corrected robust confidence intervals of Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik ( rdrobust ) are now standard.
Synthetic Control: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

In 1993 Texas began a massive expansion of its prison capacity, roughly doubling the number of beds within a few years. How much did the expansion increase the number of black men in Texas prisons? The example follows Cunningham's Causal Inference: The Mixtape . With one treated state, there is nothing to average over and no obvious control group. Which state, or average of states, shows what Texas would have looked like without the expansion? The synthetic control method (Abadie and Gardeazabal 2003; Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller 2010) answers this with weights: The weights are chosen so that the synthetic Texas matches the real Texas as closely as possible before 1993 . The effect in each later year is the gap between the two.

Why the weights are restricted Nonnegative weights that sum to one keep the synthetic unit inside the range of the actual donor states: an interpolation, not an extrapolation. The result is a transparent comparison: a reader can see which states make up synthetic Texas and judge whether they are plausible. How to write it: design We estimate the effect of the 1993 Texas prison expansion with the synthetic control method. The counterfactual for Texas is a weighted average of the other states, with nonnegative weights summing to one, chosen to reproduce the pre-1993 path of the outcome. Inference is based on placebo tests in which each donor state is in turn treated as if it had expanded its prisons.
Load the data and look at Texas

How to read it Texas has many more black male prisoners than the average state, even before 1993, so the simple average is a poor comparison: its level and trend differ. Any DiD against the average would rest on a parallel-trends assumption that the picture makes implausible. The synthetic control builds a better comparison.

How to read it Synthetic Texas is a combination of a few large states. The pre-treatment root mean squared prediction error (RMSPE) is small relative to the size of the series: the weighted combination tracks Texas closely before 1993. A poor pre-treatment fit would make any post-treatment gap uninterpretable, so always report this number. This guide matches on the outcome path only. The full method also matches on predictors (income, unemployment, demographics) with a second set of weights on those predictors; the synth packages in Stata and R do this.
The effect: actual against synthetic Texas

How to read it The two lines move together until 1993 and then separate sharply: by the late 1990s Texas held tens of thousands more black men in prison than synthetic Texas. The gap is the estimated effect in each year. It grows as the new capacity came into use.

How to read it Each grey line is a placebo: the same method applied to a state that did not expand its prisons, as if it had. If Texas's gap were unusual only by chance, many placebo gaps would look like it. The standard comparison uses the ratio of post- to pre-treatment RMSPE, which accounts for how well each synthetic unit fitted before 1993. The permutation p-value is Texas's rank among all states divided by the number of states. On this statistic Texas ranks 9th of 51 (p ≈ 0.18). But look at which states beat it: Pennsylvania's ratio is over 300 because its synthetic control fits its pre-1993 path almost perfectly, so even a modest later deviation is enormous relative to that fit . With only 8 pre-treatment years, the ratio is a fragile statistic.

A second statistic is the average post-1993 gap as a share of each state's own pre-1993 level. On this measure Texas's gap, more than its entire pre-1993 level, ranks second of 51 (p ≈ 0.04). Report both, and explain the difference: the effect is very large in size, and the conventional ratio-based p-value is weakened by placebo states with near-perfect pre-treatment fits. A standard refinement drops placebo states whose pre-treatment fit is much worse than Texas's (Abadie et al. 2010 use two or five times its pre-RMSPE); here the problem runs the other way, which is why a second statistic helps.
Robustness: leave-one-out and an in-time placebo

How to read it Leave-one-out. Dropping each state with a positive weight in turn and re-estimating should not change the conclusion. If it did, the result would hinge on one donor. In-time placebo. Pretending the expansion happened in 1989 and using only earlier years for the weights, there should be no gap between 1989 and 1992. A gap would mean synthetic Texas cannot track Texas even when nothing happens.

How to write it: results Synthetic Texas, a weighted combination of a few other large states, closely reproduces the number of black male prisoners in Texas before 1993. After the expansion of prison capacity, the two series diverge sharply: by the end of the decade Texas held tens of thousands more black men in prison than its synthetic counterpart. The result is robust to excluding any single donor state, and an in-time placebo shows no divergence before 1993. In placebo-in-space tests, the gap for Texas relative to its pre-1993 level is the second largest of 51 states (permutation p = 0.04); on the ratio of post- to pre-treatment prediction errors, Texas ranks ninth of 51, because several placebo states have near-perfect pre-treatment fits that inflate their ratios.

Common mistakes Including donors that were affected by the same policy, or by spillovers from the treated unit. Interpreting a gap when the pre-treatment fit is poor. Using conventional standard errors. With one treated unit, inference comes from placebo permutations. Choosing the pre-treatment period or the donor pool after looking at the results. Too short a pre-treatment period: the weights then fit noise.
Staggered Difference-in-Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why timing matters

The question is the one in the DiD guide: did stand-your-ground laws change homicide rates? But now all 21 adopting states are used, and they passed their laws in different years. That is the usual situation in policy evaluation: minimum-wage increases, Medicaid expansions, carbon taxes and central-bank reforms all arrive at different dates in different places. The tempting regression is the same as before: Why the conventional regression fails Goodman-Bacon (2021) showed that \(\tau^{TWFE}\) is a weighted average of every 2×2 DiD comparison in the data. Some of those comparisons use states that adopted earlier as the control group for states that adopt later . If the effect of the law grows or changes over time, the earlier adopters' outcomes are still moving because of their own treatment, and subtracting them removes part of the effect, or even flips its sign. Some weights can be negative. The fix is to estimate the effect for each adoption cohort separately, against clean controls, and then average: the group-time ATT of Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021).
The question and why timing matters

How to write it: design States enacted Castle Doctrine laws at different dates between 2006 and 2010. Because two-way fixed-effects estimates are biased under staggered adoption when treatment effects vary over time or across cohorts (Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille 2020), we estimate cohort-specific average treatment effects on the treated, using never-treated states as controls, and aggregate them following Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021).
Load the data and look at the cohorts

How to read it Five adoption cohorts, with most states adopting in 2007, and 29 states that never adopt. The never-treated states are the clean comparison group. Without them, the not-yet-treated states could serve instead.

How to read it The TWFE estimate is about 0.07: homicide about 7% higher after adoption, though not significant with clustered standard errors. This is the number many papers would report. Under staggered adoption it is not a well-defined average of the effects, so it has to be checked against estimators that are.
Group-time effects: one clean comparison per cohort and year

How to read it Each cell is a separate 2×2 comparison: cohort \(g\) against the never-treated states, between year \(t\) and the year before adoption, \(g-1\) . Cells before adoption are placebo comparisons and should be near zero; cells after adoption are effects. Nothing in this table uses an already-treated state as a control. The cohorts with one or two states (2006, 2009, 2010) are noisy, so the cells are aggregated next.
Aggregate: the event study and the overall ATT

How to read it Event study. The group-time effects are averaged by years since adoption, weighting cohorts by size. Standard errors come from a cluster bootstrap over states. Pre-trends. The leads are jointly insignificant at 5% (p ≈ 0.07). Not a clean pass: a sensitivity analysis is advisable. The overall ATT is about 0.02, a third of the TWFE estimate and far from significance. Look at the leads. They are all negative, around −0.04 to −0.10: relative to the never-treated states, homicide in adopting states was lower several years before adoption than in the year just before it. In other words, it was already rising. This estimator measures everything against the year before adoption, so it does not count that earlier rise as an effect of the law.
Aggregate: the event study and the overall ATT
The large estimate four years after adoption rests on the single 2006 adopter (Florida) and should not be over-interpreted.

How to read it The imputation estimator fits state and year effects only on untreated observations , predicts what each treated state-year would have been without the law, and averages the gaps. Like Callaway–Sant'Anna, it never uses treated observations as controls, so it is free of the staggered-adoption bias. It gives about 0.07, close to TWFE . So in this dataset the bias from comparing late with early adopters is small. The real divergence is between estimators that use all pre-treatment years as the baseline (TWFE, imputation: about 0.07) and the one that uses only the year before adoption (Callaway–Sant'Anna: about 0.02). The leads explain it: homicide in adopting states was already rising relative to controls before the laws, and an all-years baseline attributes part of that rise to the law.

The honest conclusion: the estimated effect depends on how the pre-trend is handled, and none of the estimates is statistically significant. Report all three, show the event study, and add a sensitivity analysis for violations of parallel trends (Rambachan and Roth 2023). (Standard errors for the imputation estimator are best obtained with the did_imputation package in Stata or a cluster bootstrap.)

How to write it: results Because states adopted Castle Doctrine laws at different dates, we report heterogeneity-robust estimators alongside the two-way fixed-effects estimate. The two-way fixed-effects and imputation estimators, which use all pre-adoption years as the baseline, both indicate an increase in homicide of about 7 percent; the Callaway–Sant'Anna estimator, which uses the year before adoption as the baseline, indicates about 2 percent. None of the estimates is statistically significant. The pre-adoption event-study coefficients are negative and jointly significant at the 10 but not the 5 percent level, suggesting that homicide was already rising in adopting states; the results are therefore sensitive to how this pre-trend is treated. Common mistakes

Reporting only the TWFE coefficient under staggered adoption. Running a conventional event-study regression with relative-time dummies under staggered adoption: it suffers from the same contamination (Sun and Abraham 2021). Use cohort-specific estimates. Not saying which controls are used: never-treated or not-yet-treated. They rest on different assumptions; report both if possible. Ignoring small cohorts. A cohort of one state drives the event-time estimates where it is alone.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How strongly did the Federal Reserve respond to inflation, and which shocks drove U.S. inflation? Calibration cannot answer this: it requires estimating the policy rule jointly with the rest of the economy. Bayesian estimation (Smets and Wouters 2003; An and Schorfheide 2007) combines the model's likelihood, computed with the Kalman filter, with prior information about the parameters. The model is the New Keynesian model of An and Schorfheide (2007), with a technology growth shock \(z_t\) , a demand (government spending) shock \(g_t\) and a monetary policy shock \(\varepsilon^R_t\) : and measurement equations that link the model to the data: Data and measurement are part of the model Three observables and three shocks. A linear DSGE model with fewer shocks than observables is stochastically singular : it implies an exact linear relation among the observables that the data reject. Never use more observables than shocks (or add measurement errors).
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

Demeaned data. Each observable has its sample mean removed, so the model is estimated in deviations and the constants (trend growth, the inflation target, the real rate) are not estimated. Estimating them requires that the model's steady state matches the data's means, which with these data would force a real interest rate near zero. Demeaning is a common, transparent choice; state it in the paper. Units. Output growth is in percent per quarter; inflation and the interest rate are annualised percentages, hence the factor 4. How to write it: data We estimate the model on three quarterly U.S. series for 1966Q1–2007Q4: the growth rate of real GDP, inflation measured by the GDP deflator (annualised), and the effective federal funds rate. The sample ends before the zero-lower-bound period. All series are demeaned prior to estimation.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

Parameter Meaning Prior Mean Std. dev. \(\tau\) inverse intertemporal elasticity Gamma 2.0 0.5 \(\kappa\) slope of the Phillips curve Gamma 0.2 0.1 \(\psi_1\) response to inflation Gamma 1.5 0.25 \(\psi_2\) response to the output gap Gamma 0.5 0.25 \(\rho_R, \rho_g, \rho_z\) persistence Beta 0.5, 0.8, 0.66 0.2, 0.1, 0.15 \(\sigma_R, \sigma_g, \sigma_z\) shock standard deviations Inverse gamma 0.4, 1.0, 0.5 4 (degrees of freedom) The priors follow An and Schorfheide (2007): their means are standard values from earlier studies, and their spreads allow the data to move the estimates substantially. Gamma priors keep parameters positive, Beta priors keep persistence between 0 and 1. How to read it estimated_params lists each estimated parameter with its prior: distribution, mean, standard deviation.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

varobs names the observables; their names must match the column headers of the data file. estimation first finds the posterior mode ( mode_compute = 5 , Dynare's Newton-type optimiser), then runs two independent Metropolis–Hastings chains of 10,000 draws each, discards the first half of each chain as burn-in ( mh_drop ), and reports posterior means and 90% highest-posterior-density intervals. mh_jscale scales the proposal distribution; it is tuned so that about a quarter to a third of proposals are accepted. Chains for a paper should be much longer (at least 2 × 100,000); this page uses short chains so that it can be rebuilt in minutes. The output reports, for each parameter: the prior mean, the posterior mean, the 90% HPD interval, the prior distribution and the prior standard deviation.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it Acceptance ratio. Between about 0.2 and 0.4 is the target. Too high means the sampler takes tiny steps and explores slowly; too low means it rarely moves. R-hat (Gelman and Rubin 1992) compares the variance between the two chains with the variance within them. Values close to 1 (below about 1.1) indicate that the chains have converged to the same distribution. Dynare reports the related Brooks–Gelman diagnostics graphically. Trace plots. The two chains should overlap and move freely around the same region, with no trends.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it Bars are the posterior, dashed lines the prior. Where the two differ, the data are informative. The policy rule. The response to inflation \(\psi_1\) is estimated just above 1, lower than its prior mean: over 1966–2007, which includes the high-inflation 1970s, the Federal Reserve on average barely satisfied the Taylor principle. Interest-rate smoothing \(\rho_R\) is high. The Phillips curve slope \(\kappa\) is estimated at about 0.15: inflation responds weakly to the output gap. Shock persistence. The demand and technology shocks are very persistent ( \(\rho_g\) , \(\rho_z\) near 0.97), a common finding in small models: persistent shocks absorb dynamics the model's frictions cannot generate. Where the posterior looks like the prior , the data say little about that parameter. The identification guide shows how to check this before estimating.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it Each line is the posterior mean response to a one-standard-deviation monetary policy shock; the shaded band is the 90% HPD interval, which reflects parameter uncertainty. Unlike a VAR, the DSGE model identifies the shock through its structure: every response follows from the estimated equations.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to read it The black line is demeaned inflation; the coloured areas show how much of it each smoothed shock accounts for in each quarter (plus the effect of initial conditions, not shown). In this small model the persistent technology growth shock accounts for almost all of it (94% of the squared contributions), including the Great Inflation of the 1970s and the disinflation of the 1980s; monetary policy shocks account for the rest. The demand shock does not move inflation at all: in this model it shifts output and its natural level together. That is a property of a three-shock model with no cost-push shock: a richer model would split inflation between more shocks, so read the decomposition as model-dependent.
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

How to write it: results Table 2 reports the prior and posterior distributions. The posterior mean of the response of the policy rate to inflation is about 1.2, with a 90 percent interval just above one, indicating that over 1966–2007 the Federal Reserve on average satisfied the Taylor principle only narrowly; interest rates were adjusted gradually (posterior mean of the smoothing coefficient about 0.77). The slope of the Phillips curve is estimated at about 0.15. Two Metropolis–Hastings chains were run; the Gelman–Rubin statistics are close to one for all parameters. A contractionary monetary policy shock lowers output and inflation (Figure 3). Common mistakes More observables than shocks: stochastic singularity. Data and model in different units (annualised vs quarterly, percent vs fractions, levels vs growth rates).
Bayesian Estimation of a New Keynesian Model

Reporting estimates from chains that have not converged, or from very short chains. Running the sampler without first checking the mode ( mode_check ) and identification. Priors so tight that the posterior equals the prior, then presenting the result as an estimate. Always plot priors against posteriors.
Higher-Order Solutions and Welfare: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
The question and why first order is not enough

How costly are business cycles, and does uncertainty change how the economy behaves on average? In a first-order solution, the mean of every variable equals its steady state, whatever the size of the shocks: households behave as if they were certain about the future (certainty equivalence). That makes first-order solutions unable to measure: precautionary behaviour : uncertainty raising saving and the capital stock; welfare : the average utility loss from fluctuations, which depends on variances, a second-order term; asymmetry : large positive and negative shocks having responses of different size. The model is the RBC model of the first guide with one extra equation, a recursive definition of lifetime utility:
The question and why first order is not enough

Pruning Higher-order perturbation solutions can explode in simulations, because the squared terms feed back on themselves. Pruning (Kim, Kim, Schaumburg and Sims 2008; Andreasen, Fernández-Villaverde and Rubio-Ramírez 2018) removes the terms of higher order than the approximation, keeping simulations stable and making theoretical moments available. Always use it at order 2 and above.

How to read it The policy functions now contain a constant correction and terms in squared states. The constant (the ghs2 term in Dynare's notation) is how risk enters: it shifts every variable away from its steady state even when no shock occurs in a given period. The theoretical moments below are computed from the pruned second-order solution.
Precautionary saving and the welfare cost of fluctuations

How to read it Precautionary saving. With uncertainty, the average capital stock is above its steady state: households save more as insurance against bad productivity draws. Output is higher on average as a result. A first-order solution would show zero difference for every variable. Welfare cost. The consumption-equivalent cost \(\lambda\) solves \(E[\mathcal W] = \mathcal W_{ss} + \ln(1-\lambda)/(1-\beta)\) : the share of consumption households would give up every period to live in the steady state instead of the fluctuating economy. Here it is negative , about −0.03%: households are slightly better off with fluctuations. That is not a bug. With elastic labour supply and capital, households can work and invest more when productivity is high and less when it is low, and that option is worth more than the utility lost to consumption volatility (Cho, Cooley and Kim 2015). Lucas (1987) found the cost of fluctuations to be tiny in an endowment economy; in this production economy it is tiny and of the opposite sign. Models with incomplete markets, unemployment risk or nominal rigidities typically produce positive and larger costs.
How the answer changes with the size of shocks

How to read it Size of shocks. Doubling the shock standard deviation multiplies the precautionary capital and the welfare effect by four, tripling it by nine: both are proportional to the variance of the shocks, the signature of a second-order effect. Third order. The model file can be solved at third order with dynare rbc2 -DORD=3 . With symmetric shocks, third-order terms leave average outcomes essentially unchanged; they matter for time-varying risk premia and models with stochastic volatility. Dynare provides theoretical moments only up to second order, so third-order results come from long pruned simulations.

How to read it With a linear solution the two lines would coincide exactly. At second order the squared terms add the same correction to positive and negative shocks, so their responses can differ in size. In this smooth RBC model the difference is virtually nil , even for a five-standard-deviation shock: the model is close to linear around its steady state. Strong asymmetries need strong nonlinearities, such as the occasionally binding constraint of the zero-lower-bound guide.

How to write it: results We solve the model with a second-order perturbation and pruning, which captures the effect of uncertainty on average outcomes. Productivity risk raises the average capital stock above its deterministic steady state, reflecting precautionary saving. The welfare effect of business-cycle fluctuations, measured as the permanent percentage of consumption that would make households indifferent between the stochastic economy and its deterministic steady state, is very small and slightly favourable: with elastic labour supply, households exploit productivity fluctuations by working and investing more in good times. Both effects scale with the variance of the shocks. Common mistakes Computing welfare from a first-order solution. The linear approximation of a utility function gets welfare comparisons wrong; use second order.

Simulating at order 2 or 3 without pruning. Comparing welfare across policies without a common starting point: conditional and unconditional welfare can rank policies differently. Reporting means from a first-order solution as “effects of uncertainty”: they equal the steady state by construction.
Identification Before Estimation: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Dynare code, real output and sample text.
The question and why it comes first

Which parameters can the data actually tell us about? In a DSGE model the observables depend on the parameters through the solution of the model, and some parameters may have no separate effect: they enter only in a combination, or their effect is indistinguishable from another parameter's. Such parameters are not identified . Estimating them anyway gives posteriors that mirror the priors, and conclusions that are really assumptions. Iskrev (2010) and Komunjer and Ng (2011) showed how to check identification from the model alone: a parameter is (locally) identified if the moments, or the spectrum, of the observables change when the parameter changes, in a way that no combination of other parameters can replicate. Dynare implements both checks in the identification command.
The question and why it comes first

Two kinds of problems Non-identification : a parameter has no effect on the observables, or two parameters enter only as a product or ratio. The Jacobian of the moments with respect to the parameters is rank-deficient. Weak identification : the parameter is identified in principle, but its effect is small or nearly collinear with another's, so the data are only weakly informative. The Jacobian is close to rank-deficient.

How to read it Dynare runs three tests, and they do not all agree: Komunjer and Ng (2011) , the test on the model's minimal state-space system, finds all parameters identified . The reduced-form test (Iskrev 2010) and the spectrum test (Qu and Tkachenko 2012) flag the policy-rule block ( \(\psi_1\) , \(\psi_2\) , \(\rho_R\) and the standard deviation of the monetary shock) as collinear with the other parameters: their effects on the observables can be closely mimicked by combinations of other parameters. This is not a quirk of the code. Cochrane (2011) argued that Taylor-rule coefficients are hard to identify in New Keynesian models precisely because, under determinacy, the equilibrium never shows the off-equilibrium responses those coefficients govern. In practice it means the data will be only weakly informative about the policy rule, and its posterior will lean on the prior: compare the prior and posterior of \(\psi_1\) in the estimation guide before interpreting it. The other parameters are cleanly identified.
A model that is not identified

How to read it The Phillips curve depends on the Calvo parameter \(\theta\) and the labour-supply parameter \(\varphi\) only through the slope \(\kappa\) . Many combinations of \(\theta\) and \(\varphi\) give the same \(\kappa\) , and therefore exactly the same predictions for output, inflation and interest rates. Now all three tests fail, including Komunjer–Ng, and each names the same culprit: [varphi, theta] are pairwise collinear . Unlike the weak identification of the policy rule, this is exact non-identification. This is a typical situation, not a contrived one. Small models usually identify the slope of the Phillips curve but not the structural parameters behind it. The remedies are: estimate the reduced-form coefficient ( \(\kappa\) ) and calibrate one of the structural parameters;
A model that is not identified

add data that the other parameter affects separately (hours or wages identify \(\varphi\) ); use informative priors from micro evidence, and say clearly that the posterior for that parameter reflects the prior.

How to write it: identification Before estimation, we verify local identification of the estimated parameters at the prior mean using the rank conditions of Iskrev (2010) and Komunjer and Ng (2011), as implemented in Dynare. The Komunjer–Ng test indicates that all estimated parameters are locally identified, although the reduced-form and spectral tests point to weak identification of the policy-rule parameters, a known feature of New Keynesian models (Cochrane 2011); we therefore interpret their posteriors with reference to the priors. In an alternative parameterisation in which the Calvo probability and the inverse Frisch elasticity are estimated separately, the two are not separately identified, because they enter the model only through the slope of the Phillips curve; we therefore estimate the slope directly.

Common mistakes Estimating first and checking identification only when a posterior looks like its prior. Taking a well-behaved posterior as evidence of identification: a tight prior produces a tight posterior even for an unidentified parameter. Checking identification at one parameter value only. Dynare can check it across draws from the prior ( prior_mc option), which reveals regions where it fails. Estimating more structural parameters than the observables can inform, instead of estimating reduced-form coefficients.
