Load the data and confirm the starting point

Eligible households hold far more financial assets, but they also earn more: the raw difference mixes the effect of eligibility with the effect of income. Adjusting for the controls cuts the difference roughly in half. With 12 controls (Rule B2: at least 10), DML is the method; with a binary treatment, the interactive model (Rule B3).

The AIPW score divides by \(\hat m(X)\) and \(1 - \hat m(X)\) . If some households are almost certain to be eligible, or almost certain not to be, those weights explode and the estimate becomes unstable. Before estimating anything, check overlap : the propensity scores of treated and untreated households should cover the same range, away from 0 and 1. Overlap is reasonable in the middle of the distribution, but 4.8 % of households, almost all of them not eligible (451 of the 478 below 0.05), have propensity scores outside [0.05, 0.95]: households whose characteristics almost never come with a 401(k) offer. DoubleML trims extreme scores at a threshold; the guide reports the estimate at several thresholds in Step 5.

The interactive model needs three predictions: the outcome for treated households \(\hat g(1, X)\) , for untreated households \(\hat g(0, X)\) (both from ml_g ), and the propensity score \(\hat m(X)\) (from the classifier ml_m ). Each is cross-fitted.

Both learners give an average effect of eligibility of about 8,000 dollars (8,316 with LASSO, 7,896 with random forests), close to the published DML estimates for these data, below the OLS estimate of 9,396 and less than half the raw difference. The two learners differ by a third of a standard error (Rule B4), so the result does not hinge on the choice of machine-learning method.
Robustness: trimming and the effect on the treated

Two checks belong in the paper. First, how much do the extreme propensity scores matter? Second, the average effect on the treated (ATTE), the effect for households that actually were eligible, may differ from the ATE.

How to write it: method and results We estimate the average effect of 401(k) eligibility on net financial assets with the interactive regression model of Chernozhukov et al. (2018), assuming, following Poterba, Venti and Wise, that eligibility is as good as random conditional on income, age, education, family structure and other pension and asset holdings (twelve controls including squares). The outcome regressions and the propensity score are estimated with LASSO and, alternatively, random forests, with five-fold cross-fitting repeated three times and propensity scores trimmed at 0.01. Eligibility raises net financial assets by about 8,000 dollars on average (8,316 with LASSO and 7,896 with random forests; standard errors about 1,200), less than the OLS estimate of 9,396 and far less than the raw difference of 19,559 (Table X). The estimate barely moves when propensity scores are trimmed at 0.05 or 0.10 (7,709 and 7,727). The effect on eligible households is larger, about 10,900 dollars (ATTE), consistent with larger gains for the higher-income households who are more often eligible.

Checklist for the paper Argue why treatment is as good as random given the controls. Show the propensity-score distribution and the share outside [0.05, 0.95]. Report the learners, folds, repetitions and the trimming threshold. Show DML with two learners next to OLS and the raw difference. Report the ATTE and the estimate at other trimming thresholds.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

What is the effect of actually participating in a 401(k) plan on a household's financial assets? Participation is a choice: households that save a lot anyway are more likely to join, so comparing participants with non-participants, even with controls, overstates the effect. Eligibility is a natural instrument. It is set by the employer, so (following Poterba, Venti and Wise) it is as good as random given income and the other controls; it strongly shifts participation, because only eligible workers can participate; and it plausibly affects assets only through participation. The partially linear IV model is with \(D\) participation, \(Z\) eligibility and \(X\) the controls. DML-IV predicts \(Y\) , \(D\) and \(Z\) from \(X\) by cross-fitted machine learning, and then runs IV on the residuals: \(\hat\theta = \sum \tilde Z_i \tilde Y_i / \sum \tilde Z_i \tilde D_i\) .
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

Whose effect is this? With a binary instrument and heterogeneous effects, IV estimates the effect for compliers , the households who participate because they are eligible (a local average treatment effect; Imbens and Angrist 1994). Here non-eligible households cannot participate at all (one-sided non-compliance), so the compliers are all participants and \(\theta\) is the average effect of participation on the participants.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Load the data and confirm the starting point
Nobody who is ineligible participates, and 70.5 % of the eligible do. OLS gives a large effect of participation, but it compares savers who chose to participate with households that did not.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

An instrument must move the treatment. The first-stage regression of participation on eligibility and the controls tells how strongly; the selection tool requires an F statistic of at least 10 (Rule B3). The instrument is extremely strong: eligibility raises the probability of participating by 70 percentage points (F ≈ 7,600). Weak-instrument problems do not arise here. When the F statistic is close to or below 10, report Anderson–Rubin confidence intervals, which stay valid however weak the instrument is.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

2SLS is the standard estimator, but it controls for \(X\) linearly. With income entering wealth and participation in a strongly nonlinear way, a linear adjustment may leave confounding behind. DML-IV relaxes that.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Three nuisance functions are cross-fitted: \(\ell(X) = E[Y \mid X]\) ( ml_l ), \(m(X) = E[Z \mid X]\) ( ml_m ) and \(r(X) = E[D \mid X]\) ( ml_r ).
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)
Reading the result: the intention-to-treat and the Wald ratio

With one binary instrument, the IV estimate is the effect of eligibility on assets (the intention-to-treat , ITT) divided by the effect of eligibility on participation (the first stage). Seeing the two pieces makes the result transparent:
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

How to write it: method and results Participation in a 401(k) is chosen by households and is therefore endogenous. We instrument it with eligibility, which is determined by employers and, following Poterba, Venti and Wise, is as good as random conditional on income, age, education and family characteristics. The first stage is very strong (eligibility raises participation by about 70 percentage points; F in the thousands). We estimate the partially linear IV model by double machine learning (Chernozhukov et al. 2018), with LASSO and random-forest learners, five-fold cross-fitting and three repetitions. Participation raises net financial assets by about 13,000 dollars among participants (13,641 with LASSO and 12,880 with random forests; standard errors about 1,900), close to linear 2SLS (13,526) and somewhat below OLS (14,159), which is biased upwards by the self-selection of savers into participation (Table X). The two learners differ by 0.4 standard errors.
Double Machine Learning with an Instrument (DML-IV)

Checklist for the paper Argue relevance, exclusion and as-good-as-random assignment of the instrument. Report the first stage and its F statistic; use Anderson–Rubin intervals if it is weak. State whose effect IV identifies (compliers; here, participants). Show DML-IV with two learners next to OLS and 2SLS. Report folds, repetitions and the learners for all three nuisance functions.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

Do poorer countries grow faster? The neoclassical growth model predicts conditional convergence: holding constant the determinants of a country's steady state, a lower initial income should mean faster growth. The test is the sign of \(\theta\) in where \(X_i\) are the steady-state determinants. The Barro–Lee data used by Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2011, 2014) have 90 countries and 60 candidate controls: schooling by level and sex, population growth, fertility, investment, government spending, openness, political instability, the black-market premium and more. With 60 controls and 90 countries, OLS is barely estimable, and choosing a handful of controls by hand is exactly the specification search that convergence studies have been criticised for.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

This is the partially linear model : the treatment \(D\) enters linearly with one coefficient \(\theta\) , and the controls enter through an unknown function \(g\) that machine learning can estimate. DML (Chernozhukov et al. 2018) estimates \(\theta\) in three steps: predict the outcome from the controls, \(\hat\ell(X) \approx E[Y\mid X]\) , and the treatment from the controls, \(\hat m(X) \approx E[D\mid X]\) , each by machine learning; form the residuals \(\tilde Y = Y - \hat\ell(X)\) and \(\tilde D = D - \hat m(X)\) ; regress \(\tilde Y\) on \(\tilde D\) : the slope is \(\hat\theta\) . Two ingredients make the standard error valid even though the predictions are regularised: the residual-on-residual form is Neyman-orthogonal (small errors in \(\hat\ell\) and \(\hat m\) have only second-order effects on \(\hat\theta\) ), and every prediction is made by cross-fitting , on observations the learner was not trained on.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

The identifying assumption is the same as for OLS DML assumes that, given \(X\) , the remaining variation in initial GDP is unrelated to unobserved determinants of growth. Machine learning makes the adjustment for \(X\) flexible; it does not make the assumption true. Argue it as you would for OLS, and if it fails, use an instrument (DML-IV) or a research design.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Load the data and confirm the starting point

Without controls, richer countries did not grow more slowly: unconditional convergence fails. With all 60 controls, OLS uses up most of the sample (29 residual degrees of freedom) and the estimate is too imprecise to say anything. That is the case for DML (Rule B2: 60 controls, far more than 10). The forest predicts growth slightly better than LASSO from the controls, and initial GDP slightly worse. Neither clearly dominates, so the guide estimates DML with both learners and checks that they agree (Rule B4).
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Why not just use LASSO to pick the controls?

The tempting shortcut is to run LASSO of growth on initial GDP and the 60 controls, keep what survives, and report OLS on the survivors. This single selection is biased: LASSO drops controls that predict growth only weakly, even if they are strongly related to initial GDP, and those are exactly the confounders that matter. Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014) show that one must also keep controls that predict the treatment . Their double selection is the simplest valid version of the DML idea: LASSO's penalty matters here. Cross-validation chooses a penalty for prediction and, with 90 observations, keeps most of the 60 controls. For selecting controls, Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen use a theory-based plug-in penalty, \(\lambda = 2c\,\hat\sigma\sqrt{n}\,\Phi^{-1}\!\big(1 - \gamma/(2p)\big)\) with \(c = 1.1\) and \(\gamma = 0.1/\log n\) , iterated on the residual variance. It keeps only controls whose signal is clearly above noise.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
Why not just use LASSO to pick the controls?

The result is a textbook illustration of the problem. LASSO of growth on the controls keeps none of them: no single control predicts growth strongly enough. Single selection therefore reduces to OLS without controls and finds no convergence. But several controls strongly predict initial GDP, and those are the confounders. Double selection keeps them and finds a clearly negative \(\theta\) , close to the \(-0.050\) (s.e. 0.016) that Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014) report with the same data.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

The DoubleML package (Bach et al. 2022) implements the estimator with cross-fitting and repeated sample splits. The learners are passed in as scikit-learn models: ml_l predicts the outcome and ml_m the treatment. With 90 observations, one random split into folds can matter, so the estimator is repeated over 10 different splits ( n_rep=10 ) and the median is reported, with a standard error that includes the variation across splits.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model
How much does the sample split matter?
The spread across splits is the price of a small sample. Report the median over many splits, never the result of one split chosen after the fact.
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

How to write it: method and results We estimate the effect of log initial GDP per capita on growth in the partially linear model \(\text{growth}_i = \theta \log \text{GDP}_{i,1965} + g(X_i) + \varepsilon_i\) , where \(X_i\) contains 60 country characteristics, using double machine learning (Chernozhukov et al. 2018). The nuisance functions are estimated with LASSO and, alternatively, with a random forest, using five-fold cross-fitting repeated over 10 random splits. Unconditionally there is no convergence ( \(\hat\theta = 0.001\) ), and OLS with all 60 controls is too imprecise to be informative (s.e. 0.032). Double machine learning gives \(\hat\theta \approx -0.04\) with both learners (s.e. about 0.015, p < 0.01), and the two learners agree within a fraction of a standard error. The estimate is close to post-double-selection LASSO with a plug-in penalty ( \(-0.042\) ), and to the \(-0.050\) reported by Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014): conditional on their steady-state determinants, poorer countries grew faster (Table X).
Double Machine Learning: Partially Linear Model

Checklist for the paper State the partially linear model and argue that the controls capture the confounders. Explain why OLS is not enough (many controls, or nonlinear controls). Report the learners, the number of folds and of repeated splits. Show DML with at least two learners, plus OLS and double selection as benchmarks. Report the variation across sample splits.
Elastic Net: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, strongly correlated predictors.

Can next quarter's U.S. inflation be forecast from the recent history of inflation, unemployment, interest rates, output and money? The file holds inflation and four lags of five series (20 predictors) for 198 quarters. The lags of each series are highly correlated with one another: inflation this quarter and last quarter move together. That is the setting for the elastic net (Zou and Hastie 2005), which combines the LASSO and ridge penalties: \(\alpha = 1\) gives LASSO and \(\alpha = 0\) ridge. In between, the ridge part makes correlated predictors share their weight, and the LASSO part still sets weak groups to zero. Both \(\lambda\) and \(\alpha\) are chosen by cross-validation.

Predictor group Columns Series Inflation infl_l1 … infl_l4 CPI inflation, annualised % Unemployment unemp_l1 … unemp_l4 Unemployment rate, % Interest rate tbilrate_l1 … tbilrate_l4 3-month Treasury bill rate, % Output gdp_growth_l1 … gdp_growth_l4 Real GDP growth, annualised % Money m1_growth_l1 … m1_growth_l4 M1 growth, annualised % Every predictor is dated before the quarter being forecast, so the model uses only information that was available at the time.
Load the data and test for unit roots

Machine learning does not remove the need to check stationarity. A model trained on a trending series learns the trend's past range: a random forest can never predict a value it has not seen, and a linear model on I(1) series risks a spurious fit. So each series is tested first, exactly as in the Time-Series Guide, and I(1) series are differenced. The T-bill rate has a unit root in levels (ADF does not reject, KPSS rejects stationarity) and is stationary after one difference; inflation, unemployment, GDP growth and money growth reject the unit root at 5 %. Following the selection tool, the four T-bill lags enter in first differences.
Load the data and test for unit roots
Several pairs of lags are correlated above 0.9, far above the 0.8 threshold: the elastic net's case.
Validate forward in time, never backward

Ordinary k-fold cross-validation shuffles the observations, so a model would be trained on 2005 and tested on 1975, using the future to predict the past. For time series, every validation fold must come after the data the model was trained on. TimeSeriesSplit does this: each split trains on an expanding window of the past and validates on the next block. The elastic net has the lowest rolling-origin error, LASSO is close, and the random forest is clearly worse: a nonlinear model does not help here (Rule A3), and with lags correlated above 0.8 the tool chooses the elastic net (Rule A4).
Grouped selection: elastic net against LASSO

Fit both on the full sample and compare which lags they keep. Within a group of correlated lags, LASSO tends to keep one or two and drop the rest; the elastic net, the more so the smaller its mixing weight α, spreads the weight. To see the effect, the table also shows an elastic net with α fixed at 0.3. Cross-validation chooses a mixing weight of α = 0.9, close to LASSO, so here the two give almost the same coefficients: the data prefer a mostly-LASSO penalty with a little ridge stabilisation. The α = 0.3 column shows what a stronger ridge component does: weight is spread across correlated lags (the third lag of inflation loses weight to the fourth, which almost triples) and one more lag ( unemp_l1 ) enters. Report the cross-validated α, and show that the main conclusions do not depend on it. In every version the first three lags of inflation dominate, followed by the T-bill rate and money growth.
A real forecasting test: recursive one-step-ahead forecasts

The honest test of a forecasting model is to simulate using it in real time. From 1990 onwards, each quarter the model is re-estimated on all data up to the previous quarter (penalty re-chosen each time) and forecasts the next quarter. The benchmark every forecasting paper must beat is a simple AR(4) model of inflation on its own four lags, estimated the same way. A ratio below 1 means the model beats the AR(4) benchmark. Here it does not : both penalised models forecast about 6 % worse than the AR(4) over 1990–2009. Whether a difference is statistically significant is tested with the Diebold–Mariano test on the loss differences (with a Newey–West variance, because forecast errors are serially correlated):

The difference is not significant (p ≈ 0.2): the twenty extra predictors neither help nor clearly hurt. This is a well-known result, not a failure of the method: since the mid-1980s, inflation has been hard to forecast with anything better than its own recent history (Atkeson and Ohanian 2001; Stock and Watson 2007). A paper must report it honestly. The elastic net is still the right tool for the question which lags carry information; the forecasting test says that, out of sample, the information beyond inflation's own lags is small. How to write it: method and results We forecast quarterly CPI inflation with an elastic net on four lags of inflation, unemployment, the change in the Treasury-bill rate (the level has a unit root), real GDP growth and M1 growth. Because lags of the same series are highly correlated (|r| up to 0.97), we prefer the elastic net to LASSO, which selects arbitrarily within correlated groups. Penalty and mixing weight are chosen by rolling-origin cross-validation, so that no model is ever validated on data earlier than its training sample. Cross-validation selects a mixing weight of 0.9, close to LASSO; the first three lags of inflation, the change in the T-bill rate and lagged money growth carry most of the weight. In recursive one-step-ahead forecasts over 1990Q1–2009Q3, re-estimating the model each quarter, the elastic net does not improve on an AR(4) benchmark: its RMSE is 2.67 percentage points against 2.52, and a Diebold–Mariano test with HAC variance does not reject equal accuracy (p = 0.18). Consistent with Atkeson and Ohanian (2001), the additional macroeconomic predictors contain little information about future inflation beyond its own history.

Checklist for the paper Test every series for a unit root and difference I(1) series before any learning. Date every predictor before the forecast target; never let future information in. Use rolling-origin (expanding-window) validation, not shuffled k-fold. Report the chosen mixing weight α and penalty λ, and which lags survive. Compare recursive out-of-sample forecasts with an AR benchmark; report the RMSE ratio and a Diebold–Mariano test.
Choosing a machine-learning method in economics: LASSO, ridge, random forest, XGBoost, double machine learning or causal forests, with step-by-step guides.

Nine routes to a finished paper
Each guide takes one real dataset through tuning, validation, diagnostics and writing, with Python code, real output and sample text for the paper.
Few controls that enter linearly With fewer than 10 controls and no sign of nonlinearity, OLS already adjusts for the confounders; report the DML estimate as a robustness check …

Selection on unobservables, no instrument Machine learning cannot fix confounding by variables you do not observe. Use a research design: difference-in-differences, synthetic control or regression discontinuity …
LASSO: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, few predictors matter.

The question is a practical one for any economics department: which student characteristics predict the final score in an introductory economics course? The file records fourteen candidate predictors for 814 students: study habits, grades, ACT scores, prior economics and calculus, attendance attitudes and family background. Some surely matter and many probably do not. Choosing among them by hand invites a specification search; LASSO makes the choice by a rule. LASSO (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator; Tibshirani 1996) estimates a linear model but adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients: The absolute-value penalty sets the coefficients of weak predictors to exactly zero , so LASSO selects variables while it estimates. The penalty weight \(\lambda\) controls how many survive: \(\lambda = 0\) gives OLS; a large \(\lambda\) drops everything.

Variable Definition Variable Definition score Course score, % (outcome) male 1 if male age Age in years calculus 1 if took calculus work Hours worked per week econhs 1 if took economics in high school study Hours studied per week attexc , attgood 1 if attendance rated excellent / good colgpa College GPA before the course fathcoll , mothcoll 1 if father / mother has a degree hsgpa High-school GPA acteng , actmth ACT English / maths score Prediction, not causation LASSO answers which variables help to predict the score . It does not say that studying more would raise a student's score: a selected variable may stand in for an omitted one, and a dropped variable may still have a causal effect that is small relative to the noise. If the question is causal, use double machine learning instead (see the DML guides).
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The selection tool's rules are met: there are more than 100 observations, the random forest does not beat LASSO out of sample (it is worse), so the relationship is treated as linear, and no two predictors are correlated above 0.8. The last check, sparsity, comes in Step 4. How to write it: data section The sample contains 814 students with complete records. The outcome is the course score (in per cent). Fourteen candidate predictors describe study effort, prior achievement, preparation in mathematics and economics, attitudes to attendance and family background. A random forest does not improve on a linear model in five-fold cross-validation, so we model the score as a linear function of the predictors and use LASSO to select among them.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The penalty treats every coefficient alike, so the predictors must be on the same scale: a coefficient on hours per week and one on a 0/1 dummy are otherwise not comparable. Standardise first (mean 0, standard deviation 1), inside the pipeline, so that each cross-validation fold is standardised with its own training data. \(\lambda\) is chosen by five-fold cross-validation. Two choices are standard (Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman 2009): \(\lambda_{\min}\) : the penalty with the lowest cross-validated error, the best for prediction ; \(\lambda_{1se}\) : the largest penalty whose error is within one standard error of the minimum, the more conservative choice for selection , because it keeps only predictors whose contribution is clearly above noise.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The error curve is flat near its minimum and rises steeply once the penalty starts to remove the strong predictors. The one-standard-error rule moves to the right along the flat part: a simpler model that predicts almost as well.

The coefficients are in units of the score per one standard deviation of each predictor, so their sizes can be compared directly. At \(\lambda_{1se}\) LASSO keeps fewer than half of the predictors: the problem is sparse, which is the condition for LASSO in the selection tool (Rule A4). College GPA and the ACT maths score carry most of the signal; high-school GPA, calculus, work hours and sex add smaller amounts. The coefficient path shows the whole story at once: as the penalty falls (to the right), predictors enter one by one.

A single LASSO fit can be fragile: with a slightly different sample a borderline predictor may enter or leave. A simple check is to refit LASSO on many bootstrap samples, with the same \(\lambda_{1se}\) , and count how often each predictor is kept (the idea behind stability selection ; Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010). Predictors kept in nearly every bootstrap sample are robust findings. Predictors kept about half the time are borderline: report them as such and do not build an argument on them. Reading the frequencies A common rule is to call a predictor stable if it is selected in at least 80 % of the resamples (Meinshausen and Bühlmann suggest thresholds between 60 % and 90 %). Below that, the evidence that it adds predictive power is weak, even if the full-sample fit keeps it.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

Cross-validation chose \(\lambda\) , so the cross-validated error at \(\lambda_{\min}\) is slightly optimistic. The honest test is nested cross-validation: an outer loop holds out each fold in turn, and the whole procedure, including the choice of \(\lambda\) , is run on the other four. LASSO predicts slightly better than OLS with all fourteen predictors (an RMSE of 10.18 against 10.26 points), while setting five of them to zero even at \(\lambda_{\min}\) ; both explain about 40 % of the variance out of sample, far better than predicting the mean. The forest is worse. When OLS and LASSO predict equally well, the advantage of LASSO is the interpretation : it shows which few predictors carry the signal.
Post-LASSO OLS, and why its p-values are not valid

A common next step is to re-estimate OLS on the predictors LASSO selected ( post-LASSO ; Belloni and Chernozhukov 2013). This removes the shrinkage bias in the kept coefficients and gives them their natural units. Do not report these p-values as tests The predictors were chosen because they fit well in this sample, so the usual standard errors are too small and the p-values too optimistic (the post-selection inference problem). Report post-LASSO coefficients as descriptions of the selected model. If you need a valid test of one variable's effect, use the double-selection or DML methods in the causal guides, which are designed for exactly that.

How to write it: results We select predictors of the course score with LASSO, choosing the penalty by five-fold cross-validation and using the one-standard-error rule for selection. Of the fourteen candidate predictors, LASSO keeps six (Table X): college GPA and the ACT mathematics score are the strongest, followed by high-school GPA, a calculus background, hours of paid work (negative) and sex. College GPA and the ACT mathematics score are selected in every one of 200 bootstrap resamples and calculus in 97 %; high-school GPA and work hours in about 80 %, and sex in only 55 %, so we treat sex as a borderline predictor. In nested cross-validation, LASSO predicts the score with an RMSE of 10.2 points (out-of-sample R² of 0.42), slightly better than OLS with all fourteen predictors and far better than the sample mean (13.3 points); a random forest does not improve on it. Because the predictors were chosen on the same data, we report the post-LASSO coefficients as descriptive and do not interpret their p-values as tests.

Checklist for the paper State the aim (prediction or selection) and why a penalised model is used. Report how λ was chosen (CV folds, λ min or λ 1se) and that predictors were standardised. Show the selected predictors, the coefficient path, and the selection frequencies. Report out-of-sample accuracy against OLS and a mean-only benchmark (nested CV). Do not give causal readings or post-selection p-values.
Random Forest: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Nonlinear, fewer than 1,000 observations.

How well can a baseball player's salary be predicted from his career record? The file holds the 1993 salaries of 353 Major League Baseball players and fifteen career statistics: years in the league, games, at-bats, runs, hits, home runs, runs batted in, batting average, walks, strikeouts, stolen bases, fielding percentage, all-star seasons and race. Salaries are not linear in performance: rookies are paid little whatever they do, salaries jump once players can bargain, and stars are paid far more than a linear model would suggest. A random forest (Breiman 2001) averages many regression trees. Each tree is grown on a bootstrap sample of the players, and at every split it may choose only from a random subset of the predictors. A single deep tree fits the sample closely but is very unstable; averaging hundreds of decorrelated trees keeps the flexibility and removes most of the instability:

What a forest can and cannot do A forest captures thresholds, curvature and interactions without being told about them. It cannot extrapolate: a forest never predicts a value outside the range of the outcomes it was trained on. And it gives no coefficients; Steps 6 and 7 show how to describe what it has learned.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The forest's error is far below LASSO's, much more than the 5 % threshold (Rule A3): salaries are strongly nonlinear in the career record. With only 353 players, below 1,000, the selection tool chooses a random forest over gradient boosting (Rule A5). How to write it: data section The sample contains 353 Major League Baseball players with 1993 salaries and career statistics. The outcome is the log salary. In five-fold cross-validation a random forest predicts log salaries with an error about 28 % lower than LASSO, indicating strong nonlinearities and interactions between career statistics and pay; given the modest sample, we use a random forest rather than a boosted model, which has more tuning parameters to overfit.
Grow the forest: how many trees?

More trees never overfit: they only reduce the variance of the average. The question is how many are needed before the error stops falling. The out-of-bag (OOB) error answers it for free: each player is left out of about a third of the bootstrap samples, and the trees that did not see him predict his salary. The error is essentially flat beyond a few hundred trees. Use 500: cheap, and safely on the flat part.
Tune the two parameters that matter

Two parameters control how flexible each tree is: min_samples_leaf : the smallest number of players in a final leaf. Larger leaves make smoother, less variable predictions. max_features : the share of predictors each split may consider. Smaller values decorrelate the trees more. The surface is flat near the optimum: forests are forgiving, and any setting in the low-error region gives similar predictions. Report the chosen values and the grid.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

The tuning above used the same folds that measured the error, which flatters the winner. Nested cross-validation repeats the tuning inside each outer fold. The forest explains a much larger share of the out-of-sample variance than OLS or LASSO. That gap is what justifies its loss of interpretability.

The forest has no coefficients. Permutation importance measures how much the held-out error rises when one predictor's values are shuffled, breaking its link with salary while leaving everything else intact. Compute it on a test set the forest did not see; the impurity-based importance that scikit-learn reports by default is computed on the training data and favours predictors with many distinct values. Correlated predictors share their importance At-bats, hits, runs and runs batted in are almost the same variable (correlations above 0.95). When one is shuffled, the forest still learns from the others, so each looks less important than the group is. Read the importances by group, or shuffle a correlated group together, before concluding that a statistic does not matter.
How do the key predictors affect salary? Partial dependence

A partial-dependence plot shows the average prediction as one predictor is varied over its range, with the others held at their observed values. It is the forest's answer to "what is the coefficient?", but it can bend. The curves are far from straight lines: salary rises steeply over the first years of a career and then flattens, which is the nonlinearity a linear model misses and the reason the forest predicts so much better.

How to write it: results We predict the log salary with a random forest of 500 trees, tuning the minimum leaf size and the share of predictors considered at each split by five-fold cross-validation. In nested cross-validation the forest's out-of-sample error is far below that of OLS and LASSO, and it explains a substantially larger share of the variance (Table X). Permutation importance on a held-out sample shows that years in the league and cumulative career output (at-bats, runs batted in, hits) dominate the predictions. Partial-dependence plots show that predicted salaries rise steeply over the first years of a career and then level off, a nonlinearity that linear models cannot capture.

Checklist for the paper Show why a nonlinear model is needed (forest vs LASSO, cross-validated). Report the number of trees, the tuned parameters and the tuning grid. Report nested out-of-sample accuracy against OLS, LASSO and the mean. Use permutation importance on held-out data, and read correlated predictors as a group. Show partial-dependence plots for the main predictors; do not call them causal effects.
Ridge Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Linear, many small effects.

How well can a man's wage be predicted from his ability, schooling, experience and background? The Blackburn–Neumark data, used throughout Wooldridge's textbook, record 15 candidate predictors for 663 men with complete data: two test scores (IQ and the Knowledge of the World of Work test), schooling, experience, tenure, age, marital status, race, region, urban residence, siblings, birth order and both parents' education. Unlike the exam-score example in the LASSO guide, nearly all of these plausibly matter a little. That is the setting for ridge. Ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard 1970) adds a squared penalty to the least-squares objective: The squared penalty pulls every coefficient towards zero but, unlike the LASSO penalty, never sets one exactly to zero. It trades a little bias for a large reduction in variance, and it has a closed-form solution: \(\hat\beta = (X'X + \lambda I)^{-1}X'y\) .

Variable Definition Variable Definition lwage Log monthly wage (outcome) married 1 if married hours Average weekly hours black 1 if black IQ IQ score south , urban 1 if in the South / an SMSA KWW Knowledge of world of work score sibs Number of siblings educ Years of schooling brthord Birth order exper , tenure Years of experience / with employer meduc , feduc Mother's / father's schooling age Age in years When is ridge the right choice? When the true model is dense (many predictors with small effects), LASSO's habit of setting coefficients to zero throws away real signal, and ridge predicts better. When it is sparse (a few strong effects), LASSO wins. The selection tool decides with the share of predictors LASSO keeps at the one-standard-error penalty: half or more means dense, so ridge.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

All three conditions for ridge hold: the forest does not beat the linear model, no correlation exceeds 0.8, and LASSO keeps well over half of the predictors even at its conservative penalty. The signal is spread across many variables. How to write it: data section The sample contains 663 men with complete records from the Blackburn–Neumark extract of the National Longitudinal Survey. The outcome is the log monthly wage in 1980. Fifteen predictors describe measured ability, schooling, labour-market experience, demographics and family background. A random forest does not improve on a linear model in five-fold cross-validation, and a LASSO fit retains most predictors, indicating many small effects; we therefore use ridge regression.
Standardise, then choose the penalty by cross-validation

The penalty acts on the size of the coefficients, so the predictors must be on a common scale; standardise them inside the pipeline. Then search a grid of \(\lambda\) values. For ridge, leave-one-out cross-validation has a closed form and is almost free ( RidgeCV uses it by default), but five-fold CV is shown here to match the other guides. The error curve is shallow: moderate shrinkage helps a little, and only very large penalties (which shrink everything towards zero) hurt. That is typical of a dense, well-measured problem: ridge improves on OLS at the margin rather than dramatically.
How much does ridge shrink each coefficient?

Coefficients are per standard deviation of each predictor. Ridge keeps every predictor and shrinks the vector of coefficients as a whole; most individual estimates move towards zero (siblings by a third, experience by a fifth), but a few correlated ones grow slightly (the KWW score, age, father's education), because ridge spreads weight across predictors that carry overlapping information. The ridge path shows how all coefficients move smoothly towards zero as the penalty grows, without any of them hitting zero:

Ridge does not drop variables, so "number of predictors" no longer measures model complexity. The effective degrees of freedom do: with \(d_j\) the singular values of the standardised \(X\) , which equals \(p\) at \(\lambda = 0\) (OLS) and falls towards 0 as \(\lambda\) grows. Report this number: it tells the reader how much the penalty actually constrained the model.
Accuracy on data the model has not seen

Choosing \(\lambda\) on the same folds that measure the error flatters the model. Nested cross-validation repeats the whole procedure, including the choice of \(\lambda\) , inside each outer fold. The differences between the three linear models are small relative to their variation across folds: with 663 observations and 15 predictors, OLS is not badly overfitted, and ridge's gain is modest. That is an honest and common finding. Ridge earns its place when \(p\) is large relative to \(n\) or when predictors are noisy; report the comparison either way.

How to write it: results We predict the log wage with ridge regression on fifteen standardised predictors, choosing the penalty by five-fold cross-validation. Because LASSO retains most predictors even at its one-standard-error penalty, the signal appears to be spread across many variables, the setting in which ridge's proportional shrinkage is preferable to variable selection. The largest standardised coefficients belong to urban residence, schooling, marital status, IQ and weekly hours (negative), followed by experience and tenure (Table X); race and the South enter negatively. The chosen penalty (λ = 73) reduces the effective degrees of freedom from 15 to 13. In nested cross-validation ridge has the lowest error of the models compared (RMSE 0.357 against 0.358 for OLS and 0.359 for LASSO), although the differences are small relative to their variation across folds; all three explain about a quarter of the out-of-sample variance, and a random forest does not improve on them.

Checklist for the paper Explain why the problem is dense (LASSO keeps most predictors) and why ridge is used. State the standardisation, the λ grid and the CV scheme; report λ and the effective degrees of freedom. Show OLS and ridge coefficients side by side, and the ridge path. Report nested out-of-sample accuracy against OLS, LASSO and a mean-only benchmark. Ridge coefficients are shrunk on purpose: do not attach OLS-style standard errors to them.
Gradient Boosting (XGBoost): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How long will an injured worker stay out of work? Workers' compensation insurers and labour economists both want to know. The file covers 6,822 workers injured in Kentucky and Michigan around benefit increases studied by Meyer, Viscusi and Durbin (1995). The outcome is the log number of weeks on temporary disability benefits; the eighteen predictors describe the worker (age, sex, marital status, previous earnings), the injury (medical costs, hospitalisation, body part, occupational disease), the industry, the state, and whether the injury happened after the benefit increase. Durations depend on these in strongly nonlinear ways: medical costs matter a great deal up to a point, and the type of injury changes how much.

Gradient boosting (Friedman 2001) builds trees one after another. Each new tree is fitted to the errors that the current model still makes and is added with a small weight \(\eta\) , the learning rate: A random forest averages many independent deep trees; boosting adds many small dependent ones, each correcting the last. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016) adds penalties on tree size and leaf weights, and is the standard implementation in applied work. Variable Definition Variable Definition ldurat Log weeks on benefits (outcome) ltotmed Log total medical costs afchnge 1 if injured after the benefit increase hosp 1 if hospitalised highearn 1 if earnings above the benefit cap head … lowextr

Body part injured (dummies) lprewage Log weekly wage before the injury occdis 1 if occupational disease age , male , married Worker characteristics manuf , construc Industry dummies ky 1 if Kentucky (0 = Michigan)
Load the data and confirm the starting point

The forest beats LASSO by more than the 5 % threshold (Rule A3), so the relationship is nonlinear, and with almost 7,000 workers there is enough data to tune a boosted model (Rule A5). Validation must respect the structure of the data Here every row is a different worker, so ordinary shuffled folds are fine. If the same unit appears several times (a firm over years, a route in several years), keep all of its rows in the same fold ( GroupKFold ); otherwise the model memorises units and looks better than it is. With time series, validate forward in time only (see the Elastic net guide). The nonlinearity test is only as honest as its folds: on panel data, shuffled folds can make a forest look far better than it is.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

How to write it: data section The sample contains 6,822 workers injured in Kentucky and Michigan (Meyer, Viscusi and Durbin 1995). The outcome is the log number of weeks on temporary disability benefits; eighteen predictors describe the worker, the injury, the industry, the state and the timing of the injury relative to a benefit increase. In five-fold cross-validation a random forest predicts log durations with an error about 8 % lower than LASSO, so we model durations with gradient-boosted trees.
The parameters that matter, and early stopping

Boosting has more tuning parameters than a forest, and unlike a forest it can overfit if it runs too long. The ones that matter most: learning rate \(\eta\) : smaller is better but needs more trees; 0.03 to 0.1 is usual; number of trees : chosen by early stopping , i.e. stop adding trees when the error on a validation set has not improved for a while; max_depth : the depth of each tree, which sets how many variables can interact; min_child_weight , subsample , colsample_bytree : regularisation, as in a forest. The training error keeps falling as trees are added; the validation error falls, flattens and then creeps up as the model starts to fit noise. Early stopping picks the number of trees at the bottom of the validation curve.
Trees of depth 3 do best: durations depend on interactions between a few variables at a time, not on deep combinations, and depth 6 overfits. The minimum leaf weight hardly matters.
A fair comparison with the alternatives
Nested cross-validation: the boosted model is tuned inside each outer training sample, then scored on the held-out fold.
Open the black box: SHAP values

SHAP values (Lundberg and Lee 2017) split each prediction into additive contributions from each predictor, measured from the average prediction. XGBoost computes them exactly for trees ( pred_contribs=True ).

Medical costs do almost all the work: predicted durations are flat for the cheapest injuries (log costs below about 4.5, roughly $90) and then rise steeply. Age and the previous wage shift predictions far less. These are predictive patterns, not causal effects. The benefit increase ( afchnge ), for example, is the treatment in the original study; its causal effect needs a difference-in-differences design (see the Causal Inference Guide), not a prediction model.

How to write it: results We predict log benefit durations with gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost) with a learning rate of 0.03, choosing the number of trees by early stopping and the tree depth and minimum leaf weight by five-fold cross-validation. In nested cross-validation the boosted model has the lowest out-of-sample error of the models compared: it explains 44 % of the out-of-sample variance, against 43 % for a random forest and 31 % for OLS and LASSO (Table X). SHAP values show that medical costs dominate the predictions (a mean absolute contribution of 0.64 log weeks, ten times that of the next predictor, age), followed by head injuries, the previous wage, industry and hospitalisation. The partial-dependence plot for medical costs is flat for the cheapest injuries and then rises steeply and almost linearly in log costs, a threshold that a linear model misses; age and the previous wage matter much less. We interpret these patterns as predictive, not causal.

Checklist for the paper Build validation folds that respect the data's structure (groups, time). Report the learning rate, early stopping and the tuned depth and regularisation. Compare with a random forest and with linear models in nested cross-validation. Interpret with SHAP values and partial dependence, and say that the patterns are predictive.

Cross-Sectionally Augmented ARDL: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is the same as in the PMG guide: what are the long-run price and income elasticities of cigarette demand? This time the data are used as they are. Cigarette consumption in every state was driven by national forces: the 1964 Surgeon General's report, advertising bans, changing social norms, federal excise taxes. These common factors affect states to different degrees, and they are correlated with prices and incomes. A model that ignores them confuses the national anti-smoking trend with the effect of price. For each state \(i\) , CS-ARDL(1,1) estimates where \(x = (p, y)\) are the log real price and log real income, and \(\bar z_t\) are the cross-sectional averages of \(c\) and \(x\) in year \(t\) , with \(p_T\) lags. Each state's long-run effect is \(\theta_i = (\beta_{0i} + \beta_{1i}) / (1 - \lambda_i)\) , and the estimate reported is the mean group average of the \(\theta_i\) .

The neighbours' price used in the PMG guide is left out here. It moves almost one-for-one with the state's own real price, and once the cross-sectional averages absorb the national component, the two can no longer be separated in 29 annual observations per state: with both included, the state-level long-run estimates become erratic. With CS-ARDL, keep the model small. Why the cross-sectional averages work If the errors contain unobserved common factors \(f_t\) with state-specific loadings, the cross-sectional averages of the observed variables are (as N grows) a linear combination of those factors. Adding them, and their lags, to each state's regression with state-specific coefficients controls for the factors without having to name or measure them. Because every state gets its own coefficients on the averages, states can respond to the common shocks to different degrees, which year dummies cannot do.

How to write it: model section We estimate state-specific ARDL(1,1) models of cigarette demand augmented with the contemporaneous and lagged cross-sectional averages of all variables, following Chudik et al. (2016). The averages proxy unobserved common factors, such as national anti-smoking campaigns and federal tax changes, to which states may respond heterogeneously. Long-run elasticities are computed for each state and averaged across states (mean group).
Load the data and run the pre-tests

How to read it Cross-sectional dependence is overwhelming: CD statistics above 100 and average absolute correlations between states of 0.7 to 0.9. The states are driven by national forces. Unit roots (CIPS). Sales and income are I(1); the real price rejects a unit root in levels and is I(0). A mix of I(0) and I(1), none I(2): the ARDL family applies. Slopes are heterogeneous. Mixed integration orders and strong cross-sectional dependence: this is the combination for which the model selection tool recommends CS-ARDL. It is the result the tool gives for this example dataset.
What goes wrong if the common factors are ignored

How to read it PMG and MG on the raw data assume independent states. The CD test on the PMG residuals shows that the assumption fails badly: the residuals are strongly correlated across states. With common factors in the errors that are also correlated with the regressors, these long-run estimates are biased. The clearest symptom is income: real incomes rose everywhere while smoking fell everywhere for reasons unrelated to income (health information, social norms), so the national trend cancels the income effect in PMG and turns it negative in MG. The PMG guide deals with this by demeaning; CS-ARDL deals with it inside the model.

How to read it Price. Once the common factors are absorbed, the long-run price elasticity is about −0.9: a 10% rise in the real price lowers sales by about 9% in the long run. The estimate is close to the PMG estimate on demeaned data (−0.77), which used a different way of dealing with the same common shocks. Two methods agreeing is strong evidence. Income. Positive and significant, about 0.6: cigarettes are a normal good once the national anti-smoking trend is no longer confounded with rising incomes. Adjustment. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant: each state's consumption returns towards its long-run relationship. Adjustment is faster than in PMG on demeaned data, because the averages also absorb slow-moving national trends.
Standard errors are mean-group standard errors, from the dispersion of the 46 state estimates. They are valid whatever the heterogeneity across states.
Test 1: are the common factors removed?

How to read it The CD statistic falls from the very large value of the raw PMG residuals to a small one: the cross-sectional averages have absorbed the common factors. Report this test; it is the evidence that the augmentation did its job. A remaining small, insignificant or weakly significant CD statistic is normal, since the averages approximate the factors only up to an error that shrinks with N.
Robustness: the number of lags of the averages

How to read it Chudik et al. recommend about \(T^{1/3}\) lags of the averages, which is 3 here. But each state regression has only 29 observations, and every lag adds four regressors, so with this many variables the number of lags must stay small. Show that the results do not depend on the choice: here the long-run price elasticity stays between −0.73 and −0.88 and the income elasticity between 0.51 and 0.61. The results are robust to the lag length.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Put the estimators that ignore the common factors next to CS-ARDL, with the residual CD test in the table, so the reader sees both the bias and its correction. Column (3) is the preferred estimate. Cite the PMG-on-demeaned-data estimate as a second robustness check.

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator All variables exhibit strong cross-sectional dependence (Pesaran CD tests), reflecting national anti-smoking trends and federal policy. CIPS tests indicate a mixture of I(0) and I(1) variables, and the Pesaran–Yamagata test rejects slope homogeneity. Because estimators that assume cross-sectional independence would be biased, and because states may respond differently to common shocks, we estimate the long-run elasticities with the cross-sectionally augmented ARDL (CS-ARDL) approach of Chudik et al. (2016). How to write it: results The mean group long-run price elasticity is about −0.9 and the income elasticity about 0.6 (Table 6, column 3). The price elasticity is close to the estimate from a pooled mean group model on cross-sectionally demeaned data, and both are robust to the number of lags of the cross-sectional averages. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant, confirming adjustment towards a long-run relationship. The CD test on the CS-ARDL residuals indicates that the cross-sectional averages successfully absorb the common factors, in contrast with PMG and MG estimates on the raw data, whose residuals remain strongly dependent.

Common mistakes Adding too many lags of the averages relative to T. Each lag costs one regressor per variable in every unit regression. Using CS-ARDL with small N. The averages approximate the common factors only as N grows; with fewer than about 15 units they are poor proxies. Reporting the long run without the residual CD test, which is the evidence that the method worked. Forgetting that the mean group long run is an average of unit-specific ratios: a few units with \(\lambda_i\) close to 1 produce extreme \(\theta_i\) . Check the distribution, and report the median as well.
Panel Model in First Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question: how does gasoline demand respond to income and to the price of gasoline? The dataset is the one Baltagi and Griffin used to compare panel estimators of gasoline demand across OECD countries, before and during the oil shocks of the 1970s. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(\ln G_{it}\) lgaspcar Log gasoline consumption per car dependent variable \(\ln Y_{it}\) lincomep Log real income per capita positive: income elasticity \(\ln P_{it}\) lrpmg Log real price of gasoline negative: price elasticity \(\ln C_{it}\) lcarpcap Log cars per capita negative: more cars, each driven less In first differences, the coefficients are short-run elasticities : how much gasoline use per car changes in the year that income or the price changes.

Why differences, and what you give up If the variables are I(1) and cointegrated, a long-run relationship in levels exists and an error-correction model (the PMG or CS-ARDL guides) estimates it. If they are I(1) and not cointegrated, there is no long-run relationship to estimate: a regression in levels would be spurious, and the valid model is in differences. You give up the long-run elasticities, which is why the cointegration tests deserve care. How to write it: model section We relate the growth of gasoline consumption per car to the growth of real income per capita, the real price of gasoline and the stock of cars per capita, \(\Delta \ln G_{it} = \beta_1 \Delta \ln Y_{it} + \beta_2 \Delta \ln P_{it} + \beta_3 \Delta \ln C_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) . The coefficients are short-run elasticities.
Load the panel and run the pre-tests

How to read it Cross-sectional dependence is strong for every variable (the oil shocks hit every country), so CIPS is the unit-root test to use. Unit roots. CIPS does not reject a unit root in levels for any variable, and rejects it in first differences for all of them: all four are I(1) . Slopes are heterogeneous: the Δ test rejects. This will matter for the choice of cointegration test and of estimator.

How to read it In levels, fixed effects gives large, highly significant elasticities and a high within R-squared. This is exactly what a spurious regression looks like. With I(1) variables, the t-statistics do not follow the t distribution, and trending series appear related whether or not they are. These numbers are only meaningful if the variables are cointegrated, which is the next test.

How to read it The null hypothesis of both tests is no cointegration . Kao pools the fixed-effects residuals and assumes the same slopes in every country. It rejects narrowly, at the 5% level. Fisher–Engle–Granger runs an Engle–Granger test for each country, with its own slopes, and combines the p-values. Its Z version does not reject (p = 0.25); its P version comes close only at the 10% level. The tests disagree, and the pre-tests tell us which to believe: the slopes are heterogeneous , which violates Kao's assumption. A Kao test applied to heterogeneous panels can reject spuriously, because the pooled residuals mix different long-run relationships. The model selection tool therefore uses the heterogeneous test here, and concludes that there is no cointegration.

This is a close call, and the paper must say so: report both tests, and add the Westerlund (2007) error-correction tests with bootstrap critical values, which allow for both heterogeneity and cross-sectional dependence ( xtwest in Stata). With T = 19, every panel cointegration test has limited power.
Estimate the model in first differences

How to read it Differencing removes the country fixed effects (permanent differences in levels), so the pooled regression on differences needs no country dummies. Compare the elasticities with the spurious levels regression: the income and price responses are much smaller in differences , as one would expect when drivers can adjust only gradually. (The cars coefficient is similar, because the stock of cars and fuel use per car are linked almost mechanically in every year.) Price. A 10% rise in the real price of gasoline reduces consumption per car by roughly 1–3% within the year, depending on the estimator. Income. The short-run income elasticity is positive. Cars per capita. More cars means each car is driven less, so consumption per car falls.
Estimate the model in first differences

With heterogeneous slopes and cross-sectional dependence, CCE-MG is the preferred estimator : it averages the country-specific elasticities and removes the common factors (the oil shocks) through the cross-sectional averages. Its standard errors are larger, because they reflect the cross-country dispersion of the elasticities.

How to read it The pooled regression in differences leaves strong common shocks in the residuals. In the CCE-MG residuals the CD statistic is close to zero and no longer significant: the cross-sectional averages absorb the common oil-price and business-cycle shocks.
Build the results table for the paper
How to read it Including the levels regression in column (1) shows the reader the spurious result the paper avoids. Column (4) is the preferred estimate.

How to write it: pre-tests CIPS tests, which allow for the strong cross-sectional dependence indicated by the CD test, do not reject a unit root in levels for any variable but reject it in first differences. Because the Pesaran–Yamagata test rejects slope homogeneity, we test for cointegration with the Fisher-type combination of country-level Engle–Granger tests, which allows the long-run coefficients to differ across countries; it does not reject the null of no cointegration. The Kao test, which assumes homogeneous slopes, rejects at the 5 percent level. Given the heterogeneity of slopes, we treat the evidence for cointegration as weak and estimate the model in first differences. How to write it: results

Table 4 reports short-run elasticities. In the common correlated effects mean group model (column 4), gasoline consumption per car rises with income and falls with the real price and with the number of cars per capita. The short-run income and price elasticities are much smaller than the coefficients of the levels regression in column 1, which, given the absence of cointegration, should not be interpreted. Common mistakes Running a levels regression on I(1) variables without testing for cointegration, and interpreting the t-statistics. Choosing the cointegration test that gives the desired answer. Choose it from the pre-tests (homogeneous or heterogeneous slopes, dependence or not), and report the others. Calling short-run elasticities from a model in differences “long-run” effects.
Ignoring cross-sectional dependence in the differenced model. Common shocks remain after differencing.
Fixed Effects: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Unit effects correlated with the regressors.

The question is a classic of labour economics: do union members earn more than comparable non-members? A cross-section cannot answer it, because workers who join unions may differ in ability, motivation or occupation in ways the data do not record. A panel that follows the same workers over time can: it compares each worker with himself, in years with and without union membership. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(\ln w_{it}\) lwage Log hourly wage dependent variable \(union_{it}\) union 1 if wage set by a union contract positive: the union wage premium \(married_{it}\) married 1 if married positive: the marriage premium \(exper^2_{it}\) expersq Years of experience, squared negative: wage growth slows with experience

\(\alpha_i\) — Worker fixed effect: ability, motivation, occupation unobserved \(\lambda_t\) — Year effect: inflation, the business cycle common to all workers Experience itself is not in the model. Every worker gains exactly one year of experience per year, so with worker and year effects the level of experience is perfectly collinear and cannot be estimated. Its square still varies within workers. Before you estimate anything Write down what the fixed effect \(\alpha_i\) stands for in your application and why it may be correlated with the regressor of interest. Here: more able workers may be less likely to join a union and also earn more. If that is true, pooled OLS mixes the union effect with the ability effect, and only the within-worker comparison isolates it. That argument is the reason for using fixed effects, and the paper must make it.

How to write it: model section We estimate \(\ln w_{it} = \beta_1 union_{it} + \beta_2 married_{it} + \beta_3 exper^2_{it} + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}\) , where \(\alpha_i\) is a worker fixed effect and \(\lambda_t\) a year effect. The worker effect absorbs all time-invariant characteristics, including unobserved ability, which may be correlated with union status. The union premium \(\beta_1\) is therefore identified from workers who change union status during the sample.
Load the panel and confirm the starting point

How to read it The panel is balanced and short : 545 workers, each observed in all 8 years. With so few periods, unit-root tests are not the issue; the question is how to treat the worker effects. The model selection tool ran that sequence on this file and recommended fixed effects (the F, LM and Mundlak tests are repeated below). The within standard deviations matter most. Union status has a within standard deviation of about 0.28: plenty of workers move in and out of union jobs, and the line below shows how many. Those switchers identify the fixed-effects estimate. Education has a within standard deviation of zero: it never changes for these men, so fixed effects cannot estimate its return.

How to read it Pooled OLS treats the 4,360 rows as if they were 4,360 different people. It puts the union premium at about 18%. This estimate uses both the comparison across workers (union members against non-members) and the comparison over time, so if union members differ in unobserved ways, the premium is biased. Even in pooled OLS, the standard errors must be clustered by worker : the same man appears eight times, and his errors are correlated across years. Unclustered standard errors would be far too small.

How to read it Union. Comparing the same worker in union and non-union years, union membership raises the wage by about 8%. That is less than half the pooled OLS premium: much of the cross-sectional premium reflects who joins unions, not what unions pay. Married. The marriage premium falls from about 15% in pooled OLS to about 5%, significant only at the 5% level. Much of the cross-sectional marriage premium is a selection effect. Experience squared. Negative and highly significant: wage growth slows with experience. Standard errors. Clustered by worker, which allows for any pattern of heteroskedasticity and serial correlation within each worker. This is the standard choice for a short panel with many units.
The constant reported by PanelOLS is the average of the fixed effects and has no economic meaning.
Test 1: do the workers differ? The F test

How to read it The null hypothesis is that every worker has the same intercept, in which case pooled OLS would be enough. The F statistic is large and the p-value is essentially zero: the worker effects are jointly significant , so ignoring them is not an option. The remaining question is whether to treat them as fixed or random.
Test 2: fixed or random? Hausman and Mundlak

How to read it Random effects is more efficient than fixed effects, but only consistent if the worker effects are uncorrelated with union status, marriage and experience. Hausman test. It compares the FE and RE coefficients. Under the null both are consistent and differ only by sampling error. Here the gap is large and the test rejects strongly. Mundlak test. It adds each worker's average union status, marriage rate and squared experience to the RE model. If the worker effect is correlated with the regressors, those averages pick it up. The test uses clustered standard errors, so unlike the conventional Hausman test it remains valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation. It also rejects.
Test 2: fixed or random? Hausman and Mundlak

A useful check. In the Mundlak model, the coefficient on union is identical to the fixed-effects estimate. This is an exact algebraic result, and it is why the Mundlak model is also called correlated random effects. Conclusion: random effects is rejected, and fixed effects is the estimator to report.
Diagnostic tests: serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence

How to read it Serial correlation. The Wooldridge test rejects: the errors of the same worker are correlated over time, as they almost always are in wage data. This does not bias the FE coefficients, but it invalidates conventional standard errors. Clustering by worker already corrects for it , which is why the clustered standard errors are the ones to report. Cross-sectional dependence. With T = 8, the residual correlation between any two workers rests on eight observations and is very noisy, so a mean absolute correlation of this size is what pure noise would produce. The average signed correlation is close to zero: once year effects are included, there is no common shock left. Year effects are the standard way to deal with common shocks in short micro panels.

How to read it First differences is the other estimator that removes the worker effect. It compares adjacent years only, so it is more sensitive to measurement error in union status: a misreported switch in one year looks like two genuine switches. The FD premium is smaller, which is the usual sign of measurement error in a binary regressor. Report it, and explain the difference. Correlated random effects adds the worker averages of the time-varying regressors. Its union and marriage coefficients equal the fixed-effects ones, but it can also estimate the effect of time-invariant variables such as education and race. This is the answer when a referee asks for the return to education in a fixed-effects paper.
The ranking pooled > RE > FE for the union premium is exactly what positive selection on unobserved ability predicts.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it A panel results table shows the main estimator next to the benchmarks, so the reader can see how much the unit effects matter. Report under the table: the number of workers and years, that standard errors are clustered by worker, that all columns include year effects (except where they are differenced away), and the F, Hausman and Mundlak statistics. Column (3) is the preferred estimate.

How to write it: specification tests An F test rejects the hypothesis that the worker effects are jointly zero, so pooled OLS is inappropriate. A Hausman test rejects the consistency of random effects, and a cluster-robust Mundlak test, which remains valid under heteroskedasticity and serial correlation, leads to the same conclusion. We therefore estimate the model by fixed effects with worker and year effects, and cluster standard errors by worker; a Wooldridge test confirms serial correlation within workers. How to write it: results Table 1 reports the estimates. Pooled OLS puts the union wage premium at about 18 percent (column 1). Once time-invariant worker characteristics are controlled for, the premium falls to about 8 percent (column 3), and it remains significant at the 1 percent level. The decline is consistent with workers of higher unobserved ability being less likely to hold union jobs. The first-difference estimate is smaller (column 4), as expected if union status is measured with error.

Common mistakes Reporting unclustered standard errors. In a panel they are almost always too small. Including a regressor that moves one-for-one with time (age, experience) together with year effects. It is collinear and either drops out or gives a meaningless coefficient. Claiming the FE coefficient on a variable that never changes. It is not identified; use correlated random effects instead. Treating fixed effects as a cure for all endogeneity. It removes time-invariant confounders only. If union status responds to wage shocks in the same year, FE is still biased, and you need an instrument or a dynamic model. Using only the conventional Hausman test. Report the robust Mundlak version as well.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

The question: in the OECD economies of 1967–1990, how was output growth related to unemployment and to changes in trade openness? Macro panels like this one, a few dozen countries over a few decades, are typical of empirical papers in international and environmental economics. Their defining feature is that the countries share the same shocks: the oil crises of 1973 and 1979 and the recessions that followed hit all of them at once. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(g_{it}\) gdp_growth Real GDP growth, % dependent variable \(u_{it}\) unem Unemployment rate, % negative: slack and low growth go together (Okun's law) \(\Delta open_{it}\) d_trade Change in trade (exports + imports) as % of GDP
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

positive if openness raises growth \(\alpha_i\) — Country fixed effect permanent differences in growth Before you estimate anything In a macro panel, three properties decide the estimator, and each needs a test: cross-sectional dependence (do the countries share shocks?), stationarity (do the variables have unit roots?) and slope homogeneity (is \(\beta\) the same in every country?). The next three steps run them. Fixed effects with Driscoll–Kraay errors is the answer when the variables are stationary and the slopes are homogeneous. How to write it: model section We estimate \(g_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_1 u_{it} + \beta_2 \Delta open_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) for 14 OECD countries over 1967–1990, where \(g_{it}\) is real GDP growth, \(u_{it}\) the unemployment rate and \(\Delta open_{it}\) the change in trade openness, and \(\alpha_i\) are country fixed effects.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Load the panel and test for cross-sectional dependence

How to read it A balanced panel of 14 countries over 24 years. The Pesaran CD test rejects cross-sectional independence for every variable, decisively. The average absolute correlation between two countries' growth rates is about 0.45: the OECD economies move together . Two consequences follow. Unit-root tests must allow for this (CIPS rather than Fisher-ADF), and standard errors that treat countries as independent will be too small.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to read it Stationarity. Because the variables are cross-sectionally dependent, CIPS is the test to use. It rejects a unit root in levels for all three: every variable is I(0) . Notice that for unemployment the first-generation Fisher test does not reject. It ignores the common shocks, and the two tests disagree; CIPS is the valid one here. Slope homogeneity. The adjusted Δ test does not reject: there is no evidence that the effects of unemployment and openness differ across countries. Pooling the slopes is defensible. These are the conditions under which the model selection tool recommends fixed effects with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Estimate fixed effects with three kinds of standard errors

How to read it The coefficients are the same in every column; only the standard errors differ. Unemployment. A one-point higher unemployment rate goes with growth about a third of a point lower. Significant under every choice of standard errors. Trade openness. With conventional or clustered standard errors, the negative coefficient looks significant. With Driscoll–Kraay standard errors it is not. Clustering by country allows for correlation over time within a country, but still treats countries as independent of each other. Driscoll–Kraay standard errors also allow for correlation across countries in the same year , which the CD test showed is strong. Openness moves together across countries (world trade booms and slumps), so its standard error is the one most affected.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Estimate fixed effects with three kinds of standard errors

The Driscoll–Kraay estimator needs a reasonably long T, since it averages over years rather than countries; with 24 years it is appropriate. The bandwidth (lags of the Newey–West kernel) is set to 3, roughly \(T^{1/3}\) .
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to read it Residual dependence. Even after the two regressors, the residuals of different countries remain correlated: the common shocks are not explained by the model. This is exactly the case Driscoll–Kraay standard errors are built for. Serial correlation. The residuals are positively autocorrelated, as is usual for annual macro data. The Bartlett kernel in the Driscoll–Kraay estimator corrects for it. But there is a deeper question. Driscoll–Kraay fixes the standard errors . If the common shocks are also correlated with the regressors, the coefficients themselves are biased, and no standard-error correction helps. The robustness checks test this.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Robustness: are the coefficients driven by common shocks?

How to read it This is the most important table in a macro-panel paper. Bandwidth. A longer kernel changes the standard errors only a little. Year effects. Adding a dummy for each year removes everything common to all countries in that year. The unemployment coefficient shrinks towards zero and the openness coefficient turns positive and significant . CCE pooled removes common factors through cross-sectional averages, allowing each country to respond to them differently. It tells the same story as the year effects. The interpretation: in the baseline, both coefficients mostly reflected the common OECD cycle . In the 1970s oil shocks, growth fell everywhere while unemployment rose and the value of trade (inflated by oil prices) rose. Once the common shocks are removed, countries whose openness rose faster than the OECD average grew faster. The baseline coefficient was biased by the common shocks, not just its standard error.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors
Robustness: are the coefficients driven by common shocks?

So for this question the robustness check changes the conclusion: report the model with year effects or CCE as the main specification, and the plain FE-DK as the comparison. The model selection tool flagged the residual cross-sectional dependence; this step is how you act on it.
