Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Report the pre-tests (CD, CIPS, slope homogeneity) in a separate table before this one. In this table, the progression from column (1) to columns (2) and (3) shows the reader how much of the raw correlation is due to common shocks.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator Pesaran's CD test rejects cross-sectional independence for all variables, so we test for unit roots with the CIPS test, which rejects a unit root in levels for each series. The Pesaran–Yamagata test does not reject slope homogeneity (adjusted Δ, p = 0.16). We therefore estimate a fixed-effects model with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, which are robust to heteroskedasticity, serial correlation and cross-sectional dependence. How to write it: results In the fixed-effects model, higher unemployment is associated with lower growth, and the change in trade openness has a negative but insignificant coefficient once standard errors allow for cross-sectional dependence (Table 2, column 1). Because the residuals remain cross-sectionally dependent, we also control for common shocks with year effects and with the common correlated effects estimator. In both specifications, increases in trade openness relative to the OECD average are associated with significantly higher growth (columns 2 and 3), indicating that the baseline estimate was confounded by the common business cycle.
Fixed Effects with Driscoll–Kraay Standard Errors

Common mistakes Clustering by country in a macro panel and calling the standard errors robust. They are not robust to common shocks. Using Driscoll–Kraay with a short T. The estimator averages over time periods, so it needs many of them. Thinking Driscoll–Kraay solves cross-sectional dependence. It corrects the inference only; if the common factor is correlated with the regressors, the coefficients are biased. Always compare with year effects or CCE. Using first-generation unit-root tests (LLC, IPS, Fisher) when the CD test rejects.
Difference GMM for Dynamic Panels: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.
The question and why the usual estimators fail

The question: how persistent is firm employment, and how does it respond to wages and capital? Employment adjusts slowly because hiring and firing are costly, so this year's employment depends on last year's. That makes the model dynamic: with all variables in logs: employment \(n\) , the real wage \(w\) , capital \(k\) (current and two lags) and industry output \(ys\) (current and two lags). \(\eta_i\) is a firm fixed effect. Estimator Problem with a lagged dependent variable Bias in \(\alpha_1\) Pooled OLS \(n_{i,t-1}\) contains \(\eta_i\) , which is in the error upwards Fixed effects demeaning makes \(n_{i,t-1}\) correlated with the demeaned error (Nickell bias, of order 1/T) downwards Difference GMM
The question and why the usual estimators fail

first-difference to remove \(\eta_i\) , then instrument \(\Delta n_{i,t-1}\) with \(n_{i,t-2}, n_{i,t-3}, \dots\) consistent as N grows, if the instruments are valid When to use this guide, and when not GMM for dynamic panels is designed for many units and few periods . Its consistency comes from N growing, not T. With 20 countries over 40 years the Nickell bias is small, the instruments multiply out of control, and fixed effects (or the macro-panel guides) are the better choice. The model selection tool sends a panel here only when T is short (below 15), N is large (at least 30 units) and you say the model is dynamic. With fewer units it recommends bias-corrected fixed effects (LSDVC) instead.
The question and why the usual estimators fail

How to write it: model section We estimate a dynamic labour-demand equation in which log employment depends on its own two lags, the current and lagged log real wage, and current and lagged log capital and industry output, together with year effects \(\lambda_t\) and firm effects \(\eta_i\) . Because the lagged dependent variable is correlated with the firm effect, pooled OLS is biased upwards, and because T is short, the within estimator is subject to the Nickell bias. We therefore use the difference GMM estimator of Arellano and Bond (1991).
Load the panel and build the lags

How to read it This is the shape GMM needs: 140 firms and 7 to 9 years each . The model selection tool ran the static tests on this file (fixed effects is preferred to random effects) and then asked whether the model is dynamic. Because employment adjusts gradually, the answer is yes, which leads here. Download the helper file and the data .
Step 1: pooled OLS and fixed effects give the bounds

How to read it The coefficient on lagged employment is above 1 by pooled OLS and about 0.73 by fixed effects. Because the first is biased upwards and the second downwards, a credible GMM estimate should lie between them, or close to the fixed-effects bound . This check (Bond 2002) costs two regressions and is the first thing to run in any dynamic panel study.

How to read it These are one-step estimates with standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and to correlation within each firm. They reproduce the published Arellano–Bond results for this dataset (0.686 on lagged employment), which is how the helper function was checked. Persistence. About 0.69 on the first lag. Employment adjusts gradually. Wages. A 1% rise in the real wage lowers employment by about 0.6% in the same year; the long-run elasticity, which allows for the dynamics, is about −0.5. Capital. A 1% rise in capital raises employment by about 0.36% at once, and by about 0.7% in the long run. The bounds. The GMM persistence lies slightly below the fixed-effects estimate. That is a warning sign of weak instruments in the differenced equation: when employment is highly persistent, its lagged levels predict its differences poorly. Step 4 returns to this.

How to read it A dynamic panel GMM table is not complete without these. AR(1) in the differenced residuals is expected: differencing creates it. It says nothing about validity. AR(2) is the test that matters. If the errors in levels are serially uncorrelated, the differenced errors have no second-order correlation. Here it is not rejected, so levels dated \(t-2\) are valid instruments. If it were rejected, the instruments would have to start at \(t-3\) . Hansen J. The null is that all instruments are valid. It is not rejected. Be suspicious of p-values very close to 1: that is a symptom of too many instruments, not of very good ones.
Instrument count. The count must stay well below the number of firms. Too many instruments overfit the endogenous variable, pull GMM towards the biased OLS estimate and weaken the Hansen test.
Step 4: robustness to the instrument set

How to read it Referees always ask whether the results depend on the instruments. Report a table like this one. The wage and capital effects are stable across all instrument sets: they are the robust findings. The persistence coefficient is not. It moves with the lag depth, and with collapsed instruments its standard error grows. Persistence is the parameter for which difference GMM is known to be weak when the series are highly persistent. What to do. Report the baseline, show this table, and estimate system GMM (Blundell and Bond 1998), which adds the equations in levels instrumented by lagged differences and is much stronger when persistence is high. In Stata: xtabond2 n L(1/2).n w L.w k L(1/2).k ys L(1/2).ys i.year, gmm(L.n, collapse) iv(w L.w k L(1/2).k ys L(1/2).ys i.year) twostep robust (see the Stata workflow on the main page).
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Columns (1) and (2) are the bounds, columns (3) and (4) the GMM estimates. Always report the AR(2) and Hansen p-values and the instrument count in the table itself, not only in the text.

How to write it: estimation strategy Because the model includes lagged employment and firm fixed effects, and T is short, both pooled OLS and the within estimator are inconsistent, with biases of opposite sign. We use the Arellano–Bond difference GMM estimator, instrumenting the differenced lags of employment with levels dated \(t-2\) and earlier and treating wages, capital and output as strictly exogenous. We report one-step estimates with standard errors robust to heteroskedasticity and within-firm correlation. How to write it: results The Arellano–Bond test does not detect second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals, and the Hansen test does not reject the validity of the instruments (Table 1, column 3). A 1 percent increase in the real wage reduces employment by about 0.6 percent on impact and by about 0.5 percent in the long run. The wage and capital elasticities are robust to the choice of instrument lags and to collapsing the instrument matrix, whereas the estimated persistence of employment is sensitive to the instrument set, consistent with weak instruments for highly persistent series.

Common mistakes Using GMM with few units (say, 20 countries). The asymptotics need large N, and the instrument count quickly exceeds the number of units. Not reporting the instrument count, or using all available lags without collapsing in longer panels. Treating a Hansen p-value of 0.99 as reassuring. It usually means too many instruments. Ignoring the bounds check. A GMM persistence estimate above pooled OLS or well below fixed effects signals a problem. Treating endogenous regressors as exogenous. If wages respond to employment shocks, they must be instrumented with their own lags, just like the lagged dependent variable.

1. Panel structure and the common-factor problem

Let \(i=1,\ldots,N\) index countries or other macro units and \(t=1,\ldots,T\) index time. A heterogeneous panel regression is where \(\alpha_i\) is a unit-specific intercept, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_i\) is a potentially heterogeneous slope vector, \(\mathbf{f}_t\) is a vector of unobserved common factors, and \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i\) contains unit-specific factor loadings. Global interest rates, commodity prices, financial conditions, technology and common policy shocks can induce dependence across countries even after observed controls are included. For macro panels, asymptotics often require both \(N\) and \(T\) to be sufficiently informative. A large-\(N\), short-\(T\) micro-panel design is not interchangeable with a country panel having moderate or large \(T\).

After a baseline model is estimated, let \(\widehat{\rho}_{ij}\) be the pairwise correlation between residuals for units \(i\) and \(j\). Pesaran's CD statistic is based on The null is cross-sectional independence. Rejection indicates that conventional first-generation panel procedures relying on cross-sectional independence may not be appropriate without adjustment. The test should be considered alongside the economic structure of common shocks and residual diagnostics. Implementation: Stata's xtcd2 is distributed with xtdcce2 . Run it on the variables or, more importantly, on residuals from a defensible baseline model.

In a homogeneous specification, \(\boldsymbol{\beta}_i=\boldsymbol{\beta}\) for all \(i\). The Pesaran–Yamagata delta test assesses this restriction using dispersion in unit-specific slope estimates relative to a pooled estimate. The economic question is whether a common response is credible across countries with different institutions, production structures, energy mixes and policy regimes. If homogeneity is defensible, pooled estimators may gain precision. If slopes differ, Mean Group or CCE-MG/AMG estimators allow unit-specific slopes. PMG imposes a common long-run coefficient vector but allows short-run coefficients and adjustment speeds to vary.
4. Panel unit roots: first versus second generation

Family Examples Key maintained structure First generation LLC, IPS, Fisher-ADF, Fisher-PP Cross-sectional independence, or an adjustment that makes it credible. Second generation CADF and CIPS Cross-sectional averages proxy unobserved common factors. The cross-sectionally augmented Dickey–Fuller regression includes lagged levels and cross-sectional averages. The CIPS statistic is the cross-sectional average of individual CADF statistics: In Stata, xtcips implements the Pesaran CIPS test and requires a balanced panel. Deterministic terms (intercept or trend), lag selection and sample comparability must be specified and reported. A test result should not be treated as an integration-order label independent of those choices.

Cointegration is considered when variables are appropriately established as I(1) and theory supports a long-run equilibrium relation. Residual-based tests include Pedroni and Kao. Westerlund's error-correction tests ask whether deviations from long-run equilibrium generate adjustment. The null in the Westerlund error-correction framework is no error correction (no cointegration); the alternative can allow adjustment in some or all panel members depending on the statistic. When cross-sectional dependence is material, bootstrap inference or a dependence-aware implementation is important. Cointegration tests do not by themselves establish a common long-run coefficient vector.

Estimate a separate time-series regression for each unit and average the coefficients: MG allows slope heterogeneity but does not automatically remove bias from unobserved common factors. It is a useful heterogeneous benchmark when each unit has enough time observations.

CCE augments unit-specific regressions with cross-sectional averages of the dependent and explanatory variables, and where needed their lags. These averages proxy the unobserved common factors. CCEMG averages the unit-specific CCE slope estimates. The rank condition and the number of cross-sectional averages relative to the factor structure matter.

AMG estimates a common dynamic process from a pooled first-difference model with time effects, then includes that process in unit-specific regressions. It allows heterogeneous slopes while controlling for an estimated common dynamic component.

For an error-correction representation, PMG constrains the long-run vector to be common, while allowing short-run coefficients, intercepts, variances and adjustment speeds to differ: The long-run restriction \(\boldsymbol{\theta}_i=\boldsymbol{\theta}\) is substantive. Compare PMG with MG and dependence-aware estimators; do not select PMG solely because it produces a smaller standard error.

CS-ARDL augments a dynamic heterogeneous ARDL with current and lagged cross-sectional averages. Unit-specific long-run effects can be formed from the distributed-lag coefficients and then averaged. This combines dynamic adjustment with a proxy for unobserved common factors.

Describe \(N\), \(T\), balancedness, missingness, frequency and the economic comparability of units. Estimate transparent baseline FE/RE specifications and inspect residual dependence. Test cross-sectional dependence and slope homogeneity. Choose first- or second-generation unit-root procedures accordingly; specify intercepts, trends and lags. Test cointegration only when the integration orders and theoretical relation warrant it. Compare MG, CCE-MG, AMG, PMG and CS-ARDL under explicit restrictions. Report residual dependence, serial correlation, adjustment coefficients, lag sensitivity, sample sensitivity and long-run coefficient comparisons.

Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

The question is one of the oldest in growth economics: do countries that save more grow faster? In the Solow model a higher saving rate raises the level of income and, during the transition, the growth rate. But there is no reason to expect the same relationship in Japan, Chile and Nigeria: financial systems, openness and the use of saving differ. Symbol Variable Definition Expected sign \(g_{it}\) growth Growth of real GDP per capita, % (computed below) dependent variable \(s_{it}\) sr Saving rate, % of GDP positive \(\beta_i\) — Country-specific effect of saving on growth what we want to average The model lets every country have its own slope \(\beta_i\) . The parameter of interest is the average slope \(\beta\) .
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

Pooled or mean group? Fixed effects imposes \(\beta_i = \beta\) for all countries. If that is wrong, the FE estimate is a weighted average of the \(\beta_i\) , with weights that depend on the variance of each country's saving rate, not on anything economically meaningful, and its standard error ignores the slope heterogeneity. The mean group estimator (Pesaran and Smith 1995) estimates each \(\beta_i\) separately and averages them. Its standard error comes from the dispersion of the \(\beta_i\) across countries, so it is valid whatever the heterogeneity. It needs T large enough to estimate a regression for each country. How to write it: model section We allow the effect of saving on growth to differ across countries, \(g_{it} = \alpha_i + \beta_i s_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\) , and estimate the average effect \(\beta = E(\beta_i)\) with the mean group estimator of Pesaran and Smith (1995), and with the common correlated effects mean group estimator of Pesaran (2006), which in addition controls for unobserved common factors.

Load the data and run the pre-tests

How to read it 125 countries over 25 years : long enough to estimate a regression for each country. Cross-sectional dependence. The CD test rejects for both variables. World growth has a common cycle, so CIPS is the right unit-root test. Stationarity. CIPS rejects a unit root for both growth and the saving rate: both are I(0), and a model in levels is valid. Slope heterogeneity. The Δ test rejects decisively. The effect of saving on growth differs across countries , so pooling the slopes is not defensible. Stationary variables with heterogeneous slopes: this is where the model selection tool recommends mean-group estimation.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

How to read it The histogram is the reason for this guide. The country slopes are spread widely, and a substantial minority are negative. A single pooled coefficient would hide all of this. The mean group estimate is the simple average of these slopes , and its standard error is their standard deviation divided by \(\sqrt{N}\) . The extreme slopes come from small countries with volatile data and few effective observations. Because every country gets the same weight, a few of them can move the mean; the robustness step checks this.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group
Mean group, CCE mean group and the pooled comparison

How to read it Mean group. On average across countries, a saving rate one percentage point higher goes with growth about 0.35 points higher, and the effect is significant. CCE mean group adds the cross-sectional averages of growth and saving to each country's regression. They proxy the unobserved common factors (the world business cycle, oil prices, world interest rates), and each country can respond to them differently. The average effect is a bit larger and remains significant. Pooled fixed effects gives a smaller slope. The difference is the weighting: FE gives more weight to countries whose saving rate varies more, and those are not the countries with the largest effects. With heterogeneous slopes the FE number has no clear interpretation, which is the point of the Δ test.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group
Diagnostic test: are the common shocks removed?

How to read it The plain mean-group residuals are still cross-sectionally dependent: country regressions with only their own saving rate leave the world cycle in the error. With the cross-sectional averages included, the CD statistic falls from about 26 to about 0.2 and is no longer significant: the common factors have been removed. This is why CCE-MG is the preferred estimator when the CD test rejects. If the common factors were correlated with saving, plain MG would be biased. (The mean absolute correlation barely changes, because with T = 25 any two countries' residuals are correlated by chance; the CD test looks at the signed correlations, which are what common shocks create.)
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

How to read it Because the mean group gives every country equal weight, report the trimmed mean and the median alongside it. Here they matter. The distribution of country slopes is skewed to the right: a few countries have very large slopes (the largest is 6.8), and they pull the mean up. Trimming the extreme 5% at each end, or taking the median, gives an effect of about 0.23 : smaller than the baseline mean group, but still positive and, for the trimmed mean, more precisely estimated. The sign is robust; the size depends on how much weight the extreme countries get. Say so in the paper.

How to read it Report the pooled estimates for comparison, but make column (4) the main result: it allows for both heterogeneous slopes and common shocks, the two features the pre-tests found.
Mean Group and CCE Mean Group

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator The CD test indicates strong cross-sectional dependence, and the CIPS test rejects a unit root for both growth and the saving rate. The Pesaran–Yamagata test strongly rejects slope homogeneity, so pooled estimators would average heterogeneous country effects with arbitrary weights. We therefore estimate the average effect with the mean group (MG) estimator and, to account for unobserved common factors, with the common correlated effects mean group (CCE-MG) estimator. How to write it: results The CCE-MG estimate implies that a saving rate one percentage point higher is associated with growth of GDP per capita about 0.5 percentage points higher on average (Table 3, column 4). The effect varies considerably across countries: it is negative in about a fifth of them, and the distribution is skewed by a few countries with very large effects. Excluding the most extreme 5 percent of country estimates at each end, or using the median country slope, yields a smaller but still positive effect of 0.2 to 0.3. Pooled fixed-effects estimates are smaller still, consistent with the arbitrary weighting of heterogeneous slopes.

Common mistakes Reporting a pooled FE coefficient after the slope-homogeneity test rejects, without comment. Using mean group estimators with short T. Each country regression needs enough observations; with T below about 20 the unit estimates are noisy and MG can be badly biased in dynamic models. Forgetting the common factors: MG with cross-sectionally dependent errors can be biased. Use CCE-MG and report the residual CD test. Reading the average slope as causal. Saving and growth are jointly determined; this is a conditional correlation unless you have a source of exogenous variation.
Panel Local Projections: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

How does the outcome of a unit evolve after a shock to that unit? For each horizon \(h = 0, 1, \dots, H\) the panel local projection estimates where \(\alpha_{i,h}\) is a unit effect, \(\delta_{t,h}\) is an optional time effect, \(s_{i,t}\) is the shock and \(x_{i,t}\) holds the controls (lags of the outcome, of the shock and of other variables, and any variables ordered before the shock). The coefficient \(\beta_h\) is the impulse response at horizon \(h\) . Because every horizon is a separate fixed-effects regression, the method is robust to misspecification of the dynamics and does not require a balanced panel. Four checks before you trust a panel local projection

Is the shock plausibly exogenous to the unit's own outcome? The shock should be a change that is not driven by anticipated changes in the outcome (a tax change, a policy reform, an external shock). A price that responds to expected demand is not a shock. Which effects? Unit effects remove permanent differences between units. Time effects also remove everything common to all units in a period, so the response is identified from differences across units only, and the average effect of a common shock is lost. Which standard errors? The horizon- \(h\) errors overlap across horizons and are correlated within a unit, so cluster by unit. If shocks hit all units at once, errors are also correlated across units, and Driscoll-Kraay errors (which need a long time dimension) or time effects are needed.

Is T large enough? With unit effects and lagged outcomes among the controls, a short panel has Nickell bias. Check that the response is stable to the number of lags. How to write it: the model We estimate the dynamic effect of a cigarette-price increase on sales with panel local projections (Jordà 2005). For each horizon \(h = 0, \dots, 8\) years we regress log per-capita sales at \(t+h\) on the change in the log real price at \(t\) , on the contemporaneous change in log income, on two lags of the price change, of income growth and of log sales, and on state fixed effects. The price change is scaled to one standard deviation. Standard errors are clustered by state.
Load the panel and check its structure

How to read it The panel is balanced: 46 states observed for 30 years (1963-92). Log sales and log price are persistent, so the shock used is the one-year change in log price ( d_log_price , mean 0.011, s.d. 0.060). The per-state unit-root test rejects a unit root in none of the states for the levels and in only 13% for the change, but with 30 years per state and two lags the test has little power, so treat it as a warning about persistence, not proof. Because every state has all 30 years, no grid gaps need filling.

How to read it Each row is a separate regression of log sales at t+h on the price shock, with state effects, two lags and the contemporaneous income change, scaled to a one-standard-deviation shock. Sales fall by 1.9% on impact (-0.0192, s.e. 0.0015), the response deepens to a peak of -0.0369 at horizon 3, and decays to -0.0255 by horizon 8. Every horizon is significant at 1%, and the 95% band stays well away from zero. The observation count drops from 1,242 to 874 as the horizon grows because later outcomes need more future years.
Choose the effects: pooled, unit or unit and time

How to read it The effects choice matters for the shape. Pooled and unit-effects responses are almost identical (about -0.036 at horizon 4), so state-level differences in average sales do not drive the result. Adding year effects shrinks the response (-0.018 at horizon 4, -0.008 at horizon 8) because common national shocks, such as federal tax changes and health campaigns, move prices and sales together. Report which comparison you mean: unit effects give the within-state response to a price change; two-way effects give the response relative to other states in the same year.

How to read it Driscoll-Kraay errors are two to six times larger than clustered errors and grow with the horizon (0.0081 versus 0.0020 at horizon 4, 0.0185 versus 0.0028 at horizon 8). Clustering by state allows arbitrary serial correlation within a state but assumes states are independent; Driscoll-Kraay also allows common shocks across states, which matters here because the years are shared. With only 30 periods, the Driscoll-Kraay errors are the more cautious choice; the response stays significantly negative through horizon 8 under both.
Robustness: lags, outcome, controls and leave-one-state-out

How to read it The impact and peak responses barely move: -0.018 to -0.020 at horizon 0 and -0.033 to -0.039 at horizon 4 across one lag, four lags and no income control. The far horizon is less stable (-0.008 with four lags against -0.032 with one), so quote the horizon 8 value with care. The change-since-t-1 outcome matches the baseline exactly because the regression includes a lag of the outcome, as expected. Dropping any one state leaves the horizon 4 response between -0.0369 and -0.0357, and all 46 runs are negative, so no single state drives it.

How to write it: results A one-standard-deviation increase in the annual change in log cigarette price (about 6 percentage points) lowers per-capita sales by 1.9% on impact. The response grows to a peak of 3.7% after three years (95% CI -4.0% to -3.3%, state-clustered) and is still 2.6% below its starting path after eight years. The estimates use local projections with state fixed effects, two lags of sales and the price change, and a contemporaneous income control. The impact and peak responses are stable across lag length, outcome definition and leave-one-state-out checks. Driscoll-Kraay standard errors are larger but the response remains significant through horizon 8. With year effects the response is smaller (1.8% at horizon 4), so the result partly reflects national co-movement of prices and sales. With T = 30 and lagged outcomes among the regressors, fixed-effect estimates carry a small Nickell-type bias.

The question: what are the long-run price and income elasticities of cigarette demand? Smoking is addictive, so consumption adjusts slowly to price changes, and the long-run response is what matters for tax policy. The data also contain the minimum price in neighbouring states, which captures cross-border buying (“bootlegging”). The panel ARDL(1,1) model in error-correction form is Symbol Variable Definition Expected sign of \(\theta\) \(c_{it}\) log_sales Log packs per capita dependent variable \(p_{it}\) log_price Log real price per pack negative: the long-run price elasticity \(y_{it}\) log_income Log real disposable income per capita positive if cigarettes are a normal good \(pn_{it}\) log_pimin Log real minimum price in neighbouring states positive: cheaper neighbours draw buyers away

\(\phi_i\) — Speed of adjustment to the long run negative, between −2 and 0 PMG restricts the long-run coefficients \(\theta\) to be the same in every state, and lets \(\phi_i\) , the short-run coefficients \(\gamma_i\) and the intercepts differ. MG lets everything differ and averages. Dynamic fixed effects (DFE) restricts everything except the intercepts. Why PMG suits this question Long-run elasticities are often similar across units, because they reflect preferences and technology, whereas short-run adjustment depends on local institutions (here, state tax changes and their timing). PMG imposes the restriction where it is plausible and estimates it efficiently. Whether the restriction holds is tested by comparing PMG with MG. How to write it: model section

We estimate an ARDL(1,1) model of cigarette demand in error-correction form, in which the long-run elasticities of per-capita sales with respect to the real price, real income and the real minimum price in neighbouring states are common across states, while the short-run coefficients and the speed of adjustment are state-specific. The model is estimated by the pooled mean group (PMG) estimator of Pesaran, Shin and Smith (1999).
Load the data and remove the common shocks

How to read it In the raw data every variable is strongly cross-sectionally dependent: national trends (the 1964 Surgeon General's report, federal taxes, inflation) move all states together. Cross-sectional demeaning , subtracting each year's average across states, removes common shocks that affect all states equally. It is the standard first step before PMG, which assumes independent units. Demeaning removes almost all of the dependence: the CD statistics fall from above 100 to about −3. What is left is small and negative , partly a mechanical by-product of demeaning (subtracting the cross-state average makes deviations slightly negatively correlated). Demeaning cannot remove common shocks to which states respond differently; for those, use CS-ARDL (see that guide, which uses the same data without demeaning). The test that matters is the CD test on the PMG residuals, below.

How to read it Unit roots. The variables are a mix: some do not reject a unit root in levels, others do. Every variable is stationary in first differences, and none is I(2). This mix of I(0) and I(1) is the case the panel ARDL is designed for : the bounds-testing logic of ARDL does not require all variables to share the same order of integration. Slope heterogeneity. The static Δ test rejects. That does not rule PMG out: PMG lets the short-run coefficients differ, and only restricts the long run. Whether the long-run restriction is acceptable is tested directly in the Hausman step.
Estimate PMG, MG and dynamic fixed effects

How to read it PMG long run. A 10% rise in the real price lowers cigarette sales by about 7.7% in the long run. Income has a positive long-run effect, and a higher price in neighbouring states raises sales at home: when the neighbours are cheap, smokers cross the border. All three are precisely estimated, because PMG pools the long-run information from all 46 states. MG estimates each state separately. Its price elasticity is larger in absolute value and its income and neighbour-price effects are imprecise: with 29 years per state, individual long-run coefficients are noisy, and averaging noisy ratios inflates the standard errors. DFE pools everything, including the adjustment speed, which biases the long run when dynamics differ across states.
Estimate PMG, MG and dynamic fixed effects

Speed of adjustment. \(\phi\) is negative and significant, which supports the long-run relationship: deviations from it are corrected. With PMG, about a fifth of the gap closes each year, a half-life of about three years. Smoking adjusts slowly, as addiction models predict.
Test 1: is the common long run acceptable? Hausman PMG vs MG

How to read it Under the null that the long-run coefficients are the same in every state, both PMG and MG are consistent and PMG is efficient. Under the alternative, only MG is consistent. The test does not reject, so the common long-run restriction is accepted, and PMG is the preferred estimator. This is the test referees expect in every PMG paper.
Test 2: residual cross-sectional dependence and the adjustment speeds

How to read it Residual dependence. PMG assumes the states' errors are independent. The CD test on the residuals rejects narrowly (p = 0.03), but the remaining dependence is weak and negative, of the kind demeaning itself induces, not the strong positive dependence of common shocks in the raw data (CD above 100). Report this honestly, and use CS-ARDL as the robustness check: it handles any remaining common factors. Adjustment speeds. Every state should have \(-2 < \phi_i < 0\) for a stable long-run relationship. None is below −2, but 7 of the 46 states have a small positive \(\phi_i\) : for them, sales show no tendency to return to the long-run relationship within the sample. Report the range, and check that the results survive without those states.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it The standard PMG table: long-run coefficients and the error-correction coefficient for PMG, with MG and DFE alongside, and the Hausman statistic in the notes. Report the short-run coefficients in an appendix table.

How to write it: pre-tests and estimator To remove common national shocks, all variables are expressed as deviations from their cross-state means in each year. CIPS tests indicate a mixture of I(0) and I(1) variables, none of them I(2), which motivates a panel ARDL specification. We estimate it by the pooled mean group estimator, which constrains the long-run elasticities to be equal across states while allowing state-specific short-run dynamics. A Hausman test does not reject the long-run homogeneity restriction against the mean group estimator, and the remaining cross-sectional dependence in the PMG residuals is weak (CD = −2.1). How to write it: results The long-run price elasticity of cigarette demand is about −0.77 (Table 5, column 1): a 10 percent increase in the real price reduces per-capita sales by 7.7 percent in the long run. A higher minimum price in neighbouring states raises home-state sales, consistent with cross-border purchases. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant, implying that about one fifth of a deviation from long-run equilibrium is corrected each year.

Common mistakes Running PMG on cross-sectionally dependent data. Demean first, test the residuals, and switch to CS-ARDL if dependence remains. Skipping the Hausman test against MG. The common long run is a restriction and must be tested. Using PMG with an I(2) variable, or with short T. Each state's short-run dynamics are estimated separately and need enough years. Reporting only the long run. The error-correction coefficient is the evidence that a long-run relationship exists.
Pooled OLS: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. Short panel, no significant unit effects.

Pooled OLS is rarely the right model for variables in levels: firms, workers and countries almost always differ permanently. It often becomes the right model once the variables are growth rates , because differencing removes the permanent differences in levels. The question here: how does a firm's employment growth respond to the growth of its wages, capital and industry demand? \(\lambda_t\) — Year effects: the 1980–81 recession common to all firms Before you estimate anything Pooling assumes that all units share the same intercept and the same slopes. With growth rates the first assumption is plausible: a firm with permanently high employment does not need to have permanently high employment growth . But it is still an assumption, and the F and LM tests below check it. If they reject, use the fixed- or random-effects guide instead. How to write it: model section We relate employment growth to the growth of the real wage, the capital stock and industry output, \(\Delta \ln n_{it} = \beta_1 \Delta \ln w_{it} + \beta_2 \Delta \ln k_{it} + \beta_3 \Delta \ln ys_{it} + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}\) , where \(\lambda_t\) are year effects. Specifying the model in growth rates removes permanent firm-specific differences in employment levels.
Load the data and build the growth rates

How to read it The panel is short and unbalanced: 140 firms with 6 to 8 growth observations each. Taking differences loses the first year of every firm. Employment fell on average over the period, the years of the early-1980s recession in British manufacturing. The model selection tool, run on this file, finds no significant firm effects and recommends pooled OLS. The next steps show why.
Test for firm effects: F and Breusch–Pagan LM

How to read it F test. Null: all 140 firms have the same intercept. It is not rejected, so firm-specific intercepts do not improve the fit. Breusch–Pagan LM test. Null: the variance of a random firm effect is zero. It is not rejected either. With neither test rejecting, pooling the firms is defensible. Fixed effects would estimate 139 extra intercepts for no gain in fit, and lose precision.
Estimate the pooled model with clustered standard errors

How to read it Wages. A 1 percentage point faster growth of the real wage lowers employment growth by about 0.4 points in the same year. Capital. Faster capital growth is associated with faster employment growth: firms that invest also hire. Industry output. Faster growth of demand in the firm's industry raises employment growth: about half a point for each point of output growth. Clustered standard errors are not optional. Even without firm effects, the errors of the same firm can be correlated across years and their variance can differ across firms. The second table compares them: the clustered standard error of the wage coefficient is more than three times the conventional one. With conventional standard errors you would overstate the precision of every estimate. Report the clustered ones.
Diagnostic tests: serial correlation and heteroskedasticity

How to read it Serial correlation. Regressing each residual on the same firm's residual a year earlier gives a small positive coefficient (0.09), significant only at the 10% level. The serial correlation that remains is weak. Heteroskedasticity. The Breusch–Pagan test rejects clearly: the error variance differs across observations, as is usual with firm data (small firms have more volatile growth). Both problems leave the pooled OLS coefficients unbiased; they only affect the standard errors. Clustering by firm corrects for both , which is why it was used from the start.

How to read it Fixed effects gives coefficients close to pooled OLS. This is what the F test predicted, and it is the strongest evidence a referee will accept that pooling is harmless. Random effects is identical to pooled OLS. The estimated variance of the firm effect is zero, so the random-effects transformation subtracts nothing: this is the LM test result seen from the other side. Without year effects the output coefficient changes the most: industry output and the recession move together, so without year effects output growth picks up the common cycle. Keep the year effects. Dropping the most extreme 1% of employment growth (mergers, plant closures) leaves the capital and output effects similar, but halves the wage effect , to −0.21. It remains significant, but its size depends on a few firm-years with very large swings. Report this check: a reader needs to know that the magnitude, though not the sign, is fragile.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Column (1) is the preferred estimate; columns (2) and (3) show that it does not depend on the treatment of firm effects. The F and LM statistics in the notes are the justification for pooling.

How to write it: specification Because the model is specified in growth rates, permanent differences in employment levels across firms are differenced out. Consistent with this, an F test does not reject the hypothesis that firm-specific intercepts are jointly zero, and a Breusch–Pagan LM test does not reject the absence of random firm effects. We therefore estimate the model by pooled OLS with year effects, and cluster standard errors by firm to allow for heteroskedasticity and serial correlation within firms. How to write it: results Real wage growth has a negative and significant effect on employment growth: a one percentage point faster increase in the real wage reduces employment growth by about 0.4 percentage points (Table 1, column 1). Capital growth and industry output growth are positively associated with employment growth. Fixed- and random-effects estimates are very close to the pooled estimates (columns 2 and 3), confirming that unobserved firm heterogeneity does not drive the results. The magnitude of the wage effect is, however, sensitive to a small number of extreme observations: excluding the top 1 percent of absolute employment changes reduces it to about −0.2, still significant.

Common mistakes Pooling variables in levels without testing for unit effects. In levels the F test almost always rejects. Reporting conventional standard errors. Pooled observations on the same unit are not independent; cluster by unit. Omitting year effects. Common shocks then load onto whichever regressor moves with the cycle. Using pooled OLS for a dynamic model with a lagged dependent variable. Pooled OLS is then biased upwards; see the GMM guide.
Panel Threshold Regression (Hansen): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Does the slope change when a threshold variable crosses a value? With unit effects \(\mu_i\) , a regressor \(x_{it}\) , controls \(z_{it}\) and a threshold variable \(q_{it}\) , the one-threshold model is The unit effects are removed by the within transformation. For each candidate \(\gamma\) the model is linear in the slopes, so \(\gamma\) is estimated by least squares: the value that gives the smallest sum of squared residuals over a grid. Inference has two nonstandard parts. Under the null of no threshold, \(\gamma\) is not identified, so the usual \(F\) test fails and Hansen's bootstrap supplies the \(p\) -value. The confidence interval for \(\gamma\) is the set of values at which the likelihood-ratio statistic stays below a critical value, not a symmetric interval around the estimate.

Three checks before you trust a threshold model Is there a threshold at all? Look at the bootstrap \(p\) -value of the test against a linear model first. If it does not reject, the regime estimates are descriptive. Is the threshold precisely located? A wide likelihood-ratio interval or a flat likelihood means the data barely locate the threshold, and the regime slopes depend on where you put it. Is each regime well populated? A regime with few observations or few units gives noisy slopes. The trimming fraction keeps every regime above a minimum share of the sample. How to write it: the model We estimate a panel threshold regression (Hansen 1999) in which the effect of the probability of arrest on the crime rate may differ across counties with low and high police presence. The crime rate and the probability of arrest are in logs, the model includes county fixed effects, and the probability of conviction and the average sentence enter with a common slope. The threshold variable is log police per capita. The threshold is searched over 100 grid points between the 5th and 95th percentiles of the threshold variable, the test against a linear model uses a bootstrap with 300 replications, and standard errors of the slopes are clustered by county.
Load the data and look at the threshold variable

How to read it The panel is balanced: 90 counties observed for seven years (1981-87), 630 observations. The threshold variable, log police per capita, has a median of -6.54 and a 5th to 95th percentile range of -7.17 to -5.74. Seventy-eight percent of its variance is between counties, so the regimes are mostly defined by which counties are well policed, while the slope is identified from changes within counties over time. A regime that is almost a fixed county characteristic is worth knowing about before interpreting the result as an effect of changing police levels.
Test for a threshold and estimate it

How to read it The bootstrap test rejects a linear model: the F statistic is 31.5 and the bootstrap p-value is 0.027, with 5% and 1% critical values of 24.8 and 33.4. The threshold is -6.38 in log police per capita, which puts 69% of the observations (432 of 630) in the low-police regime. The 95% confidence interval runs from -6.49 to -5.76; its upper end is the upper edge of the grid (the 95th percentile of the threshold variable), so the likelihood-ratio statistic stays flat above the estimate and the data cannot rule out a higher threshold. The likelihood-ratio chart shows the same: a sharp dip at the estimate and a long flat stretch to the right.

How to read it The slope of the crime rate on the probability of arrest is -0.153 (standard error 0.122) in counties with police per capita at or below the threshold and -0.289 (0.105) above it. Only the high-police slope is significantly different from zero (p = 0.006); the 95% intervals of the two slopes overlap (-0.39 to 0.09 against -0.49 to -0.08). The linear fixed-effects slope is -0.194 (0.112), roughly the average of the two regimes. The pattern fits the view that a higher arrest probability deters crime more where enforcement is stronger, but the data support it only moderately: the threshold is detected, while the difference between the two slopes is imprecisely estimated.

How to read it The test of one threshold against two does not reject (F = 12.7, bootstrap p = 0.19, 5% critical value 18.9), so one threshold is enough and the engine reports the single-threshold model. The second threshold is searched with the first fixed at its estimate, which is valid because the first estimate converges faster.
Robustness: grid, trimming, bootstrap seed and controls

How to read it The threshold estimate is stable: -6.37 to -6.41 under every variant. The test against a linear model rejects at 5% in every case except without controls (p = 0.073), where both arrest slopes are smaller in size (-0.044 and -0.160) but the high-police slope is still about three times the low-police slope. When the slope of the probability of conviction is also allowed to change with the regime, the arrest slopes become -0.164 and -0.312, so the difference is, if anything, larger. A grid of 50, 100 or 200 points, trimming of 5% to 15% and a different bootstrap seed change the threshold by at most 0.01 and the bootstrap p-value stays between 0.003 and 0.027.
Robustness: grid, trimming, bootstrap seed and controls

How to read it Dropping one year at a time moves the threshold estimate between -6.67 and -5.72 (it is -6.37 to -6.45 in four of seven cases) and the bootstrap p-value between 0.00 and 0.06, with only 1981 pushing it above 5% (p = 0.06). The result does not depend on a single year, though with seven years a leave-one-year-out check has little power to distinguish. Report the range.

How to write it: results A test against a linear model rejects at the 5% level (Hansen bootstrap, F = 31.5, p = 0.027) and locates a threshold at -6.38 in log police per capita, with 69% of the county-years below it (95% confidence interval -6.49 to -5.76, bounded above by the edge of the search grid). Below the threshold the elasticity of the crime rate with respect to the probability of arrest is -0.15 (clustered standard error 0.12); above it, -0.29 (0.10). A second threshold is not supported (p = 0.19). The threshold is stable across grid size, trimming, the bootstrap seed and the choice of controls, and the high-police slope is larger in size in every variant, but the confidence intervals of the two slopes overlap, so we read the evidence as consistent with stronger deterrence where policing is heavier rather than as a precise estimate of the difference. Because 78% of the variation in police per capita is between counties, the regimes largely separate counties rather than periods.

Random Effects: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is a central one in labour economics and in macroeconomic models of the labour market: how much do men change their working hours when their wage changes? The answer, the labour-supply elasticity, governs how taxes affect work and how much hours move over the business cycle. Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(\ln h_{it}\) lnhr Log annual hours worked dependent variable \(\ln w_{it}\) lnwg Log hourly wage positive and small: the labour-supply elasticity \(kids_{it}\) kids Number of children positive: more needs to provide for \(age_{it}\) age Age in years negative over the life cycle \(disab_{it}\) disab 1 if a health limitation is reported negative \(u_i\) —

Worker effect: tastes for work, occupation treated as random In the random-effects model the worker effect \(u_i\) is part of the error, with variance \(\sigma_u^2\) . The key assumption is that \(u_i\) is uncorrelated with every regressor in every year . The tests below check it. Before you estimate anything Random effects is not a weaker version of fixed effects. If its assumption holds, it is consistent and more efficient, and it can estimate the effect of variables that do not change over time. If the assumption fails, it is biased. So the choice is made by a test, and the paper must report it. How to write it: model section

We model log annual hours as \(\ln h_{it} = \beta_1 \ln w_{it} + \beta_2 kids_{it} + \beta_3 age_{it} + \beta_4 disab_{it} + \lambda_t + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}\) , where \(\lambda_t\) are year effects and \(u_i\) is a worker-specific effect capturing persistent differences in tastes for work. The coefficient \(\beta_1\) is the elasticity of hours with respect to the wage.
Load the panel and look at the variation

How to read it A balanced, short panel: 532 men, each observed for 10 years. The model selection tool ran the specification tests on this file and recommended random effects; this guide repeats them in full. Look at the wage. Its between standard deviation (0.39) is more than twice its within standard deviation (0.17): most of the wage variation is across men, not over time for the same man. Fixed effects throws the between variation away. Random effects uses it, which is why it will be much more precise here, provided its assumption holds.

How to read it Wage elasticity. A 10% higher wage is associated with about 1.2% more hours, significant at the 5% level. This is small, as the literature on prime-age men consistently finds. Children raise hours slightly; a health limitation lowers them by about 7%. Variance components. About a third of the unexplained variation in hours is a permanent worker effect ( \(\rho\) ); the rest changes from year to year. \(\theta\) . Random effects subtracts a fraction \(\theta\) of each man's average from his data. With \(\theta = 0\) it would be pooled OLS, with \(\theta = 1\) fixed effects. Here \(\theta\) is about 0.6, so RE sits between the two: it is a weighted average of the within and between estimators.
Test 1: are there worker effects at all? Breusch–Pagan LM

How to read it The null hypothesis is \(\sigma_u^2 = 0\) : no worker effect, in which case pooled OLS would do. The statistic is very large, so the worker effects are real . Pooled OLS with clustered standard errors would still be consistent here, but random effects is more efficient, and the clustered pooled standard errors would hide this structure.
Test 2: is the random-effects assumption credible? Hausman and Mundlak

How to read it The two tests disagree, and the reason matters for every panel paper. Conventional Hausman test. It compares the FE and RE coefficients using the textbook variance formula, which assumes that RE is fully efficient: homoskedastic errors and no correlation over time other than the worker effect. It rejects (p = 0.001). Mundlak test. It adds each man's average wage, number of children, age and disability to the RE model. If tastes for work were correlated with these averages, their coefficients would be significant. Because it uses clustered standard errors, it stays valid when the errors are heteroskedastic or serially correlated. It does not reject (p = 0.16).
Test 2: is the random-effects assumption credible? Hausman and Mundlak

Hours data are strongly heteroskedastic: a few men have very low hours in some years (the minimum of log hours is 2.8, about 16 hours a year). Under heteroskedasticity the conventional variance formula is wrong, so the conventional test cannot be trusted. The robust test is the one to base the decision on, and it supports random effects , which, as the more efficient estimator, is the one to report. Two cautions. Failing to reject is not proof that the assumption holds. And because the two tests disagree, report both, and report fixed effects alongside as the robustness check.

How to read it The point estimates are close: the FE wage elasticity is somewhat larger, but the gap is well inside the confidence intervals. The main difference is precision : fixed effects uses only the small within variation in wages, so its standard error is larger. This is the efficiency gain that random effects buys when its assumption holds.

How to read it The random-effects model assumes that, apart from the permanent worker effect, the errors are uncorrelated over time. The Wooldridge test checks this: if the errors in levels are serially uncorrelated, the first-differenced errors have a correlation of exactly −0.5. Here the estimate is −0.41 and the test does not reject at 5% (p = 0.11), so there is no strong evidence of serial correlation beyond the worker effect , which supports the RE error structure. Had it rejected, the RE point estimates would remain consistent but the textbook standard errors would be wrong. The clustered standard errors used throughout this guide are valid either way , which is why they are the ones to report.
Build the results table for the paper

How to read it Column (2) is the preferred estimate. Columns (1) and (3) show that the conclusion does not depend on how the worker effects are treated, and column (4) shows the Mundlak model, whose coefficients on the worker averages are the basis of the test. The three test statistics belong in the table notes.

How to write it: specification tests A Breusch–Pagan LM test strongly rejects the absence of worker-specific effects, so pooled OLS is inefficient. The conventional Hausman test rejects random effects, but it assumes homoskedastic errors, which is implausible for hours data; its cluster-robust Mundlak version does not reject the hypothesis that the worker effects are uncorrelated with the regressors (p = 0.16). We therefore estimate the model by random effects, with year effects and standard errors clustered by worker, and report fixed-effects estimates as a robustness check. How to write it: results The estimated elasticity of hours with respect to the wage is about 0.12 and significant at the 5 percent level (Table 1, column 2). A 10 percent rise in the hourly wage is thus associated with a 1.2 percent increase in annual hours, in line with the small elasticities typically found for prime-age men. A reported health limitation reduces hours by about 7 percent. The fixed-effects estimate of the wage elasticity is somewhat larger, 0.17, but much less precise (column 3).

Common mistakes Choosing random effects because fixed effects “loses too many variables”. That is a reason to use the Mundlak model, not to assume the RE condition holds. Reporting only the conventional Hausman test. With heteroskedastic or serially correlated errors it is invalid, as this example shows, and it can even be negative. Report the Mundlak test too. Reading “do not reject” as “random effects is proven”. Show that the FE estimates tell the same story. Interpreting the wage elasticity causally. Wages may respond to hours (overtime pay, measurement error in hours, which also enters the wage as earnings divided by hours). The serious literature instruments the wage.

Exercise 1.1 — Estimating the elasticity of intertemporal substitution from the Euler equation

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real consumption realcons and ex-post real interest rate realint , 1959–2009. The log-linearized Euler equation is \(\Delta\log c_{t+1}=\text{const}+\psi\,r_t+\varepsilon_{t+1}\) , where \(\psi\) is the elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS). The realized real rate is measured with error and correlated with the expectational error, so use instrumental variables (Hall, 1988). Estimate \(\psi\) by OLS. Estimate it by 2SLS, instrumenting \(r_t\) with variables dated \(t-2\) and \(t-3\) (lagged real rate, inflation and consumption growth). Report the first-stage \(F\) . What does the estimate imply for the coefficient of relative risk aversion if preferences are CRRA ( \(\gamma=1/\psi\) )? Output: OLS and 2SLS both give an EIS of about 0.2–0.3, and the 2SLS confidence interval includes zero. This is Hall's (1988) classic finding: aggregate consumption growth responds little to the real interest rate, so the EIS is small (and, under CRRA, risk aversion \(1/\psi\) would be large, around 4 or more). The first-stage \(F\) of about 13 is only moderately strong. Instruments dated \(t-2\) and earlier are used because time aggregation of quarterly consumption makes \(t-1\) instruments invalid. Many macro models assume an EIS near 0.5–1, which is hard to reconcile with this evidence.

Exercise 1.2 — Is consumption a random walk? The Campbell–Mankiw test

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real consumption and real disposable income. Hall's (1978) permanent-income hypothesis implies that consumption growth is unpredictable. Campbell and Mankiw (1989) nest it in \(\Delta\log c_t=\mu+\lambda\,\Delta\log y_t+\varepsilon_t\) , where \(\lambda\) is the share of income going to "rule-of-thumb" (hand-to-mouth) consumers. Estimate \(\lambda\) by OLS and by 2SLS, using lags 2–4 of income growth, consumption growth and the change in the T-bill rate as instruments. Test \(\lambda=0\) . What does the estimate say about the importance of hand-to-mouth households — a central ingredient of TANK and HANK models (Lectures 12–13)? Output: The 2SLS estimate of \(\lambda\) is about 0.65 and strongly significant, so consumption growth is far from unpredictable: predictable income growth passes into consumption. Taken at face value, around half or more of income goes to rule-of-thumb consumers — Campbell and Mankiw (1989) found about 0.5. Two warnings: the first-stage \(F\) of about 4 signals weak instruments (Lecture 5 of Econometrics), so the 2SLS point estimate is unreliable and weak-IV-robust inference is needed; and the over-identification test rejects, so the instruments disagree. The qualitative conclusion — a sizable hand-to-mouth share — is what motivates TANK and HANK models.

Exercise 2.1 — Building a capital stock and a Solow residual for the U.S.

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real GDP, real investment, unemployment rate and population, 1959–2009. Build a capital stock with the perpetual-inventory method \(K_{t+1}=(1-\delta)K_t+I_t\) , \(\delta=0.025\) per quarter, initializing \(K_0=I_0/(g+\delta)\) with \(g\) the average investment growth rate. Proxy labor input by employment, \(N_t=pop_t(1-u_t/100)\) , and compute the Solow residual \(\log z_t=\log Y_t-\alpha\log K_t-(1-\alpha)\log N_t\) with \(\alpha=1/3\) . Decompose average annual growth of output per worker into capital deepening and TFP growth, before and after 1973. Output: The perpetual-inventory capital stock rises relative to output over the sample. Growth accounting shows the post-1973 productivity slowdown: output per worker growth fell from about 2.8% to 1.9% a year, and almost all of the decline is TFP (from about 1.7% to 0.9%), while the contribution of capital deepening was stable at about 1 point. This replicates the classic finding with a crude employment measure; using hours and a capital measure that excludes residential structures changes the levels but not the story.

Exercise 2.2 — Tobin's q: does market value predict investment?

Data: grunfeld (statsmodels) — investment, market value and capital stock of 11 large U.S. firms, 1935–1954. With adjustment costs, investment depends on Tobin's \(q\) . Grunfeld's data give firm value \(V\) and capital \(K\) ; use \(V/K\) as a (crude) average- \(q\) proxy. Regress the investment rate \(I_{it}/K_{it}\) on lagged \(V/K\) , with firm fixed effects. Interpret the coefficient as \(1/\phi\) for quadratic adjustment costs \(\frac{\phi}{2}(I/K)^2K\) , and report the implied \(\phi\) . Why does the \(q\) theory typically explain investment poorly, and what does measurement error in \(q\) do to the coefficient? Output: The coefficient on lagged \(V/K\) is positive and significant, but small: it implies an adjustment-cost parameter of about 34, so firms would take decades to close a gap between \(q\) and one. That is the well-known failure of \(q\) theory — implausibly slow adjustment. One reason is measurement: \(V/K\) is average q, the relevant concept is marginal q, and market values are noisy, so the coefficient is attenuated (Erickson and Whited, 2000). With 11 firms, the clustered standard error also rests on few clusters.

Exercise 3.1 — The Ramsey model: steady state, saddle path and transition

Data: Calibrated to standard annual U.S. values: \(\alpha=1/3\) , \(\beta=0.96\) , \(\delta=0.08\) , \(\sigma=2\) . In discrete time, the resource constraint is \(k_{t+1}=k_t^{\alpha}+(1-\delta)k_t-c_t\) and the Euler equation is \(c_t^{-\sigma}=\beta c_{t+1}^{-\sigma}(\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}+1-\delta)\) . Compute the steady state \((k^*,c^*)\) and the saving rate. Find the saddle path by shooting : from \(k_0=0.5k^*\) , search for the initial \(c_0\) such that the path converges to the steady state (bisection on \(c_0\) ). Report the transition: how many years until capital closes half of the gap? How does the saving rate evolve along the path? Output: The steady-state saving rate is about 22%. Shooting finds the unique initial consumption (about 75% of its steady-state level) that puts the economy on the saddle path; any other choice leads to capital exhaustion or oversaving. Capital closes half the gap in about 9 years. Along the path, the saving rate falls from 26.5% toward 22%: with \(\sigma=2\) , poor households save more while the return to capital is high. Unlike in Solow, the saving rate is an outcome, not a parameter.

Exercise 4.1 — U.S. business-cycle facts with the HP filter

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real GDP, consumption, investment and government spending, 1959–2009. HP-filter the logs of real GDP, consumption, investment and government spending ( \(\lambda=1600\) ). Report for each the standard deviation (%), the standard deviation relative to output, the correlation with output, and the first-order autocorrelation. Which facts must a business-cycle model reproduce? Which of them does the basic RBC model struggle with? Output: These are the classic stylized facts: investment is about 4.7 times as volatile as output and strongly procyclical; consumption is smoother (0.8 times as volatile) and procyclical; employment is procyclical and persistent; government spending is essentially acyclical; all series are persistent (autocorrelations of 0.8–0.9). A business-cycle model must reproduce these relative volatilities and co-movements. The basic RBC model does well on investment and consumption, but it generates too little employment volatility and too much correlation between productivity and output.

Exercise 4.2 — Simulating the stochastic growth model with full depreciation

Data: TFP process estimated from the U.S. Solow residual of Lecture 2 (rebuilt here); model calibration \(\alpha=1/3\) , \(\beta=0.99\) . With log utility and full depreciation (Brock–Mirman), the policy functions are known in closed form: \(k_{t+1}=\alpha\beta z_tk_t^{\alpha}\) and \(c_t=(1-\alpha\beta)z_tk_t^{\alpha}\) . Re-estimate an AR(1) for the (linearly detrended) U.S. log Solow residual. Simulate the model for 10,000 quarters, HP-filter simulated output, consumption and investment, and compute the same moments as in the previous exercise. Compare with the data. Why does the model make consumption exactly as volatile as output, and what feature of the full RBC model (with \(\delta<1\) ) fixes this? Output: The estimated TFP process ( \(\rho\approx0.96\) , \(\sigma\approx0.7\%\) ) is close to the standard RBC calibration. But with full depreciation and log utility, consumption and investment are constant shares of output, so all three series have exactly the same volatility and are perfectly correlated — far from the data, where investment is about six times as volatile as consumption. With \(\delta<1\) , capital is a durable stock: households smooth consumption by letting investment absorb shocks, which generates the observed volatility ranking. The simple model is useful as a check on numerical methods (Lecture 10), not as a model of the cycle.

Exercise 5.1 — From price stickiness to the slope of the Phillips curve

Data: Calibration: \(\beta=0.99\) , \(\sigma=1\) , \(\varphi=1\) (Galí, 2015, ch. 3, without strategic complementarities). In the Calvo model, a share \(\theta\) of firms cannot reset prices each quarter, so the average price duration is \(1/(1-\theta)\) , and the NKPC slope on the output gap is \(\kappa=\frac{(1-\theta)(1-\beta\theta)}{\theta}(\sigma+\varphi)\) . Compute \(\kappa\) for average durations of 2, 3, 4, 6 and 8 quarters. Micro evidence (Bils and Klenow, 2004; Nakamura and Steinsson, 2008) suggests durations of 4–11 months for regular prices. What range of \(\kappa\) does that imply? Invert the mapping numerically: what duration is implied by a slope of \(\kappa=0.01\) , roughly what many macro estimates find? Output: The slope \(\kappa\) falls steeply with price duration: from 1.0 at 2 quarters to 0.17 at one year and 0.04 at two years. Micro evidence on regular price durations of 4–11 months implies \(\kappa\) of 0.2 or more. Yet a slope of 0.01, typical of aggregate estimates, would require prices to stay fixed for almost four years on average. This micro–macro gap is why models add strategic complementarities (real rigidities), which flatten the Phillips curve for a given frequency of price changes.

Replace \(E_t\pi_{t+1}\) with realized \(\pi_{t+1}\) and estimate by 2SLS with instruments dated \(t-1\) and earlier (lags 1–4 of inflation, lags 1–2 of the gap and of the T-bill rate). Output: The estimates put most weight on expected future inflation ( \(\gamma_f\approx0.85\) ) and little on lagged inflation, with the two summing to slightly below one. The slope on the unemployment gap is positive but imprecise — not significantly different from zero: the Phillips curve is flat and poorly identified. The first-stage \(F\) of about 13 looks acceptable, but NKPC estimates are notoriously sensitive to the instrument set, the gap measure and the sample, because lagged variables predict future inflation only weakly once current inflation is controlled for (Mavroeidis, Plagborg-Møller and Stock, 2014). Exercise 6.1 — Solving the three-equation NK model by undetermined coefficients

Data: Calibration following Galí (2015, ch. 3): \(\beta=0.99\) , \(\sigma=1\) , \(\kappa=0.17\) , \(\phi_\pi=1.5\) , \(\phi_y=0.125\) , monetary shock persistence \(\rho_v=0.5\) . The model: \(x_t=E_tx_{t+1}-\frac1\sigma(i_t-E_t\pi_{t+1})\) ; \(\pi_t=\beta E_t\pi_{t+1}+\kappa x_t\) ; \(i_t=\phi_\pi\pi_t+\phi_yx_t+v_t\) , \(v_t=\rho_vv_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) . Guess \(x_t=\psi_xv_t\) , \(\pi_t=\psi_\pi v_t\) , and solve for the coefficients with sympy . Compute impulse responses of the output gap, inflation, the nominal rate and the real rate to a 25 basis-point shock (annualized: 1 percentage point). Repeat for shock persistence \(\rho_v=0.8\) and \(0.9\) . Why can the nominal rate fall after a contractionary monetary shock, while the real rate rises? Output: A 25 basis-point (1 point annualized) contractionary shock lowers the output gap by about 0.26% and annualized inflation by about 0.35 points on impact; both responses decay at the shock's rate \(\rho_v\) . The real rate rises by more than the nominal rate because expected inflation falls. With more persistent shocks, the fall in inflation and output is so large that the Taylor rule's endogenous response lowers the nominal rate on impact even though policy is tighter: with \(\rho_v=0.8\) , the nominal rate falls by about 0.5 points while the real rate still rises. The nominal interest rate is a poor indicator of the policy stance.

Exercise 6.2 — The Taylor principle and determinacy

Data: Same calibration ( \(\beta=0.99\) , \(\sigma=1\) , \(\kappa=0.17\) ). Write the model without shocks as \(E_tz_{t+1}=Mz_t\) with \(z_t=(x_t,\pi_t)'\) . With two forward-looking variables, the equilibrium is determinate when both eigenvalues of \(M\) lie outside the unit circle. Derive \(M\) and compute its eigenvalues on a grid of \(\phi_\pi\in[0,3]\) for \(\phi_y=0\) and \(\phi_y=0.5\) . Find the critical \(\phi_\pi\) numerically and compare with the analytical condition \(\kappa(\phi_\pi-1)+(1-\beta)\phi_y>0\) (Bullard and Mitra, 2002). Interpret: why does the central bank have to raise the nominal rate more than one-for-one with inflation? Output: With \(\phi_y=0\) , determinacy requires \(\phi_\pi>1\) — the Taylor principle — and the numerical boundary matches the Bullard–Mitra condition. Responding to the output gap relaxes it slightly: with \(\phi_y=0.5\) , \(\phi_\pi>0.97\) suffices, because in the long run a permanent rise in inflation also raises the output gap by \((1-\beta)/\kappa\) . Below the threshold, one eigenvalue lies inside the unit circle and sunspot equilibria exist: self-fulfilling inflation expectations are not ruled out, because the real rate falls when inflation rises.

Exercise 7.1 — Taylor rules before and after Volcker

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly 3-month T-bill rate, CPI inflation and real GDP. Clarida, Galí and Gertler (2000) argue that U.S. policy was "passive" ( \(\phi_\pi<1\) ) before 1979 and "active" ( \(\phi_\pi>1\) ) afterwards. Construct four-quarter inflation and the HP output gap. Estimate a Taylor rule with interest-rate smoothing, \(i_t=(1-\rho)(c+\phi_\pi\pi_t+\phi_xx_t)+\rho i_{t-1}+e_t\) , by nonlinear least squares for 1960–1979 and 1987–2007. Report the long-run responses \(\phi_\pi,\phi_x\) with delta-method standard errors, and relate them to the determinacy condition of Lecture 6. Output: For 1960–79, the long-run inflation response is about 0.56, well below one: policy accommodated inflation, consistent with Clarida, Galí and Gertler (2000). For 1987–2007, this simple specification does not find \(\phi_\pi>1\) : the point estimate is similar but has a huge standard error (0.73), because inflation varied little after the mid-1980s and smoothing is high, so the inflation response is poorly identified. CGG use expected future inflation (GMM), the GDP deflator, the federal funds rate and a different gap measure, and find about 2. Specification choices matter a lot for this famous result — an honest lesson.
Lecture 7: Monetary Policy: Rules, Commitment, and the Effective Lower Bound
Exercise 7.2 — The effective lower bound in 2009: what did a Taylor rule prescribe?

Data: macrodata — U.S. data through 2009Q3. Compute the rate prescribed by Taylor's (1993) original rule, \(i_t=1+1.5\pi_t+0.5x_t\) , for each quarter of 2008–2009, using an output gap whose trend is estimated only through 2007 (to avoid the end-point problem of the HP filter). Compare it with the actual T-bill rate and with the rule estimated on 1987–2007 in the previous exercise. In which quarter did the prescribed rate first fall below zero, and how negative did it get? What tools did the Fed use when the rule called for negative rates (forward guidance, asset purchases), and how does a "shadow rate" summarize them? Output: Taylor's 1993 rule would have called for a negative policy rate from 2008Q4, reaching about −5.8% in 2009Q2 — close to estimates in the literature (Rudebusch, 2009). The rule estimated on 1987–2007 gives absurd values (below −18%), because its large output-gap coefficient was estimated in a period of small gaps — an extrapolation warning. The T-bill rate was stuck near zero. With conventional policy constrained, the Fed turned to forward guidance and large-scale asset purchases; "shadow rate" estimates (Wu and Xia, 2016) translate their effect into an equivalent negative policy rate of a few percent.

Exercise 8.1 — Debt dynamics and the debt-stabilizing primary surplus

Output: Over this sample, the average real T-bill rate (about 1%) was well below real growth (about 3%), so \(r-g\approx-2\) points. With \(r<g\) , debt stabilizes even with a primary deficit : about 1.2% of GDP at a 60% debt ratio. With a balanced primary budget, debt falls from 60% to about 33% in 30 years. Exercise 8.2 — A government-spending multiplier from a recursive VAR

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real government spending, real GDP and real consumption, per capita, 1959–2009. Following Blanchard and Perotti (2002), assume government spending does not respond to output within the quarter, so spending is ordered first in a Cholesky VAR. Estimate a VAR(4) in log real per-capita government spending, GDP and consumption, with a linear trend. Compute the impulse responses to a spending shock, and convert them into dollar multipliers using the sample average ratios \(Y/G\) and \(C/G\) . Report the impact and cumulative 8-quarter multipliers \(\sum\Delta Y/\sum\Delta G\) . Does consumption rise or fall? Output: On impact, output rises by about $0.50 per dollar of spending, but the effect turns negative within a few quarters, and the cumulative 8-quarter multiplier is slightly negative, with consumption falling. That is lower than Blanchard and Perotti's (2002) estimates (around 1), which use tax data, quarterly fiscal series and a different trend specification. Exercise 10.1 — Linearize the Ramsey model and solve it with the QZ decomposition

Data: Calibration as in Lecture 3: \(\alpha=1/3\) , \(\beta=0.96\) , \(\delta=0.08\) , \(\sigma=2\) . Exercise 10.2 — Value function iteration versus the exact solution

Data: Brock–Mirman model: log utility, full depreciation, \(\alpha=1/3\) , \(\beta=0.96\) — the exact policy \(k'=\alpha\beta k^{\alpha}\) is known. Solve the deterministic model \(V(k)=\max_{k'}\{\log(k^{\alpha}-k')+\beta V(k')\}\) by value function iteration on grids of 100, 300 and 1,000 points (vectorized). Report the number of iterations, computing time, and the maximum error of the policy function relative to the exact \(k'=\alpha\beta k^{\alpha}\) . Why does the error fall only slowly with the number of grid points, and what methods (interpolation, endogenous grids — Lecture 12) do better? Output: VFI converges in about 450 iterations regardless of the grid, because the contraction rate is \(\beta\) . Output: EGM converges in a few hundred iterations without any root-finding: inverting the Euler equation on a grid of next-period assets gives consumption directly. The stationary distribution has a wealth Gini of about 0.49 — far below the U.S. value of about 0.8 — and only 1.6% of households at the borrowing constraint. The average annual MPC is 0.08, close to the permanent-income benchmark. One-asset models with these parameters generate too few constrained households and too little wealth inequality; HANK models fix this with two assets (Kaplan, Moll and Violante, 2018) or with a lower discount factor.

Exercise 12.2 — Hand-to-mouth households and wealth inequality in U.S. survey data

Data: 401ksubs — 9,275 U.S. households, 1991 SIPP: family income inc and net total financial assets nettfa (thousands of dollars). Kaplan, Violante and Weidner (2014) classify households as hand-to-mouth (HtM) if their liquid wealth is below about half a month of income. Compute the share of households with non-positive financial assets, and the share with financial assets below half a month of income. Compute the Gini coefficient of financial wealth (allowing negative values) and the share of financial wealth held by the top 10%. Break the HtM share down by income quintile. Why does the presence of HtM households at all income levels matter for fiscal policy? Output: In these 1991 data, 35% of households have non-positive financial assets, and 46% hold less than half a month of income in financial assets — somewhat above Kaplan, Violante and Weidner's (2014) estimate of about one third, which uses a broader liquid-wealth measure and later survey years. Financial wealth is extremely concentrated (Gini 0.98, top 10% share 72%; the mean is ten times the median). The hand-to-mouth share falls with income but remains above 20% even in the top income quintile. Those are the "wealthy hand-to-mouth" — households with illiquid wealth (housing, pensions) but little cash — which is why transfers raise spending even among middle-income households.

Exercise 13.1 — Who spends a transfer? MPCs across the wealth distribution

Data: The stationary Aiyagari distribution from Lecture 12's exercise (re-solved here so the code is self-contained). Re-solve the Aiyagari household and its stationary distribution (same calibration). Compute the average MPC by wealth quintile. By how much does targeting raise the spending response per dollar? Output: MPCs fall steeply with wealth: about 0.20 in the poorest wealth quintile and about 0.04 at the top.
