Exercise 13.2 — A TANK multiplier with a data-based hand-to-mouth share

Data: 401ksubs — the share of hand-to-mouth households from Lecture 12's exercise. In a two-agent New Keynesian (TANK) model with a share \(\lambda\) of hand-to-mouth households who consume their income, and Ricardian households who smooth consumption, a deficit-financed transfer \(T\) given equally to all households has a first-round output effect of approximately \(\Delta Y=\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda\,\mu}T\) under a fixed real rate, where \(\mu\) is the share of income that HtM households receive relative to their population share (set \(\mu=1\) for simplicity) — a simple "Keynesian cross" among HtM households. Compute the HtM share \(\lambda\) from the data (half-month-of-income rule) and from the stricter "non-positive wealth" rule. Compute the transfer multiplier \(\Delta Y/T\) for each, and for \(\lambda\in\{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\}\) .

Exercise 13.2 — A TANK multiplier with a data-based hand-to-mouth share

Compare with the Campbell–Mankiw \(\lambda\) estimated in Lecture 1's exercise. Why do HANK models with wealthy hand-to-mouth households give larger multipliers than this simple TANK calculation? Output: With the half-month-of-income rule ( \(\lambda\approx0.46\) ), the stylized transfer multiplier is about 0.87; with the stricter rule ( \(\lambda\approx0.35\) ), about 0.54. The multiplier is convex in \(\lambda\) because hand-to-mouth households spend the income created by each other's spending. Campbell and Mankiw's \(\lambda\) (Lecture 1) points to a similar range. HANK models produce larger and more persistent effects than this calculation because many households are only partly constrained, MPCs are high for several quarters, and the "intertemporal Keynesian cross" works through future income too (Auclert, Rognlie and Straub, 2024).

Exercise 14.1 — Local projections of a monetary shock measured as a Taylor-rule residual

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly data, 1960–2007. Estimate a Taylor rule with smoothing on 1960–2007 (as in Lecture 7) including two lags of inflation and the output gap, and treat its residual as a monetary policy shock (a Romer–Romer-style shortcut). Estimate local projections of the unemployment rate and inflation on the shock for \(h=0,\dots,12\) quarters, controlling for four lags of unemployment, inflation and the T-bill rate. Use HAC standard errors. Report the responses to a 100 bp shock. Do you find a price puzzle? What identification assumption is doing the work? Output: The Taylor-rule residual is a crude shock: the rule explains 92% of the T-bill rate, and the residual still contains the Fed's reaction to information not in the rule. The responses show it. Unemployment falls for the first year after a "tightening" and rises only after about two years, peaking near 0.12 points; inflation is flat at first and then falls by about 0.6 points after three years. The early unemployment response has the wrong sign, a symptom of residual endogeneity — the same problem as the price puzzle. Narrative (Romer and Romer, 2004) or high-frequency shocks (Gertler and Karadi, 2015) give cleaner identification. The identification assumption here is that the residual is uncorrelated with all other shocks affecting the outcomes.

Exercise 14.2 — Okun's law: estimation and parameter stability

Data: okun — U.S. annual real GDP growth pcrgdp and the change in the unemployment rate cunem , 1959–2005. Estimate Okun's law \(\Delta u_t=a+b\,g_t+e_t\) . Compute the implied "normal" growth rate \(-a/b\) at which unemployment is stable, with a delta-method standard error. Test whether \(b=-0.5\) (the textbook rule of thumb). Test for a break in 1983 with a Chow test, and estimate the two subsamples. Has the relationship changed? Output: Each extra point of GDP growth lowers unemployment by about 0.38 points, and unemployment is stable when growth is about 3.3%. The textbook coefficient of −0.5 is rejected. The Chow test detects a break in 1983: the slope is similar across subperiods, but the growth rate needed to keep unemployment stable fell from about 3.9% to 2.9%, reflecting slower labor-force and productivity growth. The break is in the intercept , which is why rule-of-thumb versions of Okun's law need periodic updating.

Exercise 1.1 — From discrete to continuous compounding with real interest rates

Data: intqrt — U.S. 3-month Treasury bill yields ( r3 , % per year), quarterly. Take the average T-bill yield \(r\) in the sample. Compute the growth factor of $1 after one year, \((1+r/n)^n\) , for \(n=1,2,4,12,365,10^6\) . Show numerically that the sequence converges to \(e^r\) , and that the error behaves like \(r^2e^r/(2n)\) . Use sympy to prove the limit symbolically. Why does the choice between annual and continuous compounding matter more when rates are high (as in 1981)? Output: At the sample's average yield of 6.45%, the growth factor rises from 1.0645 (annual compounding) toward \(e^{0.0645}=1.0666\) . The gap shrinks in proportion to \(1/n\) , exactly as the second-order expansion \(r^2e^r/(2n)\) predicts: doubling \(n\) halves the error. sympy confirms \(\lim_{n\to\infty}(1+x/n)^n=e^x\) . The difference between annual and continuous compounding is of order \(r^2/2\) , so it grows quadratically with the rate: at the 16.5% peak of 1981 it was 1.4 percentage points a year — enough to matter when quoting or comparing yields.

Exercise 1.2 — Arc elasticity converges to point elasticity: demand for eco-labeled apples

Data: apple — 660 households in a 1990s survey that randomly assigned prices of eco-labeled ( ecoprc ) and regular ( regprc ) apples and recorded pounds demanded ( ecolbs ). Estimate an exponential demand curve \(E[q\mid p]=\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1p_{eco}+\beta_2p_{reg})\) by Poisson regression (which handles the many zero purchases). At the mean prices, compute the arc elasticity \(\frac{\Delta q/q}{\Delta p/p}\) for price changes of 20, 10, 1 and 0.1 cents. Show that it converges to the point elasticity \(\beta_1p\) as \(\Delta p\to0\) , and that the error is roughly proportional to \(\Delta p\) . Why would the same exercise with a linear demand curve show no convergence at all? Output: At mean prices, the point elasticity of demand for eco-labeled apples is about \(-2.2\) : demand is elastic. The arc elasticity approaches it as the price step shrinks, and the error divided by \(\Delta p\) settles near a constant: the error is first order in \(\Delta p\) , as a Taylor expansion of \(e^{\beta_1\Delta p}\) predicts. For a linear demand curve, the one-sided arc elasticity \((\Delta q/q)/(\Delta p/p)=\beta_1p/q\) is exact for every step size, so there is nothing to converge — the last line shows the same number for 20 cents and 0.1 cent. Prices were randomized in this survey, so the slope can be read as a causal demand response for stated purchases.

A sequence \((a_n)\) converges to \(L\) if for every \(\varepsilon>0\) , there exists \(N\) such that \(n\ge N\) implies \(|a_n-L|<\varepsilon\) . Limits are unique and convergent sequences are bounded. A sequence is Cauchy if its terms become arbitrarily close to each other; completeness of \(\mathbb R\) ensures every Cauchy sequence converges.

Every monotone increasing sequence bounded above converges to its supremum. Every monotone decreasing sequence bounded below converges to its infimum. This result is useful for recursive sequences and iterative economic processes.

The series \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) converges when its partial sums \(S_N=\sum_{n=1}^N a_n\) converge. A necessary condition is \(a_n\to0\) , but this is not sufficient. The geometric series has sum \(a/(1-r)\) for \(|r|<1\) .

The p-series \(\sum n^{-p}\) converges iff \(p>1\) . Use comparison and limit comparison for nonnegative terms. The ratio test uses \(L=\lim|a_{n+1}/a_n|\) : convergence if \(L<1\) , divergence if \(L>1\) , and no conclusion if \(L=1\) . The root test uses \(\limsup |a_n|^{1/n}\) . Alternating-series convergence follows when positive terms decrease to zero.

Absolute convergence means \(\sum|a_n|\) converges and implies convergence of \(\sum a_n\) . Conditional convergence occurs when the original series converges but its absolute-value series diverges. Rearrangement can change the sum of a conditionally convergent real series.

A power series \(\sum a_n(x-c)^n\) has radius of convergence \(R\) . It converges absolutely for \(|x-c|<R\) , diverges for \(|x-c|>R\) , and endpoints must be checked separately. Termwise differentiation and integration are valid inside the interval of convergence.

Exercise 2.1 — Log differences versus percent changes: a Taylor series for growth rates

Data: macrodata (statsmodels) — U.S. quarterly real GDP and CPI, 1959–2009. Economists often measure growth as \(\Delta\log y\) instead of \(\Delta y/y\) . Since \(\log(1+g)=g-g^2/2+g^3/3-\dots\) , the two differ at second order. Compute quarterly percent changes and log differences of real GDP and of the CPI. Report the largest gap between them. Show that adding the second-order term, \(g-g^2/2\) , removes most of the gap. Annualize quarterly growth in two ways — \(4\times\) the quarterly rate and \((1+g)^4-1\) — and compare for the most extreme quarter. Output: Quarterly changes are small, so log differences and percent changes differ by at most 0.08 percentage points. Adding the \(-g^2/2\) term cuts the gap by a factor of about 40, and the cubic term by another 30 — the Taylor series converges fast for small \(g\) . Annualization matters more: for GDP's strongest quarter, simple multiplication by four gives 15.7%, true compounding 16.7%, and four times the log difference 15.4%. Always state which convention a reported growth rate uses.

Data: intqrt — U.S. Treasury yields; we use the sample's average 12-month yield r12 as a discount rate. A perpetuity pays $100 per year forever. Write its value as a geometric series and sum it with sympy . Compute the partial sums for 10, 30 and 100 years. How many years of payments make up 90% of the perpetuity's value? Output: sympy sums the geometric series to \(100/R\) , about $1,444 at a 6.9% discount rate. Data: macrodata — annual averages of U.S. real GDP, 2000–2008, used to give a stylized project realistic cash flows that grow with the economy. A project costs $1,000 today and returns cash flows \(C_1,\dots,C_9\) proportional to annual U.S. real GDP growth paths. The IRR solves \(NPV(r)=-1000+\sum_t C_t/(1+r)^t=0\) . Derive \(NPV'(r)\) analytically. Implement Newton's method \(r_{k+1}=r_k-NPV(r_k)/NPV'(r_k)\) from \(r_0=0\) . Print each iteration and show quadratic convergence (the number of correct digits roughly doubles). Check with scipy.optimize.brentq . Output: Newton's method converges to the IRR of about 8.27% in five iterations. The errors fall from \(10^{-2}\) to \(10^{-3}\) , \(10^{-6}\) , \(10^{-11}\) and machine precision: the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step, which is quadratic convergence. It works so well here because \(NPV(r)\) is smooth, decreasing and convex. Data: volat — monthly S&P 500 returns ( rsp500 , % per year) and 3-month T-bill yields ( i3 ), 1947–1993. Using the empirical distribution of monthly gross returns \(R\) , compute the exact certainty equivalent \(CE=u^{-1}(E[u(R)])\) and risk premium \(E[R]-CE\) for \(\gamma=2,5,10\) . Compare with the second-order Taylor (Arrow–Pratt) approximation \(\pi\approx\tfrac12\gamma\operatorname{Var}(R)/E[R]\) (relative risk aversion form). The table tells a familiar story: the 1960s had the fastest real growth; the 1970s had nominal growth above 10% driven by inflation of almost 7%; and per-capita growth slowed steadily to about 1.4% in the 2000s. Exercise 7.2 — Partial elasticities and a total derivative in a hedonic price function

Data: hprice1 — 88 house sales. Fit \(\log(price)=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(sqrft)+\beta_2 bdrms+\beta_3\log(lotsize)\) . Compute the partial effect of one more bedroom, holding square footage fixed. Why can it be small or even negative? In the data, bigger houses have more bedrooms: estimate the auxiliary relation \(bdrms=\gamma_0+\gamma_1\log(sqrft)\) . Use the chain rule to compute the total derivative \(\frac{d\log price}{d\log sqrft}=\beta_1+\beta_2\gamma_1\) and compare it with the slope from regressing \(\log price\) on \(\log sqrft\) and \(\log lotsize\) only. Output: Holding size fixed, one more bedroom raises price by only about 4% (and insignificantly): at a fixed floor area, an extra bedroom means smaller rooms. But bigger houses have more bedrooms, so the total derivative of log price with respect to log size, \(\beta_1+\beta_2\gamma_1\approx0.76\) , exceeds the partial effect of 0.70. It equals the short-regression slope exactly — the chain rule here is the omitted-variable bias formula of Econometrics Lecture 3, read the other way round.

Let \(f(x,y)=-(x^2+2y^2)+4x+8y\) . The gradient is \((-2x+4,-4y+8)'\) , giving \((2,2)\) . The Hessian is diagonal with entries -2 and -4, so it is negative definite and the point is a strict global maximum.

Exercise 8.1 — Least squares as unconstrained optimization: gradient and Hessian checks

Data: wage1 — 526 workers. Write the sum of squared residuals \(SSR(b)=(y-Xb)'(y-Xb)\) for \(\log wage\) on \((1, educ, exper, tenure)\) . Minimize it numerically with BFGS from \(b=0\) , supplying the analytic gradient \(-2X'(y-Xb)\) . At the optimum, check that the gradient is (numerically) zero and that the Hessian \(2X'X\) is positive definite (eigenvalues). Report the condition number and explain what it means for numerical accuracy. Compare with the closed-form solution. Output: BFGS converges to the closed-form OLS solution in five iterations, and the gradient is zero to 12 decimals. The Hessian \(2X'X\) is positive definite, so the SSR is strictly convex and the minimum is unique. Its condition number of about 18,000 comes from regressors on very different scales (a constant, years of education, years of tenure). Standardizing the regressors reduces it to about 4, which is why numerical optimizers and ridge-type penalties work better on standardized data. Here the problem is still well conditioned enough for double-precision arithmetic.

Exercise 8.2 — Newton–Raphson for a logit likelihood, by hand

Data: mroz — 753 married women; inlf = labor force participation. Write the logit log-likelihood \(\ell(\beta)=\sum_i[y_i x_i'\beta-\log(1+e^{x_i'\beta})]\) , its gradient \(X'(y-p)\) and Hessian \(-X'WX\) with \(W=\text{diag}(p_i(1-p_i))\) . Run Newton–Raphson from \(\beta=0\) with regressors \((1, educ, exper, age, kidslt6, nwifeinc)\) . Print the log-likelihood and the gradient norm at each iteration. Show that the Hessian is negative definite everywhere (so \(\ell\) is globally concave and the maximum is unique), and compare with statsmodels . Output: Starting from zero, Newton–Raphson reaches the maximum in about five iterations: the gradient norm falls from 2,700 to \(10^{-10}\) , with the quadratic convergence typical near the optimum. The largest eigenvalue of the Hessian stays negative at every iterate: the logit log-likelihood is globally concave, because \(-X'WX\) is negative definite whenever \(X\) has full rank. The maximum is therefore unique, and the estimates match statsmodels (which uses the same algorithm) to every printed digit.

At an interior constrained optimum, the objective gradient is parallel to the constraint gradient. The objective's level surface is tangent to the constraint surface. The multiplier scales the constraint normal and measures the marginal value of relaxing the constraint under the stated sign convention.

Let \(V(c)=\max_{g(x)=c}f(x)\) . Under regularity and differentiability, the envelope result gives \(V'(c)=\lambda^*\) for the Lagrangian convention above. The multiplier is a local shadow value, not necessarily a globally constant effect.

The Hessian of the Lagrangian is evaluated along feasible directions tangent to the constraint. For a maximum, the quadratic form must be nonpositive on the tangent space; negative definiteness on nonzero feasible directions gives a strict local maximum. The unrestricted Hessian of the objective alone is not the correct constrained test.
Lecture 9: Equality Constraints and Lagrange Multipliers

Maximize \(x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\) subject to \(p_xx+p_yy=m\) , with positive prices and income. Using log utility gives FOCs \(\alpha/x=\lambda p_x\) and \((1-\alpha)/y=\lambda p_y\) , plus the budget equation. Solving yields \(x^*=\alpha m/p_x\) , \(y^*=(1-\alpha)m/p_y\) .

Derive FOCs for a two-variable equality-constrained problem. Interpret the multiplier under a clearly stated Lagrangian sign convention. Solve Cobb–Douglas utility maximization. Derive the expenditure-minimization dual problem. Explain why constrained SOCs use feasible directions.

Exercise 9.1 — Cobb–Douglas demand and the multiplier as marginal utility of income

Data: engel (statsmodels) — 235 Belgian working-class households (Engel's 19th-century data): annual income and food expenditure. A household maximizes \(u(f,o)=\alpha\log f+(1-\alpha)\log o\) subject to \(f+o=m\) (prices normalized to 1). Solve the Lagrangian with sympy for the demands and the multiplier \(\lambda\) . Calibrate \(\alpha\) to the average food budget share in Engel's data and compute the demands for the median household. Verify the envelope theorem numerically: \(dV/dm=\lambda\) , where \(V(m)\) is maximized utility. Cobb–Douglas implies a constant budget share. Check this against the data by regressing the food share on log income. What does Engel's law say? Output: The Lagrangian gives the familiar Cobb–Douglas demands \(f=\alpha m\) and \(o=(1-\alpha)m\) , with \(\lambda=1/m\) . The envelope theorem holds to six decimals: the multiplier is the marginal utility of income. Calibrated to Engel's data, the average household spends 66% of income on food. But Cobb–Douglas implies a constant budget share, and the data reject it: the food share falls by about 8.6 percentage points for each log point of income. That is Engel's law — food is a necessity — and it calls for non-homothetic preferences such as Stone–Geary.
Lecture 9: Equality Constraints and Lagrange Multipliers
Exercise 9.2 — Restricted least squares via a Lagrangian: constant returns in investment

Data: grunfeld (statsmodels) — 11 U.S. firms, 1935–1954. In \(\log I=\beta_0+\beta_1\log V+\beta_2\log K+u\) , impose \(\beta_1+\beta_2=1\) . Write the Lagrangian for minimizing SSR subject to \(R\beta=r\) and derive \(\tilde\beta=\widehat\beta-(X'X)^{-1}R'[R(X'X)^{-1}R']^{-1}(R\widehat\beta-r)\) . Compute \(\tilde\beta\) and the multiplier, and check the result by substituting the constraint into the regression. Compute the \(F\) statistic from the restricted and unrestricted SSRs. Interpret the size of the multiplier. Output: The unrestricted elasticities sum to 1.18. Imposing \(\beta_1+\beta_2=1\) through the Lagrangian reproduces the substitution method exactly. The large multiplier says the constraint is costly in terms of fit, and the \(F\) test rejects it decisively ( \(F\approx36\) ): investment rises more than proportionally with the scale of the firm. The Lagrange multiplier and the \(F\) statistic carry the same information, which is the logic of the LM test.

Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_j(x)\le0\) , \(j=1,\ldots,m\) , and equality constraints as needed. Define For a differentiable problem, KKT conditions include stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility \(\mu_j\ge0\) , and complementary slackness \(\mu_jg_j(x)=0\) .
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

An inactive constraint has \(g_j(x^*)<0\) , implying \(\mu_j=0\) . An active constraint binds and may have a positive multiplier. Complementary slackness links scarcity values to binding restrictions. Multipliers are local shadow prices under regularity.
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

KKT conditions are not automatically necessary for every nonlinear program. Conditions such as LICQ or an appropriate weaker qualification ensure the existence of multipliers at a local optimum. State the qualification used rather than treating KKT as universally necessary.
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

For a convex minimization problem—convex objective and convex feasible set—any feasible KKT point is globally optimal. Strict convexity can give uniqueness. In nonconvex problems, KKT points may be local minima, maxima, or saddle points.
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

Capacity, non-negativity, borrowing, labor-supply, and resource constraints generate inequality restrictions. A binding resource constraint can have a positive shadow value; a slack resource constraint has zero multiplier under complementary slackness.
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

Minimize \((x-3)^2\) subject to \(x\le2\) . Write \(g(x)=x-2\le0\) . The constrained optimum is \(x^*=2\) , with multiplier \(\mu=2\) , satisfying stationarity \(2(x-3)+\mu=0\) , feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness.
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions

State all KKT conditions for a problem with two inequalities. Identify active constraints in a numerical solution. Solve a one-dimensional constrained quadratic. Explain the role of LICQ. State conditions under which KKT conditions are sufficient for global optimality.

Exercise 10.1 — Stocks or bills? A portfolio choice with no borrowing and no short sales

Data: volat — monthly S&P 500 returns and 3-month T-bill yields, 1947–1993. A mean–variance investor chooses the share \(w\) in stocks (the rest in T-bills) to maximize \(w\mu_e-\tfrac{\gamma}{2}w^2\sigma^2\) , where \(\mu_e\) and \(\sigma^2\) are the mean and variance of the monthly excess return, subject to \(0\le w\le1\) . Write the KKT conditions with multipliers for both bounds. Estimate \(\mu_e\) and \(\sigma\) from the data. Solve for \(w^*\) and the multipliers for \(\gamma=1,2,5,10\) . For which \(\gamma\) is the borrowing constraint \(w\le1\) binding, and what is its shadow value? Check complementary slackness. Output: Over 1947–1993, stocks earned about 0.6% a month over T-bills, with a Sharpe ratio of about 0.6 a year. That premium is so large relative to the risk that a mean–variance investor with \(\gamma\le5\) would like to borrow to hold more than 100% in stocks; with borrowing ruled out, the constraint \(w\le1\) binds. Its multiplier is the marginal gain from relaxing it and falls as risk aversion rises. At \(\gamma=10\) , the interior solution of about 52% is feasible, and both multipliers are zero. Complementary slackness holds in every case. (The large equity premium relative to risk is the "equity premium puzzle" of Mehra and Prescott, 1985.)
Lecture 10: Inequality Constraints and Karush–Kuhn–Tucker Conditions
Exercise 10.2 — Synthetic weights as a KKT problem

Data: statecrime (statsmodels) — U.S. states: % high-school graduates, % in poverty, % single-parent households, % urban. A synthetic-control-style problem: find non-negative weights summing to one so that a weighted average of other states matches California's characteristics as closely as possible: \(\min_w\|x_{CA}-X_0w\|^2\) s.t. \(w\ge0\) , \(\sum w=1\) . Solve it with scipy.optimize.minimize (SLSQP), using standardized characteristics. Report the states with positive weight, and the fit. Check the KKT conditions: for states with \(w_j=0\) , the gradient component must be at least as large as for states with \(w_j>0\) (whose gradient components are all equal, to the multiplier on the adding-up constraint). Output: Only two states get positive weight — Texas (57%) and Rhode Island (43%). Corner solutions with most weights at zero are typical of synthetic control. The synthetic unit matches California's poverty and single-parent shares well but not its very high urban share or low high-school graduation, because no convex combination of other states reaches those extremes. The KKT conditions hold: the gradient components of the two active states are equal (the common multiplier on the adding-up constraint), and every inactive state's gradient component is at least as large, so moving weight to it would not lower the loss.

Exercise 11.1 — Comparative statics of the Solow steady state with the implicit function theorem

Data: macrodata — U.S. investment share of GDP and population growth, used to calibrate the model. In the Solow model, steady-state capital per worker \(k^*\) solves \(F(k,s)=s\,k^{\alpha}-(n+\delta)k=0\) . Calibrate \(s\) as the average ratio of real investment to real GDP and \(n\) as average annual population growth; set \(\alpha=1/3\) , \(\delta=0.05\) . Solve for \(k^*\) numerically ( brentq ), without using the closed form. Use the implicit function theorem, \(dk^*/ds=-F_s/F_k\) , to compute the effect of a higher saving rate, and the elasticity \(\frac{dk^*}{ds}\frac{s}{k^*}\) . Compare with a finite difference and with the closed-form elasticity \(1/(1-\alpha)\) . Output: Calibrated to the U.S. (investment share 13%, population growth 1.1%), the numerical root matches the closed-form steady state. The implicit function theorem gives \(dk^*/ds=-F_s/F_k\) without solving for \(k^*\) explicitly, and it agrees with the finite difference. \(F_k<0\) at the steady state, which is both the condition for the IFT to apply and the condition for stability. The elasticity of steady-state capital with respect to the saving rate is exactly \(1/(1-\alpha)=1.5\) .
Lecture 11: Implicit and Inverse Function Theorems
Exercise 11.2 — Yield to maturity as an inverse function, and duration

Data: intqrt — U.S. 12-month Treasury yield (average, used as a reference yield). The price of a bond is a decreasing function of its yield, \(P(y)=\sum_t c_t/(1+y)^t\) . Its inverse \(y(P)\) is the yield to maturity. For a 10-year bond with a 6% annual coupon and face value 100, compute \(P\) at the average 12-month yield. Invert numerically: find \(y\) from \(P\) , and check that the round trip recovers the yield. By the inverse function theorem, \(dy/dP=1/P'(y)\) . Compute it, and the modified duration \(-P'(y)/P\) . Use duration to approximate the price change from a 1-point yield rise and compare with the exact change. Output: Because the price is strictly decreasing in the yield, the inverse function exists, and the numerical inversion recovers the yield to ten decimals. The inverse function theorem gives \(dy/dP=1/P'(y)\) : a $1 price fall raises the yield by about 15 basis points. Modified duration (7.2 years) predicts a 7.2% price fall for a 1-point yield rise, against an exact fall of 6.9%. The gap is convexity: the price–yield curve is convex, so duration overstates losses and understates gains (Finance, Lecture 7).

Exercise 12.1 — A bivariate normal probability by double integration

Data: econmath — ACT math scores and college GPA of 814 students. Fit a bivariate normal to (actmth, colgpa) . Compute \(P(\text{ACT math}\ge28,\ GPA\ge3.5)\) by numerical double integration of the density ( scipy.integrate.dblquad ). Check it with the bivariate normal CDF and with Monte Carlo integration (one million draws). Compare with the empirical frequency in the data. What does any gap say about the normal model? Output: Double integration, the CDF formula and Monte Carlo all give about 2.2% for the joint event. In the data, 3.2% of students (26 of 814) have both an ACT math score of 28 or more and a GPA of 3.5 or more — about 45% more than the normal model predicts. Exercise 12.2 — Change of variables: from log wages to wages

Data: wage1 — hourly wages. If \(Z=\log W\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) , the density of \(W=e^Z\) follows from the change-of-variables formula \(f_W(w)=f_Z(\log w)\,|dz/dw|=f_Z(\log w)/w\) . Output: sympy produces the lognormal density through the Jacobian \(1/w\) . Numerically it integrates to one, and its mean equals \(e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}\approx\$5.84\) , close to the sample mean of $5.90. The lognormal overstates the share of very low wages (16% below $3 against 12% in the data), because the 1976 minimum wage of $2.30 truncates the lower tail of actual wages. The change of variables is exact; the model's fit is the empirical question.

A differential equation relates an unknown function to its derivatives. A separable equation \(\dot x=a(x)b(t)\) can be rearranged and integrated when division is valid. A linear equation \(\dot x+p(t)x=q(t)\) uses integrating factor \(M(t)=e^{\int p(t)dt}\) .

For \(\dot x=Ax\) , solutions are governed by eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A\) . If all eigenvalues have negative real parts, the origin is asymptotically stable; if any eigenvalue has positive real part, it is unstable. Zero real parts require further analysis.

A steady state \(x^*\) solves \(f(x^*)=0\) . Local dynamics around it are approximated by \(\dot u=J_f(x^*)u\) , where \(u=x-x^*\) . Eigenvalues of the Jacobian determine local stability for hyperbolic steady states.

Capital accumulation may be written \(\dot k=s f(k)-(n+g+\delta)k\) . A steady state equates investment per effective worker with break-even investment. Local stability follows from the derivative of the dynamic law at the steady state.

For \(\dot k=sk^\alpha-\delta k\) , with \(0<\alpha<1\) , the positive steady state satisfies \(k^*=(s/\delta)^{1/(1-\alpha)}\) . The derivative is \(s\alpha k^{\alpha-1}-\delta\) , which is negative at the positive steady state, giving local asymptotic stability.

Solve a separable first-order ODE with an initial condition. Solve a linear ODE using an integrating factor. Classify roots of a second-order characteristic equation. Determine stability from a two-dimensional Jacobian. Derive and assess a capital-accumulation steady state.

Simulate ODE paths using numerical solvers. Compare analytical and numerical solutions; plot phase diagrams and trajectories near stable and unstable steady states.
Lecture 13: Differential Equations and Continuous-Time Dynamics
Exercise 13.1 — The continuous-time Solow model calibrated to the U.S.

Data: macrodata — U.S. investment share and population growth (calibration as in Lecture 11). Capital per worker follows \(\dot k=s\,k^{\alpha}-(n+\delta)k\) . Solve the ODE numerically with solve_ivp starting from half the steady-state capital. Linearize around \(k^*\) : \(\dot k\approx-\lambda(k-k^*)\) with \(\lambda=(1-\alpha)(n+\delta)\) . Compute the implied half-life \(\ln2/\lambda\) . Measure the half-life in the numerical solution. Why is it close but not identical to the linear prediction? Output: Starting at half the steady state, capital per worker closes 90% of the gap after about 40 years. Linearization predicts a half-life of 17.1 years; the numerical solution takes about 18.5. The linear approximation is accurate only near \(k^*\) : starting far below, the true dynamics are slower at the beginning in terms of the proportional gap, because \(\dot k/k=sk^{\alpha-1}-(n+\delta)\) is not linear in \(k\) . The calibrated convergence rate of about 4% a year is in the range of empirical estimates (2–3%) only roughly; a higher capital share brings it down.
Lecture 13: Differential Equations and Continuous-Time Dynamics
Exercise 13.2 — Exponential growth: fitting \(\dot y=gy\) to U.S. real GDP

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real GDP, 1959–2009. The solution of \(\dot y=gy\) is \(y(t)=y_0e^{gt}\) , so \(\log y\) is linear in \(t\) . Estimate \(g\) by regressing \(\log GDP\) on time (in years). Compute the implied doubling time \(\ln2/g\) and compare with the actual doubling time in the data. Plot (or tabulate) the deviation of log GDP from the fitted exponential path at business-cycle troughs (1975Q1, 1982Q4, 1991Q1, 2009Q2). Is the growth rate constant over 1959–2009? Compare \(g\) for 1959–1983 and 1984–2009. Output: Real GDP grew at about 3.2% a year on average, implying a doubling time of about 22 years. It actually doubled faster, in 18.5 years (by 1977), because growth was higher early in the sample: 3.4% a year in 1959–83 against 3.0% in 1984–2009. The constant-growth model is a first approximation. The deviations from trend at recession troughs grow over time, ending 10.6% below trend in 2009 — partly because of the deep recession and partly because the trend slowed, which a single exponential cannot capture.

Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics
A discrete dynamic process has form \(x_{t+1}=f(x_t)\) . A fixed point satisfies \(x^*=f(x^*)\) . The path depends on the initial condition and the global properties of \(f\) .
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics

For \(x_{t+1}=a+bx_t\) , if \(b\ne1\) , the fixed point is \(x^*=a/(1-b)\) . The solution is Thus convergence occurs iff \(|b|<1\) ; positive \(b\) gives monotone convergence, while negative \(b\) gives oscillatory convergence.
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics

For nonlinear \(x_{t+1}=f(x_t)\) , linearize around a fixed point: If \(|f'(x^*)|<1\) , the fixed point is locally asymptotically stable; if \(|f'(x^*)|>1\) , it is unstable. The boundary cases require higher-order analysis.
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics

For \(x_{t+1}=F(x_t)\) , the Jacobian at a fixed point determines local dynamics. If all eigenvalues have modulus below one, the fixed point is locally asymptotically stable; if any eigenvalue has modulus above one, it is unstable. Unit-modulus eigenvalues require additional analysis.
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics

Applications include cobweb price adjustment, debt dynamics, adaptive expectations, inventory adjustment, and discrete capital accumulation. Stability depends on adjustment parameters and the slope of the map, not merely on the existence of a steady state.
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics
For \(x_{t+1}=4+0.5x_t\) , the fixed point is 8 and \(x_t-8=0.5^t(x_0-8)\) . Every initial condition converges geometrically to 8.

Solve a first-order linear difference equation. Classify convergence for positive and negative slopes. Apply the derivative stability criterion to a nonlinear map. Determine stability of a two-dimensional linear system. Analyze a cobweb model under alternative supply and demand slopes.
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics

Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics
Exercise 14.1 — A first-order difference equation for unemployment

Data: phillips — U.S. annual unemployment, 1948–2003. Estimate \(u_t=a+bu_{t-1}+e_t\) by OLS. Find the fixed point \(u^*=a/(1-b)\) and check stability ( \(|b|<1\) ). Write the general solution \(u_t=u^*+b^t(u_0-u^*)\) and simulate the deterministic path from the 2003 level for 10 years. Plot the phase diagram: \(u_t\) against \(u_{t-1}\) with the 45° line. How many years until the gap halves? Output: The fitted equation has a fixed point at about 5.8% and a root of 0.74, so it is stable, and any gap closes by 26% a year — a half-life of 2.3 years. Starting from 6.0% in 2003, the deterministic path converges slowly to 5.8%. The deterministic solution describes the expected path only; the actual path is hit by new shocks every year (Econometrics Lecture 9).
Lecture 14: Difference Equations and Discrete-Time Dynamics
Exercise 14.2 — Business cycles from a second-order difference equation

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real GDP growth, 1959–2009. Samuelson's multiplier–accelerator model produces a second-order difference equation, \(y_t=a_1y_{t-1}+a_2y_{t-2}\) . Estimate an AR(2) for quarterly GDP growth (in deviations from the mean). Find the roots of the characteristic equation \(\lambda^2-a_1\lambda-a_2=0\) . Are they real or complex? Is the system stable? If complex, compute the implied cycle period \(2\pi/\theta\) where \(\lambda=re^{\pm i\theta}\) , and the damping factor \(r\) . Compute the impulse response for 16 quarters. Repeat for an AR(2) in the level of the unemployment rate ( unemp ). Which series shows a clearer cycle? Output: For GDP growth, both roots are real and small: shocks die out within two or three quarters with no oscillation. Growth rates have little persistence. The unemployment rate behaves differently: its roots are complex with modulus 0.83, so a shock produces a hump-shaped response that peaks after a few quarters and then decays with a cycle. The implied period of about 58 quarters is long, and the damping is strong, so the "cycle" is barely visible. Samuelson's oscillations exist, but the data favor damped, mostly monotone dynamics.

Prove \(\lim_{x\to2}(3x+1)=7\) using epsilon-delta. Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to0}(\sqrt{1+x}-1)/x\) . Construct examples of removable, jump, and infinite discontinuities. Guidance: For Question 1, choose \(\delta=\varepsilon/3\) , since \(|3x+1-7|=3|x-2|\) . For Question 2, rationalize the numerator before taking the limit.

Determine convergence of \(a_n=(2n+1)/(n+3)\) . Test \(\sum_{n=1}^\infty1/[n(n+1)]\) and find its sum. Determine absolute or conditional convergence of \(\sum(-1)^{n+1}/n\) . Guidance: Use the sequence limit for Question 1. For Question 2, use partial fractions and telescoping. For Question 3, apply the alternating-series test and separately test absolute convergence.

Differentiate \(x^2e^{3x}\) . Differentiate \(\log(1+x^2)\) . Use the mean value theorem to prove a monotonicity result. Guidance: Apply product and chain rules; state the interval and regularity assumptions for the theorem.

Obtain the second-order Taylor polynomial of \(e^x\) at zero. Find and classify stationary points of \(f(x)=x^3-3x\) . Maximize \(20q-q^2-16\) over \(q\ge0\) . Guidance: Solve the FOC, apply the SOC, and compare with boundary values when the domain is constrained.

Evaluate \(\int_0^1xe^{x^2}dx\) . Evaluate \(\int xe^x dx\) . Determine when \(\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx\) converges. Guidance: Use substitution, integration by parts, and an improper-integral limit, respectively.

Question 1 (10 marks). True, false or uncertain? Explain in at most three sentences each. (a) "If \(E[Xu]=0\) , then OLS is unbiased." (b) "Robust standard errors correct for omitted-variable bias." (c) "A first-stage \(F\) statistic of 12 guarantees that 2SLS \(t\) -tests have correct size." (a) False. Unbiasedness needs \(E[u\mid X]=0\) . Orthogonality only delivers consistency (Lectures 1–2). (b) False. They correct the variance estimator for heteroskedasticity. They do nothing about the probability limit of \(\widehat\beta\) . (c) False. \(F>10\) controls the bias of 2SLS relative to OLS (Stock–Yogo). For a 5% \(t\) -test to have correct size with \(|t|>1.96\) , \(F\) must be around 104.7 (Lee et al., 2022). Otherwise use the tF adjustment or Anderson–Rubin.

Question 2 (15 marks). In \(y=X\beta+u\) with \(E[u\mid X]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(u\mid X)=\sigma^2I\) , let \(\tilde\beta=(X'X+\lambda I)^{-1}X'y\) for \(\lambda>0\) (ridge regression). (a) Is \(\tilde\beta\) unbiased? (b) Derive \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta\mid X)\) . (c) Does this contradict Gauss–Markov? (a) \(E[\tilde\beta\mid X]=(X'X+\lambda I)^{-1}X'X\beta\neq\beta\) unless \(\beta=0\) : biased toward zero. (b) \(\sigma^2(X'X+\lambda I)^{-1}X'X(X'X+\lambda I)^{-1}\) , which is smaller than \(\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\) in the positive semidefinite sense. (c) No. Gauss–Markov compares linear unbiased estimators only. Ridge is linear but biased, and it can have lower MSE. Question 3 (15 marks). True model: \(\log w=\beta_0+\beta_1S+\beta_2A+u\) . You omit \(A\) (ability). The auxiliary regression of \(A\) on \(S\) has slope 0.15, and \(\beta_2=0.08\) . Schooling is also measured with error, with reliability ratio 0.85. If the true \(\beta_1=0.07\) , what is the probability limit of the short-regression OLS estimate? Which bias dominates?

Treat the errors-in-variables problem as acting on the short regression. The OVB term is \(0.15\times0.08=0.012\) , so with true schooling the short regression gives \(0.082\) . Attenuation scales this by 0.85: \(0.082\times0.85\approx0.070\) . The two biases almost exactly offset. (A full answer notes that the precise formula depends on how the measurement error interacts with the auxiliary regression, since the auxiliary slope of \(A\) on observed \(S\) is also attenuated. Under classical error independent of \(A\) , both terms scale by the reliability ratio, giving \(0.85\times(0.07+0.012)\) .) Question 4 (20 marks). A study uses rainfall in the farmer's district as an instrument for agricultural income, to estimate the effect of income on children's schooling. The first-stage effective \(F\) is 31, the OLS estimate is 0.05 and the 2SLS estimate is 0.21 (s.e. 0.07). (a) State the two instrument conditions in this context and assess each. (b) Give two distinct reasons why 2SLS could exceed OLS. (c) Who are the compliers, and what does that imply for policy relevance?

(a) Relevance: rainfall shifts harvests and incomes. With \(F=31\) , relevance is adequate for bias, though a tF adjustment of the \(t\) -test is advisable. Exclusion: rainfall could affect schooling directly (flooded roads, disease, child labor demand on the farm, school closures), so the exclusion restriction is doubtful. (b) Measurement error in income (attenuating OLS); heterogeneous effects with a LATE for households whose income is sensitive to rainfall (poorer, credit-constrained households may have larger effects); a violated exclusion restriction (for example, through child labor demand). (c) Compliers are households whose income responds to rainfall: rain-fed, non-diversified farmers. The estimate is informative for transfers to such households, less so for urban or diversified households.

Question 5 (20 marks). Consider the system \(q=\alpha p+\gamma y+u_d\) (demand), \(q= eta p+\delta w+u_s\) (supply), with \(y,w\) exogenous. (a) Derive the reduced form for \(p\) . (b) Check the order and rank conditions for each equation. (c) If \(\delta=0\) , what can be estimated consistently? (a) \(p=(\delta w-\gamma y+u_s-u_d)/(\alpha- eta)\) . (b) Each equation excludes one exogenous variable and has one RHS endogenous variable: just identified by the order condition. Rank for demand requires that \(w\) moves \(p\) : \(\delta
eq0\) . Rank for supply requires \(\gamma
eq0\) . (c) If \(\delta=0\) , demand is not identified (no supply shifter), but supply remains identified by \(y\) if \(\gamma
eq0\) . Question 6 (20 marks). You estimate the effect of a state-level policy on individual earnings with 1.2 million workers in 48 states over 15 years. Policy timing varies by state. Describe (a) the variance estimator you would use and why, (b) how many effective observations you have for inference, (c) one finite-sample check, and (d) one concern about the point estimate if you use static TWFE.

(a) Cluster by state, the level of policy assignment, allowing arbitrary serial correlation within states. (b) Effectively 48 clusters, not 1.2 million or 720 state-years. (c) Wild cluster bootstrap p-values with the null imposed, or CR2 with Bell–McCaffrey degrees of freedom; check the number of treated clusters. (d) With staggered adoption and heterogeneous or dynamic effects, TWFE uses already-treated states as controls and can put negative weights on some group-time effects. Use Callaway–Sant'Anna, Sun–Abraham or imputation estimators (Lecture 13).

Derive Nickell bias for \(T=2\) , and show that Anderson–Hsiao IV is consistent. When is it weak? Show that FE equals the Mundlak coefficient in a balanced panel, and describe a cluster-robust test of RE against FE. Explain why the Engle–Granger residual-based test needs non-standard critical values, and why OLS standard errors in the cointegrating regression are invalid. In a 3-variable VAR, count the restrictions for exact identification. Compare Cholesky and proxy-SVAR identification of a monetary shock. 23 min read 2 OLS Inference: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Tests, and Confidence Intervals By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. state the convergence concepts and limit theorems used in econometrics (WLLN, CLT, continuous mapping, Slutsky, delta method); 2. prove consistency and asymptotic normality of OLS for the linear projection model; 3. derive the exact finite-sample distribution of \(t\) and \(F\) statistics in the normal regression model; 4. construct and interpret asymptotic \(t\) tests, Wald tests, and confidence intervals, including for nonlinear functions of \(\beta\) ; 5. explain size, power, and the duality between tests and confidence sets. 20 min read 3 Functional Form, Partial Effects, and Omitted-Variable Bias By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. interpret coefficients in level, log and mixed specifications exactly, not only approximately; 2. compute partial effects, turning points and their standard errors in models with polynomials and interactions; 3. derive the omitted-variable bias formula in finite samples and in the limit, and sign the bias; 4. derive attenuation bias from classical measurement error, and explain why "bad controls" bias regression coefficients; 5. use specification tests (RESET) and sensitivity analysis responsibly.

19 min read 4 Heteroskedasticity, Dependence, and Robust Inference By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. derive the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC) covariance estimators and explain the finite-sample corrections HC1–HC3; 2. test for heteroskedasticity and decide when weighted least squares is worth using; 3. derive the cluster-robust variance estimator and the Moulton factor, and explain what goes wrong with few clusters; 4. derive the long-run variance and the Newey–West HAC estimator for time-series regressions; 5. choose the level of clustering from the sampling and assignment design. 19 min read Part II · Endogeneity and identification 5 Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. classify sources of endogeneity and show why each makes OLS inconsistent; 2. derive the IV and 2SLS estimators, prove consistency and asymptotic normality, and compute correct standard errors; 3. diagnose weak instruments and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin); 4. test overidentifying restrictions and endogeneity, and state what each test can and cannot establish; 5. interpret IV estimates with heterogeneous effects as local average treatment effects (LATE).

21 min read 6 Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. write a system of simultaneous equations in structural and reduced form, and derive simultaneity bias; 2. state and apply the order and rank conditions for identification of a single equation; 3. estimate an identified equation by 2SLS and LIML, and a full system by 3SLS, and compare their properties; 4. explain identification through covariance restrictions and heteroskedasticity; 5. connect the identification problem in simultaneous equations to structural VARs (Lecture 11). 18 min read Part III · Panel data 7 Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects By the end of this lecture you should be able to: 1. write the unobserved-effects model and explain what panel data can and cannot identify; 2. derive the fixed-effects (within) and first-difference estimators and state the strict-exogeneity assumption each needs; 3. derive the random-effects GLS estimator as quasi-demeaning and explain when it is consistent; 4. use the Mundlak (correlated random effects) device and a robust Hausman test to choose between FE and RE; 5. conduct inference with clustered standard errors, and recognize the limits of two-way fixed effects.

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: define the conditional expectation function (CEF) and prove that it is the best predictor of \(Y\) given \(X\) in mean square; define the best linear predictor (linear projection), derive its coefficients, and explain how it relates to the CEF; derive the OLS estimator in matrix form and interpret it as the sample analogue of the projection coefficient; state and prove the algebraic properties of the projection matrices \(P_X\) and \(M_X\) , including the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem; prove unbiasedness of OLS and the Gauss–Markov theorem, and state exactly which assumptions each result uses.
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

Almost every empirical paper in economics reports a regression. Before asking whether a regression coefficient is causal , we need to know what it is : what population object the estimator converges to, under what conditions, and with what precision. This lecture builds the regression model from probability alone. The key message is that a linear regression always estimates something well defined — the linear projection — whether or not the conditional mean is linear and whether or not the model has a causal interpretation. Assumptions are added only when we want more: unbiasedness, efficiency, or a structural interpretation.
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

Let \((Y, X')'\) be a random vector with \(E[Y^2]<\infty\) , where \(Y\) is scalar and \(X\) is \(k\times 1\) . The conditional expectation function is \(m(x)=E[Y\mid X=x]\) . Define the CEF error \(e=Y-m(X)\) , so that This is a decomposition , not a model: it holds for any joint distribution with a finite first moment. Theorem 1.1 (Properties of the CEF error). Let \(e = Y - m(X)\) . Then \(E[e\mid X]=0\) ; \(E[e]=0\) ; \(E[h(X)\,e]=0\) for any function \(h\) with \(E|h(X)e|<\infty\) . Proof. (1) \(E[e\mid X]=E[Y\mid X]-m(X)=0\) . (2) By the law of iterated expectations (LIE), \(E[e]=E\{E[e\mid X]\}=0\) . (3) \(E[h(X)e]=E\{h(X)E[e\mid X]\}=0\) , again by the LIE, because \(h(X)\) is known once we condition on \(X\) . ∎
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

Property 3 says the CEF error is uncorrelated with every function of \(X\) . This is much stronger than being uncorrelated with \(X\) itself. Theorem 1.2 (The CEF is the best predictor). If \(E[Y^2]<\infty\) , then for every function \(g\) with \(E[g(X)^2]<\infty\) , with equality if and only if \(g(X)=m(X)\) almost surely. Proof. Write \(Y-g(X) = e + (m(X)-g(X))\) . Expanding the square, The cross term is zero by Theorem 1.1(3) with \(h=m-g\) . The last term is non-negative and equals zero only when \(g(X)=m(X)\) a.s. ∎ Variance decomposition. Since \(m(X)\) and \(e\) are uncorrelated, \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{Var}(m(X))+E[e^2]\) , and \(E[e^2]=E[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]\) . This is the law of total variance: total variation equals explained variation plus average conditional variance.
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

The CEF can be any function. In practice we often approximate it with a linear function \(X'\beta\) . Define the best linear predictor (BLP) or linear projection as the minimizer of mean squared prediction error over linear functions: Theorem 1.3 (Projection coefficient). Assume \(E[Y^2]<\infty\) , \(E\|X\|^2<\infty\) , and \(Q_{XX}=E[XX']\) is positive definite. Then the unique minimizer is and the projection error \(u=Y-X'\beta\) satisfies \(E[Xu]=0\) . Proof. \(S(b)=E[Y^2]-2b'E[XY]+b'E[XX']b\) . This is a strictly convex quadratic in \(b\) because \(E[XX']\) is positive definite. The first-order condition \(-2E[XY]+2E[XX']b=0\) gives the formula. Substituting, \(E[Xu]=E[XY]-E[XX']\beta=0\) . ∎ Three facts follow, and they are worth memorizing. The BLP always exists under moment conditions alone. No linearity of the CEF, no homoskedasticity, no normality and no causal story is required.

If \(X\) includes a constant , then \(E[u]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(X_j,u)=0\) for every regressor \(j\) . \(E[Xu]=0\) is weaker than \(E[u\mid X]=0\) . The projection error is uncorrelated with \(X\) but may be correlated with nonlinear functions of \(X\) . The two conditions coincide exactly when the CEF is linear: \(m(X)=X'\beta\) . The BLP also approximates the CEF. Because \(Y=m(X)+e\) with \(E[Xe]=0\) , so the projection coefficient is the best linear approximation to the CEF itself. This is why regression remains informative when the CEF is nonlinear. Simple regression. With \(X=(1,x)'\) , solving the two normal equations gives the familiar formulas

3. Linear regression models and their assumptions

The literature uses several different "linear regression models". They are nested, and it pays to keep them separate. Model Defining assumption What it buys Linear projection \(E[Xu]=0\) (by construction) OLS is consistent for \(\beta\) Linear CEF \(E[u\mid X]=0\) OLS is unbiased; \(X'\beta\) is the best predictor Homoskedastic linear CEF adds \(E[u^2\mid X]=\sigma^2\) Gauss–Markov efficiency; simple variance formula Normal regression adds \(u\mid X\sim N(0,\sigma^2)\) exact finite-sample \(t\) and \(F\) distributions Structural (causal) model \(\beta\) measures the effect of an intervention on \(X\) economic interpretation; requires identification arguments (Lectures 5–6, 13) A common error is to treat a statement in the bottom row as if it followed from the rows above it. It does not: no amount of statistical structure turns a projection coefficient into a causal effect.

Observe a random sample \(\{(Y_i,X_i)\}_{i=1}^n\) . Stack the data as \(y=(Y_1,\dots,Y_n)'\) ( \(n\times1\) ) and \(X=(X_1,\dots,X_n)'\) ( \(n\times k\) ). OLS replaces population moments with sample moments: Equivalently, \(\widehat\beta\) minimizes the sum of squared residuals \(SSR(b)=(y-Xb)'(y-Xb)\) . The first-order conditions are the normal equations the sample analogue of \(E[Xu]=0\) . The estimator exists and is unique if and only if \(X\) has full column rank, \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=k\) . Perfect multicollinearity, such as including a full set of dummies together with an intercept, violates this. Method-of-moments view. OLS is the method-of-moments estimator for the moment condition \(E[X(Y-X'\beta)]=0\) . This view generalizes directly to instrumental variables (Lecture 5) and GMM (Lecture 8).
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

Define the \(n\times n\) matrices Then fitted values are \(\widehat y=X\widehat\beta=P_Xy\) and residuals are \(\widehat u=y-\widehat y=M_Xy\) . Theorem 1.4 (Projection algebra). \(P_X\) and \(M_X\) are symmetric and idempotent; \(P_XX=X\) ; \(M_XX=0\) ; \(P_XM_X=0\) ; \(\operatorname{tr}(P_X)=k\) ; and \(\operatorname{tr}(M_X)=n-k\) . Proof. Symmetry is immediate because \((X'X)^{-1}\) is symmetric. Idempotence: \(P_XP_X=X(X'X)^{-1}X'X(X'X)^{-1}X'=P_X\) . Then \(M_XM_X=I-2P_X+P_X=M_X\) , \(P_XX=X\) and \(M_XX=X-X=0\) . For the traces, \(\operatorname{tr}(P_X)=\operatorname{tr}\big((X'X)^{-1}X'X\big)=\operatorname{tr}(I_k)=k\) , using \(\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\) . ∎ Geometrically, \(P_X\) projects \(y\) orthogonally onto the column space of \(X\) , and \(M_X\) projects it onto the orthogonal complement. The decomposition \(y=P_Xy+M_Xy\) is orthogonal, so When \(X\) contains a constant, the same holds after demeaning, giving \(SST=SSE+SSR\) and the coefficient of determination \(R^2=1-SSR/SST\in[0,1]\) . \(R^2\) measures in-sample linear predictive fit. It is not a test of the model, and adding regressors can never lower it.

Leverage. The diagonal elements \(h_{ii}=X_i'(X'X)^{-1}X_i\) of \(P_X\) satisfy \(0\le h_{ii}\le1\) and \(\sum_ih_{ii}=k\) . An observation with large leverage has unusual regressor values and pulls the fitted line toward itself. Leverage will matter again for robust variance estimators (Lecture 4).

Partition \(X=[X_1\;X_2]\) and \(\widehat\beta=(\widehat\beta_1',\widehat\beta_2')'\) . Let \(M_1=I-X_1(X_1'X_1)^{-1}X_1'\) . Theorem 1.5 (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell). The OLS coefficient on \(X_2\) in the long regression of \(y\) on \([X_1\;X_2]\) equals the coefficient from regressing the residuals \(M_1y\) on the residuals \(M_1X_2\) . The residuals of the two regressions are identical. Proof. Start from \(y=X_1\widehat\beta_1+X_2\widehat\beta_2+\widehat u\) and premultiply by \(M_1\) . Since \(M_1X_1=0\) , and \(M_1\widehat u=\widehat u\) because \(X_1'\widehat u=0\) , Premultiply by \(X_2'\) . Since \(X_2'\widehat u=0\) , we get \(X_2'M_1y=X_2'M_1X_2\widehat\beta_2\) . Solving gives the result. The same equation shows that the residuals of the short regression of \(M_1y\) on \(M_1X_2\) equal \(\widehat u\) . ∎ FWL makes "holding other variables constant" precise: a multiple-regression coefficient measures the association between \(y\) and the part of \(X_2\) that is not linearly explained by \(X_1\) . Applications appear throughout the course: demeaning with an intercept, detrending, and the within estimator for panel data (Lecture 7), which is FWL with individual dummies in \(X_1\) .

Substituting \(y=X\beta+u\) gives the sampling-error representation Every property of OLS is a property of this expression. Assumptions. (A1) \(y=X\beta+u\) . (A2) Random sampling. (A3) \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=k\) . (A4) \(E[u\mid X]=0\) . (A5) \(E[uu'\mid X]=\sigma^2I_n\) . Theorem 1.6 (Unbiasedness and variance). Under A1–A4, \(E[\widehat\beta\mid X]=\beta\) . Under A1–A5, \(\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1}\) . Proof. \(E[\widehat\beta-\beta\mid X]=(X'X)^{-1}X'E[u\mid X]=0\) . For the variance, Note what A4 rules out: with only the projection condition \(E[Xu]=0\) , OLS is generally biased in finite samples (but still consistent, Lecture 2). Theorem 1.7 (Gauss–Markov). Under A1–A5, OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE): for any estimator \(\tilde\beta=Ay\) with \(A\) a function of \(X\) and \(E[\tilde\beta\mid X]=\beta\) , the matrix \(\operatorname{Var}(\tilde\beta\mid X)-\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta\mid X)\) is positive semidefinite.
Lecture 1: From Probability to the Linear Regression Model

Proof. Unbiasedness for every \(\beta\) requires \(AX=I_k\) . Write \(A=(X'X)^{-1}X'+D\) . Then \(AX=I_k+DX\) , so \(DX=0\) . Hence because the cross terms \((X'X)^{-1}X'D'\) vanish when \(DX=0\) . The difference \(\sigma^2DD'\) is positive semidefinite. ∎ Gauss–Markov does not require normality. It does require homoskedasticity and no serial correlation; without A5, generalized least squares is more efficient and the OLS variance formula is wrong (Lecture 4). The theorem also restricts the comparison to linear unbiased estimators; biased or nonlinear estimators can have lower mean squared error. Estimating \(\sigma^2\) . Using \(\widehat u=M_Xu\) and the trace result, so \(s^2=\widehat u'\widehat u/(n-k)\) is unbiased for \(\sigma^2\) . The divisor \(n-k\) is a degrees-of-freedom correction: \(k\) dimensions of \(u\) are "used up" in fitting \(\widehat\beta\) .

Returns to schooling, two ways. Suppose \(\log w = \beta_0+\beta_1\,educ+\beta_2\,exper+u\) . By FWL, \(\widehat\beta_1\) can be computed in two steps: regress \(educ\) on \((1,exper)\) and keep the residual \(\tilde r\) , the part of schooling not linearly predicted by experience; regress \(\log w\) on \(\tilde r\) : the slope is \(\widehat\beta_1=\sum_i\tilde r_i\log w_i/\sum_i\tilde r_i^2\) . Numerically, both routes give identical coefficients and identical residuals, which you should verify in the lab. Interpretation: \(\widehat\beta_1\) estimates the projection coefficient — the approximate percentage wage difference associated with one more year of schooling among workers with the same experience. Whether it is the return to schooling depends on whether \(E[u\mid educ,exper]=0\) has a causal justification; unobserved ability is the classic reason to doubt it (Lecture 3 derives the resulting bias).

CEF and BLP. Let \(X\sim U[0,1]\) and \(Y=X^2+\varepsilon\) , with \(\varepsilon\) independent of \(X\) , \(E[\varepsilon]=0\) . (a) Find \(m(x)\) . (b) Find the BLP of \(Y\) on \((1,X)\) . (c) Show that the projection error is uncorrelated with \(X\) but not mean-independent of \(X\) . Solution (a) \(m(x)=x^2\) . (b) \(\beta_1=\operatorname{Cov}(X,X^2)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\) . With \(E[X]=1/2\) , \(E[X^2]=1/3\) and \(E[X^3]=1/4\) : \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,X^2)=1/4-1/6=1/12\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/12\) , so \(\beta_1=1\) and \(\beta_0=1/3-1/2=-1/6\) . The BLP is \(X-1/6\) . (c) \(u=X^2-X+1/6+\varepsilon\) . By construction \(E[u]=0\) and \(E[Xu]=0\) , but \(E[u\mid X]=X^2-X+1/6\neq0\) . CEF and BLP. (c) Show that the projection error is uncorrelated with \(X\) but not mean-independent of \(X\) .

Solution (a) \(m(x)=x^2\) . (b) \(\beta_1=\operatorname{Cov}(X,X^2)/\operatorname{Var}(X)\) . Use FWL with \(X_1=\iota\) (a column of ones) to show that the slope coefficients in a regression with an intercept equal the coefficients from regressing demeaned \(y\) on demeaned regressors. Exercise 1.1 — The CEF of wages given schooling, and its best linear approximation

Data: wage1 — 526 U.S. workers, Current Population Survey 1976 (hourly wage, years of education). Estimate the conditional expectation function \(E[wage\mid educ]\) nonparametrically, as the mean wage in each education cell. Estimate the linear projection of wage on (1, educ) by OLS. Show numerically that OLS on the individual data equals weighted least squares of the cell means on educ , with cell sizes as weights. This is the "regression approximates the CEF" result. Where does the linear approximation fit worst? What does that say about the true shape of the CEF? Output: The two slopes are identical: OLS on the micro data is exactly a weighted regression of the CEF on educ (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, §3.1). The gaps are positive at the extremes and negative in the middle (for example, the CEF is below the line around 9–11 years and above it at 16–18 years). The CEF is convex in schooling. The linear projection is still well defined, but it understates returns at high education. That is one motivation for the log specification in Lecture 3.

Exercise 1.2 — Frisch–Waugh–Lovell and leverage, by hand

Data: wage2 — 935 men from the National Longitudinal Survey, 1980 (monthly earnings, education, experience, tenure, IQ). Estimate \(\log(wage)=\beta_0+\beta_1 educ+\beta_2 exper+\beta_3 tenure+u\) with matrix algebra ( numpy , no regression package). Verify FWL: partial exper and tenure (and the constant) out of both educ and log(wage) , and regress residual on residual. Compute the leverage values \(h_{ii}\) , check that they sum to \(k\) , and list the three highest-leverage workers. Why are they unusual? Output: The FWL slope matches the full-regression coefficient on educ to every printed digit. The leverages sum to \(k=4\) , as \(\operatorname{tr}(P_X)=k\) requires. The highest-leverage workers have unusual combinations of regressors, not extreme wages. Two of the three report tenure longer than total experience (16 years with the employer but 4 years of experience), which is logically impossible: leverage diagnostics are a quick way to find data errors. Leverage depends on \(X\) only, which is why it enters the HC2/HC3 corrections of Lecture 4.

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: state the convergence concepts and limit theorems used in econometrics (WLLN, CLT, continuous mapping, Slutsky, delta method); prove consistency and asymptotic normality of OLS for the linear projection model; derive the exact finite-sample distribution of \(t\) and \(F\) statistics in the normal regression model; construct and interpret asymptotic \(t\) tests, Wald tests, and confidence intervals, including for nonlinear functions of \(\beta\) ; explain size, power, and the duality between tests and confidence sets.
Lecture 2: OLS Inference: Sampling Distributions, Hypothesis Tests, and Confidence Intervals

An estimate without a standard error is not a result. Lecture 1 characterized what OLS estimates; this lecture asks how precisely. There are two routes to inference. The exact route assumes normal errors and delivers \(t\) and \(F\) distributions that hold for every \(n\) . The asymptotic route drops normality and homoskedasticity and relies on large-sample approximations. Modern applied work uses the asymptotic route almost exclusively, but the exact theory explains where the familiar formulas and degrees-of-freedom corrections come from.

Let \(Z_n\) be a sequence of random vectors. Definition 2.1. \(Z_n\) converges in probability to \(c\) , written \(Z_n\to_p c\) , if \(P(\|Z_n-c\|>\varepsilon)\to0\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\) . \(Z_n\) converges in distribution to \(Z\) , written \(Z_n\to_d Z\) , if \(P(Z_n\le z)\to P(Z\le z)\) at every continuity point \(z\) of the distribution of \(Z\) . The four workhorse results: Weak law of large numbers (WLLN). If \(W_i\) are i.i.d. with \(E\|W_i\|<\infty\) , then \(\bar W_n\to_pE[W_i]\) . Central limit theorem (CLT). If \(W_i\) are i.i.d. with \(E\|W_i\|^2<\infty\) , then \(\sqrt n(\bar W_n-E[W_i])\to_dN(0,\operatorname{Var}(W_i))\) . Continuous mapping theorem (CMT). If \(Z_n\to_pc\) (or \(\to_dZ\) ) and \(g\) is continuous at \(c\) (or on the support of \(Z\) ), then \(g(Z_n)\to_pg(c)\) (or \(\to_dg(Z)\) ).

If \(\sqrt n(\widehat\theta-\theta)\to_dN(0,V)\) and \(g:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^q\) is continuously differentiable at \(\theta\) with Jacobian \(G=\partial g(\theta)/\partial\theta'\) , then Proof sketch. By the mean value theorem, row by row, \(g(\widehat\theta)-g(\theta)=G(\bar\theta)(\widehat\theta-\theta)\) for some \(\bar\theta\) between \(\widehat\theta\) and \(\theta\) . Since \(\widehat\theta\to_p\theta\) , \(G(\bar\theta)\to_pG\) by the CMT. Slutsky then gives the result. ∎

Work in the projection model of Lecture 1: \(Y_i=X_i'\beta+u_i\) with \(E[X_iu_i]=0\) , i.i.d. sampling, and \(Q_{XX}=E[X_iX_i']\) positive definite. Theorem 2.2 (Consistency). Under these assumptions and \(E\|X_i\|^2<\infty\) , \(E[Y_i^2]<\infty\) : \(\widehat\beta\to_p\beta\) . Proof. Write By the WLLN, \(\tfrac1n\sum X_iX_i'\to_pQ_{XX}\) and \(\tfrac1n\sum X_iu_i\to_pE[X_iu_i]=0\) . For \(H_0:R\beta=r\) , Under homoskedasticity with \(\widehat V^0_\beta\) , \(W=qF\) , so for large \(n\) the \(F\) test and the Wald test agree. Likelihood ratio and score (LM) tests. Under normality the LR statistic is \(n\log(SSR_r/SSR_u)\) . The LM statistic is computed from the restricted model only, as \(nR^2\) from regressing restricted residuals on all regressors. Wald, LR and LM are asymptotically equivalent under the null and local alternatives; they differ in finite samples and in what must be estimated.

6. Confidence intervals and the duality with tests

A \(1-\alpha\) confidence interval for \(\beta_j\) is the set of values not rejected by a level- \(\alpha\) test: Interpretation. Coverage is a property of the procedure : in repeated samples, intervals constructed this way contain the fixed true \(\beta_j\) with probability approaching \(1-\alpha\) . A computed interval either does or does not contain \(\beta_j\) ; it is not a probability statement about \(\beta_j\) . Joint confidence regions for \(q\) coefficients are ellipsoids \(\{b: n(R\widehat\beta-b)'(R\widehat V_\beta R')^{-1}(R\widehat\beta-b)\le\chi^2_{q,1-\alpha}\}\) . Two individual 95% intervals do not form a 95% joint region.

7. Size, power, and what a p-value is

The size of a test is its rejection probability under \(H_0\) . An asymptotic test has correct size in the limit; in finite samples the actual size can differ, sometimes badly (heavy tails, high leverage, few clusters, weak instruments). Power is the rejection probability under an alternative. For a fixed alternative \(\beta_j\neq\beta_j^0\) , \(|T_j|\to_p\infty\) , so a consistent test has power approaching one. To study power meaningfully, consider local alternatives \(\beta_j=\beta_j^0+h/\sqrt n\) : then \(T_j\to_dN(h/\sigma_j,1)\) , and power depends on the signal-to-noise ratio \(h/\sigma_j\) . A p-value is the probability, computed under \(H_0\) , of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and a small p-value does not imply an economically important effect.

Exercise 2.1 — Testing a hedonic price model: classical versus robust inference

Data: hprice1 — 88 house sales in Boston-area communities, 1990 (price, lot size, square footage, bedrooms). Estimate \(\log(price)=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(lotsize)+\beta_2\log(sqrft)+\beta_3 bdrms+u\) . Report classical and HC1 standard errors side by side. Test \(H_0:\beta_1+\beta_2=1\) (a 1% increase in both lot size and floor space raises price by 1%) with a robust Wald test, and build a 95% confidence interval for \(\beta_1+\beta_2\) . Test the joint null \(\beta_1=\beta_3=0\) . Output: The point estimate of \(\beta_1+\beta_2\) is about 0.87, but the robust 95% interval runs from about 0.66 to 1.08 and contains one, so the test does not reject proportionality. With 88 houses, the data cannot distinguish a size elasticity of 0.87 from 1. The combined standard error uses the estimated covariance between the two coefficients, which a calculation from the two separate standard errors would ignore. Robust standard errors are 8–20% larger than classical ones here. The joint test that lot size and bedrooms both have no effect is rejected decisively, driven by lot size.

Exercise 2.2 — Delta method versus bootstrap for a turning point

Data: wage1 — 526 workers, CPS 1976. Estimate \(\log(wage)=\beta_0+\beta_1 educ+\beta_2 exper+\beta_3 exper^2+u\) . Compute the experience level at which predicted log wages peak, \(x^*=-\beta_2/(2\beta_3)\) , with a delta-method standard error (robust covariance). Compute a pairs-bootstrap 95% percentile interval (999 draws, seed 42) and compare. Output: Predicted log wages peak after about 29 years of experience. The bootstrap interval is shifted to the right of the symmetric delta-method interval and is wider, reflecting the ratio form of \(x^*\) : the bootstrap standard error is about 15% larger. With a less precise quadratic term, the delta method would be much less reliable (Lecture 2, Problem 3). About a quarter of the sample lies beyond the estimated peak, so the decline at high experience is supported by data rather than pure extrapolation — but a quadratic forces the profile to turn down; a more flexible specification (splines) would test that.

Lecture 1 showed that OLS estimates a linear projection. In applied work we choose which projection: which transformations of the variables, which interactions, which controls. Each choice changes what the coefficient means. This lecture is about two failure modes: reading a coefficient as something it is not (an interpretation error), and leaving out a variable that matters (an identification error). The omitted-variable bias formula is the most useful single equation in applied econometrics, because it turns a vague worry ("maybe ability matters") into a signed, quantitative argument.

Quadratics. In \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2x^2+u\) , the partial effect is \(\beta_1+2\beta_2x\) . If \(\beta_2<0\) , it turns negative at \(x^*=-\beta_1/(2\beta_2)\) . A turning point is only meaningful if it lies well inside the support of the data. Its standard error follows from the delta method with gradient Interactions. In \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+\beta_2z+\beta_3xz+u\) , the effect of \(x\) is \(\beta_1+\beta_3z\) . Hence: \(\beta_1\) is the effect of \(x\) at \(z=0\) , which may be outside the data. Centering \(z\) at its mean makes \(\beta_1\) the effect at the average \(z\) . A test of \(\beta_1=0\) is not a test of "no effect of \(x\) ". The hypothesis \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_3=0\) is. The standard error of the effect at \(z_0\) is \(\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_1)+z_0^2\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta_3)+2z_0\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_1,\widehat\beta_3)}\) .

upward bias Two facts that are often missed. There is no bias if the omitted variable is irrelevant ( \(\beta_2=0\) ) or uncorrelated with the included regressors ( \(\Gamma=0\) ). Randomized experiments work through the second channel. Adding a control changes the coefficient of interest by exactly \(\widehat\Gamma\widehat\beta_2\) . Coefficient movement when controls are added is therefore informative about selection on observables. Oster (2019) formalizes how far one can extrapolate from it to selection on unobservables.

Classical error in the regressor. Let the true model be \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x^*+u\) , but we observe \(x=x^*+v\) , with \(v\) independent of \(x^*\) and \(u\) , mean zero, and variance \(\sigma_v^2\) . Then \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1x+(u-\beta_1v)\) , and the composite error is correlated with \(x\) . OLS satisfies The factor \(\lambda\) is the reliability ratio : the estimate is attenuated toward zero. With other controls, the attenuation worsens because the controls absorb part of the true signal in \(x^*\) but none of the noise: replace \(\sigma^2_{x^*}\) by the residual variance of \(x^*\) after partialling out the controls. Fixed-effects and first-difference estimators can therefore amplify attenuation (Lecture 7). Error in the dependent variable. If \(y=y^*+w\) with \(w\) uncorrelated with \(X\) , OLS remains consistent; only precision falls. Non-classical error, for example misreporting correlated with the true value, can bias in either direction.

Remedies. Use an instrument such as a second, independent measurement (Lecture 5), a validation sample, or bounds based on assumed reliability ratios.

More controls are not always better. A bad control is a variable that is itself an outcome of the regressor of interest. Example: when estimating the effect of a college degree on earnings, controlling for occupation conditions on a channel through which the degree works. It also introduces selection bias, because people in the same occupation with and without degrees differ in unobserved ways. In the language of causal graphs, conditioning on a mediator removes part of the effect, and conditioning on a collider opens a spurious path. Rule: good controls are determined before the treatment (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, §3.2.3).

RESET (Ramsey, 1969). Add \(\widehat y^2,\widehat y^3\) to the regression and test their joint significance with a robust Wald test. Rejection indicates that the conditional mean is nonlinear in a way the specification misses. RESET is not a test for omitted variables in general: an omitted variable that is linearly related to the included ones leaves no trace in the fitted values. Model choice. Between non-nested specifications (for example, level versus log of \(Y\) ), \(R^2\) values are not comparable when the dependent variables differ. Compare on a common scale, use out-of-sample prediction error, or use economic theory. A specification search conducted on the same data used for inference invalidates nominal p-values. Report the search, or hold out data.

Ability bias in returns to schooling. Let the long model be \(\log w=\beta_0+\beta_1S+\beta_2A+u\) , where \(A\) is standardized ability. Suppose \(\beta_2=0.10\) (one SD of ability raises wages by about 10%), and the auxiliary regression of \(A\) on \(S\) has slope \(\gamma=0.20\) (each year of schooling is associated with 0.2 SD more ability). The short regression then gives If the short regression returns 0.10, the ability-adjusted return is about 0.08: the omission inflates the return by two percentage points. Now add classical measurement error in schooling with reliability \(\lambda=0.9\) . Attenuation pulls the estimate down by about 10%, partly offsetting the upward ability bias. This tension is exactly why IV estimates of the return to schooling (Card, 1999) are often larger than OLS: they correct measurement error as well as ability bias. They may also estimate a local average effect for compliers (Lecture 5).

OVB with multiple regressors. Show that with two included regressors \((x_1,x_2)\) and one omitted \(x_3\) , the bias in \(\widehat\beta_1\) is \(\beta_3\delta_1\) , where \(\delta_1\) is the coefficient on \(x_1\) in the regression of \(x_3\) on \((1,x_1,x_2)\) . Explain why the sign of the bias cannot be read from \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_1,x_3)\) alone. Solution Apply Theorem 3.1 with \(X_1=(1,x_1,x_2)\) and \(X_2=x_3\) ; \(\Gamma\) is the vector of auxiliary-regression coefficients, whose \(x_1\) entry is \(\delta_1\) . By FWL, \(\delta_1\) is the partial association of \(x_3\) with \(x_1\) given \(x_2\) , which can have the opposite sign from the simple covariance. Attenuation with controls. Prove that, with a correctly measured control \(w\) , \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_1=\beta_1\,\sigma^2_{r}/(\sigma^2_{r}+\sigma^2_v)\) , where \(r\) is the residual from projecting \(x^*\) on \((1,w)\) . Solution By FWL, \(\widehat\beta_1\) is the slope from regressing \(y\) on the residual of \(x=x^*+v\) after projecting on \((1,w)\) . Since \(v\) is independent of \(w\) , that residual is \(r+v\) asymptotically. Applying the one-regressor attenuation result to \(r+v\) gives the formula. Because \(\sigma^2_r\le\sigma^2_{x^*}\) , attenuation is weakly worse.

Exercise 3.1 — Ability bias in the return to schooling, with IQ as a proxy

Data: wage2 — 935 men, NLS 1980; IQ is an IQ test score. Estimate the short regression of log(wage) on educ , exper , tenure , married , south , urban , black . Add IQ (the long regression). How much does the return to schooling fall? Verify the omitted-variable bias identity \(\widehat\beta^S_{educ}=\widehat\beta_{educ}+\widehat\gamma\,\widehat\beta_{IQ}\) exactly, where \(\widehat\gamma\) is the coefficient on educ in the auxiliary regression of IQ on all the short-regression regressors. Express the bias as a percentage of the short-regression estimate. Output: Each year of schooling is associated with a few more IQ points, and IQ raises wages, so omitting IQ biases the return to schooling upward . The identity holds to machine precision, as Theorem 3.1 says it must. Controlling for IQ lowers the return from about 6.5% to 5.4% per year — the bias is about one sixth of the short estimate. IQ is only a proxy for ability: if it measures ability with error, part of the bias remains, and the true ability-adjusted return could be lower still. Remember the offsetting attenuation bias from measurement error in schooling (Lecture 3, worked example).

Exercise 3.2 — Exact percentage effects, interactions and RESET

Data: wage1 — 526 workers, CPS 1976. Estimate log(wage) on female , educ , exper , exper² , tenure . Report the exact percentage gender gap \(100(e^{\delta}-1)\) with a delta-method standard error. Add female × educ . Does the return to education differ by gender? What is the gender gap at 12 and at 16 years of schooling? Run a RESET test (add \(\widehat y^2\) and \(\widehat y^3\) ) for the model of part 1, using robust inference. Output: The exact gap is a few points smaller in absolute value than the approximate one, because \(e^{\delta}-1>\delta\) for negative \(\delta\) . The interaction is small and statistically insignificant: in 1976 the return to education was similar for women and men, so the gender gap is roughly constant across schooling levels. The \(t\) -test on female alone in the interaction model would be the gap at zero years of education — not a meaningful quantity. RESET rejects strongly (p < 0.001): the specification misses some nonlinearity — candidates include a quadratic in tenure or interactions of experience with education. RESET signals that the conditional mean is misspecified; it does not say how.
