By the end of this lecture you should be able to: derive the heteroskedasticity-robust (HC) covariance estimators and explain the finite-sample corrections HC1–HC3; test for heteroskedasticity and decide when weighted least squares is worth using; derive the cluster-robust variance estimator and the Moulton factor, and explain what goes wrong with few clusters; derive the long-run variance and the Newey–West HAC estimator for time-series regressions; choose the level of clustering from the sampling and assignment design.

Point estimates come from the moment condition \(E[X_iu_i]=0\) . Standard errors come from the variance of the score \(\sum_iX_iu_i\) , and that variance depends on how errors are related across observations and how their variance changes with the regressors. Getting this wrong does not bias \(\widehat\beta\) , but it can make a 5% test reject 30% or 50% of the time. Much of the replication debate in applied economics has turned on standard errors rather than coefficients. The organizing principle of this lecture is simple: the variance estimator must match the dependence structure of the scores.

From Lecture 2, \(\operatorname{avar}(\widehat\beta)=Q^{-1}\Omega Q^{-1}/n\) with \(\Omega=E[X_iX_i'u_i^2]\) . Conditional on \(X\) , with independent observations, The White (1980) insight is that we do not need to estimate each \(\sigma_i^2\) consistently. We only need the \(k\times k\) average \(n^{-1}\sum_iX_iX_i'\sigma_i^2\) , and replacing \(\sigma_i^2\) by \(\widehat u_i^2\) does this. Estimator Weight on \(\widehat u_i^2\) Rationale HC0 \(1\) White (1980); consistent, biased downward in small samples HC1 \(n/(n-k)\) degrees-of-freedom scaling; Stata's robust HC2 \(1/(1-h_{ii})\) unbiased under homoskedasticity HC3 \(1/(1-h_{ii})^2\) approximates the jackknife; best small-sample size in most simulations Why leverage matters. Under homoskedasticity, \(E[\widehat u_i^2]=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})\) . Residuals at high-leverage points are shrunk because the fit chases those points. HC2 undoes this exactly; HC3 over-corrects, which protects against the remaining downward bias under heteroskedasticity. With \(n\) in the thousands and no extreme leverage, the four estimators agree. With small samples or a few influential observations, they can differ substantially. Report HC3, or check that conclusions survive it (Long and Ervin, 2000; MacKinnon and White, 1985).

Breusch–Pagan / White tests. Regress \(\widehat u_i^2\) on a set of variables \(Z_i\) (the regressors for BP, regressors plus squares and cross-products for White) and use \(nR^2\to_d\chi^2_{\dim Z-1}\) under homoskedasticity. A rejection says the classical variance formula is wrong. Because robust standard errors are valid either way, the test matters mainly for deciding whether efficiency gains from reweighting are worthwhile. Weighted least squares. If \(\operatorname{Var}(u_i\mid X_i)=\sigma^2h(X_i)\) with \(h\) known, OLS on the transformed model \(Y_i/\sqrt{h_i}=(X_i/\sqrt{h_i})'\beta+u_i/\sqrt{h_i}\) is BLUE (GLS). With \(h(X_i;\gamma)\) estimated in a first step, feasible GLS is asymptotically efficient if the variance model is correct. Practical advice (Romano and Wolf, 2017): use WLS for efficiency and robust standard errors for validity, because the variance model is almost never exactly right. Note that WLS and OLS estimate the same \(\beta\) only when the CEF is linear. Under misspecification, they converge to different weighted projections.

Suppose observations come in \(G\) groups (villages, schools, firms, states), indexed by \(g\) , with \(n_g\) members. Errors are independent across clusters but arbitrarily correlated within them. Writing \(X_g\) and \(u_g\) for the cluster's stacked data, The cluster-robust (CR) estimator (Liang and Zeger, 1986; Arellano, 1987) replaces \(E[u_gu_g']\) by \(\widehat u_g\widehat u_g'\) : It is consistent as \(G\to\infty\) with cluster sizes bounded. The effective sample size for inference is \(G\) , not \(n\) . The Moulton factor. Why does clustering matter so much? Take equal cluster sizes \(m\) , a regressor \(x\) with within-cluster correlation \(\rho_x\) , and an error with within-cluster correlation \(\rho_u\) . Then When the regressor is constant within clusters ( \(\rho_x=1\) ), as with a state-level policy, and \(m=100\) individuals per state with \(\rho_u=0.05\) , the variance ratio is about \(5.95\) . Conventional standard errors are then too small by a factor of about \(\sqrt{5.95}=2.4\) (Moulton, 1990).
Lecture 4: Heteroskedasticity, Dependence, and Robust Inference

Few clusters. With \(G\) below roughly 30–50, or with very unbalanced clusters, CR \(t\) -tests over-reject even with the \(c\) correction. Remedies: use \(t_{G-1}\) critical values rather than normal ones; use the CR2 estimator (Bell–McCaffrey) with Imbens–Kolesár degrees of freedom; use the wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed (Cameron, Gelbach and Miller, 2008; Roodman et al., 2019). With very few treated clusters, every method struggles; randomization inference may be the honest option (MacKinnon and Webb, 2017). Where to cluster. Abadie, Athey, Imbens and Wooldridge (2023) show that clustering is justified by the design : sampling clusters from a population (sampling-based clustering) or assigning treatment at the cluster level (design-based clustering). Clustering "because the errors might be correlated" at the coarsest available level is not always conservative, and it can be very imprecise. Rule of thumb: cluster at the level at which treatment is assigned. In panels, cluster at least at the unit level to allow arbitrary serial correlation (Bertrand, Duflo and Mullainathan, 2004).

In a time-series regression \(y_t=x_t'\beta+u_t\) , the score \(s_t=x_tu_t\) may be serially correlated. Then the long-run variance : the spectral density of \(s_t\) at frequency zero, times \(2\pi\) . The sample autocovariances \(\widehat\Gamma_j=T^{-1}\sum_t\widehat s_t\widehat s_{t-j}'\) cannot simply be summed over all lags: the result is not consistent and need not be positive semidefinite. Newey and West (1987) down-weight with a Bartlett kernel: which is positive semidefinite by construction and consistent if \(L\to\infty\) with \(L/T\to0\) . Bandwidth. A common rule is \(L=\lfloor0.75\,T^{1/3}\rfloor\) (Stock and Watson). Andrews (1991) gives data-dependent choices. Small \(L\) with persistent scores gives size distortions; large \(L\) gives noisy estimates. Recent work recommends larger bandwidths combined with fixed- \(b\) critical values, or equal-weighted cosine (EWC) estimators with \(t\) critical values (Lazarus, Lewis, Stock and Watson, 2018).

HAC does not fix dynamic misspecification. If \(y_t\) depends on \(y_{t-1}\) and the lag is omitted, the problem is in the conditional mean, not just the variance. In particular, a regression with a lagged dependent variable and serially correlated errors is inconsistent (Lecture 9).

State minimum wage policy. A researcher regresses teen employment for 200,000 individuals on a state minimum-wage indicator, using 50 states over 10 years. The robust (HC1) standard error is 0.004, and the coefficient is 0.012 ( \(t=3.0\) ). The policy varies only at the state-year level, and employment shocks are correlated within states over time. Clustering by state gives a standard error of 0.011 ( \(t=1.09\) ). What happened? The regressor is perfectly correlated within state-years and highly persistent within states. The Moulton factor is therefore large, and the HC1 standard error treats 200,000 correlated observations as independent. The correct inference uses \(G=50\) clusters, at the level of policy assignment, with \(t_{49}\) critical values. A wild cluster bootstrap p-value is a useful check.

HC2 is unbiased under homoskedasticity. Show that \(E[\widehat u_i^2\mid X]=\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})\) when \(\operatorname{Var}(u\mid X)=\sigma^2I\) . Conclude that HC2 is conditionally unbiased in this case. Solution \(\widehat u=M_Xu\) , so \(E[\widehat u\widehat u'\mid X]=\sigma^2M_X\) , whose \(i\) -th diagonal element is \(\sigma^2(1-h_{ii})\) . HC2 weights \(\widehat u_i^2\) by \(1/(1-h_{ii})\) , so the meat has expectation \(\sum_iX_iX_i'\sigma^2\) , the true meat. HC2 is unbiased under homoskedasticity. Moulton factor. Derive \(1+(m-1)\rho_x\rho_u\) for a single regressor with equal cluster sizes, equicorrelated errors ( \(\operatorname{Corr}(u_{ig},u_{jg})=\rho_u\) ), and a regressor with within-cluster correlation \(\rho_x\) . Solution With demeaned \(x\) , \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{g,i}x_{ig}u_{ig})=\sigma_u^2\sum_g\big[\sum_ix_{ig}^2+\rho_u\sum_{i\neq j}x_{ig}x_{jg}\big]\) . The second sum is approximately \(\rho_x(m-1)\sum_ix_{ig}^2\) on average. Dividing by the OLS variance \(\sigma^2_u\sum x_{ig}^2\) gives the factor. Moulton factor. Derive \(1+(m-1)\rho_x\rho_u\) for a single regressor with equal cluster sizes, equicorrelated errors ( \(\operatorname{Corr}(u_{ig},u_{jg})=\rho_u\) ), and a regressor with within-cluster correlation \(\rho_x\) . Solution With demeaned \(x\) , \(\operatorname{Var}(\sum_{g,i}x_{ig}u_{ig})=\sigma_u^2\sum_g\big[\sum_ix_{ig}^2+\rho_u\sum_{i\neq j}x_{ig}x_{jg}\big]\) . The second sum is approximately \(\rho_x(m-1)\sum_ix_{ig}^2\) on average. Dividing by the OLS variance \(\sigma^2_u\sum x_{ig}^2\) gives the factor. Positive semidefiniteness. Show by example ( \(T=3\) , \(L=1\) , unweighted sum) that \(\widehat\Gamma_0+\sum_{j=1}^{L}(\widehat\Gamma_j+\widehat\Gamma_j')\) can be negative for a scalar score. Then explain why Bartlett weights guarantee non-negativity. Solution Take \(\widehat s=(1,-1,1)\) . Then \(\widehat\Gamma_0=1\) and \(\widehat\Gamma_1=-2/3\) , so the truncated unweighted sum is \(1-4/3=-1/3<0\) : a negative "variance". (Summing all \(T-1\) lags gives \((\sum_t\widehat s_t)^2/T\ge0\) , but that estimator is inconsistent.) The Bartlett estimator equals a scaled average of squared partial sums of length \(L+1\) , which is a variance and so non-negative.

Positive semidefiniteness. Show by example ( \(T=3\) , \(L=1\) , unweighted sum) that \(\widehat\Gamma_0+\sum_{j=1}^{L}(\widehat\Gamma_j+\widehat\Gamma_j')\) can be negative for a scalar score. Then explain why Bartlett weights guarantee non-negativity. Solution Take \(\widehat s=(1,-1,1)\) . Then \(\widehat\Gamma_0=1\) and \(\widehat\Gamma_1=-2/3\) , so the truncated unweighted sum is \(1-4/3=-1/3<0\) : a negative "variance". (Summing all \(T-1\) lags gives \((\sum_t\widehat s_t)^2/T\ge0\) , but that estimator is inconsistent.) The Bartlett estimator equals a scaled average of squared partial sums of length \(L+1\) , which is a variance and so non-negative. Choosing the cluster level. A randomized trial assigns a training program at the classroom level (200 classrooms in 20 schools). Students are the unit of observation. At which level should you cluster, and why not at the school level by default? Solution Cluster at the classroom level, the unit of assignment (design-based justification). Clustering at the school level is not required by the design, leaves only 20 clusters with poor finite-sample behavior, and inflates variance without reducing bias in the variance estimate (Abadie et al., 2023).

Clustering at the school level is not required by the design, leaves only 20 clusters with poor finite-sample behavior, and inflates variance without reducing bias in the variance estimate (Abadie et al., 2023). WLS under misspecification. Show with a simple example that when the CEF is nonlinear, OLS and WLS converge to different coefficients, so a Hausman-type comparison of OLS and WLS is a specification test. Solution WLS converges to \(E[w XX']^{-1}E[wXY]\) , the projection under weights \(w(X)\) . With \(Y=X^2+e\) , \(X\sim U[0,1]\) and \(w=X\) , the weighted slope is \(\operatorname{Cov}_w(X,X^2)/\operatorname{Var}_w(X)\) , which differs from the unweighted slope of 1. If the CEF is linear, both equal \(\beta\) , so a significant difference indicates misspecification.
Lecture 4: Heteroskedasticity, Dependence, and Robust Inference

WLS under misspecification. Show with a simple example that when the CEF is nonlinear, OLS and WLS converge to different coefficients, so a Hausman-type comparison of OLS and WLS is a specification test. Solution WLS converges to \(E[w XX']^{-1}E[wXY]\) , the projection under weights \(w(X)\) . With \(Y=X^2+e\) , \(X\sim U[0,1]\) and \(w=X\) , the weighted slope is \(\operatorname{Cov}_w(X,X^2)/\operatorname{Var}_w(X)\) , which differs from the unweighted slope of 1. If the CEF is linear, both equal \(\beta\) , so a significant difference indicates misspecification.

Goal: see the Moulton problem and its fixes. Tasks: (i) compare the HC rejection rate with the Moulton prediction \(1+(m-1)\rho_u\) ; (ii) reduce \(G\) to 10 and observe the cluster-robust size; (iii) implement a wild cluster bootstrap with Rademacher weights and the null imposed. In R, use fixest::feols(y ~ d, cluster = ~g) and fwildclusterboot::boottest() . In Stata, use reg y d, vce(cluster g) and boottest .

Exercise 4.1 — Heteroskedasticity in house prices: tests, HC0–HC3 and WLS

Data: hprice1 — 88 house sales. Estimate price (in levels) on lotsize , sqrft , bdrms . Run the Breusch–Pagan and White tests. Compare classical, HC0, HC1, HC2 and HC3 standard errors. Re-estimate in logs. Does heteroskedasticity remain? What does this suggest about functional form? Estimate by WLS with weights \(1/sqrft\) and report robust standard errors. Output: In levels, both tests reject homoskedasticity: the spread of prices grows with house size. Robust standard errors are larger than classical ones, and the HC3 standard error on lotsize is far larger than the classical one, because a few very large lots have high leverage. In logs, the Breusch–Pagan test no longer rejects: the log model is the more natural specification for prices, and it also fixes most of the heteroskedasticity. WLS changes the point estimates, which is a sign that the CEF is not exactly linear in levels (Problem 5): WLS and OLS then estimate different weighted projections.
Lecture 4: Heteroskedasticity, Dependence, and Robust Inference
Exercise 4.2 — Clustering in a worker panel

Data: wagepan — 545 young men followed annually 1980–1987 (NLSY), 4,360 person-years. Estimate pooled OLS of lwage on union , educ , black , hisp , exper , expersq , married and year dummies. Compare the standard error on union under (a) classical, (b) HC1 and (c) clustering by worker ( nr ). Estimate the within-worker correlation of the residuals and of union , and compare the ratio of the clustered to the HC1 variance with the Moulton approximation \(1+(m-1)\rho_x\rho_u\) , with \(m=8\) . Output: Both union status and the wage residual are highly persistent within workers (within-worker correlations of about 0.5), so clustering raises the standard error on union by about 70% — the variance by a factor of 2.8. The simple Moulton formula, 2.7, approximates the ratio well. The HC1 standard error treats 4,360 strongly correlated observations as independent. Inference here rests on 545 worker clusters — the level of the sampling design — and on the remaining issue that pooled OLS ignores the unobserved worker effect, which Exercise 7.1 addresses.

Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: classify sources of endogeneity and show why each makes OLS inconsistent; derive the IV and 2SLS estimators, prove consistency and asymptotic normality, and compute correct standard errors; diagnose weak instruments and use weak-instrument-robust inference (Anderson–Rubin); test overidentifying restrictions and endogeneity, and state what each test can and cannot establish; interpret IV estimates with heterogeneous effects as local average treatment effects (LATE).
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Economic data are generated by choices. People choose their schooling, firms choose their inputs, and governments choose policies in response to conditions. When a regressor is chosen with knowledge of factors that also affect the outcome, the regressor is correlated with the error and OLS no longer recovers the coefficient of interest. Instrumental variables offer a way out: find a source of variation in the regressor that is unrelated to the error. The method is powerful and widely misused. Its validity rests on an untestable exclusion restriction, its precision on instrument strength, and its interpretation on assumptions about who responds to the instrument.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

A regressor \(X_j\) in the structural equation \(Y=X'\beta+u\) is endogenous if \(E[X_ju]\neq0\) . Here \(\beta\) is the causal or structural parameter, not the projection coefficient. OLS then converges to \(\beta+Q_{XX}^{-1}E[Xu]\neq\beta\) . The classic sources are: omitted variables (Lecture 3): ability in a wage equation; simultaneity (Lecture 6): price and quantity determined jointly by supply and demand; measurement error (Lecture 3): observed schooling equals true schooling plus noise; selection on gains : those who expect larger returns choose more treatment.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Partition \(X=(X_1',X_2')'\) into exogenous regressors \(X_1\) (including the constant) and endogenous \(X_2\) . An instrument vector \(Z=(X_1',Z_2')'\) , with \(\ell\ge k\) elements, must satisfy: Instrument conditions. (i) Exogeneity: \(E[Zu]=0\) . (ii) Relevance: \(Q_{ZX}=E[ZX']\) has full column rank \(k\) . The order condition \(\ell\ge k\) (at least as many excluded instruments as endogenous regressors) is necessary for (ii). Exogeneity has two parts: the instrument is as good as randomly assigned with respect to \(u\) , and it affects \(Y\) only through \(X\) (the exclusion restriction ). With \(\ell=k\) (just identification), premultiplying \(Y=X'\beta+u\) by \(Z\) and taking expectations gives \(E[ZY]=E[ZX']\beta\) , so One regressor, one instrument. \(\beta_1=\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)/\operatorname{Cov}(Z,X)\) : the ratio of the reduced form to the first stage . With a binary instrument this is the Wald estimator
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

With \(\ell>k\) (over-identification), \(E[Z(Y-X'b)]=0\) is \(\ell\) equations in \(k\) unknowns. 2SLS uses the combination that projects \(X\) onto the instruments: Two-stage interpretation. Stage 1 regresses each column of \(X\) on \(Z\) to get \(\widehat X=P_ZX\) . Stage 2 regresses \(y\) on \(\widehat X\) . The point estimates coincide, because \(\widehat X'\widehat X=X'P_ZX\) and \(\widehat X'y=X'P_Zy\) . The second-stage OLS standard errors are wrong , because they use residuals \(y-\widehat X\widehat\beta\) instead of \(y-X\widehat\beta\) . Always use a dedicated IV routine. Never do "forbidden regressions". Plugging in fitted values from a nonlinear first stage (probit, squared fitted values) does not give a consistent estimator in general. Linear projection of \(X\) onto \(Z\) is what makes the first-stage residuals orthogonal to everything in the second stage.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Theorem 5.1 (Asymptotics of 2SLS). Under i.i.d. sampling, \(E[Zu]=0\) , \(\operatorname{rank}(Q_{ZX})=k\) , \(Q_{ZZ}\) positive definite, and finite fourth moments, with \(\Omega=E[ZZ'u^2]\) . Under homoskedasticity, \(V=\sigma^2(Q_{XZ}Q_{ZZ}^{-1}Q_{ZX})^{-1}\) . Proof. \(\widehat\beta-\beta=\big[(\tfrac{X'Z}{n})(\tfrac{Z'Z}{n})^{-1}(\tfrac{Z'X}{n})\big]^{-1}(\tfrac{X'Z}{n})(\tfrac{Z'Z}{n})^{-1}\tfrac{Z'u}{n}\) . Apply the WLLN to each moment matrix, the CLT to \(n^{-1/2}Z'u\to_dN(0,\Omega)\) , and Slutsky. ∎ 2SLS is the efficient GMM estimator under homoskedasticity. With heteroskedasticity, two-step GMM with weight matrix \(\widehat\Omega^{-1}\) is more efficient (Lecture 8). IV is less precise than OLS. In the just-identified single-regressor case under homoskedasticity, \(\operatorname{avar}(\widehat\beta_{IV})=\operatorname{avar}(\widehat\beta_{OLS})/\rho^2_{XZ}\) , where \(\rho_{XZ}\) is the correlation between \(X\) and \(Z\) . With \(\rho_{XZ}=0.2\) , the variance is 25 times larger. IV trades bias for variance.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

When the first stage is weak, the asymptotic normal approximation of Theorem 5.1 is poor even in large samples. Bias toward OLS. With many weak instruments, 2SLS is biased toward the OLS probability limit. Approximately, \(E[\widehat\beta_{2SLS}]-\beta\approx(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{OLS}-\beta)/(F+1)\) , where \(F\) is the population first-stage \(F\) statistic (Staiger and Stock, 1997). Size distortion. Nominal 5% Wald tests can reject far more often than 5%, and confidence intervals undercover. Bound et al. (1995) showed that quarter-of-birth estimates of the return to schooling with many weak instruments could be reproduced with randomly generated instruments. Diagnosis. With one endogenous regressor, report the first-stage \(F\) for the excluded instruments, computed with a variance estimator matching the error structure. Under heteroskedasticity or clustering, use the effective \(F\) of Montiel Olea and Pflueger (2013). The rule of thumb \(F>10\) (Stock and Yogo, 2005) limits the 2SLS bias to about 10% of the OLS bias. Lee, McCrary, Moreira and Porter (2022) show that a 5% \(t\) -test with \(|t|>1.96\) requires a first-stage \(F\) of about 104.7 for correct size, or else adjusted critical values (the tF procedure ).
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Robust inference. The Anderson–Rubin (AR) test of \(H_0:\beta=\beta_0\) regresses \(Y-X_2'\beta_0\) on \(Z\) and tests the coefficients on the excluded instruments \(Z_2\) . Under \(H_0\) this is a valid test however weak the instruments are, because \(Y-X_2'\beta_0=X_1'\gamma+u\) has no endogenous regressor. Inverting the AR test over a grid of \(\beta_0\) yields a confidence set with correct coverage. The set may be unbounded when instruments are weak: that is an honest statement that the data are uninformative. In the just-identified case, AR is efficient among robust tests. With over-identification, the conditional likelihood ratio (CLR) test of Moreira (2003) has better power.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Over-identification (Sargan–Hansen \(J\) ). With \(\ell>k\) , test whether all moment conditions can hold simultaneously: Under homoskedasticity, \(J=nR^2\) from regressing the 2SLS residuals on \(Z\) (Sargan). Limitations: \(J\) tests coherence among instruments, not validity. If all instruments are invalid in the same direction, \(J\) has no power. And with heterogeneous effects, different valid instruments identify different LATEs, so \(J\) can reject even when all instruments are valid. Endogeneity (Durbin–Wu–Hausman). Regress the endogenous regressor on \(Z\) , save the first-stage residual \(\widehat v\) , and add it to the structural equation (the control function regression). The OLS coefficients on \(X\) in this augmented regression equal 2SLS. A robust \(t\) test on \(\widehat v\) tests \(H_0:E[X_2u]=0\) . Failing to reject is not evidence of exogeneity when the instruments are weak, because the test then has little power.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Let \(D\in\{0,1\}\) be a treatment with potential outcomes \(Y(1),Y(0)\) , and \(Z\in\{0,1\}\) an instrument with potential treatments \(D(1),D(0)\) . The population divides into compliers ( \(D(1)=1,D(0)=0\) ), always-takers , never-takers and defiers . Theorem 5.2 (Imbens and Angrist, 1994). Assume (i) independence: \((Y(1),Y(0),D(1),D(0))\perp Z\) ; (ii) exclusion: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(D\) ; (iii) first stage: \(P(D=1\mid Z=1)\neq P(D=1\mid Z=0)\) ; (iv) monotonicity: \(D(1)\ge D(0)\) , so there are no defiers. Then Proof. \(Y=Y(0)+D\,(Y(1)-Y(0))\) . By independence and exclusion, \(E[Y\mid Z=1]-E[Y\mid Z=0]=E[(D(1)-D(0))(Y(1)-Y(0))]\) . Under monotonicity, \(D(1)-D(0)\in\{0,1\}\) , so this equals \(P(\text{complier})\cdot E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid\text{complier}]\) . The denominator equals \(P(\text{complier})\) . ∎ The Wald/IV estimand is therefore the average effect for compliers , the people whose treatment the instrument changes. It is not, in general, the ATE, nor the effect on the treated. Different instruments move different people and identify different LATEs. External validity has to be argued, not assumed. The characteristics of compliers can be described from the data (Abadie, 2003), which helps that argument.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Draft lottery and earnings (Angrist, 1990). The instrument is draft eligibility \(Z\) , assigned by lottery number; the treatment is Vietnam-era military service \(D\) . Use stylized numbers. Among eligible men, 35% served; among ineligible men, 19% served. Mean annual earnings are $15,300 for eligible and $15,650 for ineligible men. Then Interpretation: military service reduced annual earnings by about $2,200 for men who served because they were draft-eligible (compliers). The lottery makes independence credible. The exclusion restriction could fail if eligibility changed behavior directly, for example through staying in school to obtain deferments. Always-takers (volunteers) and never-takers (the exempt) do not contribute to the estimate.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

IV with a binary instrument. Show that \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)/\operatorname{Cov}(Z,X)\) equals the Wald estimator when \(Z\) is binary. Solution For binary \(Z\) with \(p=P(Z=1)\) , \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W)=p(1-p)\big(E[W\mid Z=1]-E[W\mid Z=0]\big)\) for any \(W\) . Take the ratio for \(W=Y\) and \(W=X\) ; the factor \(p(1-p)\) cancels. IV with a binary instrument. Show that \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,Y)/\operatorname{Cov}(Z,X)\) equals the Wald estimator when \(Z\) is binary. Solution For binary \(Z\) with \(p=P(Z=1)\) , \(\operatorname{Cov}(Z,W)=p(1-p)\big(E[W\mid Z=1]-E[W\mid Z=0]\big)\) for any \(W\) . Take the ratio for \(W=Y\) and \(W=X\) ; the factor \(p(1-p)\) cancels. Measurement error and IV. Two independent noisy measures of schooling are available: \(x_1=x^*+v_1\) and \(x_2=x^*+v_2\) . Show that using \(x_2\) as an instrument for \(x_1\) consistently estimates \(\beta\) in \(y=\beta x^*+u\) . Solution \(y=\beta x_1+(u-\beta v_1)\) . Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_2,u-\beta v_1)=0\) because \(v_1,v_2,u,x^*\) are mutually independent except through \(x^*\) , and \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_2,x_1)=\operatorname{Var}(x^*)\neq0\) . So \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{IV}=\beta\operatorname{Var}(x^*)/\operatorname{Var}(x^*)=\beta\) .
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Measurement error and IV. Two independent noisy measures of schooling are available: \(x_1=x^*+v_1\) and \(x_2=x^*+v_2\) . Show that using \(x_2\) as an instrument for \(x_1\) consistently estimates \(\beta\) in \(y=\beta x^*+u\) . Solution \(y=\beta x_1+(u-\beta v_1)\) . Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_2,u-\beta v_1)=0\) because \(v_1,v_2,u,x^*\) are mutually independent except through \(x^*\) , and \(\operatorname{Cov}(x_2,x_1)=\operatorname{Var}(x^*)\neq0\) . So \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{IV}=\beta\operatorname{Var}(x^*)/\operatorname{Var}(x^*)=\beta\) . 2SLS standard errors. Explain precisely why manual two-step 2SLS yields incorrect standard errors, and write the correct homoskedastic variance estimator. Solution The second step estimates \(\sigma^2\) from \(y-\widehat X\widehat\beta=u+(X-\widehat X)\beta\) , which contains first-stage error. The correct estimator is \(\widehat\sigma^2(X'P_ZX)^{-1}\) with \(\widehat\sigma^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-X_i'\widehat\beta)^2\) , using the original \(X\) . 2SLS standard errors. Explain precisely why manual two-step 2SLS yields incorrect standard errors, and write the correct homoskedastic variance estimator.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Solution The second step estimates \(\sigma^2\) from \(y-\widehat X\widehat\beta=u+(X-\widehat X)\beta\) , which contains first-stage error. The correct estimator is \(\widehat\sigma^2(X'P_ZX)^{-1}\) with \(\widehat\sigma^2=n^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i-X_i'\widehat\beta)^2\) , using the original \(X\) . Anderson–Rubin. In a just-identified model with one endogenous regressor, show that the AR confidence set is unbounded whenever the first stage is not significant at the chosen level. Solution The AR statistic for \(\beta_0\) is the Wald statistic for \(\pi_Y-\beta_0\pi_X=0\) , where \(\pi_Y\) and \(\pi_X\) are the reduced-form and first-stage coefficients. As \(|\beta_0|\to\infty\) , it converges to the Wald statistic for \(\pi_X=0\) . If that is below the critical value, every sufficiently large \(|\beta_0|\) is accepted, so the set is unbounded. Anderson–Rubin. In a just-identified model with one endogenous regressor, show that the AR confidence set is unbounded whenever the first stage is not significant at the chosen level.
Lecture 5: Endogeneity, Instrumental Variables, and Two-Stage Least Squares

Solution The AR statistic for \(\beta_0\) is the Wald statistic for \(\pi_Y-\beta_0\pi_X=0\) , where \(\pi_Y\) and \(\pi_X\) are the reduced-form and first-stage coefficients. As \(|\beta_0|\to\infty\) , it converges to the Wald statistic for \(\pi_X=0\) . If that is below the critical value, every sufficiently large \(|\beta_0|\) is accepted, so the set is unbounded. LATE. In the draft example, suppose 2% of men are defiers (they serve only if not eligible). Write the Wald estimand in terms of complier and defier effects, and explain why it need not lie between them. Solution The numerator is \(\pi_c\Delta_c-\pi_d\Delta_d\) and the denominator \(\pi_c-\pi_d\) , where \(\pi\) and \(\Delta\) are shares and average effects. The ratio is a weighted average with a negative weight on defiers, so it can lie outside \([\Delta_c,\Delta_d]\) , even with the opposite sign when effects are heterogeneous.

Exercise 5.1 — Card (1995): college proximity as an instrument for schooling

Data: card — 3,010 men from the NLS Young Men cohort, earnings in 1976; nearc4 = grew up near a four-year college. Estimate OLS of lwage on educ , exper , expersq , black , smsa , south , smsa66 and regional dummies reg662 – reg669 . Estimate the first stage ( educ on nearc4 and the controls). Report the robust first-stage \(F\) . Estimate 2SLS with linearmodels (robust standard errors), treating exper and expersq as exogenous as in Card's simplest specification. Compute the Anderson–Rubin 95% confidence set by inverting the AR test over a grid of \(\beta_0\) . Output: The 2SLS return (about 13%) is close to double the OLS estimate (7.5%), with a standard error about fifteen times larger. The first-stage \(F\) is above 10 but well below the ~105 needed for the usual \(t\) -test to have exactly correct size (Lee et al., 2022). The Anderson–Rubin set is therefore wider than the Wald interval and asymmetric , extending further to the right. It is valid regardless of instrument strength. Interpretation: a LATE for men whose schooling responded to living near a college, who plausibly face higher marginal returns. The exclusion restriction is open to challenge — proximity to a college correlates with urban labor markets and family background, which the controls only partly capture.

Exercise 5.2 — Returns to education for married women: over-identification and endogeneity tests

Data: mroz — 753 married women, PSID 1975 (428 in the labor force); fatheduc , motheduc = parents' education. For women in the labor force ( inlf == 1 ), estimate lwage on educ , exper , expersq by OLS and by 2SLS using fatheduc and motheduc as instruments for educ . Report the first-stage \(F\) for the two excluded instruments. Test the over-identifying restriction (robust Hansen \(J\) / Wooldridge score test). Test the endogeneity of educ with the control-function regression. Output: The 2SLS estimate is smaller than OLS and much less precise. The instruments are strong, and the over-identification test does not reject, so the two parental-education instruments give mutually consistent answers. That does not prove both are valid: if both are correlated with unobserved ability in the same direction, the test has no power. The control-function coefficient on educ equals 2SLS exactly, and the endogeneity test is not significant at 10% (p ≈ 0.11), so the data cannot sharply distinguish OLS from 2SLS here. Note also the sample selection: wages are observed only for women who work, so these regressions condition on participation (Heckman, 1979).

Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: write a system of simultaneous equations in structural and reduced form, and derive simultaneity bias; state and apply the order and rank conditions for identification of a single equation; estimate an identified equation by 2SLS and LIML, and a full system by 3SLS, and compare their properties; explain identification through covariance restrictions and heteroskedasticity; connect the identification problem in simultaneous equations to structural VARs (Lecture 11).
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

The Cowles Commission developed econometrics in the 1940s around one problem. Equilibrium prices and quantities are determined jointly by supply and demand, so a scatter of price–quantity pairs traces out neither curve. That problem — learning about behavioral relationships from data generated by their interaction — is still the central identification problem in industrial organization, macroeconomics and trade. The tools of this lecture are the order and rank conditions, which formalize exactly how much a priori information is needed to recover a structural equation.
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

Consider a market with demand and supply where \(y_t,w_t\) are exogenous and \((u^d_t,u^s_t)\) are structural shocks with mean zero, uncorrelated with \((y_t,w_t)\) . Solving for the endogenous variables gives the reduced form In general, write \(G\) equations as where \(y_t\) is the \(G\times1\) vector of endogenous variables and \(x_t\) is the \(K\times1\) vector of exogenous variables. The reduced form is a set of regressions on exogenous variables, so \(\Pi\) is always consistently estimable by OLS. Identification asks whether \((B,\Gamma)\) can be recovered from \(\Pi\) .
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

In the demand equation, price depends on \(u^d_t\) through the reduced form, so when the two shocks are uncorrelated. With no exogenous shifters and uncorrelated shocks, the OLS regression of \(q\) on \(p\) converges to a variance-weighted average of the demand and supply slopes. If supply shocks dominate ( \(\sigma_s^2\gg\sigma_d^2\) ), the equilibria trace out the demand curve. If demand shocks dominate, they trace out supply. Otherwise OLS estimates neither.
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

Identification of the demand equation needs a variable that shifts supply but is excluded from demand: weather \(w_t\) . Shifting supply along a fixed demand curve traces out demand. Symmetrically, income identifies supply. This idea generalizes. Write equation \(g\) after normalization as \(y_{1t}=y_{2t}'\gamma+x_{1t}'\delta+u_t\) , with \(G_g\) included right-hand-side endogenous variables and \(K_g\) included exogenous variables, out of \(K\) exogenous variables in the system. Theorem 6.1 (Order and rank conditions). With exclusion restrictions only: Order condition (necessary): the number of excluded exogenous variables is at least the number of included right-hand-side endogenous variables, \(K-K_g\ge G_g\) . Rank condition (necessary and sufficient): the submatrix of reduced-form coefficients \(\Pi_{21}\) , relating the included endogenous regressors \(y_{2t}\) to the excluded exogenous variables, has rank \(G_g\) .
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

The equation is just identified if \(K-K_g=G_g\) and over-identified if \(K-K_g>G_g\) . Proof sketch. Substituting the reduced form into the equation and matching coefficients on the excluded exogenous variables gives \(\pi_{1,\text{excl}}=\Pi_{21}'\gamma\) , where \(\pi_{1,\text{excl}}\) holds the reduced-form coefficients of \(y_1\) on the excluded variables. This is a linear system of \(K-K_g\) equations in \(G_g\) unknowns. It has a unique solution if and only if \(\Pi_{21}\) has full column rank \(G_g\) , which requires at least as many equations as unknowns. Once \(\gamma\) is known, \(\delta\) follows from the coefficients on the included exogenous variables. ∎ The rank condition is the relevance condition. It is the population version of "the excluded instruments jointly predict the endogenous regressors" from Lecture 5, and it can fail even when the order condition holds. For example, the excluded variable may have a zero coefficient in the relevant reduced-form equation (no weather variation actually moves supply), or two excluded variables may move the endogenous variables only in fixed proportion. The rank condition is testable through the first stage; the exclusion restrictions are not.
Lecture 6: Simultaneous Equations and Structural Identification

Normalization and other restrictions. One coefficient in each equation is normalized to 1. Identification can also come from restrictions on \(\Gamma\) other than exclusions (for example, known ratios), from restrictions on the covariance matrix \(\Sigma=E[\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t']\) , or from cross-equation restrictions implied by theory.

Single-equation methods. An identified equation can be estimated by 2SLS (Lecture 5) using all exogenous variables in the system as instruments. This is consistent whether or not other equations are correctly specified, which is a big robustness advantage. Its finite-sample properties deteriorate with many or weak instruments. LIML. Limited-information maximum likelihood minimizes the least-variance ratio and belongs to the \(k\) -class of estimators \(\widehat\beta(k)=[W'(I-kM_X)W]^{-1}W'(I-kM_X)y_1\) , where \(W=[Y_2\;X_1]\) . Here \(k=0\) gives OLS, \(k=1\) gives 2SLS, and \(k=\widehat\kappa_{\min}\) gives LIML. LIML is approximately median-unbiased and much less biased than 2SLS with many or weak instruments, at the cost of thicker tails. Fuller's modification, \(k=\widehat\kappa-a/(n-K)\) , restores finite moments. System methods. 3SLS (Zellner and Theil, 1962) applies GLS to the stacked 2SLS system, using the cross-equation error covariance \(\widehat\Sigma\) from 2SLS residuals. FIML maximizes the full Gaussian likelihood. Both are asymptotically more efficient than equation-by-equation 2SLS when every equation is correctly specified and \(\Sigma\) is not diagonal. Both are inconsistent for all equations if any one equation is misspecified. This is the classic efficiency–robustness trade-off of system estimation.

5. Covariance restrictions and identification through heteroskedasticity

Without exclusion restrictions, information about \(\Sigma\) can identify the structure. Recursive systems. If \(B\) is triangular and \(\Sigma\) is diagonal, every equation can be estimated consistently by OLS: each right-hand-side endogenous variable depends only on shocks orthogonal to the current equation's shock. This is the logic of the Cholesky identification of a VAR (Lecture 11). Identification through heteroskedasticity (Rigobon, 2003). Suppose the structural parameters are stable but the variances of the shocks change between two regimes (for example, crisis and calm periods). Each regime gives a reduced-form covariance matrix \(\Omega_r=B^{-1}\Sigma_rB^{-1\prime}\) . For a 2×2 system, the two regimes provide six moments, against six unknowns (two slopes and four variances), so the system is just identified as long as the relative variances change. The method needs no instruments, but it requires that the slopes do not change across regimes and that the shocks are uncorrelated.

The Fulton fish market (Graddy, 1995; Angrist, Graddy and Imbens, 2000). Daily data on whiting sold in New York. Demand is \(\log q_t=\alpha_0+\alpha_1\log p_t+\text{day dummies}+u^d_t\) . Weather at sea (wave height, wind speed) affects how much fish boats can land, but plausibly not how much buyers in New York demand. Weather therefore shifts supply and is excluded from demand. OLS of \(\log q\) on \(\log p\) gives an elasticity of about \(-0.5\) : too small in absolute value, because demand shocks also move price. IV using "stormy" weather as the instrument gives an elasticity close to \(-1\) . Identification checks: the first stage (does stormy weather raise prices?) is strong; the exclusion restriction requires that weather at sea does not affect the demand of fish buyers, which is plausible but should be argued, for example by noting that the market is indoors. The supply equation is not identified from these data: there is no variable that shifts demand but is excluded from supply. Day-of-week dummies are a candidate, if they shift demand only.

OLS in a market. Derive \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\alpha_1^{OLS}\) in the model of Section 1 with no exogenous variables and uncorrelated shocks, and show that it is a weighted average of \(\alpha_1\) and \(\beta_1\) . Solution \(p=(u^s-u^d)/(\alpha_1-\beta_1)\) and \(q=(\alpha_1u^s-\beta_1u^d)/(\alpha_1-\beta_1)\) , dropping constants. Then \(\operatorname{Cov}(q,p)=(\alpha_1\sigma_s^2+\beta_1\sigma_d^2)/(\alpha_1-\beta_1)^2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(p)=(\sigma_s^2+\sigma_d^2)/(\alpha_1-\beta_1)^2\) . The ratio gives the result, with weights \(\sigma_s^2/(\sigma_s^2+\sigma_d^2)\) and \(\sigma_d^2/(\sigma_s^2+\sigma_d^2)\) . OLS in a market. Order and rank. A three-equation macro model has endogenous \((C_t,I_t,Y_t)\) and exogenous \((1,G_t,r_t,Y_{t-1})\) : \(C_t=a_0+a_1Y_t+u_{1t}\) ; \(I_t=b_0+b_1r_t+b_2Y_{t-1}+u_{2t}\) ; \(Y_t=C_t+I_t+G_t\) . Check the order condition for the consumption equation and explain what the rank condition requires. Solution The consumption equation has one RHS endogenous variable ( \(Y_t\) ) and excludes three exogenous variables ( \(G_t,r_t,Y_{t-1}\) ): over-identified by 2. Rank requires that at least one excluded variable has a nonzero reduced-form coefficient in the \(Y_t\) equation. Here \(\partial Y_t/\partial G_t=1/(1-a_1)\neq0\) , so it holds whenever \(a_1\neq1\) . Order and rank. System misspecification. Explain why 3SLS estimates of the demand equation become inconsistent if the supply equation wrongly omits a relevant exogenous variable, while 2SLS estimates of demand remain consistent. Solution 3SLS weights equations by \(\widehat\Sigma^{-1}\) , so the misspecified supply equation's error, now correlated with the instruments, contaminates the demand estimates through the off-diagonal weights. 2SLS for demand only uses \(E[x_tu^d_t]=0\) , which is unaffected. Heteroskedasticity identification. In \(p=\beta q+\varepsilon\) , \(q=\alpha p+\eta\) , with \(\varepsilon\perp\eta\) , suppose \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta)\) changes between regimes but \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) does not. Show that \(\beta=\Delta\operatorname{Cov}(p,q)/\Delta\operatorname{Var}(q)\) , where \(\Delta\) denotes the difference across regimes. Solution Solving, \(q=(\alpha\varepsilon+\eta)/(1-\alpha\beta)\) and \(p=(\varepsilon+\beta\eta)/(1-\alpha\beta)\) . A change in \(\sigma^2_\eta\) by \(\Delta\) changes \(\operatorname{Var}(q)\) by \(\Delta/(1-\alpha\beta)^2\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(p,q)\) by \(\beta\Delta/(1-\alpha\beta)^2\) . The ratio is \(\beta\) : this is an IV estimator with regime dummies interacted with \(q\) as instruments. Heteroskedasticity identification. In \(p=\beta q+\varepsilon\) , \(q=\alpha p+\eta\) , with \(\varepsilon\perp\eta\) , suppose \(\operatorname{Var}(\eta)\) changes between regimes but \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon)\) does not. Show that \(\beta=\Delta\operatorname{Cov}(p,q)/\Delta\operatorname{Var}(q)\) , where \(\Delta\) denotes the difference across regimes. Solution Solving, \(q=(\alpha\varepsilon+\eta)/(1-\alpha\beta)\) and \(p=(\varepsilon+\beta\eta)/(1-\alpha\beta)\) . A change in \(\sigma^2_\eta\) by \(\Delta\) changes \(\operatorname{Var}(q)\) by \(\Delta/(1-\alpha\beta)^2\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(p,q)\) by \(\beta\Delta/(1-\alpha\beta)^2\) . The ratio is \(\beta\) : this is an IV estimator with regime dummies interacted with \(q\) as instruments.

Exercise 6.1 — Labor supply and wage offers of married women as a simultaneous system

Data: mroz — working married women (428 observations). Wooldridge (2020, Example 16.5) writes a two-equation system: labor supply: hours on lwage , educ , age , kidslt6 , nwifeinc ; wage offer: lwage on hours , educ , exper , expersq . Check the order condition for each equation. Estimate each equation by OLS and by 2SLS, using all exogenous variables in the system as instruments. Interpret the implied labor supply elasticity at the mean of hours . Check the rank condition empirically: in the first stage for lwage , are exper and expersq jointly significant? Output: Each equation excludes enough exogenous variables: supply excludes exper and expersq (just enough for one endogenous regressor, plus one over-identifying restriction), and the wage-offer equation excludes three. OLS finds a negative effect of wages on hours, because of simultaneity bias. 2SLS reverses the sign and implies a labor supply elasticity of about 1.3. The first-stage \(F\) for the supply equation's instruments is only about 6 — below the rule of thumb of 10 — so the estimate is imprecise and weak-instrument-robust inference (Lecture 5) is needed before taking the elasticity seriously. The exclusion of experience from the supply equation is itself debatable.

Exercise 6.2 — Inflation and openness: a cross-country simultaneous system (Romer, 1993)

Data: openness — 114 countries, averages 1973–1990: inflation inf , imports as share of GDP open , log land area lland , log per capita income lpcinc . Romer (1993) argues that more open economies have less incentive to inflate. Openness is plausibly endogenous, but small countries are mechanically more open, so land area can shift openness without affecting inflation directly. Estimate inf on open and lpcinc by OLS. Estimate the first stage of open on lland and lpcinc . Estimate 2SLS with lland instrumenting open . Compare. Discuss the exclusion restriction. Output: Land area is a strong instrument: larger countries trade less. Both OLS and 2SLS give a negative effect of openness on inflation, and 2SLS is larger in absolute value, consistent with Romer's argument. Exclusion requires that country size affects inflation only through openness. Size could also matter through the political economy of central banking or seigniorage needs, so the restriction is an assumption to be argued, not a fact.

Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: write the unobserved-effects model and explain what panel data can and cannot identify; derive the fixed-effects (within) and first-difference estimators and state the strict-exogeneity assumption each needs; derive the random-effects GLS estimator as quasi-demeaning and explain when it is consistent; use the Mundlak (correlated random effects) device and a robust Hausman test to choose between FE and RE; conduct inference with clustered standard errors, and recognize the limits of two-way fixed effects.
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

Cross-sectional regressions compare different people, firms or countries. Panel data follow the same units over time, and so can compare each unit with itself . If the confounders that worry us are stable over time — management quality, ability, geography, institutions — differencing them out removes omitted-variable bias without ever measuring them. That is the promise. The price is that we learn only from within-unit variation, which can be small, noisy and dominated by measurement error, and that we need a strong exogeneity assumption about the whole history of the regressors.
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

For units \(i=1,\dots,N\) and periods \(t=1,\dots,T\) , where \(c_i\) is a time-invariant unobserved effect and \(u_{it}\) is the idiosyncratic error. Asymptotics are for \(N\to\infty\) with \(T\) fixed, the typical micro panel. Two questions organize everything that follows: Is \(c_i\) correlated with \(x_{it}\) ? If so, pooled OLS and random effects are inconsistent; fixed effects and first differences are not. Is \(u_{it}\) uncorrelated with \(x_{is}\) for all \(s,t\) (strict exogeneity), or only for \(s\le t\) (sequential exogeneity)? FE and FD need strict exogeneity; dynamic panels (Lecture 8) need only sequential exogeneity, with GMM. Strict exogeneity. \(E[u_{it}\mid x_{i1},\dots,x_{iT},c_i]=0\) for all \(t\) . It rules out feedback from past shocks to future regressors (for example, a firm raising investment after a good productivity shock) and lagged dependent variables among the regressors.
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

Pooled OLS regresses \(y_{it}\) on \(x_{it}\) with composite error \(v_{it}=c_i+u_{it}\) . It is consistent only if \(E[x_{it}c_i]=0\) and \(E[x_{it}u_{it}]=0\) . Even then, \(v_{it}\) is serially correlated within units (through \(c_i\) ), so standard errors must be clustered by unit.
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

Average the model over time for each unit, \(\bar y_i=\bar x_i'\beta+c_i+\bar u_i\) , and subtract: The unobserved effect is gone. The FE estimator is pooled OLS on demeaned data: Theorem 7.1 (FE consistency). Under strict exogeneity and the rank condition \(\operatorname{rank}\big(\sum_tE[\ddot x_{it}\ddot x_{it}']\big)=k\) , \(\widehat\beta_{FE}\to_p\beta\) as \(N\to\infty\) with \(T\) fixed, whatever the correlation between \(c_i\) and \(x_{it}\) . Proof. \(\widehat\beta_{FE}-\beta=\big(N^{-1}\sum_i\ddot X_i'\ddot X_i\big)^{-1}N^{-1}\sum_i\ddot X_i'u_i\) , using \(\ddot X_i'\ddot u_i=\ddot X_i'u_i\) because demeaning is idempotent. By the WLLN across \(i\) , the second factor converges to \(E[\ddot X_i'u_i]=\sum_tE[\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]\) . Since \(\ddot x_{it}=x_{it}-\bar x_i\) involves regressors from every period, strict exogeneity makes each term zero. ∎ Three equivalent views. (i) OLS on demeaned data. (ii) LSDV : OLS with a dummy for each unit, which by Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (Lecture 1) gives identical slopes, because partialling out unit dummies is demeaning. (iii) A GMM estimator using the moments \(E[\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]=0\) .
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

What FE cannot do. Coefficients on time-invariant regressors (gender, distance, initial conditions) are not identified, because they are absorbed into \(c_i\) . Their interactions with time-varying regressors are identified. Degrees of freedom. When computing the error variance by hand, divide by \(N(T-1)-k\) , not \(NT-k\) : demeaning uses up \(N\) degrees of freedom. Software that estimates LSDV does this automatically; manual demeaning followed by OLS does not. Inference. Use standard errors clustered by unit. They are robust to arbitrary serial correlation and heteroskedasticity in \(u_{it}\) and valid as \(N\to\infty\) (Arellano, 1987).
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

Difference adjacent periods: \(\Delta y_{it}=\Delta x_{it}'\beta+\Delta u_{it}\) , for \(t=2,\dots,T\) . FD also needs strict exogeneity ( \(\Delta x_{it}\) involves \(x_{i,t-1}\) , and \(\Delta u_{it}\) involves \(u_{it}\) ). With \(T=2\) , FD and FE are numerically identical. With \(T>2\) , they differ in efficiency: if \(u_{it}\) is serially uncorrelated, FE is more efficient; if \(u_{it}\) is a random walk, \(\Delta u_{it}\) is serially uncorrelated and FD is more efficient. A large discrepancy between FE and FD is a symptom of violated strict exogeneity or of measurement error, since the two estimators are affected differently. Measurement error is amplified. With classical error in \(x_{it}\) , within-unit variation in the true regressor is often small while the noise is not, so the reliability ratio of \(\ddot x_{it}\) or \(\Delta x_{it}\) can be much lower than that of \(x_{it}\) . This often explains why FE estimates are smaller than OLS (Griliches and Hausman, 1986).

Assume additionally \(E[c_i\mid x_{i1},\dots,x_{iT}]=0\) , so \(c_i\) is part of the error, plus homoskedasticity: \(\operatorname{Var}(c_i)=\sigma_c^2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(u_{it})=\sigma_u^2\) , with no serial correlation in \(u_{it}\) . Then \(v_i=c_i\iota_T+u_i\) has the equicorrelated covariance matrix \(\Omega=\sigma_u^2I_T+\sigma_c^2\iota_T\iota_T'\) . GLS is efficient, and it can be computed as pooled OLS on quasi-demeaned data: The cases \(\theta=0\) (pooled OLS, when \(\sigma_c^2=0\) ) and \(\theta\to1\) (FE, as \(T\sigma_c^2/\sigma_u^2\to\infty\) ) bracket RE. Feasible RE estimates \(\sigma_u^2\) from FE residuals and \(\sigma_c^2\) from pooled or between residuals. When to use RE. RE is more efficient than FE and identifies coefficients on time-invariant regressors. But it is inconsistent if \(c_i\) is correlated with any regressor , which is precisely the concern that motivates panel data in observational economics. RE is natural when units are sampled at random and the regressor of interest is randomly assigned (for example, in an experiment with repeated measurements).

6. Correlated random effects and the Hausman test

Mundlak (1978). Model the correlation explicitly: \(c_i=\bar x_i'\xi+a_i\) with \(E[a_i\mid x_i]=0\) . Substituting, Estimating this equation by pooled OLS or RE gives \(\widehat\beta\) numerically identical to FE (with a balanced panel). It also allows time-invariant regressors and makes the FE-versus-RE question a test of \(H_0:\xi=0\) . Hausman test. The classic statistic is \(H=(\widehat\beta_{FE}-\widehat\beta_{RE})'[\widehat V_{FE}-\widehat V_{RE}]^{-1}(\widehat\beta_{FE}-\widehat\beta_{RE})\) . It relies on RE being fully efficient under \(H_0\) , which fails with heteroskedasticity or serial correlation. The variance difference can then be non-positive-definite. Use the cluster-robust Wald test of \(\xi=0\) in the Mundlak regression instead. It is valid under arbitrary within-unit dependence. Interpretation. Not rejecting \(\xi=0\) does not prove that RE is valid. The test has low power when within-unit variation is small. And FE remains consistent under both hypotheses.

7. Two-way fixed effects and their limits

Adding time effects, \(y_{it}=x_{it}'\beta+c_i+\lambda_t+u_{it}\) , removes common shocks. With balanced panels, this is OLS on double-demeaned data \(z_{it}-\bar z_i-\bar z_t+\bar z\) . Two warnings: FE removes time-invariant confounding only. Unit-specific trends, time-varying shocks correlated with \(x_{it}\) , and reverse causality remain. When \(x_{it}\) is a binary treatment adopted at different times and effects are heterogeneous across units or over time, the TWFE coefficient is a weighted average of unit-time effects in which some weights can be negative (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille, 2020; Goodman-Bacon, 2021). Lecture 13 develops the alternatives.

Union wage premium. In a panel of workers, pooled OLS of \(\log w_{it}\) on union status and controls gives about 0.18; FE gives about 0.08 (orders of magnitude similar to Freeman, 1984). How should we read the drop? Selection on stable traits: if more productive workers sort into union jobs, \(c_i\) is positively correlated with union status, and pooled OLS is biased upward. FE removes this. Measurement error: union status is misreported in a few percent of observations. Most within-worker changes in union status are real switches, but some are reporting errors, so the reliability of \(\Delta union\) is much lower than that of the level. Some of the drop is attenuation.
Lecture 7: Panel Data: Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Correlated Effects

Strict exogeneity: if workers move into union jobs after a negative wage shock (for example, after a layoff), union status depends on past \(u_{is}\) , and FE is biased. The honest conclusion is a range, supported by robustness checks: an FE–FD comparison, event-study plots around switches, and validation data on misreporting.

FD versus FE with \(T=2\) . Show that the two estimators are identical when \(T=2\) . Solution With \(T=2\) , \(\ddot z_{i1}=-(z_{i2}-z_{i1})/2\) and \(\ddot z_{i2}=(z_{i2}-z_{i1})/2\) . Then \(\sum_t\ddot x_{it}\ddot x_{it}'=\Delta x_i\Delta x_i'/2\) and \(\sum_t\ddot x_{it}\ddot y_{it}=\Delta x_i\Delta y_i/2\) . The factors of \(1/2\) cancel in the ratio. FD versus FE with \(T=2\) . Show that the two estimators are identical when \(T=2\) . Solution With \(T=2\) , \(\ddot z_{i1}=-(z_{i2}-z_{i1})/2\) and \(\ddot z_{i2}=(z_{i2}-z_{i1})/2\) . Then \(\sum_t\ddot x_{it}\ddot x_{it}'=\Delta x_i\Delta x_i'/2\) and \(\sum_t\ddot x_{it}\ddot y_{it}=\Delta x_i\Delta y_i/2\) . The factors of \(1/2\) cancel in the ratio. Feedback. Suppose \(x_{it}=\rho x_{i,t-1}+\gamma u_{i,t-1}+e_{it}\) , with \(\gamma\neq0\) . Show that strict exogeneity fails and derive the sign of the FE bias for small \(T\) when \(\gamma>0\) and \(\beta=0\) . Solution For \(s>t\) , \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=\gamma\rho^{s-t-1}\sigma_u^2\neq0\) : today's shock moves future regressors, so strict exogeneity fails (sequential exogeneity, \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=0\) for \(s\le t\) , still holds). With \(\beta=0\) , \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{FE}=E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]/E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}^2]\) , and \(E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]=\sum_tE[x_{it}u_{it}]-T\,E[\bar x_i\bar u_i]=-\tfrac1T\sum_{s>t}\gamma\rho^{s-t-1}\sigma_u^2<0\) for \(\gamma>0,\rho\ge0\) . The bias is negative and of order \(1/T\) , vanishing as \(T\to\infty\) .

Feedback. Suppose \(x_{it}=\rho x_{i,t-1}+\gamma u_{i,t-1}+e_{it}\) , with \(\gamma\neq0\) . Show that strict exogeneity fails and derive the sign of the FE bias for small \(T\) when \(\gamma>0\) and \(\beta=0\) . Solution For \(s>t\) , \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=\gamma\rho^{s-t-1}\sigma_u^2\neq0\) : today's shock moves future regressors, so strict exogeneity fails (sequential exogeneity, \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=0\) for \(s\le t\) , still holds). With \(\beta=0\) , \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta_{FE}=E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]/E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}^2]\) , and \(E[\sum_t\ddot x_{it}u_{it}]=\sum_tE[x_{it}u_{it}]-T\,E[\bar x_i\bar u_i]=-\tfrac1T\sum_{s>t}\gamma\rho^{s-t-1}\sigma_u^2<0\) for \(\gamma>0,\rho\ge0\) . The bias is negative and of order \(1/T\) , vanishing as \(T\to\infty\) . Mundlak equals FE. Show that in a balanced panel the pooled OLS coefficient on \(x_{it}\) in the regression of \(y_{it}\) on \((1,x_{it},\bar x_i)\) equals \(\widehat\beta_{FE}\) . Solution By FWL, partial out \((1,\bar x_i)\) from \(x_{it}\) . The residual is \(\ddot x_{it}\) , because \(x_{it}=\bar x_i+\ddot x_{it}\) and \(\ddot x_{it}\) is orthogonal to any function of \(i\) in a balanced panel. Regressing \(y_{it}\) on \(\ddot x_{it}\) gives \(\widehat\beta_{FE}\) .

Mundlak equals FE. Show that in a balanced panel the pooled OLS coefficient on \(x_{it}\) in the regression of \(y_{it}\) on \((1,x_{it},\bar x_i)\) equals \(\widehat\beta_{FE}\) . Solution By FWL, partial out \((1,\bar x_i)\) from \(x_{it}\) . The residual is \(\ddot x_{it}\) , because \(x_{it}=\bar x_i+\ddot x_{it}\) and \(\ddot x_{it}\) is orthogonal to any function of \(i\) in a balanced panel. Regressing \(y_{it}\) on \(\ddot x_{it}\) gives \(\widehat\beta_{FE}\) . Clustering in panels. A researcher with \(N=40\) states and \(T=30\) years clusters standard errors by year "because there are more years than states would allow". Comment. Solution Clustering by year allows correlation across states within a year but assumes independence over time within a state. That is usually the wrong assumption, since state-level shocks and policies are persistent. Cluster by state (40 clusters, with small- \(G\) corrections or a wild bootstrap) or two-way by state and year. The number of clusters is not a reason to choose the wrong dimension.

Exercise 7.1 — The union wage premium: pooled OLS, random effects, fixed effects and first differences

Data: wagepan — 545 men, 1980–1987. Estimate the union premium in lwage by pooled OLS, RE, FE and FD, with year effects and the controls married , exper² (and educ , black , hisp where identified). Use standard errors clustered by worker. Run the Mundlak (correlated random effects) test of RE against FE, adding worker means of the time-varying regressors. Interpret the ranking of the estimates. Output: Pooled OLS gives the largest premium, RE an intermediate one, and FE and FD the smallest. The Mundlak regression reproduces the FE coefficient exactly, and its cluster-robust test rejects \(\xi=0\) decisively, so the worker effect is correlated with the regressors and RE is inconsistent. The drop from pooled OLS to FE is consistent with positive selection of higher-wage workers into union jobs. Part of it may also be attenuation, because misreported switches in union status loom large in within-worker variation (Lecture 7, worked example). The difference between FE and FD hints at remaining measurement error or a failure of strict exogeneity.

Exercise 7.2 — Crime and deterrence across North Carolina counties

Data: crime4 — 90 North Carolina counties, 1981–1987 (Cornwell and Trumbull, 1994). Estimate lcrmrte (log crimes per person) on log probability of arrest lprbarr , conviction lprbconv , prison lprbpris , log average sentence lavgsen and log police per capita lpolpc , with year effects, by pooled OLS and by county fixed effects. Cluster by county. Compare the deterrence elasticities. Why could FE still be biased for lpolpc ? Output: Fixed effects shrink the deterrence elasticities for arrest and conviction probabilities substantially compared with pooled OLS: counties with persistently low crime also have high arrest rates for reasons that FE removes. The police coefficient is positive in both models. That is the classic sign of reverse causality — counties hire police when crime rises — which county fixed effects cannot fix because the feedback is time-varying. This is exactly the failure of strict exogeneity discussed in Lecture 7, and it calls for an instrument or a dynamic model.

Lecture 8: Dynamic Panels, Difference GMM, and System GMM

Many economic relationships are dynamic: employment adjusts slowly, consumption is habit-forming, and growth depends on initial income. A lagged dependent variable in a panel with unit effects creates a problem that the tools of Lecture 7 cannot handle. The lag is correlated with the unit effect by construction, so pooled OLS is biased, and it violates strict exogeneity, so fixed effects are biased too. The solution — using deeper lags as instruments in a GMM framework — is among the most widely used and most widely misused tools in empirical economics.
Lecture 8: Dynamic Panels, Difference GMM, and System GMM
1. The dynamic model and Nickell bias

Pooled OLS is biased upward for \(\rho\) , because \(y_{i,t-1}\) contains \(c_i\) . Fixed effects is biased downward. After demeaning, \(\ddot y_{i,t-1}=y_{i,t-1}-\bar y_{i,-1}\) is correlated with \(\ddot u_{it}=u_{it}-\bar u_i\) : the time average \(\bar u_i\) contains \(u_{i,t-1}\) , which is part of \(y_{i,t-1}\) . Theorem 8.1 (Nickell, 1981). In the pure AR(1) panel with i.i.d. \(u_{it}\) and stationary initial conditions, as \(N\to\infty\) with \(T\) fixed, for moderately large \(T\) . The bias is \(O(1/T)\) and does not disappear as \(N\) grows. With \(T=5\) and \(\rho=0.5\) , the bias is about \(-0.375\) , so FE would report a persistence of about 0.12. Bias in \(\rho\) also contaminates \(\widehat\beta\) when \(x_{it}\) is correlated with \(y_{i,t-1}\) . A practical consequence: with persistent data, pooled OLS and FE bracket the true \(\rho\) (upward and downward bias respectively), a useful sanity check on any GMM estimate.

Let \(g_i(\theta)\) be an \(\ell\times1\) vector of moment functions with \(E[g_i(\theta_0)]=0\) , and \(\ell\ge k=\dim\theta\) . With \(\bar g_n(\theta)=n^{-1}\sum_ig_i(\theta)\) and a positive definite weight matrix \(W_n\) , the GMM estimator is Theorem 8.2 (GMM asymptotics). Under identification, regularity conditions and \(W_n\to_pW\) , with \(G=E[\partial g_i(\theta_0)/\partial\theta']\) and \(S=E[g_ig_i']\) , The variance is minimized by \(W=S^{-1}\) , giving \((G'S^{-1}G)^{-1}\) (Hansen, 1982). Two-step GMM first estimates \(\theta\) with a convenient \(W\) , forms \(\widehat S\) from first-step residuals, and re-estimates with \(W=\widehat S^{-1}\) . Linear IV is the special case \(g_i=Z_i(y_i-X_i'\theta)\) . With \(W=(Z'Z/n)^{-1}\) , GMM is 2SLS (Lecture 5). The \(J\) test. \(J=n\,\bar g_n(\widehat\theta)'\widehat S^{-1}\bar g_n(\widehat\theta)\to_d\chi^2_{\ell-k}\) under correct specification. Finite-sample caveats. Two-step standard errors are severely downward-biased in small samples, because they ignore the estimation of \(\widehat S\) . The Windmeijer (2005) correction fixes this and should always be used. With many moments, two-step GMM is biased toward OLS (as in Lecture 5), and \(\widehat S\) becomes poorly estimated.

Step 1: difference out \(c_i\) . \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}=y_{i,t-1}-y_{i,t-2}\) is correlated with \(\Delta u_{it}=u_{it}-u_{i,t-1}\) through \(u_{i,t-1}\) . Step 2: find instruments. Under sequential exogeneity and serially uncorrelated \(u_{it}\) , levels dated \(t-2\) and earlier are uncorrelated with \(\Delta u_{it}\) : Anderson and Hsiao (1981) use \(y_{i,t-2}\) (or \(\Delta y_{i,t-2}\) ) as a single instrument in 2SLS. Arellano and Bond (1991) use all available lags in each period, which gives a block-diagonal instrument matrix yielding \(T(T-1)/2\) moment conditions for the lagged dependent variable alone. Regressors are instrumented according to their exogeneity status: Status of \(x_{it}\) Valid instruments for the differenced equation strictly exogenous all of \(x_{i1},\dots,x_{iT}\) (or just \(\Delta x_{it}\) ) predetermined: \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=0\) for \(s\le t\)

\(x_{i,t-1},x_{i,t-2},\dots\) endogenous: \(E[x_{is}u_{it}]=0\) for \(s<t\) \(x_{i,t-2},x_{i,t-3},\dots\) Weakness when \(\rho\) is near 1. If \(y_{it}\) is highly persistent, lagged levels are nearly uncorrelated with subsequent differences. In the AR(1) with \(\rho\to1\) , the first-stage coefficient of \(\Delta y_{i,t-1}\) on \(y_{i,t-2}\) goes to zero. Difference GMM then suffers the weak-instrument bias toward OLS-on-differences, which in this case means downward bias (Blundell and Bond, 1998).

Blundell and Bond (1998) add the levels equation, instrumented with lagged differences : This moment holds if deviations from the long-run mean are uncorrelated with \(c_i\) . In the AR(1), the mean-stationarity condition is which says the initial observation is drawn from the steady-state distribution relative to each unit's own long-run mean. System GMM stacks the differenced and levels equations. With persistent series, it can be much more precise than difference GMM. The assumption is substantive. Mean stationarity fails, for example, when units start far from their steady state: young firms in a firm panel, or countries early in a convergence process. It is directly relevant to growth regressions (Bond, Hoeffler and Temple, 2001). A difference-in-Hansen test compares the full system with difference GMM and checks the additional moments, but its power is limited when instruments are numerous.

Serial correlation tests (Arellano–Bond). If \(u_{it}\) is serially uncorrelated, then \(\Delta u_{it}\) has first-order autocorrelation (because \(\operatorname{Cov}(\Delta u_{it},\Delta u_{i,t-1})=-\sigma^2_u\) ) but no second-order autocorrelation . Expect to reject in AR(1) and not to reject in AR(2). Rejection in AR(2) invalidates \(t-2\) instruments; use \(t-3\) and deeper. Hansen \(J\) . The test of over-identifying restrictions (use the robust Hansen version, not Sargan). A very high p-value (close to 1) is a warning sign, not reassurance. With many instruments, \(\widehat S\) is poorly estimated, and \(J\) loses power and "passes" almost always. Instrument proliferation (Roodman, 2009). The instrument count grows quadratically in \(T\) . Too many instruments overfit the endogenous variables, bias estimates toward OLS/FE, and weaken the \(J\) test. Remedies:

Labor demand (Arellano and Bond, 1991). Firm employment \(n_{it}\) depends on its own lag, wages and capital, with \(N=140\) UK firms and \(T=7\) –9. The published estimates follow a well-known pattern (approximate magnitudes; see Blundell and Bond, 1998, and the replication in Roodman, 2009, for exact figures and specifications): Estimator \(\widehat\rho\) on \(n_{i,t-1}\) Pooled OLS ≈ 1.05 (upward biased) Within (FE) ≈ 0.73 (Nickell bias, downward) Difference GMM ≈ 0.6–0.7 (below FE) System GMM ≈ 0.8–0.9 (inside the bracket) The difference-GMM estimate lies below FE, outside the OLS–FE bracket. This is the symptom of weak instruments with persistent series. System GMM moves back inside the bracket, which is consistent with Blundell and Bond's diagnosis, provided mean stationarity is believable for these firms. A careful paper would report the instrument count, AR(2) and difference-in-Hansen tests, and estimates with collapsed and lag-limited instrument sets.

Nickell bias with \(T=2\) . In \(y_{it}=\rho y_{i,t-1}+c_i+u_{it}\) with observations \(t=0,1,2\) , the FE estimator uses \(t=1,2\) and equals the FD estimator. Show that \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\rho_{FD}=\rho-(1+\rho)/2\) under stationarity, so the bias is \(-(1+\rho)/2\) . Solution \(\widehat\rho_{FD}\to\operatorname{Cov}(\Delta y_2,\Delta y_1)/\operatorname{Var}(\Delta y_1)\) . Write \(\Delta y_2=\rho\Delta y_1+\Delta u_2\) . Exercise 8.1 — Wage persistence: the OLS–FE bracket and Anderson–Hsiao IV

Data: wagepan — 545 men, 1980–1987. Model \(lwage_{it}=\rho\,lwage_{i,t-1}+\beta\,union_{it}+\lambda_t+c_i+u_{it}\) . Estimate \(\rho\) by pooled OLS and by fixed effects. Which way should each be biased? Estimate the first-differenced equation by 2SLS, instrumenting \(\Delta lwage_{i,t-1}\) with the level \(lwage_{i,t-2}\) (Anderson–Hsiao). Report the first-stage \(F\) . Does the IV estimate fall inside the OLS–FE bracket? Test for second-order serial correlation in the differenced residuals. Output: Pooled OLS is biased up (the lag contains the worker effect) and FE is biased down (Nickell bias with only \(T=8\) ). They bracket the true \(\rho\) widely. The Anderson–Hsiao estimate lies inside the bracket, which is a reassuring sanity check. Its first stage is strong here because wages are only moderately persistent once worker effects are removed. The AR(2) check is what licenses the \(t-2\) instrument: a significant lag-2 correlation of the differenced residuals would mean serial correlation in \(u_{it}\) , and deeper lags would be needed. Arellano–Bond GMM uses all available lags; try pydynpd and compare, reporting the instrument count.

Exercise 8.2 — Grunfeld investment: how instrument count changes GMM

Data: grunfeld (statsmodels) — investment, market value and capital of 11 large U.S. firms, 1935–1954. With only \(N=11\) firms and \(T=20\) , the Arellano–Bond instrument count explodes relative to \(N\) . Estimate \(invest_{it}=\rho\,invest_{i,t-1}+\beta_1 value_{it}+\beta_2 capital_{it}+c_i+u_{it}\) by pooled OLS and FE. Count how many Arellano–Bond moment conditions "all lags" would use for the lagged dependent variable alone. Estimate the differenced equation by just-identified IV (lag-2 level) and by an over-identified IV with lags 2–4 (collapsed). Compare. Explain why "panel GMM" is a poor tool for this dataset. Output: "All lags" would use 171 moment conditions for the lagged dependent variable alone — with 11 firms, the GMM weight matrix cannot even be estimated. The two IV estimates differ wildly (about 0.01 with one instrument, 0.80 with three), and both have standard errors above 0.2: the instruments carry little reliable information. With \(T=20\) , the Nickell bias of FE is modest (order \(1/T\) ), so FE is already a reasonable estimator here; difference-GMM methods are designed for large \(N\) , small \(T\) , the opposite of this dataset. The clustered standard errors rest on only 11 clusters, so even they should not be trusted (Lecture 4). Choosing the estimator to fit the dimensions of the data is part of the econometrics.

In a cross-section, observations are independent draws. In a time series we observe a single realization of a stochastic process, one draw per period, and today's value depends on yesterday's. Inference is still possible, because a stationary, weakly dependent process "forgets" its past fast enough for time averages to behave like population averages. This lecture sets up that framework. Lectures 10–12 relax stationarity, and Lecture 11 extends it to systems.
Lecture 9: Time-Series Foundations: Stationarity, ARMA, and Forecasting

A process \(\{y_t\}\) is strictly stationary if the joint distribution of \((y_{t},\dots,y_{t+h})\) does not depend on \(t\) , for every \(h\) . It is weakly (covariance) stationary if \(E[y_t]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(y_t,y_{t-j})=\gamma_j\) do not depend on \(t\) . The autocorrelation function (ACF) is \(\rho_j=\gamma_j/\gamma_0\) . Stationarity alone does not justify time averages: \(y_t=Z\) for all \(t\) , with \(Z\) random, is stationary, but \(\bar y_T=Z\) never learns \(E[Z]\) . Ergodicity rules this out. Loosely, it requires that observations far apart are nearly independent. Theorem 9.1 (Ergodic theorem). If \(\{y_t\}\) is strictly stationary and ergodic with \(E|y_t|<\infty\) , then \(\bar y_T\to_{a.s.}E[y_t]\) . Theorem 9.2 (CLT for martingale differences). If \(\{g_t\}\) is a stationary, ergodic martingale difference sequence ( \(E[g_t\mid g_{t-1},g_{t-2},\dots]=0\) ) with \(E[g_tg_t']=S\) finite, then \(T^{-1/2}\sum_tg_t\to_dN(0,S)\) .

Let \(\varepsilon_t\) be white noise: mean zero, variance \(\sigma^2\) , uncorrelated over time. MA(q). \(y_t=\mu+\varepsilon_t+\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}+\dots+\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}\) . It is always stationary, and \(\gamma_j=0\) for \(j>q\) : the ACF cuts off after lag \(q\) . It is invertible (expressible as an AR( \(\infty\) ) in current and past \(y\) ) if the roots of \(\theta(z)=1+\theta_1z+\dots+\theta_qz^q\) lie outside the unit circle. AR(1). \(y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) . By repeated substitution, if \(|\phi|<1\) , The ACF decays geometrically. The effect of a shock on \(y_{t+h}\) is \(\phi^h\) , and the half-life of a shock is \(\ln0.5/\ln|\phi|\) . With \(\phi=0.9\) per quarter, it is about 6.6 quarters. AR(p). \(\phi(L)y_t=c+\varepsilon_t\) , with \(\phi(L)=1-\phi_1L-\dots-\phi_pL^p\) and \(L\) the lag operator. It is stationary if all roots of \(\phi(z)=0\) lie outside the unit circle. Equivalently, all eigenvalues of the companion matrix

lie inside the unit circle. The autocovariances satisfy the Yule–Walker equations \(\gamma_j=\phi_1\gamma_{j-1}+\dots+\phi_p\gamma_{j-p}\) for \(j\ge1\) . Complex roots generate damped cycles in the ACF and in impulse responses. ARMA(p,q). \(\phi(L)y_t=c+\theta(L)\varepsilon_t\) : a parsimonious representation of long autocorrelation patterns. Theorem 9.3 (Wold decomposition). Every weakly stationary, purely non-deterministic process can be written as \(y_t=\mu+\sum_{j=0}^\infty\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}\) , with \(\psi_0=1\) , \(\sum\psi_j^2<\infty\) , and \(\varepsilon_t\) the one-step linear forecast error (white noise). The Wold theorem justifies linear time-series models as approximations: any stationary process has an MA( \(\infty\) ) representation, and finite ARMA models are parsimonious approximations to it. But the \(\varepsilon_t\) are forecast errors , not structural shocks. That distinction drives Lecture 11.

Autoregressions by OLS. For a stationary AR(p) with MDS errors, OLS of \(y_t\) on \((1,y_{t-1},\dots,y_{t-p})\) is consistent and asymptotically normal, by Theorems 9.1–9.2. It is biased in finite samples, because \(E[\varepsilon_t\mid y_{t+1}]\neq0\) : strict exogeneity fails although contemporaneous exogeneity holds. In the AR(1), the Kendall bias is approximately \(-(1+3\phi)/T\) (with an intercept). This is non-trivial for persistent series in short samples. MA terms require nonlinear least squares or maximum likelihood, using the Kalman filter or conditional sums of squares. A lagged dependent variable with serially correlated errors. Suppose \(y_t=\beta y_{t-1}+u_t\) with \(u_t=\rho u_{t-1}+e_t\) . Then \(y_{t-1}\) depends on \(u_{t-1}\) , which is correlated with \(u_t\) , so OLS is inconsistent . HAC standard errors do not fix this: the problem is in the conditional mean. The remedy is to model the dynamics fully: here \(y_t=(\beta+\rho)y_{t-1}-\beta\rho y_{t-2}+e_t\) is an AR(2) with white-noise errors. Test for remaining serial correlation with the Breusch–Godfrey LM test, which, unlike Durbin–Watson, is valid with lagged dependent variables.

Under quadratic loss, the optimal forecast is the conditional mean \(\widehat y_{T+h\mid T}=E[y_{T+h}\mid\mathcal F_T]\) . For the AR(1), Forecasts revert to the mean, and forecast uncertainty grows toward the unconditional variance. Iterating a one-step model ("iterated") and regressing \(y_{t+h}\) on information at \(t\) ("direct") are both common. Iterated forecasts are more efficient if the model is correct; direct forecasts are more robust to misspecification. Reported intervals usually ignore parameter uncertainty, which matters in small samples. Evaluation. Use pseudo out-of-sample forecasts: estimate on data up to \(t\) , forecast \(t+h\) , roll forward, and compute the root mean squared forecast error (RMSFE). Compare two forecasts with the Diebold–Mariano test: with loss differential \(d_t=e_{1t}^2-e_{2t}^2\) , the statistic \(\bar d/\widehat{se}(\bar d)\to_dN(0,1)\) , where the standard error is HAC because \(h\) -step errors are MA( \(h-1\) ). For nested models, the DM test is non-standard. Use Clark and West (2007).

U.S. inflation persistence. Quarterly CPI inflation is often summarized by an AR(p) chosen by BIC, typically with \(p\) between 1 and 4. Suppose the fitted AR(1) has \(\widehat\phi=0.85\) and \(\widehat\mu=2.8\%\) , and current inflation is 5%. Then: one-quarter-ahead forecast: \(2.8+0.85(2.2)=4.67\%\) ; four quarters ahead: \(2.8+0.85^4(2.2)=2.8+0.522\times2.2=3.95\%\) ; half-life of a shock: \(\ln0.5/\ln0.85=4.3\) quarters. Caveats: inflation persistence has changed over time (high in the 1970s, low after the mid-1990s; Stock and Watson, 2007), so a constant-parameter AR(1) estimated on the full sample can mislead. Lecture 10 discusses breaks. And with \(T=160\) and \(\widehat\phi=0.85\) , the Kendall bias of about \(-(1+2.55)/160\approx-0.022\) means true persistence is likely a little higher than estimated.
