Exercise 9.1 — Forecasting U.S. inflation: AR(p) by BIC against a random walk

Data: macrodata (statsmodels) — U.S. quarterly macro series, 1959Q1–2009Q3; infl = annualized CPI inflation. Plot the ACF and PACF of inflation and choose an AR order by BIC on the 1960–1984 sample. Produce pseudo out-of-sample one-quarter-ahead forecasts for 1985Q1–2009Q3 from (a) an AR( \(p\) ) re-estimated each quarter on an expanding window and (b) a random walk (the forecast is the last observed value). Report the RMSFE of each and a Diebold–Mariano test with a HAC standard error. Output: Inflation in 1960–84 is highly persistent: the ACF decays slowly and the PACF cuts off after a few lags, pointing to a low-order AR. Out of sample, after 1985, the AR model beats the random walk, because quarterly CPI inflation became noisy and much less persistent during the Great Moderation; the random walk then carries every transitory spike forward. That is the opposite of the 1970s pattern, and a reminder that forecasting rankings depend on the sample (Stock and Watson, 2007). The DM test uses HAC standard errors; the sharp 2008Q4 deflation spike dominates the loss differential — check how sensitive the result is to excluding it.

Exercise 9.2 — The persistence of unemployment: AR(1), half-life and the Kendall bias

Data: phillips — U.S. annual unemployment and inflation, 1948–2003. Estimate an AR(1) for the unemployment rate unem . Compute the half-life of a shock. Correct \(\widehat\rho\) for the Kendall bias \(-(1+3\rho)/T\) and recompute the half-life. Check the residuals for remaining autocorrelation with a Ljung–Box test. Forecast unemployment for 2004–2008 with 95% intervals (ignoring parameter uncertainty). Output: Annual unemployment is persistent: \(\widehat\rho\approx0.74\) , a half-life of about 2.3 years. Because OLS is biased downward in a sample of 56 years, the bias-corrected estimate (about 0.80) implies a half-life of about 3 years — a large difference for a policy question such as how long a recession's unemployment lingers. The Ljung–Box test does not detect remaining autocorrelation, but with annual data it has little power, and a business-cycle AR(2) is worth trying. The intervals widen quickly toward the unconditional variance. Actual U.S. unemployment in 2004–2008 was 5.5, 5.1, 4.6, 4.6 and 5.8% — all inside the intervals. But 2009's 9.3% would have been far above them: an AR(1) cannot anticipate a financial crisis.

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: distinguish trend-stationary from difference-stationary (integrated) processes, and explain why the distinction matters for inference and policy; derive the Dickey–Fuller regression, state its non-standard limiting distribution, and choose the correct deterministic terms and critical values; use ADF, DF-GLS and KPSS tests together, and understand their size and power trade-offs; test for structural breaks with known and unknown break dates (Chow, Andrews sup- \(F\) , Bai–Perron); explain why ignored breaks bias unit-root tests toward non-rejection, and how break-robust tests respond.
Lecture 10: Unit Roots, Structural Breaks, and Persistence

Many macroeconomic and financial series — GDP, prices, exchange rates, interest rates — wander without an obvious tendency to revert to a fixed mean. Whether shocks to such series are permanent (a unit root) or transitory (stationary around a trend) changes forecasts, the interpretation of business cycles, and the validity of every regression in which these series appear. Yet the question is statistically hard: over a few decades of data, a unit root and a root of 0.97 are nearly indistinguishable. This lecture gives the tools and an honest sense of their limits.
Lecture 10: Unit Roots, Structural Breaks, and Persistence

A process is integrated of order \(d\) , \(I(d)\) , if it must be differenced \(d\) times to become stationary. The prototype \(I(1)\) process is the random walk with drift: Compare the trend-stationary model \(y_t=\alpha+\mu t+u_t\) , with \(u_t\) stationary. Trend-stationary Difference-stationary (unit root) Effect of a shock on \(y_{t+h}\) dies out as \(h\to\infty\) permanent \(\operatorname{Var}(y_t)\) bounded grows linearly in \(t\) Forecast interval as \(h\to\infty\) bounded widens without limit Appropriate transformation detrend difference Beveridge–Nelson decomposition. Any \(I(1)\) process with \(\Delta y_t=\mu+\psi(L)\varepsilon_t\) can be written as a random-walk permanent component \(\tau_t=\tau_{t-1}+\mu+\psi(1)\varepsilon_t\) plus a stationary transitory component . The long-run impact of a shock is \(\psi(1)=\sum_j\psi_j\) . A process that is "nearly" trend-stationary has \(\psi(1)\) close to zero.

2. Why unit roots break standard inference

In \(y_t=\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) with \(\phi=1\) , the OLS estimator is super-consistent : \(T(\widehat\phi-1)\) converges to a non-degenerate distribution, so \(\widehat\phi\) converges at rate \(T\) , not \(\sqrt T\) . The limit is non-normal and skewed to the left. It is expressed through a standard Brownian motion \(W(r)\) on \([0,1]\) : These results follow from the functional CLT ( \(T^{-1/2}\sum_{s\le rT}\varepsilon_s/\sigma\Rightarrow W(r)\) ) and the continuous mapping theorem. The second limit is the Dickey–Fuller distribution . Its 5% critical value is about \(-1.95\) with no deterministics, \(-2.86\) with a constant, and \(-3.41\) with a constant and trend, far from the normal \(-1.645\) . Spurious regression. Regressing one independent random walk on another yields "significant" \(t\) statistics with probability approaching one, and \(R^2\) does not go to zero (Granger and Newbold, 1974; Phillips, 1986). The \(t\) statistic diverges at rate \(\sqrt T\) . A telltale sign is a high \(R^2\) together with a Durbin–Watson statistic near zero. Lecture 12 explains when a regression in levels of \(I(1)\) variables is meaningful (cointegration).

Rewrite the AR(1) as \(\Delta y_t=\pi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t\) , with \(\pi=\phi-1\) , and test \(H_0:\pi=0\) (unit root) against \(H_1:\pi<0\) (stationarity). Three versions differ in their deterministic terms: Choosing deterministics. The alternative must be plausible: for a trending series (log GDP), include a trend, so the alternative is trend-stationarity. For a non-trending series (interest rates, unemployment), include only a constant. Including unnecessary trends costs power; omitting necessary ones can make the test inconsistent. Augmented DF (ADF). Serial correlation in \(\Delta y_t\) is absorbed by lagged differences: The \(t\) statistic on \(\pi\) has the same DF limit distribution. Choose \(p\) by the modified AIC of Ng and Perron (2001), or by a general-to-specific sequence starting from \(p_{\max}=\lfloor12(T/100)^{1/4}\rfloor\) . Too few lags distort size; too many lose power.

Phillips–Perron corrects the DF statistic non-parametrically with a long-run variance estimate instead of adding lags. It has poor size when there is a large negative MA root, as in many inflation series. Low power and DF-GLS. Against near-unit-root alternatives such as \(\phi=0.95\) , ADF tests have very low power in samples of typical macro length. DF-GLS (Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock, 1996) first detrends by GLS under a local alternative, then runs the ADF regression without deterministics. It is nearly efficient and should be the default. KPSS (stationarity as the null). Kwiatkowski, Phillips, Schmidt and Shin (1992) test \(H_0\) : stationary (around a level or trend), using the scaled sum of squared partial sums of residuals with a long-run variance estimate. Using ADF/DF-GLS and KPSS together gives four possible outcomes:

Known break date (Chow test). For a break at \(T_b\) , interact all regressors with a post-break dummy and test the interactions jointly with a robust Wald test. The break date must be chosen without looking at the data. Choosing the date where the series visibly changes invalidates the critical values. Unknown break date (Andrews, 1993; Quandt). Compute the Chow statistic \(F(\tau)\) for every candidate break fraction \(\tau\in[\tau_0,1-\tau_0]\) , typically with 15% trimming, and use which has a non-standard limit (a supremum of a squared Brownian-bridge process) with tabulated critical values. Andrews and Ploberger (1994) propose average and exponential versions with optimal power properties. The break date estimator \(\widehat T_b=\arg\min SSR(T_b)\) is consistent at rate \(T\) .
Lecture 10: Unit Roots, Structural Breaks, and Persistence

Multiple breaks (Bai and Perron, 1998, 2003). These methods sequentially test \(\ell\) versus \(\ell+1\) breaks, estimate break dates by global minimization of the SSR using dynamic programming, and provide confidence intervals for the break dates. Parameter instability without discrete breaks. CUSUM tests of recursive residuals (Brown, Durbin and Evans, 1975) and the Nyblom (1989) test detect gradual drift. Time-varying-parameter models estimate it directly.

Perron (1989) showed that a stationary series with a one-time break in level or trend looks highly persistent to an ADF test that ignores the break. The test is then biased toward non-rejection of the unit root. Allowing for the 1929 crash and the 1973 oil-price slowdown, he rejected unit roots in many of the Nelson–Plosser (1982) series. When the break date is unknown, treating it as known biases the test the other way. Zivot and Andrews (1992) and Lumsdaine–Papell search over break dates under the unit-root null, with appropriately larger critical values. Practical conclusion. Unit-root and break tests are complements. Persistence, breaks, nonlinearity (for example, threshold adjustment) and long memory (fractional integration) can all produce similar-looking data. Choose the model that the economics supports, and show robustness to the alternatives.

Is U.S. real GDP trend-stationary? Take quarterly log real GDP, 1960Q1–2019Q4 ( \(T=240\) ), with an ADF regression including a constant, a trend and 2 lags. Typical results: ADF \(t\) -statistic around \(-2.5\) , against a 5% critical value of \(-3.41\) : do not reject the unit root; KPSS with trend: reject trend-stationarity at 5%; the sup- \(F\) test for a break in the trend slope identifies a break near 1973 (the productivity slowdown) and rejects stability. Reading: the evidence is consistent with a unit root, but also with trend-stationarity around a broken trend (Perron, 1989). A Zivot–Andrews test with an endogenous break typically comes close to rejecting, depending on the sample and lag choice. For forecasting at short horizons, the distinction matters little. For long-horizon forecasts and for business-cycle measurement — the size of the "cycle" depends on the trend model — it matters a lot. Spurious regression. Simulate two independent random walks with \(T=100\) , regress one on the other 1,000 times, and record how often \(|t|>1.96\) . Repeat with \(T=1{,}000\) . Explain the pattern. Solution The rejection rate is about 75% at \(T=100\) and higher at \(T=1{,}000\) , because the \(t\) statistic diverges at rate \(\sqrt T\) (Phillips, 1986). Chow with a data-chosen date. Why does choosing \(T_b\) to maximize the Chow statistic, and then using \(F\) critical values, over-reject? Exercise 10.1 — Is U.S. real GDP trend-stationary?

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real GDP, 1959Q1–2009Q3. Run ADF (with constant and trend, AIC lag choice) and KPSS (trend) tests on log(realgdp) . Run the same tests on GDP growth, \(\Delta\log(realgdp)\) , with a constant only. Run the Zivot–Andrews test that allows a break in the trend. What do the four results say together? Output: The ADF test does not reject a unit root in log GDP, and KPSS rejects trend-stationarity: both point to a stochastic trend. Growth is clearly stationary by both tests, so log GDP behaves as I(1). Allowing for one endogenous break in level and trend, Zivot–Andrews still does not reject the unit root at 5% in this sample. The conclusion "GDP has a unit root" is therefore robust to a single break here, but remember the low power of these tests against roots of 0.95–0.98 in 200 quarters (Lecture 10, lab), and that the sample ends in the middle of the Great Recession.

Exercise 10.2 — A structural break in the Nile: Chow, sup-F and the effect on unit-root tests

Data: nile (statsmodels) — annual flow of the Nile at Aswan, 1871–1970. The first Aswan dam was completed in 1902; hydrologists date a drop in flow to about 1898. Compute the Chow statistic for a break in the mean at every candidate year (15% trimming) and find the sup- \(F\) and its date. Compare the sup- \(F\) with Andrews' 5% critical value for one parameter (about 8.7). Run an ADF test on the raw series and on the series demeaned with a separate mean before and after the estimated break. Explain the difference. Output: The sup- \(F\) statistic is far above Andrews' critical value, and the estimated break falls at the end of the 1890s, matching the historical record: mean flow drops by roughly a fifth. On the raw series, the ADF test rejects less strongly than on the break-adjusted series, where the evidence of stationarity is overwhelming. This is Perron's (1989) point in miniature: an ignored level shift makes a stationary series look more persistent. (Strictly, after estimating the break date, the second ADF test needs adjusted critical values, as in Zivot–Andrews.)

Macroeconomists want answers to questions such as: what happens to output and inflation, quarter by quarter, after an unexpected monetary tightening? Sims (1980) proposed letting a small system of variables speak with minimal theoretical restrictions: the vector autoregression. A VAR summarizes the joint dynamics of the data, but its residuals are forecast errors, not economic shocks. Getting from one to the other requires identifying assumptions, and the credibility of every structural VAR result rests on them. This lecture is the time-series counterpart of the simultaneous-equations problem in Lecture 6.

For an \(n\times1\) vector \(y_t\) , a VAR( \(p\) ) is Estimation. Each equation has the same regressors, so equation-by-equation OLS is identical to SUR/GLS and is efficient (Zellner's result). Under Gaussian errors, it is also the conditional MLE. Stability. Stack \(Y_t=(y_t',\dots,y_{t-p+1}')'\) to get the companion form \(Y_t=\mathbf c+\mathbf AY_{t-1}+U_t\) . The VAR is stable (stationary) if all eigenvalues of \(\mathbf A\) have modulus less than one. Lag length. Use AIC, BIC or Hannan–Quinn computed on a common sample, check residual autocorrelation (multivariate portmanteau or LM tests), and be aware of the parameter count: \(n(np+1)\) coefficients. A VAR with 7 variables and 4 lags has 203. Bayesian VARs with Minnesota-type shrinkage priors handle larger systems (Bańbura, Giannone and Reichlin, 2010).

Granger causality. \(y_2\) does not Granger-cause \(y_1\) if lags of \(y_2\) do not help predict \(y_1\) given lags of \(y_1\) : a Wald test that the relevant blocks of \(A_1,\dots,A_p\) are zero. It is a statement about incremental predictability , not causation. Forward-looking variables such as asset prices Granger-cause the variables they anticipate.

2. Moving-average representation, impulse responses and variance decompositions

A stable VAR has the Wold representation \(\Psi_h\) gives the response of \(y_{t+h}\) to a reduced-form innovation at \(t\) . But reduced-form innovations are correlated ( \(\Sigma_u\) is not diagonal), so "a shock to \(u_{1t}\) holding \(u_{2t}\) fixed" is not meaningful. Structural shocks. Suppose \(u_t=B_0^{-1}\varepsilon_t\) , with structural shocks \(\varepsilon_t\) mutually uncorrelated and normalized to \(E[\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t']=I_n\) . Then the structural impulse responses are and the forecast-error variance decomposition gives the share of the \(h\) -step forecast error variance of variable \(i\) due to shock \(j\) :

The data identify \(\Sigma_u\) , which has \(n(n+1)/2\) distinct elements. The structure requires the \(n^2\) elements of \(B_0^{-1}\) , linked by If \(B_0^{-1}\) satisfies this, so does \(B_0^{-1}Q\) for any orthogonal matrix \(Q\) . We therefore need at least \(n(n-1)/2\) additional restrictions for exact identification: 1 for \(n=2\) , 3 for \(n=3\) , 21 for \(n=7\) . Identification can also target a single shock of interest, which needs fewer restrictions.

(a) Short-run (recursive) restrictions. Set \(B_0^{-1}=P\) , the lower-triangular Cholesky factor of \(\Sigma_u\) . Variable 1 then responds on impact only to shock 1, variable 2 to shocks 1 and 2, and so on. The ordering is the identifying assumption . Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (1999) order output and prices before the federal funds rate: the policy rate responds within the period to output and prices, but they respond to policy only with a lag. The assumption is plausible for slow-moving real variables at monthly or quarterly frequency, and implausible for financial variables that react instantly. (b) Long-run restrictions (Blanchard and Quah, 1989). Restrict the cumulative effect \(\Theta(1)=\Psi(1)B_0^{-1}\) , where \(\Psi(1)=(I-A_1-\dots-A_p)^{-1}\) . For example, "demand shocks have no long-run effect on the level of output", with output entering in differences. Since \(\Theta(1)\Theta(1)'=\Psi(1)\Sigma_u\Psi(1)'\) , a lower-triangular Cholesky factor of the right-hand side delivers \(\Theta(1)\) , and \(B_0^{-1}=\Psi(1)^{-1}\Theta(1)\) . Long-run restrictions depend on estimates of \(\Psi(1)\) , which are imprecise in finite samples (Faust and Leeper, 1997).
Lecture 11: VAR and Structural VAR: Dynamic Interactions and Shock Identification

(c) Sign restrictions (Faust, 1998; Uhlig, 2005). Require responses to have particular signs for some horizons: a monetary tightening raises the policy rate and does not raise prices for six months. Draw orthogonal \(Q\) at random, keep the rotations \(PQ\) that satisfy the signs, and report the set of accepted responses. The result is set identification. The usual "median and percentile bands" mix sampling uncertainty with uniform-prior weighting over the identified set. That prior is informative about the responses themselves (Baumeister and Hamilton, 2015). Report the bounds of the identified set, or state explicit priors. (d) External instruments / proxy SVAR (Stock and Watson, 2012, 2018; Mertens and Ravn, 2013). Suppose an external series \(z_t\) is correlated with the shock of interest and uncorrelated with all other structural shocks:

Then \(E[z_tu_t]=b_1\alpha\) , where \(b_1\) is the first column of \(B_0^{-1}\) . The impact responses are therefore identified up to scale by regressing each \(u_{it}\) on \(z_t\) , normalized so the shock raises \(y_{1t}\) by one unit. High-frequency surprises in interest-rate futures around FOMC announcements (Gertler and Karadi, 2015) and narrative series (Romer and Romer, 2004) are leading proxies. The weak-instrument issues of Lecture 5 apply in full: report the first-stage \(F\) of the proxy on \(u_{1t}\) . (e) Other routes. Identification through heteroskedasticity (Rigobon, 2003; Lecture 6) and through non-Gaussianity (independent component analysis) use higher moments of the data.

Local projections (Jordà, 2005). Estimate impulse responses directly, horizon by horizon: where \(s_t\) is an identified shock (or a proxy, estimated by IV) and \(w_t\) contains lagged controls. In population, with the same information set, LPs and VARs estimate the same impulse responses (Plagborg-Møller and Wolf, 2021). In finite samples, LPs have lower bias at long horizons but much higher variance. VARs are more efficient but can be badly biased if the lag length is too short (Li, Plagborg-Møller and Wolf, 2024). LP residuals are serially correlated, so use HAC standard errors or include lags of the shock and outcome ("lag-augmented" LP; Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller, 2021). Inference for impulse responses. Delta-method bands can be poor because responses are highly nonlinear functions of the VAR coefficients. Bootstrap methods (residual-based, wild for heteroskedasticity, or Kilian's 1998 bias-corrected bootstrap-after-bootstrap) are standard. Pointwise bands do not describe the uncertainty about the whole response path. Joint (simultaneous) bands are wider. With persistent or near-unit-root data, VAR-based bands at long horizons undercover.

A monetary-policy VAR. Take quarterly U.S. data on log real GDP, log GDP deflator, a commodity price index, and the federal funds rate (in that order), with 4 lags in levels, recursive identification, and the policy shock as the last shock. The classic findings (Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans, 1999) are: after a 100 bp tightening, output falls with a hump-shaped response, reaching a trough after 6–8 quarters, and then recovers; prices respond sluggishly. In specifications without commodity prices, the price level often rises for several quarters: the price puzzle . Including commodity prices, which proxy for information the Fed has about future inflation, largely removes it. This illustrates that a recursive VAR can confound policy shocks with the Fed's endogenous response to anticipated inflation.

Later work using high-frequency proxies (Gertler and Karadi, 2015) finds similar output effects without the price puzzle, at the cost of weaker instruments in some samples. The lesson for practice: report results under several identification schemes, and explain which economic assumption each one embodies.

A lower-triangular \(B_0^{-1}\) has 6 zeros above the diagonal, so a recursive ordering exactly identifies all four shocks. Counting restrictions. With \(\Sigma_u=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix}\) , compute \(P\) and the impact responses to each structural shock. Reverse the ordering and recompute. What changes, and why? Solution \(P=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) : a shock 1 raises \(y_1\) by 2 and \(y_2\) by 1; shock 2 moves only \(y_2\) , by 2. Reversed ordering: the Cholesky factor of \(\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is \(\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt5&0\\2/\sqrt5&\sqrt{16/5}\end{pmatrix}\) . Now the shock that moves \(y_2\) first also moves \(y_1\) by \(2/\sqrt5\approx0.89\) on impact. The covariance \(2\) is attributed to whichever shock is ordered first.

Granger causality is not causality. Construct an example in which stock prices Granger-cause GDP although stock prices have no causal effect on GDP. Solution Let GDP be driven by a news shock \(n_t\) : \(g_{t+1}=n_t+e_{t+1}\) . The stock price is the expected discounted value of future GDP, so \(s_t\) moves with \(n_t\) at time \(t\) . Lagged \(s\) then predicts \(g\) , but intervening on \(s\) (for example, by a transaction tax) would not change \(g\) .

Exercise 11.1 — A three-variable monetary VAR for the U.S.

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly data, 1959Q1–2009Q3: real GDP, CPI inflation, 3-month T-bill rate. Build a VAR in GDP growth (annualized, %), inflation, and the T-bill rate. Choose the lag by AIC and BIC (max 8). Check stability (eigenvalues of the companion matrix). Test whether the T-bill rate Granger-causes GDP growth. Compute recursive (Cholesky) impulse responses to a one-standard-deviation interest-rate shock, ordering growth, inflation, rate. Report the response of GDP growth and inflation over 12 quarters. Report the 12-quarter forecast-error variance decomposition of GDP growth. Output: AIC and BIC disagree on the lag length, a typical outcome; we use four lags (one year), a common compromise for quarterly data. The system is stable. Interest rates Granger-cause GDP growth strongly — but as Problem 3 explains, that may reflect the Fed reacting to information about future growth, not a causal effect of policy. After a recursive interest-rate shock, output growth first rises and then falls in the second quarter, and inflation rises for several quarters: the price puzzle of Lecture 11. The recursive ordering attributes to "policy shocks" some of the Fed's response to anticipated inflation. The FEVD shows that interest-rate shocks explain only about 4% of the variance of growth at a 3-year horizon; almost 90% is due to growth's own shocks.

Exercise 11.2 — How much does the ordering matter?

Data: macrodata , same VAR as above. Re-estimate the Cholesky responses with the rate ordered first (the policy rate cannot respond within the quarter to output and inflation). Compare the impact responses and the 8-quarter responses of growth to the rate shock under the two orderings. Compute the correlation of the reduced-form residuals. Why does the ordering matter more when this correlation is large? Output: With the rate ordered last, growth cannot respond on impact by construction. With the rate ordered first, the impact response is whatever the residual correlation implies. That correlation is positive: in the data, unexpected rate rises come with unexpectedly strong growth, because the Fed responds within the quarter. Ordering the rate first therefore attributes that co-movement to the policy shock, and growth appears to rise on impact after a tightening — an implausible result. Identification is an economic assumption about timing, and the data alone cannot settle it. External instruments (high-frequency surprises) are the modern response.

Lecture 12: Cointegration, VECM, and ARDL Models

Lecture 10 showed that regressing one random walk on another usually produces nonsense. But economic theory often predicts that non-stationary variables move together in the long run: consumption and income, money and nominal output, prices at home and abroad, short and long interest rates. If a linear combination of \(I(1)\) variables is stationary, the variables share a common stochastic trend. The levels regression then estimates a genuine equilibrium relationship, and deviations from it predict future adjustment. That is cointegration, and it reconciles the statistical finding of unit roots with economic models of long-run equilibrium.
Lecture 12: Cointegration, VECM, and ARDL Models

Cointegration (Engle and Granger, 1987). The components of an \(n\times1\) vector \(y_t\) are cointegrated of order \((1,1)\) if each is \(I(1)\) and there exists a nonzero vector \(\beta\) such that \(\beta'y_t\) is \(I(0)\) . The vector \(\beta\) is a cointegrating vector . There can be up to \(r\le n-1\) linearly independent cointegrating vectors; \(r\) is the cointegrating rank . With \(r\) cointegrating relations, the system is driven by \(n-r\) common stochastic trends (Stock and Watson, 1988). Example: if short and long interest rates are both \(I(1)\) and the term spread is \(I(0)\) , then \(\beta=(1,-1)'\) , and there is one common trend: the level of interest rates.

2. Error correction and the Granger representation theorem

Start from a VAR( \(p\) ) in levels, \(y_t=c+A_1y_{t-1}+\dots+A_py_{t-p}+u_t\) . It can always be rewritten as If \(\operatorname{rank}(\Pi)=0\) , there is no cointegration: a VAR in differences is appropriate. If \(\operatorname{rank}(\Pi)=n\) , then \(y_t\) is stationary: a VAR in levels is appropriate. If \(0<\operatorname{rank}(\Pi)=r<n\) , then \(\Pi=\alpha\beta'\) , with \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) both \(n\times r\) . where \(\beta'y_{t-1}\) is \(I(0)\) . Cointegrated systems have error-correction representations, and vice versa. Interpretation. \(\beta'y_{t-1}\) measures disequilibrium, and the loading (adjustment) coefficients \(\alpha\) say how fast each variable moves to restore equilibrium. If a row of \(\alpha\) is zero, that variable is weakly exogenous for \(\beta\) : it does not respond to disequilibrium, and the other variables do the adjusting. Weak exogeneity of a variable means it drives the common trend.

2. Error correction and the Granger representation theorem

Consequences for VARs in levels. A VAR in levels remains consistent when variables are cointegrated, and many coefficient tests are standard (Sims, Stock and Watson, 1990). Some tests, including Granger causality, can have non-standard distributions. The Toda–Yamamoto (1995) lag-augmentation approach restores standard Wald inference. Differencing a cointegrated system throws away the error-correction term: a misspecification.

Step 1. Estimate the levels regression \(y_{1t}=\mu+\gamma'y_{2t}+z_t\) by OLS and save \(\widehat z_t\) . Step 2. Test \(\widehat z_t\) for a unit root with an ADF regression without deterministics. Under the null of no cointegration, the test statistic has a distribution that depends on the number of regressors and the deterministics, because \(\widehat z_t\) is constructed to look as stationary as possible. Critical values come from Engle and Yoo (1987) or MacKinnon (2010); for two variables with a constant, the 5% value is about \(-3.34\) , against \(-2.86\) for an ordinary ADF test. Super-consistency and inference. If cointegrated, \(\widehat\gamma\) converges at rate \(T\) . But its limit distribution is generally non-normal and depends on nuisance parameters (endogeneity of \(\Delta y_{2t}\) and serial correlation), so OLS \(t\) -statistics in the levels regression are invalid. Johansen (1988, 1991) estimates the VECM by Gaussian (reduced-rank) maximum likelihood. Concentrating out the short-run terms, regress \(\Delta y_t\) and \(y_{t-1}\) on the lagged differences and deterministics, and keep the residuals \(R_{0t}\) and \(R_{1t}\) . With moment matrices \(S_{ij}=T^{-1}\sum_tR_{it}R_{jt}'\) , solve the eigenvalue problem giving ordered eigenvalues \(\widehat\lambda_1>\dots>\widehat\lambda_n\) , the squared canonical correlations between \(\Delta y_t\) and \(y_{t-1}\) . The MLE of \(\beta\) is given by the corresponding eigenvectors. Rank tests. Test sequentially: \(r=0\) , then \(r\le1\) , and so on, and stop at the first non-rejection. The distributions are non-standard and depend on the deterministic specification (no constant; restricted constant in the cointegrating space; unrestricted constant, giving linear trends in levels; restricted trend; unrestricted trend). The usual choice for trending macro data is an unrestricted constant or a restricted trend. The Johansen trace test is known to over-reject in small samples; Bartlett corrections or bootstrap tests help (Cavaliere, Rahbek and Taylor, 2012).

Identifying \(\beta\) . Only the cointegrating space is identified: \(\alpha\beta'=(\alpha H^{-1\prime})(\beta H)'\) for any non-singular \(r\times r\) matrix \(H\) . With \(r=1\) , normalize one coefficient to 1. With \(r>1\) , economically motivated restrictions (Johansen and Juselius, 1992) are needed, tested by LR tests that are \(\chi^2\) -distributed, because inference on \(\beta\) given the rank is asymptotically mixed normal.

5. ARDL models and the bounds test

The autoregressive distributed lag model is a single-equation conditional ECM. The long-run coefficients are \(-\theta/\phi\) , and \(\phi\in(-2,0)\) is the speed of adjustment. Bounds test (Pesaran, Shin and Smith, 2001). Test \(H_0:\phi=\theta=0\) (no level relationship) with an \(F\) statistic, and the \(t\) -statistic on \(\phi\) . The critical values depend on whether the regressors are \(I(0)\) or \(I(1)\) . PSS tabulate lower bounds (all regressors \(I(0)\) ) and upper bounds (all \(I(1)\) ). An \(F\) above the upper bound indicates a level relationship regardless of the regressors' integration order; below the lower bound, none; in between, the test is inconclusive. Use finite-sample critical values (Narayan, 2005; Kripfganz and Schneider, 2020) when \(T\) is below about 100.

5. ARDL models and the bounds test

Assumptions that are often overlooked. The bounds test (i) requires that \(y_t\) is \(I(1)\) or \(I(0)\) and that the regressors are not \(I(2)\) ; (ii) assumes at most one level relationship, with \(x_t\) weakly exogenous ( \(x\) does not error-correct toward \(y\) ); and (iii) is a single-equation method. If there may be several cointegrating relations, or feedback from \(y\) to \(x\) , use a Johansen VECM instead. "We use ARDL because our variables are a mix of I(0) and I(1)" is a valid reason only when these assumptions hold.

Long-run money demand. Let \(m_t\) be log real M2, \(y_t\) log real GDP, and \(i_t\) an opportunity-cost interest rate, with quarterly data. Suppose all three are \(I(1)\) by ADF and KPSS. A Johansen trace test with an unrestricted constant and 4 lags rejects \(r=0\) (trace 41.2 against a 5% critical value of 29.8) but not \(r\le1\) (12.1 against 15.5): one cointegrating vector. Normalizing on money gives The income elasticity is close to 1, and an LR test of \(\beta_y=1\) does not reject. The interest semi-elasticity of \(-0.045\) means a one-point rise in \(i\) lowers money demand by about 4.5%. The adjustment coefficient on the money equation is \(-0.12\) (12% of the gap closes per quarter). The output equation's loading is insignificant, so output is weakly exogenous. (Illustrative numbers. Many studies find that the stability of such relations breaks down around financial innovations, so test for parameter stability in \(\beta\) as in Lecture 10.)

Why special critical values? Explain why the ADF test on Engle–Granger residuals uses critical values more negative than the ordinary ADF test. Solution OLS chooses \(\widehat\gamma\) to minimize the residual variance, which makes \(\widehat z_t\) look as stationary as possible even when no cointegration exists. A study applies the ARDL bounds test to GDP, exports and imports, finds a level relationship, and interprets it as "exports cause growth". List three problems. Solution (i) Exports and GDP almost certainly feed back on each other, violating the weak-exogeneity assumption of the conditional ECM. (ii) With three variables there may be more than one cointegrating relation (for example, GDP–imports and GDP–exports), which the single-equation bounds test cannot handle. (iii) A level relationship is a statement about co-movement, not causation; causal claims need an identification strategy.

Exercise 12.1 — Danish money demand: Johansen's classic dataset

Data: danish_data (statsmodels) — Danish quarterly data, 1974Q1–1987Q3 (Johansen and Juselius, 1990): log real money lrm , log real income lry , bond rate ibo , deposit rate ide . Run the Johansen trace test on (lrm, lry, ibo, ide) with a constant and one lagged difference. Assuming rank 1, estimate the VECM and normalize the cointegrating vector on money. Interpret the income elasticity and the interest-rate coefficients, and the adjustment coefficients. Output: The trace test rejects \(r=0\) only narrowly (48.8 against a critical value of 47.9) and does not reject \(r\le1\) in this short sample of 55 quarters, so one cointegrating relation — as Johansen and Juselius (1990) found with seasonal dummies and a restricted constant. Under rank one, the long-run income elasticity of money demand is close to one, and the coefficients on the two interest rates have opposite signs: the bond rate (the opportunity cost of holding money) lowers money demand, and the deposit rate (the own rate on money) raises it — with similar magnitudes, so the spread matters. Money is the variable that adjusts to disequilibrium, which supports reading the relation as money demand . The sensitivity of the rank test to the deterministic terms is part of the lesson.

Exercise 12.2 — The consumption–income relation: Engle–Granger, DOLS and the error-correction model

Data: macrodata — U.S. quarterly real consumption realcons and real disposable income realdpi , 1959–2009. Test both logs for a unit root (ADF with trend). Run the Engle–Granger cointegration test of log(realcons) on log(realdpi) . Estimate the cointegrating slope by static OLS and by DOLS with 2 leads and lags (HAC standard errors). Estimate the error-correction model \(\Delta c_t=\alpha+\gamma\,\widehat z_{t-1}+\delta\,\Delta y_t+\varepsilon_t\) . How fast does consumption close the gap? Output: Both series are I(1). The Engle–Granger test, with its special critical values, does not reject the null of no cointegration (p ≈ 0.26). That is a common finding for consumption and income in levels: the consumption–income ratio drifted upward from the 1980s as the saving rate fell, so the gap looks persistent. The remaining steps are therefore conditional on cointegration — exactly the situation where a researcher must say so explicitly. The long-run elasticity is close to but significantly above one in the DOLS regression, which uses valid HAC inference unlike the static regression. The error-correction coefficient is negative, as theory requires, but small: consumption closes only a few percent of the gap each quarter. Short-run consumption responds much less than one-for-one to income growth — the consumption smoothing that permanent-income theory predicts.

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: define causal estimands (ATE, ATT, LATE, CATE) in the potential-outcomes framework, and decompose a naive comparison into effect and selection bias; estimate effects under unconfoundedness by regression adjustment, inverse probability weighting and doubly robust methods, and check overlap; set up difference-in-differences, test its assumptions with event studies, and explain why two-way fixed effects fails with staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects; describe the synthetic control method and its inference; estimate sharp and fuzzy regression discontinuity designs with local polynomials, optimal bandwidths and robust bias-corrected inference, and validate them.

Since the "credibility revolution" (Angrist and Pischke, 2010), the most influential empirical work in economics has been organized around research designs : features of the world that make treated and untreated units comparable. This lecture collects the main designs that do not rely on instruments (Lecture 5 covered IV). The common thread is that every design replaces an untestable assumption about everything with a more transparent, partially testable assumption about something specific : random assignment, selection on observables, parallel trends, or continuity at a threshold.

Each unit \(i\) has potential outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) (treated) and \(Y_i(0)\) (untreated). We observe \(Y_i=D_iY_i(1)+(1-D_i)Y_i(0)\) . The individual effect \(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\) is never observed: the fundamental problem of causal inference . The estimands are averages: The notation embeds SUTVA : one unit's treatment does not affect another's outcomes (no spillovers), and there is a single version of treatment. Selection bias. The naive difference in means decomposes as Randomization makes \(D\) independent of \((Y(1),Y(0))\) , so the selection bias is zero and ATT = ATE. In a randomized experiment, regressing \(Y\) on \(D\) and pre-treatment covariates improves precision without introducing bias asymptotically. The fully interacted specification (Lin, 2013) is robust to heterogeneous effects.

Unconfoundedness and overlap. (i) \((Y(1),Y(0))\perp D\mid X\) : conditional on observed pre-treatment covariates, treatment is as good as random. (ii) \(0<e(x)<1\) , where \(e(x)=P(D=1\mid X=x)\) is the propensity score . Under these assumptions, \(ATE=E\big[\mu_1(X)-\mu_0(X)\big]\) , with \(\mu_d(x)=E[Y\mid D=d,X=x]\) . Three estimation approaches follow. Regression adjustment: fit \(\widehat\mu_1\) and \(\widehat\mu_0\) separately, then average \(\widehat\mu_1(X_i)-\widehat\mu_0(X_i)\) . A single regression of \(Y\) on \(D\) and \(X\) instead estimates a variance-weighted average of conditional effects, which differs from the ATE when effects are heterogeneous (Angrist, 1998; Słoczyński, 2022). Inverse probability weighting (IPW): \(\widehat{ATE}=n^{-1}\sum_i\big[D_iY_i/\widehat e(X_i)-(1-D_i)Y_i/(1-\widehat e(X_i))\big]\) . This is unstable when \(\widehat e\) is near 0 or 1; use normalized (Hájek) weights. Doubly robust (AIPW):

It is consistent if either the outcome model or the propensity model is correct. It is efficient if both are. Combined with cross-fitting, it allows flexible machine-learning estimates of the nuisance functions while preserving \(\sqrt n\) inference (double/debiased machine learning; Chernozhukov et al., 2018). Matching on covariates or on the propensity score is an alternative. Use bias-corrected matching estimators (Abadie and Imbens, 2011); bootstrap standard errors are invalid for nearest-neighbor matching. Overlap in practice. Plot \(\widehat e(X)\) by treatment group. Trim units with extreme scores (Crump et al., 2009), and report how the estimand changes. Sensitivity: unconfoundedness is untestable. Report how strong unobserved confounding would have to be to overturn the result (Imbens, 2003; Cinelli and Hazlett, 2020).

The 2×2 design. Two groups (treated \(G=1\) , control \(G=0\) ) and two periods (pre, post). The DiD estimand is Theorem 13.1. Under parallel trends , \(E[Y_{post}(0)-Y_{pre}(0)\mid G=1]=E[Y_{post}(0)-Y_{pre}(0)\mid G=0]\) , and no anticipation ( \(Y_{pre}(1)=Y_{pre}(0)\) for the treated), we have \(\tau_{DiD}=ATT\) in the post period. Proof. For the treated, \(E[Y_{post}-Y_{pre}\mid G=1]=E[Y_{post}(1)-Y_{pre}(0)\mid G=1]\) by no anticipation. Subtract and add \(E[Y_{post}(0)\mid G=1]\) to get \(ATT+E[Y_{post}(0)-Y_{pre}(0)\mid G=1]\) . By parallel trends, the second term equals the control group's observed change. ∎ The regression \(Y_{it}=\alpha+\beta G_i+\gamma Post_t+\tau(G_i\times Post_t)+\varepsilon_{it}\) gives \(\widehat\tau=\widehat\tau_{DiD}\) . Parallel trends is an assumption about untreated potential outcomes , so it is untestable in the post period and scale-dependent : it cannot hold in both levels and logs unless trends are zero (Roth and Sant'Anna, 2023). Choose the scale on economic grounds. Cluster at the level of treatment assignment (Lecture 4).

Event studies. With multiple periods, estimate dynamic effects relative to the period before treatment: where \(E_i\) is the treatment date. Pre-period coefficients near zero are consistent with parallel trends, but pre-trend tests have low power, and conditioning on passing them can distort inference (Roth, 2022). The approach of Rambachan and Roth (2023) gives inference that is robust to bounded violations of parallel trends. Staggered adoption and the TWFE problem. When units adopt treatment at different times, the static TWFE regression \(Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\tau D_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}\) is a weighted average of all 2×2 DiDs in the data. These include comparisons that use already-treated units as controls (Goodman-Bacon, 2021). If effects grow over time, those "forbidden comparisons" subtract treatment effects, and some implicit weights on group-time effects are negative . \(\widehat\tau\) can then have the wrong sign even if every unit's effect is positive (de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfœuille, 2020). Dynamic TWFE event studies suffer from the same contamination (Sun and Abraham, 2021). Heterogeneity-robust alternatives:

Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021): estimate group-time ATTs, \(ATT(g,t)\) , using never-treated or not-yet-treated units as controls, then aggregate with explicit, non-negative weights; Sun and Abraham (2021): an interaction-weighted event-study estimator; Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess (2024): imputation — fit unit and time effects on untreated observations only, impute \(Y(0)\) for the treated, and average the differences.

With a single (or few) treated aggregate unit(s) — a country, a state — and a long pre-period, Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller (2010) construct a synthetic control : a convex combination of donor units, with weights \(w_j\ge0\) and \(\sum w_j=1\) , chosen to match the treated unit's pre-treatment outcomes and predictors. The effect estimate is the post-treatment gap between the treated unit and its synthetic counterpart. The convexity constraint prevents extrapolation and makes weights interpretable. Inference uses placebo (permutation) tests: apply the method to each donor and compare the treated unit's post/pre RMSPE ratio with the placebo distribution. Extensions include synthetic DiD (Arkhangelsky et al., 2021), which combines unit and time weights, and conformal inference (Chernozhukov, Wüthrich and Zhu, 2021).

Treatment is determined, fully or partly, by whether a running variable \(X\) crosses a cutoff \(c\) . Sharp RD: \(D=1\{X\ge c\}\) . If \(E[Y(0)\mid X=x]\) and \(E[Y(1)\mid X=x]\) are continuous at \(c\) , then Fuzzy RD: the probability of treatment jumps at \(c\) but by less than one. The estimand is the ratio of the outcome jump to the treatment jump, a LATE for compliers at the cutoff. It is IV with \(1\{X\ge c\}\) as the instrument. Estimation. Use local linear regression on each side within a bandwidth \(h\) , with a triangular kernel. Avoid global high-order polynomials, which give noisy estimates and misleading inference (Gelman and Imbens, 2019). Choose \(h\) to minimize MSE (Imbens and Kalyanaraman, 2012). Because the MSE-optimal bandwidth leaves a bias of the same order as the standard error, conventional confidence intervals undercover. Use robust bias-corrected inference (Calonico, Cattaneo and Titiunik, 2014), implemented in rdrobust .

Validation. Manipulation: if agents can precisely sort around the cutoff, continuity fails. Test for a discontinuity in the density of \(X\) at \(c\) (McCrary, 2008; Cattaneo, Jansson and Ma, 2020). Covariate balance: pre-determined covariates should not jump at \(c\) . Run the RD with each covariate as the outcome. Placebo cutoffs and bandwidth sensitivity: no effects at fake cutoffs, and stable estimates across a range of bandwidths. External validity: the estimate is local to \(X=c\) . Extrapolation away from the cutoff requires further assumptions.

Two groups adopt treatment: group A in period 2, group B in period 3; \(T=3\) , no never-treated group. Effects are 1 in the first treated period and 3 in the second. Describe the 2×2 comparisons in TWFE and explain how a "forbidden" comparison biases \(\widehat\tau\) . Solution The comparisons are: A vs not-yet-treated B for periods 1→2 (clean, effect 1); B vs already-treated A for periods 2→3. In the second, A's outcome changes by its effect growth \(3-1=2\) , so the comparison yields \(1-2=-1\) for B's true effect of 1. The forbidden comparison enters with positive weight and pulls \(\widehat\tau\) down — it can even make it negative while all true effects are positive.

Manipulation. A scholarship is awarded to students scoring at least 80 on an exam graded by their own teachers. The density of scores shows excess mass at 80–81. What does this imply for the RD, and what can you do? Solution Teachers likely push marginal students over the threshold, so students just above differ systematically from those just below: continuity fails. Options: use a running variable that cannot be manipulated (an externally graded test), use a "donut" RD excluding observations near the cutoff (with caution), or bound the effect under assumptions about the manipulators (Gerard, Rokkanen and Rothe, 2020). Data: jtrain2 — the NSW randomized experiment (185 treated, 260 controls); jtrain3 — the same treated men with 2,490 non-experimental controls from the PSID. Outcome: 1978 earnings re78 (thousands of dollars). Estimate the experimental effect of training on re78 (difference in means and with covariates). Using jtrain3 , estimate the effect by (a) a naive difference, (b) regression adjustment, and (c) a doubly robust AIPW estimator with a logit propensity score. Covariates: age , agesq , educ , black , hisp , married , re74 , re75 , unem74 , unem75 . Check overlap: what share of PSID controls have propensity scores below 0.01? Exercise 13.1 — LaLonde's job training data: can observational methods recover an experimental benchmark?

Output: The experiment gives an effect of about $1,800 on 1978 earnings. With PSID controls, the naive comparison is hugely negative : trainees were far poorer than the average PSID household — classic selection bias. Regression adjustment and the doubly robust estimator move a long way toward the benchmark, but the answer depends on modeling choices, and most PSID controls have propensity scores near zero: there is almost no overlap. Trimming to the region of common support changes the estimates noticeably. This is LaLonde's (1986) lesson, refined by Dehejia and Wahba (1999): observational methods can work only when comparable controls exist, and overlap diagnostics must come first.

Exercise 13.2 — Difference-in-differences: an incinerator and house prices

Data: kielmc — 321 house sales in North Andover, Massachusetts, in 1978 (before rumors of an incinerator) and 1981 (during construction); nearinc = within 3 miles of the site. Compute the 2×2 DiD estimate of the incinerator's effect on real house prices rprice from the four group means. Estimate it by regression, rprice ~ nearinc * y81 , with robust standard errors. Add house characteristics ( age , agesq , intst , land , area , rooms , baths ). How does the estimate change, and why? Use log(rprice) to express the effect in percent. Which scale makes parallel trends more plausible? Output: Houses near the site were already cheaper in 1978. The DiD removes that level difference and attributes the change in the gap — a fall of roughly $12,000 in real (1978) dollars — to the incinerator. Without controls the estimate is imprecise. Adding house characteristics makes it larger and more precise, because the mix of houses sold near the site changed between the two years. In logs with controls, the effect is about \(-9\%\) , but with a standard error of 0.06 it is not statistically significant: the evidence is suggestive rather than conclusive with 321 sales. Parallel trends is an assumption about counterfactual price paths; the log scale is often more plausible for prices, because it allows near and far houses to share common percentage appreciation. With only two periods, pre-trends cannot be checked — a key limitation (Kiel and McClain, 1995; Wooldridge, Example 13.3).

By the end of this lecture you should be able to: move from a research question to a precisely stated estimand, an identification argument and an estimator; design, run and report a Monte Carlo study, including Monte Carlo standard errors; use the bootstrap correctly (pairs, wild, block, cluster), and know when it fails; control for multiple testing (Holm, Benjamini–Hochberg, Romano–Wolf) and report specification robustness transparently; build a replication package that meets current journal standards.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

The previous thirteen lectures supplied estimators and the assumptions under which they work. This lecture is about using them in research that others can trust and reproduce. Two facts motivate it. First, the finite-sample behavior of an estimator in your setting is often unknown, and simulation is how you find out. Second, the credibility of empirical economics has been damaged less by bad estimators than by undisclosed researcher choices, unreported specifications and code that cannot be re-run. Journals now enforce reproducibility (the AEA Data Editor has done so since 2019), and evidence of selective reporting is widespread (Brodeur, Cook and Heyes, 2020).
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

A good empirical paper answers four questions, in order. Estimand. What population quantity do you want? "The effect of class size on test scores" is not yet an estimand. "The average effect, on third-grade reading scores, of reducing class size from 22 to 15 for students in Tennessee public schools in 1985–89" is one. Identification. Under which assumptions does that quantity equal a feature of the observable distribution (a regression coefficient, a Wald ratio, a discontinuity)? State them in words and in notation, and say which can be partially tested. Estimation and inference. Which estimator, which variance estimator (matching the dependence structure, Lecture 4), and which finite-sample corrections? Validation. Placebo outcomes, placebo treatments, pre-trends, balance, density tests, sensitivity analysis.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

Pre-analysis plans. For experiments, and increasingly for observational work using new data, register the primary outcomes, specifications and hypotheses before seeing the outcome data (the AEA RCT Registry, OSF). A plan does not forbid exploration. It makes the distinction between confirmatory and exploratory results visible (Olken, 2015).
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

Purpose. Simulation answers questions that asymptotic theory leaves open: Is the bias of my estimator material at \(n=200\) ? Do my 95% intervals cover? How many clusters do I need? Design checklist. Data-generating process (DGP). Make it realistic: calibrate it to your data (sample size, number of clusters, regressor distributions, \(R^2\) , error dependence). Vary the features that theory says matter (instrument strength, persistence, heteroskedasticity). Estimators and procedures compared on the same simulated datasets (common random numbers reduce the noise in comparisons). Performance measures for an estimator \(\widehat\theta_r\) , \(r=1,\dots,R\) : Report median bias and interquartile ranges when the estimator may lack moments (just-identified IV has no finite mean). Monte Carlo standard errors. Simulation results are estimates. For a rejection rate \(\widehat p\) , the MC standard error is \(\sqrt{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)/R}\) . With \(R=1{,}000\) and true size 5%, it is 0.0069, so an observed 6.2% is not evidence of size distortion. To detect a 1-point distortion reliably, you need \(R\approx10{,}000\) .
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting
Reproducibility. Fix and report seeds, save simulated results, and parallelize with independent random streams (for example, numpy.random.SeedSequence.spawn ).

The bootstrap approximates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling from the data (Efron, 1979). The resampling scheme must mimic the dependence structure of the data. Data structure Bootstrap i.i.d. observations pairs (resample rows \((Y_i,X_i)\) ) heteroskedastic regression wild : \(Y_i^*=X_i'\widehat\beta+\widehat u_iv_i\) , with \(v_i\) Rademacher (±1) clustered resample whole clusters, or the wild cluster bootstrap (one \(v_g\) per cluster), with the null imposed time series block (moving or stationary) bootstrap, or sieve (residual-based AR) Asymptotic refinement. Bootstrapping an asymptotically pivotal statistic, such as a \(t\) -statistic, gives more accurate tests and intervals than normal approximations (the percentile- \(t\) method). Bootstrapping the estimator itself (the percentile method) does not provide this refinement.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

When the bootstrap fails. Examples: parameters on the boundary of the parameter space, the maximum of a sample, non-differentiable functionals, nearest-neighbor matching estimators (Abadie and Imbens, 2008), weak instruments, and unit-root autoregressions ( \(\phi=1\) ). Subsampling or the \(m\) -out-of- \(n\) bootstrap can help in some of these cases.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

Multiple hypotheses. Testing \(m\) hypotheses at 5% each gives a probability of at least one false rejection of up to \(1-0.95^m\) : 40% for \(m=10\) . Family-wise error rate (FWER). Bonferroni tests each hypothesis at \(\alpha/m\) . Holm's step-down procedure is uniformly more powerful: sort p-values \(p_{(1)}\le\dots\le p_{(m)}\) and reject \(H_{(j)}\) while \(p_{(j)}\le\alpha/(m-j+1)\) . Romano–Wolf (2005) uses the bootstrap to exploit the correlation between test statistics, which gives more power when outcomes are correlated. False discovery rate (FDR). Benjamini–Hochberg controls the expected share of false rejections among rejections: reject \(H_{(1)},\dots,H_{(k)}\) for the largest \(k\) with \(p_{(k)}\le k\alpha/m\) . It is appropriate for exploratory analysis with many outcomes. Anderson (2008) applies these methods to early-childhood interventions.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

Index outcomes. Combine related outcomes into a standardized summary index (Kling, Liebman and Katz, 2007), which reduces the number of tests and increases power. Specification robustness. Report how the main estimate changes across defensible choices of controls, samples, functional forms and estimators: a "specification curve" or multiverse analysis (Simonsohn, Simmons and Nelson, 2020). Robustness tables that only show specifications that work are not robustness checks.
Lecture 14: Research Design, Monte Carlo, Replication, and Reporting

Lead with effect sizes and confidence intervals in meaningful units (percent, standard deviations, dollars per person). Interpret magnitude against a benchmark. Avoid significance stars as the main message. "Not significant" is not "no effect": report the interval and what it rules out. Report the first-stage \(F\) (effective \(F\) ) for IV, the number of clusters, the variance estimator, and the number of treated units. Show the raw data where possible: binned scatter plots, event-study plots with pre-periods, RD plots with binned means. Be explicit about the estimand. LATE, ATT and ATE differ, and so do weighted and unweighted estimates.

Modern journals require a replication package that reproduces every table and figure from raw data. The AEA Data and Code Availability Policy and the Social Science Data Editors' template README set the standard. A package should contain: a README with data sources, access conditions (including for confidential data), the software and versions used, expected run time, and a table mapping every table and figure to the program that produces it; raw data (or instructions to obtain them) kept separate from derived data , with the cleaning code; a master script that runs everything in order with a single command; a fixed environment : requirements.txt or environment.yml (Python), renv.lock (R), the Stata version plus ado-files;

fixed seeds for anything random (bootstrap, simulation, sample splits); relative paths only , and no manual steps. Test it by running the package from a clean machine or container before submission. Version control with Git, with tagged releases for submitted versions, makes the history auditable.

How many replications? You want to compare the size of a cluster-robust \(t\) -test and a wild cluster bootstrap with \(G=12\) clusters, where the true size of the first test might be about 9% and of the second about 5.5%. With \(R\) replications per design, the MC standard errors are \(\sqrt{0.09\times0.91/R}\) and \(\sqrt{0.055\times0.945/R}\) . With \(R=2{,}000\) , these are 0.0064 and 0.0051. Even treating the two estimates as independent, the MC standard error of their difference is \(\sqrt{0.0064^2+0.0051^2}=0.0082\) , so a 3.5-point gap is about four standard errors from zero. Because both tests are run on the same simulated datasets, the true standard error of the difference is smaller still. With \(R=200\) , the SEs are 0.020 and 0.016, and the comparison would be uninformative. With 399 bootstrap draws per replication, the total cost is \(2{,}000\times399\approx800{,}000\) model fits: plan computing time accordingly, and use a parallel, seeded design.

MC error. In 500 replications, a test rejects 33 times at nominal 5%. Is there evidence of over-rejection? Compute an approximate 95% interval for the true rejection rate. Solution \(\widehat p=0.066\) , with MC SE \(\sqrt{0.066\times0.934/500}=0.0111\) . The 95% interval is \(0.066\pm0.022=[0.044,\,0.088]\) , which contains 0.05. That is not strong evidence; increase \(R\) . MC error. In 500 replications, a test rejects 33 times at nominal 5%. Is there evidence of over-rejection? Wrong bootstrap. A researcher bootstraps standard errors in a state-year panel by resampling individual state-year observations. Explain the problem and the fix. Solution Resampling observations independently destroys within-state serial correlation, so the bootstrap reproduces the downward bias of non-clustered standard errors. Resample states (the cluster bootstrap), or use a wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed when the number of states is small.

Exercise 14.1 — Wild cluster bootstrap with few clusters

Data: wagepan — 545 workers, 1980–1987; the dummies occ1 – occ9 give each person-year's occupation (9 groups). Many applied papers have few clusters. Build an occupation variable from the dummies occ1 – occ9 and use it (9 groups) as the cluster: Regress lwage on union , educ , exper , expersq and year dummies; report the cluster-robust \(t\) -statistic on union with 9 occupation clusters. Implement a wild cluster bootstrap-t with Rademacher weights and the null \(\beta_{union}=0\) imposed (999 draws, seed 1). Compare p-values. Why can the conventional cluster-robust p-value be misleading here? Output: With only 9 clusters, the cluster-robust variance estimator is noisy and biased downward, so normal (or even \(t_{G-1}\) ) critical values overstate significance. The wild cluster bootstrap with the null imposed gives a more honest p-value — here noticeably larger than the conventional one. With very few clusters, Rademacher weights allow only \(2^G\) distinct bootstrap samples; Webb's six-point weights are recommended for \(G<12\) . The deeper question, as in Lecture 4, is whether occupation is the right clustering level for this design at all (Abadie et al., 2023).

Exercise 14.2 — Multiple outcomes and multiple testing in the NSW experiment

Data: jtrain2 — NSW randomized experiment. Estimate the effect of training on six outcomes: re78 , unem78 , an indicator of positive 1978 earnings, earnings above $5,000, above $10,000, and the change re78 − re75 . Report unadjusted p-values and Holm, Bonferroni and Benjamini–Hochberg adjustments. Build a standardized summary index (Kling, Liebman and Katz, 2007): standardize each outcome by the control-group mean and SD (signing unem78 so higher is better), average them, and test the treatment effect on the index. Output: Four of the six outcomes are individually significant at 5%. After adjusting for six tests, only 1978 earnings survives Bonferroni and Holm (Holm's adjusted p-values are smaller, but here they cross 5% at the same point), while the Benjamini–Hochberg FDR procedure keeps four. Notice that unem78 and pos78 give identical results: they are almost the same variable (positive earnings = employed), which is a reminder to define the outcome family carefully before testing. The summary index answers the question "did training improve labor-market outcomes overall?" with a single test and more power than any one outcome. Pre-specify which family of outcomes will be adjusted and which index will be primary before seeing the data (Lecture 14, §1).

Topic Outline — Graduate econometrics course notes covering OLS, inference, IV, panel data, time series, cointegration and causal inference.

A condensed map of the core definitions and results in Econometrics. Each topic is developed in full in the lecture notes . Level: Advanced undergraduate and graduate. Scope: Probability foundations, regression, inference, endogeneity, IV, panel data, time series, causal inference, and reproducible computation.

Students will formulate estimands, derive estimators, state identification assumptions, distinguish finite-sample from asymptotic results, diagnose model failures, and implement reproducible analyses in R, Python, or Stata.

Let (Y,X) be random variables. Conditional expectation E(Y|X) is the minimum mean-square predictor among functions of X. Use iterated expectations, total variance, covariance decompositions, LLN, CLT, Slutsky's theorem, continuous mapping, and the delta method. Distinguish convergence in probability from convergence in distribution.

For y = Xβ + u, OLS minimizes (y-Xb)'(y-Xb), yielding βhat=(X'X)^(-1)X'y when X has full column rank. Define projection P_X=X(X'X)^(-1)X' and residual maker M_X=I-P_X. Then fitted values are P_Xy, residuals are M_Xy, and X'u_hat=0. Under correct linear conditional mean, full rank, E(u|X)=0, and Var(u|X)=σ²I, OLS is BLUE. Normality is not required for Gauss-Markov. Variance: Var(βhat|X)=σ²(X'X)^(-1); estimate σ² by RSS/(n-k). Derive t and F tests under normality. Explain partial regression and the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem.

Levels, log-level, level-log, log-log, polynomials, interactions, dummy variables, elasticities, marginal effects, and nonlinear transformations. For log(y)=β0+β1log(x)+u, β1 is an elasticity. Interpret coefficients conditionally; a regression coefficient is not automatically causal. Cover RESET, residual plots, leverage, studentized residuals, and Cook's distance.

Test H0:Rβ=r using Wald, likelihood-ratio, or score procedures. Explain size, power, confidence coverage, p-values, multiple testing, and economic significance. Under heteroskedasticity, use sandwich covariance (X'X)^(-1) (Σ x_i x_i' uhat_i²) (X'X)^(-1). HC0-HC3 differ in finite-sample leverage corrections. Robust standard errors do not fix endogeneity or wrong functional form.

Endogeneity arises from omitted variables, simultaneity, measurement error, or selection. Instrument z must satisfy relevance and exclusion/exogeneity. With instrument matrix Z, P_Z=Z(Z'Z)^(-1)Z' and βhat_2SLS=(X'P_ZX)^(-1)X'P_Zy. Explain first-stage partial R², weak-instrument diagnostics, weak-IV robust inference, overidentification tests, and local average treatment effects. Relevance is empirically assessable; exclusion needs institutional and economic justification.

Structural system By_t+Γx_t=ε_t and reduced form y_t=Πx_t+v_t. Explain order and rank conditions, exclusion restrictions, structural versus reduced-form parameters, 2SLS and 3SLS. A reduced-form residual does not automatically identify a structural shock.

Model y_it=x_it'β+α_i+λ_t+u_it. Derive within transformation and first differences. Compare pooled OLS, fixed effects, random effects, correlated random effects/Mundlak, two-way effects, and clustered inference. Fixed effects remove time-invariant α_i but not time-varying confounding. Discuss serial correlation, unbalanced panels, and few-cluster inference.

For y_it=ρy_i,t-1+x_it'β+α_i+u_it, explain Nickell bias for fixed T, difference GMM, system GMM, timing-based moment restrictions, instrument proliferation, AR(1)/AR(2), Hansen/Sargan tests, instrument collapsing, and sensitivity to instrument count. Students must state the exact moment conditions used.

Stationarity, weak dependence, ACF/PACF, white noise, deterministic trends, stochastic trends, unit roots, spurious regression, ARMA, lag selection, residual diagnostics, and forecast evaluation. For AR(1), y_t=ρy_t-1+ε_t, covariance stationarity requires |ρ|<1.

VAR(p): y_t=c+Σ A_j y_t-j+ε_t. Cover stability, companion form, lag selection, Granger predictability, impulse responses, forecast-error variance decomposition, and structural identification through contemporaneous restrictions, long-run restrictions, sign restrictions, or external instruments. Reduced-form innovations alone do not identify economic shocks.

Cointegration is a stationary linear combination of nonstationary I(1) variables. VECM: Δy_t=Πy_t-1+ΣΓ_jΔy_t-j+ε_t, with Π=αβ'. Explain rank, adjustment coefficients, Johansen trace and maximum-eigenvalue tests, Engle-Granger, deterministic components, ARDL bounds testing, and integration-order restrictions.

Potential outcomes Y(1),Y(0), ATE=E[Y(1)-Y(0)], ignorability, overlap, matching, weighting, regression adjustment, DiD, event studies, synthetic control, and regression discontinuity. DiD estimator: (treated post-treated pre)-(control post-control pre). State parallel trends, inspect pre-trends, and account for staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects.

Differentiate the OLS objective and derive βhat=(X'X)^(-1)X'y. In y=β1x1+β2x2+u, derive omitted-variable bias when x2 is excluded: β1 probability limit shifts by β2 Cov(x1,x2)/Var(x1). Explain relevance versus exclusion for an instrument and provide a plausible exclusion violation. Show within-demeaning removes α_i and explain why time-invariant regressors are unidentified under individual fixed effects. Explain spurious regression and how cointegration changes the interpretation.

1.1 (Projection with a nonlinear CEF). Let \(X\sim\text{Exponential}(1)\) and \(E[Y\mid X]=\log(1+X)\) . (a) Derive the BLP coefficients of \(Y\) on \((1,X)\) as integrals and evaluate them numerically. (b) Show that the projection error is uncorrelated with \(X\) but that \(E[u\mid X]\neq0\) . (c) Explain what OLS estimates in this model and why the result is still useful. 1.2 (FWL and leverage). Prove that adding a dummy variable for observation \(i\) alone to a regression sets \(\widehat u_i=0\) and gives the remaining coefficients as if observation \(i\) were deleted. Use this to derive the leave-one-out residual \(\widehat u_{(i)}=\widehat u_i/(1-h_{ii})\) . 1.3 (Delta method, computational). Using the Current Population Survey extract of your choice (or Wooldridge's wage2 data), estimate \(\log w=\beta_0+\beta_1exper+\beta_2exper^2+\beta_3educ+u\) . Report the turning point of the experience profile with a delta-method 95% interval and a pairs-bootstrap percentile- \(t\) interval (999 draws). Comment on any differences.

1.1 \(\beta_1=\operatorname{Cov}(X,\log(1+X))/\operatorname{Var}(X)\) , where \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1\) and \(E[\log(1+X)]=e\,E_1(1)\approx0.596\) ( \(E_1\) the exponential integral). Evaluate \(E[X\log(1+X)]\) numerically, giving \(\beta_1\approx0.40\) . (c) OLS estimates the best linear approximation to a concave CEF. It is useful as a summary of the average slope, weighted by the design, but not as a structural marginal effect at a particular \(x\) . 1.2 By FWL, partialling out the dummy \(e_i\) deletes row \(i\) from every other regressor. The dummy's coefficient absorbs \(y_i-X_i'\widehat\beta_{(i)}\) , so \(\widehat u_i=0\) . The leave-one-out formula follows from the Sherman–Morrison identity applied to \((X'X-X_iX_i')^{-1}\) . 1.3 With the delta method, the interval is symmetric by construction. The percentile- \(t\) interval is typically asymmetric and wider when \(\widehat\beta_2\) is imprecise, reflecting the ratio form of the turning point.

2.1 (Signing bias). In a regression of country growth on initial income and investment, explain the likely direction of bias in the investment coefficient from (a) omitting human capital and (b) classical measurement error in investment. Combine the two effects in a single formula and state the condition under which the OLS estimate is unbiased by accident. 2.2 (Moulton in practice). Using Project STAR data (student-level test scores with classroom assignment), estimate the effect of small classes with (a) HC1, (b) classroom-clustered, and (c) school-clustered standard errors. Report the intra-class correlation of the residual and compare the ratio of standard errors with the Moulton formula. Which level of clustering is justified by the design, and why?
Problem Set 2 — Specification and robust inference (Lectures 3–4)

2.3 (Leverage and HC3). Simulate \(n=40\) observations with one high-leverage point. Show by Monte Carlo ( \(R=5{,}000\) ) that HC0 under-covers and HC3 nearly fixes it. Report Monte Carlo standard errors. 2.1 Human capital is positively related to both growth and investment, giving upward bias. Measurement error attenuates. With reliability \(\lambda\) of investment after partialling out initial income, \(\operatorname{plim}\widehat\beta=\lambda(\beta+\gamma\delta)\) , where \(\gamma\delta\) is the OVB term. It is accidentally unbiased when \(\lambda(\beta+\gamma\delta)=\beta\) . 2.2 Treatment was randomized within schools, across classrooms , so the assignment unit is the classroom: cluster there and include school fixed effects. School-level clustering is not required by the design and leaves about 79 clusters with much noisier variance estimates (Abadie et al., 2023).

3.1 (Proximity to college). Using Card's (1995) NLS Young Men data, estimate the return to schooling by OLS and by IV, with an indicator for growing up near a four-year college as the instrument, controlling for experience, experience squared, race, region and urban residence. Report (a) the first stage with an effective \(F\) , (b) 2SLS with robust standard errors, (c) the Anderson–Rubin 95% confidence set, and (d) a discussion of who the compliers are and of plausible violations of the exclusion restriction. 3.2 (Many instruments). Add interactions of the instrument with region and parental education to obtain about 20 instruments. Compare 2SLS, LIML and Fuller(1). Explain the differences using the theory of Lectures 5–6.

3.3 (Order versus rank). Construct a two-equation system in which the order condition holds for the first equation but the rank condition fails. Simulate it, and show what happens to the 2SLS estimate and the first-stage \(F\) . 3.1 The IV estimate exceeds OLS (roughly 0.13 versus 0.07–0.08 in Card's specification), with a much larger standard error. The first stage is significant but not overwhelming. Compliers are men whose schooling depends on living near a college, likely from lower-income families with higher marginal returns. That is one explanation for IV > OLS, alongside measurement error. Exclusion concerns: college proximity correlates with urban labor markets and family background. 3.2 With many instruments, 2SLS moves toward OLS; LIML and Fuller stay closer to the just-identified estimate, with wider dispersion.

3.3 Example: the excluded variable enters the reduced form of the endogenous regressor with coefficient zero. The 2SLS estimate is then centered near the OLS limit, with an erratic distribution, and the first-stage \(F\) is approximately \(\chi^2_\ell/\ell\) .

4.1 (Within versus between). Prove that the RE estimator is a matrix-weighted average of the within and between estimators. Give the weights. 4.2 (Union premium). Using the NLSY or PSID worker panel (e.g., Wooldridge's wagepan ), estimate the union wage premium by pooled OLS, RE, FE and FD with unit-clustered standard errors. Run the Mundlak test. Interpret the pattern of estimates in light of selection and measurement error. 4.3 (Dynamic panel). Using the Arellano–Bond employment data ( abdata ), estimate the labor demand equation by FE, difference GMM and system GMM. For the GMM estimators, report results with all lags and with collapsed instruments limited to lags 2–4, along with instrument counts, AR(1)/AR(2) tests, Hansen tests and Windmeijer-corrected standard errors. Which estimates do you believe, and why?

4.1 \(\widehat\beta_{RE}=W\widehat\beta_B+(I-W)\widehat\beta_W\) , with \(W=[X_W'X_W+\psi X_B'X_B]^{-1}\psi X_B'X_B\) , \(\psi=\sigma_u^2/(\sigma_u^2+T\sigma_c^2)\) , where \(X_W\) and \(X_B\) are the within and between design matrices. 4.2 Expect pooled > RE > FE ≈ FD (FD smallest if measurement error dominates). A Mundlak rejection indicates correlation between the unit effect and union status. 4.3 Results should bracket the lagged-employment coefficient between FE and pooled OLS. Estimates that move substantially when instruments are collapsed signal proliferation.

5.1 (ARMA identification). Derive the ACF of an ARMA(1,1). Show that the ACF decays geometrically after lag 1, with the lag-1 value depending on both parameters. 5.2 (Inflation forecasting). Report relative RMSFEs and Diebold–Mariano tests with HAC standard errors. 5.3 (Unit roots and breaks). Report a half-life of deviations with a bias-corrected estimate of the AR coefficient. Relate your results to the "PPP puzzle" (Rogoff, 1996).

5.1 \(\rho_1=(1+\phi\theta)(\phi+\theta)/(1+2\phi\theta+\theta^2)\) and \(\rho_j=\phi\rho_{j-1}\) for \(j\ge2\) . 5.2 Since the mid-1980s, a random walk or IMA(1,1) is very hard to beat at a 4-quarter horizon. AR models do relatively better in high-volatility periods. 5.3 Typical half-lives are 3–5 years, with wide intervals: unit-root tests rarely reject in post-Bretton Woods samples, while panel or long-span data more often do.

6.1 (Long-run restrictions). In a bivariate VAR in output growth and unemployment, derive the Blanchard–Quah impact matrix in terms of \(\Sigma_u\) and \(\Psi(1)\) . Explain what happens to the identified shocks if the VAR is estimated with too few lags. 6.2 (Monetary policy). Estimate a quarterly VAR in log real GDP, log GDP deflator, a commodity price index and the federal funds rate (1965–2007). Compare recursive identification with and without commodity prices, and document the price puzzle. Then estimate impulse responses by local projections using the Romer–Romer (2004) shock series, with HAC bands. Discuss the differences. 6.3 (Term structure). Test whether 3-month and 10-year Treasury yields are cointegrated with cointegrating vector \((1,-1)\) using both Engle–Granger and Johansen. Estimate the VECM and determine which rate adjusts. Interpret the result in light of the expectations hypothesis.

6.1 \(\Theta(1)=\operatorname{chol}(\Psi(1)\Sigma_u\Psi(1)')\) and \(B_0^{-1}=\Psi(1)^{-1}\Theta(1)\) . Too few lags bias \(\Psi(1)\) , and long-run identification is very sensitive to it (Faust and Leeper, 1997). 6.2 Without commodity prices, the price level typically rises for several quarters after a tightening. Exercise 1.1 — Ninety years of U.S. stock returns: arithmetic, geometric and compounded

Data: Fama–French monthly market excess return Mkt-RF and T-bill rate RF , July 1926 – November 2018. Build monthly total market returns \(R_m=\) Mkt-RF + RF . Report annualized arithmetic and geometric mean returns for stocks and bills, and the annualized volatility of stocks. Check the approximation \(\text{geometric}\approx\text{arithmetic}-\sigma^2/2\) . Compute the value in 2018 of $1 invested in July 1926 in stocks and in bills. Report the annualized Sharpe ratio with its standard error \(\sqrt{(1+SR^2/2)/T}\) (Lo, 2002, i.i.d. case). Output: Over 92 years, U.S. stocks returned about 11.2% a year on average (arithmetic) and 9.9% compounded, against 3.3% for T-bills. The geometric mean is close to arithmetic minus \(\sigma^2/2\) : volatility drag. Compounding turns the gap into an enormous difference in wealth — $1 grew to about $6,400 in stocks versus $21 in bills. The Sharpe ratio of about 0.43 has a standard error of 0.10, even with 1,109 months: expected returns are hard to estimate precisely, which is a recurring theme of this course. (Bills look almost riskless in nominal terms here; in real terms they are not.)

Exercise 1.2 — Daily S&P 500 returns: fat tails and volatility clustering

Data: Daily S&P 500 adjusted close, 1999–2018 ( arch.data.sp500 ). Compute daily log returns. Report mean, standard deviation, skewness and excess kurtosis, and run a Jarque–Bera test. Count the days with moves larger than 4 standard deviations, and compare with the number a normal distribution predicts. Compare the autocorrelation of returns with the autocorrelation of squared returns (lags 1–5). What does the contrast say about predictability of returns versus predictability of risk? Output: Daily returns are far from normal: excess kurtosis is about 8, and there were 32 days with moves beyond four standard deviations, where a normal distribution predicts 0.3. The three worst days all fell in autumn 2008. Returns themselves have small (slightly negative) autocorrelations, but squared returns are strongly autocorrelated: large moves cluster in time. Returns are close to unpredictable; risk is highly predictable. This is the motivation for GARCH models (Lectures 13 and 15) and for fat-tailed risk measures.
