Local Projections (Impulse Responses): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

What is the path of \(y\) after a shock \(s\) ? A local projection estimates the impulse response at each horizon \(h = 0, 1, \dots, H\) with a separate regression: where \(x_t\) holds the controls dated \(t\) or earlier (lags of \(y\) , of the shock and of other variables, and any variables ordered before the shock). The coefficient \(\beta_h\) is the response of \(y_{t+h}\) to the shock, and the sequence \(\beta_0, \dots, \beta_H\) is the impulse response function. A VAR gets the same object by iterating one estimated system forward; a local projection estimates each horizon directly. That makes it less efficient but more robust: a misspecified lag length or a nonlinear dynamic does not propagate from short to long horizons.

Three checks before you trust a local projection Is the shock identified? The coefficient is a causal response only if \(s_t\) is unrelated to the other things that move \(y\) . Either the shock is exogenous by construction (a narrative or high-frequency measure, an instrument), or you control for what the shock responds to within the period (the recursive, or Cholesky, assumption). Is the transformation right? Local projections work in levels, in differences and in growth rates, but the outcome must match the question. A response of a level needs the level (or a cumulative sum of growth rates) on the left-hand side. Are the standard errors right? The horizon- \(h\) errors are a moving average of order \(h\) , so ordinary standard errors are wrong. Use Newey-West errors (with bandwidth \(h+1\) ) or lag augmentation with robust errors.

How to write it: the model We estimate the dynamic effect of a credit-spread shock on industrial production with local projections (Jordà 2005). For each horizon \(h = 0, \dots, 24\) months we regress the cumulative growth of industrial production from \(t\) to \(t+h\) on the change in the credit spread at \(t\) , on the contemporaneous stock return, and on six lags of every variable. Identification is recursive: the stock market reacts to news about credit conditions within the month, whereas industrial production and the policy rate respond with a lag. Standard errors are Newey-West with bandwidth \(h+1\) , and the shock is scaled to one standard deviation.
Load the data and check the transformation

How to read it All four series are stationary: the ADF tests reject a unit root (p ≤ 0.001) and the KPSS tests do not reject stationarity (p = 0.10 is the top of the table of available p-values). Stock returns, industrial-production growth and the changes in the fed funds rate and the credit spread are already in the form a local projection needs, so no further transformation is required. The sample has 420 months (1985–2019), and the credit-spread change has a standard deviation of 0.17 percentage points, so a "one-standard-deviation shock" is a 17 basis-point widening. If your shock or outcome were a trending level, use a change or a growth rate; local projections in levels are also valid (see lag augmentation in Step 6), but the interpretation changes.
Identify the shock and choose the controls

The choice of controls is the identification. Compare the response with and without the stock return as a contemporaneous control. How to read it The controls change the answer. If the stock return enters only through its lags, a one-standard-deviation spread shock lowers industrial production by 0.88% after 12 months; if the contemporaneous stock return is held fixed, the fall is 0.64%. The two estimates differ because stock prices and credit spreads react to the same news within the month. Holding the stock return fixed treats that news as already priced in by the stock market and attributes only the part of the spread movement that is not contemporaneously reflected in stock returns to the credit shock. Neither choice is "correct" without an argument. State the ordering you assume and report the other as a robustness check (Step 6). The baseline in the rest of the guide holds the stock return fixed, which is the more conservative of the two.

How to read it A one-standard-deviation widening of the credit spread lowers the level of industrial production by 0.06% in the month of the shock (not significant, p = 0.14), by 0.32% after three months, and by 0.64% after twelve months (95% band −1.04 to −0.23). The response keeps deepening to a maximum of −0.74% at 19 months and is significant at 5% from month 1 to month 19. After 20 months the band includes zero. Each row is a separate regression with 390 to 414 observations; the bands widen with the horizon (standard error 0.04 at h = 0, 0.21 at h = 12 and 0.40 at h = 24), which is the main cost of the method. In the output, "Peak response" is the largest absolute response and "Peak horizon" is the horizon at which it occurs.

A VAR with the same variables and the same ordering gives the same object by a different route. Agreement is reassuring; a large gap means that the VAR dynamics are misspecified or that the local projection is imprecise. How to read it The VAR and the local projection agree closely for the first year: −0.32 against −0.32 at three months, −0.64 against −0.63 at twelve months. They separate at long horizons. At 18 months the figures are −0.73 and −0.67, and at 24 months the local projection shows a recovery (−0.55) while the VAR continues to deepen (−0.69). That is the usual pattern: a VAR imposes a smooth, geometrically decaying response because it extends the short-run dynamics to every horizon, whereas a local projection lets each horizon speak for itself. The difference at 24 months (0.13) is small relative to the local-projection standard error (0.40), so the two are not statistically distinguishable. Report the local projection as the main result and the VAR as a cross-check, or the other way round, but state which.
Robustness: lags, lag augmentation, standard errors and the shock size

How to read it The sign and the timing are robust, the size is not. With three lags the response at twelve months is −0.54, with six lags −0.64 and with twelve lags −0.78; the lag-augmented specification with heteroskedasticity-robust errors gives −0.62 with a larger standard error (0.28 against 0.21). Widening the Newey-West bandwidth to 24 leaves the estimate unchanged and lowers the standard error slightly (0.19), so the significance does not depend on the bandwidth rule. The largest fall is at 19 months in every specification that holds the stock return fixed (18 months without it). The identification choice matters most: leaving the stock return out of the contemporaneous controls gives −0.88 at twelve months. In the paper, say that the response at one year is between 0.5% and 0.9% depending on lags and identification, and that all specifications agree on the shape.
A level or a growth rate? The outcome option

Industrial-production growth is a monthly growth rate. With the level outcome the response at horizon \(h\) is the effect on growth in month \(t+h\) ; with the cumulative-sum outcome it is the effect on the level of production, which is usually the question. How to read it The monthly growth effects are small (−0.06 to −0.11 percentage points per month for the first six months) and fade by the end of the first year (−0.03 at twelve months, +0.06 at 24). Read on their own, the late-horizon figures suggest that the shock has no lasting effect. The cumulative-sum outcome shows what they add up to: a level of industrial production that is 0.64% lower after twelve months and still 0.55% lower after 24. Choose the outcome to match the question, and say in the text whether the response is of a growth rate or of a level.
A level or a growth rate? The outcome option

When the shock is not observed: LP-IV If you have an external instrument for the shock (a high-frequency surprise, a narrative series), add it with the instrument option. The shock is then estimated by two-stage least squares at every horizon (LP-IV; Stock and Watson 2018), and the first-stage F statistic is reported. Check that the F statistic is well above 10 before you read the response.

How to write it: results A one-standard-deviation (17 basis-point) widening of the credit spread lowers the level of industrial production by 0.32% after three months (standard error 0.08) and by 0.64% after twelve months (standard error 0.21). The response reaches its maximum of −0.74% after 19 months, and is statistically significant at the 5% level from month 1 to month 19. The local-projection response is close to that of a VAR(6) with the same ordering for the first year; at 24 months the local projection shows a partial recovery (−0.55) while the VAR does not (−0.69). The size of the response at twelve months ranges from −0.54 to −0.88 across lag lengths and identifying assumptions; its sign and timing are the same in all of them.

Nonlinear ARDL (NARDL): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is: do corporate borrowing costs respond differently to increases and decreases in the policy rate? A standard ARDL model forces a rate rise and a rate cut of the same size to have equal and opposite effects. There are reasons to doubt that: credit risk premia, expectations about the business cycle and the behaviour of lenders can all differ between tightening and easing. The nonlinear ARDL model of Shin, Yu and Greenwood-Nimmo (2014) relaxes this restriction with one simple device. The regressor \(x_t\) is split into two partial sums , one that accumulates only its increases and one that accumulates only its decreases: The two partial sums then enter an ordinary ARDL model as separate regressors:

The long-run effects are \(L^{+} = -\delta^{+}/\rho\) for increases and \(L^{-} = -\delta^{-}/\rho\) for decreases. If \(L^{+} = L^{-}\) and the short-run coefficients are equal too, the model collapses to the linear ARDL. When to use NARDL, and when not to Use it when theory or earlier evidence gives a reason to expect asymmetry: fuel prices that rise faster than they fall, exchange-rate depreciations versus appreciations, monetary tightening versus easing. Do not use it only because it is fashionable. The symmetry tests in Steps 6 and 7 decide: if symmetry is not rejected, report the linear ARDL instead. How to write it: model section To allow increases and decreases in the policy rate to have different effects on corporate borrowing costs, we use the nonlinear ARDL model of Shin, Yu and Greenwood-Nimmo (2014). The federal funds rate is decomposed into partial sums of its positive and negative changes, \(x_t^{+} = \sum_{s \le t} \max(\Delta x_s, 0)\) and \(x_t^{-} = \sum_{s \le t} \min(\Delta x_s, 0)\) , which enter the unrestricted error-correction model as separate regressors. The long-run effects of rate increases and rate decreases are \(L^{+} = -\delta^{+}/\rho\) and \(L^{-} = -\delta^{-}/\rho\) . Long-run symmetry ( \(L^{+} = L^{-}\) ) and short-run symmetry ( \(\sum_i \lambda_i^{+} = \sum_i \lambda_i^{-}\) ) are tested with Wald tests.
Load the data and check the orders of integration
How to read it Both series are I(1), and neither is I(2). NARDL has the same requirement as ARDL: any mix of I(0) and I(1) is allowed, but no I(2) variable. The dependent variable should be I(1).

How to read it ffr_pos only ever rises and ffr_neg only ever falls. Added to the starting value, they rebuild the original series exactly, which the check confirms. Always run this check: a mistake in the partial sums invalidates everything that follows. The asymmetry tests need enough observations of both kinds. Here there are 198 months with a rise and 169 with a fall, which is well balanced. If your regressor almost always moves in one direction, NARDL cannot identify the other side. Because ffr_neg is negative and falling, read its coefficient with care: a positive coefficient on ffr_neg means that a rate cut (a fall in ffr_neg ) lowers the yield.
Choose the lags and estimate the model

How to read it The unrestricted search gives the two partial sums very different lag lengths, and BIC drops rate increases altogether. For the symmetry tests it is cleaner to give both partial sums the same lag length, so that the comparison is like for like. We use 3 lags of the yield and 3 of each partial sum, close to the AIC choice for the yield, and vary this in the robustness step.

How to read it The F-statistic of 6.88 is above the upper bound at the 1% level (5.54), so a long-run relationship exists between the Baa yield and the two partial sums. The bounds test is read exactly as in the ARDL guide; the number of regressors counted for the critical values is two, the two partial sums. The error-correction coefficient is negative and significant: 5.3% of a deviation is corrected each month, a half-life of about 13 months.
Long-run coefficients and the long-run symmetry test

How to read it Rate increases: the long-run effect is 0.07 and is not significantly different from zero. A permanent 1-point rise in the federal funds rate does not raise the Baa yield in the long run. Rate decreases: the long-run effect is 0.24 and significant. A 1-point cut lowers the Baa yield by about 0.24 points in the long run. The symmetry test has the null that the two long-run effects are equal. It is rejected at 5% (p = 0.03): the long-run response is asymmetric. The test restricts the two level coefficients to be equal, which is the same as \(L^{+} = L^{-}\) because both are divided by the same \(\rho\) .

How to read it In the month of a rate rise , the Baa yield goes up by 0.30 points per point, and this is significant. In the month of a rate cut there is no significant response. The test of equal short-run sums has a p-value of 0.07: asymmetry at the 10% level, not at 5%. Put the two tests together and a pattern appears. Rate rises pass through quickly but not permanently ; rate cuts pass through slowly but permanently . Four outcomes are possible in any NARDL study, and you should say which one you have: symmetry in both, asymmetry only in the long run, only in the short run, or in both.

The dynamic multiplier traces the path from the short run to the long run: the cumulative response of the yield, month by month, to a permanent 1-point rise and to a permanent 1-point cut. How to read it After a rise the yield jumps by 0.30 points at once and by 0.40 after one month. The effect then fades, to 0.17 after a year and 0.07 after five years. After a cut the yield does not fall at first; the point estimates for the first months are slightly positive and not significant. The decline builds slowly: −0.06 after a year, −0.16 after two years and −0.23 after five. The asymmetry line is the sum of the two. It would be zero at every horizon if the responses were mirror images. It starts positive, because rises have the larger short-run effect, crosses zero after about two years, and ends negative, because cuts have the larger long-run effect.

Both lines converge to the long-run effects from Step 6 (0.07 and −0.24), which is a useful check that the multipliers were computed correctly. The multiplier figure is usually the main figure of a NARDL paper.

How to read it Serial correlation. Not rejected (p = 0.63), so the bounds test is valid. ARCH and CUSUM. Neither rejects. Heteroskedasticity and normality. Both rejected, so the Wald tests should be based on robust standard errors. The symmetry tests with HAC standard errors give p-values of 0.08 for both the long run and the short run, compared with 0.03 and 0.07 before. Because the White test rejected, these robust p-values are the ones to rely on. That changes the wording of the conclusion: the evidence for asymmetry is significant at the 10% level, not the 5% level. Report the robust version. Choosing whichever standard errors give the smaller p-value is not acceptable practice, and referees check.

How to read it Lag length. With 2, 3 or 4 lags the long-run effects stay at about 0.05 for rises and 0.24 for cuts, and long-run symmetry is rejected each time. 1985–2007. The long-run asymmetry is unchanged, so it is not a product of the zero-rate years after 2008. Short-run asymmetry is not significant in this sample. 1990–2019. The bounds F-statistic of 3.84 lies between the bounds (3.23 and 4.32): the test is inconclusive, so the long-run results for this subsample cannot be interpreted. 1970–2019. With the high-inflation years included, the long-run effects are 0.81 and 0.82 and symmetry is clearly not rejected (p = 0.76). Over the longer sample the response is symmetric and much larger.

Linear ARDL. The symmetric model gives a single long-run effect of 0.56. The NARDL has the lower AIC, so the data from 1985 prefer the asymmetric model. The asymmetry is a feature of the period since 1985, not a constant of the economy. One reason to be careful: both yields and the policy rate trended downwards over 1985–2019, and the falling partial sum may partly capture that common decline. A paper should present the asymmetry as a finding for this period and discuss this possibility.

Section What goes in it From which step Data Sources, sample, unit-root tests, plot of the series and the partial sums Steps 2 and 3 Method Why asymmetry is expected, the partial-sum decomposition, the NARDL equation Step 1 Cointegration Bounds F-statistic with critical values Step 5 Long-run results \(L^{+}\) and \(L^{-}\) with standard errors, long-run symmetry test Step 6 Short-run results Short-run coefficients, short-run symmetry test, dynamic multiplier figure Steps 7 and 8 Robustness Diagnostics, lag lengths, samples, comparison with the linear ARDL Steps 9 and 10 How to write it: results The bounds F-statistic of 6.88 exceeds the 1% upper critical value (5.54), indicating a long-run relationship between the Baa yield and the positive and negative partial sums of the federal funds rate. The estimated long-run effects differ markedly: a one-point reduction in the policy rate lowers the Baa yield by 0.24 points in the long run (s.e. 0.11), whereas the long-run effect of a one-point increase is 0.07 and statistically insignificant. A Wald test rejects long-run symmetry at the 10% level with heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-robust standard errors (p = 0.08). In the short run the pattern is reversed: a rate increase raises the yield by 0.30 points within the month, while a rate cut has no significant immediate effect. The dynamic multipliers in Figure 3 show that the response to increases peaks after one month and then decays, while the response to cuts builds gradually over several years. The asymmetry is specific to the period since 1985; over 1970–2019 the long-run responses to increases and cuts are both about 0.8 and symmetry is not rejected.

What a referee will ask Why should the effect be asymmetric? Give the economic reason before the statistics. Is symmetry actually rejected? Report both Wald tests. If neither rejects, the linear ARDL is the right model. Are there enough rises and enough falls? Report the counts. Do the partial sums just pick up a trend? Partial sums trend by construction, one up and one down. If the dependent variable has a long trend of its own, the two can become confused. Check subsamples and, where sensible, include a trend. Where are the confidence bands on the multipliers? Journals increasingly expect bootstrap bands around the asymmetry line. Are the results stable across samples? Asymmetry found in one period often does not hold in another.
OLS Regression: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text. All variables stationary in levels.

Every empirical paper starts from a question that a regression can answer. Ours is: do macroeconomic conditions explain monthly U.S. stock returns? The model selection tool showed that all four variables are stationary in levels, so the model can be estimated by ordinary least squares in levels: Symbol Variable in the file Definition Expected sign \(r_t\) sp500_return Monthly log return on the S&P 500, in percent dependent variable \(\Delta ip_t\) ip_growth Monthly growth of industrial production, in percent positive: stronger activity raises expected cash flows \(\Delta ffr_t\) d_fedfunds Change in the federal funds rate, percentage points negative: a higher discount rate lowers prices \(\Delta cs_t\) d_credit_spread Change in the Baa–10-year Treasury spread, percentage points

negative: wider spreads signal higher risk Before you estimate anything Write down the equation, define every variable with its unit, and state the sign you expect and why. Referees look for this table. It also protects you from explaining a result only after you have seen it. How to write it: model section To examine whether macroeconomic conditions explain stock returns, we estimate \(r_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \Delta ip_t + \beta_2 \Delta ffr_t + \beta_3 \Delta cs_t + \varepsilon_t\) , where \(r_t\) is the monthly log return on the S&P 500, \(\Delta ip_t\) is the growth rate of industrial production, \(\Delta ffr_t\) is the change in the federal funds rate and \(\Delta cs_t\) is the change in the Baa–Treasury credit spread. We expect \(\beta_1 > 0\) , since stronger real activity raises expected cash flows, and \(\beta_2 < 0\) and \(\beta_3 < 0\) , since higher discount rates and higher credit risk lower equity valuations.
Load the data and confirm the starting point

How to read it There are 420 monthly observations. The ADF p-values are all below 0.05, so a unit root is rejected for every variable: all four are I(0). This is the condition for using OLS in levels. If even one variable were I(1), you would be in a different guide. Note the minimum return of −22.8%. That is October 2008. One extreme month can drive a regression, so we will check later whether the results survive without the crisis.

How to read it Coefficient. A one-percentage-point rise in the credit spread within a month is associated with a return that is 9.7 percentage points lower. A typical monthly change in the spread is 0.17 points (its standard deviation), which corresponds to about −1.7 points of return. t-statistic and p-value. Only the credit spread is significant. Industrial production growth and the change in the federal funds rate have p-values of 0.52 and 0.20, so we cannot say their effects differ from zero. R-squared. The three variables explain about 20% of the variation in monthly returns. For stock returns this is high; most of it comes from the credit spread. F-statistic. The regressors are jointly significant.
Do not report these standard errors yet. They are valid only if the residuals pass the diagnostic tests in the next steps.

OLS standard errors assume that the errors are not correlated over time. The Breusch–Godfrey test has the null hypothesis of no serial correlation . How to read it A Durbin–Watson statistic near 2 means no first-order autocorrelation; 1.61 points to positive autocorrelation. The Breusch–Godfrey p-values are far below 0.05 at every lag length, so the null of no serial correlation is rejected. There is a specific reason here. The S&P 500 series is a monthly average of daily prices, and averaging creates first-order autocorrelation in returns even when daily returns have none. Knowing your data's construction often explains a failed test. The coefficients are still unbiased, but the standard errors are wrong. The fix comes in the step on robust standard errors.

OLS standard errors also assume a constant error variance. The White and Breusch–Pagan tests have the null of homoskedasticity ; the ARCH test checks whether volatility clusters over time. How to read it All three tests reject at the 1% level. The error variance is not constant, and it clusters in time, which is the usual finding for financial returns: calm periods and turbulent periods alternate. As with serial correlation, the coefficients are unaffected but the conventional standard errors cannot be trusted.
Diagnostic test 3: normality of the residuals

How to read it The Jarque–Bera test rejects normality: the residuals are skewed to the left (−0.62) and have fat tails (kurtosis 4.6 against 3 for a normal distribution). The plots show why: a few very large negative months, above all in 1987 and 2008. With 420 observations this is not a serious problem. The t- and F-tests are still valid in large samples by the central limit theorem. State this in the paper rather than hiding the test. Normality matters much more in small samples.
Diagnostic test 4: functional form, multicollinearity and stability

How to read it RESET has the null that the linear functional form is correct. It is rejected (p < 0.001), so something nonlinear is missing from the model. This one affects the coefficients themselves, not just the standard errors, so it must be dealt with. VIF values are all close to 1. Values above 10 would signal harmful multicollinearity; here there is none. CUSUM tests whether the coefficients are stable over the sample. The test statistic rejects stability at 5% (p = 0.02), and in the plot the CUSUM line drifts down and touches its lower bound near observation 290, which is early 2009. Both point to a change in the relationship around the financial crisis, so a subsample check is needed later.
Diagnostic test 4: functional form, multicollinearity and stability

How to write it: diagnostics paragraph Diagnostic tests on the baseline specification indicate serial correlation (Breusch–Godfrey LM(6) = 23.27, p < 0.01) and heteroskedasticity (White LM = 64.77, p < 0.01) in the residuals. Inference is therefore based on Newey–West heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors throughout. The Jarque–Bera test rejects normality, reflecting a small number of extreme negative returns; given the sample of 420 observations, inference relies on asymptotic results. Variance inflation factors below 1.2 rule out multicollinearity. The RESET test rejects the linear specification (F = 28.66, p < 0.01), which motivates the nonlinear specification considered below.
Fix what failed: robust standard errors and a better specification

Two different problems need two different fixes. Serial correlation and heteroskedasticity leave the coefficients unchanged but make the standard errors wrong. The standard remedy is Newey–West (HAC) standard errors. A common rule for the lag length is \(4(T/100)^{2/9}\) , which gives 5 for 420 observations. A rejected RESET test means the model itself should change. A natural candidate is that large moves in the credit spread matter more than proportionally, so we add the squared change. How to read it With HAC standard errors the credit-spread coefficient is unchanged at −9.75, but its standard error almost doubles, from 0.95 to about 1.8. It is still strongly significant. This is typical: ignoring serial correlation and heteroskedasticity makes results look more precise than they are.
Fix what failed: robust standard errors and a better specification

In the extended model the squared term is negative and significant: large widenings of the spread hurt returns more than proportionally. RESET no longer rejects at 5% (p = 0.10), and R-squared rises from 0.20 to 0.26. The federal funds rate now has the expected negative sign and is significant at 5%. A better specification can change your conclusions about other variables, which is why the RESET result could not be ignored.

A result that holds in one specification only will not convince a referee. Check the choices a reader would question: the extreme crisis months, the dynamics, and the sample. How to read it Read down each column and ask whether the sign, size and significance survive. Credit spread. Negative in every row, and significant at 1% everywhere except 1985–2001, where it is smaller (−4.18) and significant only at 10%. The relationship is clearly stronger after 2002. That matches the CUSUM warning from Step 7, and it belongs in the paper. Federal funds rate. Between −1.6 and −2.4 in every row; significant at 5% except in the early subsample. The crisis. Dropping September 2008 to June 2009 barely changes either coefficient, so the main result is not driven by the crisis months.
Report honestly what holds and what weakens. A robustness table in which one result weakens is more credible than one in which nothing ever changes.
Build the results table for the paper

Journals expect one table with the specifications side by side, standard errors in parentheses and significance stars. How to read and format it In column 3 the squared term has a much larger standard error (7.2 against 1.0). Without the crisis months there are few large spread movements left, so the nonlinearity is estimated imprecisely. It is identified mainly from turbulent periods, and the paper should say so. Give the table a title and a note that a reader can understand without the text: the dependent variable, the sample, the type of standard errors and the meaning of the stars. For example: "Dependent variable: monthly S&P 500 log return (%). Sample: 1985:01–2019:12. Newey–West standard errors with 5 lags in parentheses. *** p<0.01, ** p<0.05, * p<0.1." To export the table to Word or LaTeX use table.as_latex() or table.tables[0].to_excel("results.xlsx") .

The analysis is finished. The paper now has a standard structure, and each step above feeds one part of it. Section What goes in it From which step 1. Introduction The question, why it matters, what you find, how it differs from earlier work Steps 1 and 10 2. Literature What is known, and the gap your paper fills your reading 3. Data Sources, sample, definitions, summary statistics, unit-root tests Step 2 and the selection tool 4. Method The equation, expected signs, estimator, standard errors Steps 1 and 8 5. Results The main table and its interpretation Steps 3, 8 and 10 6. Robustness Diagnostic tests and alternative specifications Steps 4 to 9

7. Conclusion The answer to the question, limits, implications all How to write it: results paragraph Table 2 reports the estimates. Changes in credit conditions are the dominant macroeconomic correlate of stock returns: in the baseline specification, a one-percentage-point widening of the Baa–Treasury spread is associated with a 9.7-percentage-point lower monthly return (column 1), and the relationship is nonlinear, with larger widenings having more than proportional effects (column 2). Once this nonlinearity is accounted for, increases in the federal funds rate are also associated with lower returns. Industrial production growth has no significant contemporaneous relationship with returns in any specification. The model explains 26% of the monthly variation in returns.

How to write it: abstract This paper examines whether macroeconomic conditions explain monthly U.S. stock returns over 1985–2019. Using OLS with heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors, we find that changes in the corporate credit spread are the main macroeconomic correlate of returns, with a nonlinear effect that strengthens for large spread movements. Changes in the federal funds rate are negatively related to returns once this nonlinearity is modelled, while industrial production growth is not. The results are robust to excluding the 2008–09 financial crisis and to allowing for return dynamics, and the relationship with credit spreads is markedly stronger after 2002. What a referee will ask Is this causal? No. Returns and credit spreads are determined at the same time, and both respond to news. The regression measures association. Say so, and do not write "the effect of" without an identification strategy. If you need causal claims, see the 2SLS / GMM guide.

Why these variables? Justify each from theory or earlier papers, not from what turned out significant. Are the standard errors right? State the type and the lag length. Does one episode drive the result? Show the table without the crisis. Is the relationship stable? Report subsamples, and mention the CUSUM evidence. Final checklist before you submit Every variable is defined, with its unit and source. Unit-root tests are reported, and they justify the choice of OLS in levels. All diagnostic tests are reported, including the ones that failed, with what you did about them. Every number in the text matches the tables. The code runs from the raw data file to the final table without manual steps.
Smooth-Transition Regression (LSTAR and ESTAR): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

Do the coefficients depend on the level of a state variable, and how fast do they move? In a smooth-transition regression the transition function \(G\) rises from 0 to 1 as the transition variable \(s_t\) moves through a range. In the logistic form (LSTAR), \(G = 1/\{1+\exp[-\gamma (s_t-c)/\sigma_s]\}\) : the regimes at low and high \(s_t\) differ, and \(c\) is where they are halfway between. In the exponential form (ESTAR), \(G = 1-\exp[-\gamma (s_t-c)^2/\sigma_s^2]\) : the two outer regimes are alike and differ from the middle. The slope parameter \(\gamma\) (scaled by the standard deviation of \(s_t\) ) sets the speed. As \(\gamma\to\infty\) the logistic form becomes the threshold model of the threshold regression guide .

A linear model is nested in two ways, \(\theta=0\) or \(\gamma=0\) , so the usual tests do not apply. Teräsvirta (1994) replaces \(G\) by a third-order Taylor approximation, which turns the linearity test into an F test, and the pattern of rejections chooses between LSTAR and ESTAR. Given \(\gamma\) and \(c\) , the model is linear in the other coefficients, so estimation concentrates the sum of squares on \((\gamma, c)\) , searches a grid and polishes with a simplex search. Four checks before you trust a smooth-transition model Is linearity rejected for the transition variable you use? If not, the nonlinear estimates are not determined. Try the candidate variables and delays and report the search.

Is \(\gamma\) estimated away from its limits? A very large \(\gamma\) means an abrupt switch, and its standard error is unreliable because the likelihood is almost flat. A very small \(\gamma\) makes the model a polynomial in \(s_t\) , with no meaningful location. Does the location \(c\) lie inside the data and away from the edge of its range? It is searched between the 10th and 90th percentiles of \(s_t\) , so that both regimes have observations. Are the residuals clean? Remaining serial correlation means the dynamics are too short. Add lags before interpreting the regimes. How to write it: the model We estimate a nonlinear monetary policy rule with a smooth-transition regression (Teräsvirta 1994). The federal funds rate depends on its own lag, inflation and the output gap, and all coefficients, including the intercept, move with a logistic function of the output gap lagged three quarters. The transition function has a speed \(\gamma\) and a location \(c\) . We test linearity with Teräsvirta's third-order Taylor approximation for every candidate transition variable and delay, choose the logistic or the exponential form by the sequence of tests, estimate \(\gamma\) and \(c\) by nonlinear least squares on 237 quarterly observations from 1960 to 2019, and report Newey–West standard errors.
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The sample runs from 1960Q1 to 2019Q4 (240 quarters). The federal funds rate averages 4.99% with a standard deviation of 3.65 and ranges from 0.07% to 17.78%. Inflation averages 3.20% (standard deviation 2.19). The output gap averages about zero (standard deviation 1.43) and runs from −4.80 to 3.72 points, so large positive gaps are rare. The funds rate is correlated with inflation (0.76) and weakly with the output gap (0.20), and it is persistent (ADF p = 0.33), so a lag of the funds rate is included to capture interest-rate smoothing.
Test linearity and choose the transition variable and the delay

How to read it Linearity is rejected at 5% for all eight combinations of transition variable and delay, and at 1% for seven. Two things guide the choice. First, the quality of the fit: with the output gap lagged three quarters the AIC gain over the linear model is 57.4, against 11 to 18 for the other output-gap delays and 6 to 16 for inflation. Second, whether the transition is identified. With inflation as the transition variable the slope \(\gamma\) sits at its lower limit of 0.1 for a delay of one quarter (so the model is close to a polynomial in inflation, with a location of 6.5% that carries no meaning) and at its upper limit of 500 for a delay of four. With the output gap at a delay of three quarters, \(\gamma\) is 10.0 and the location is 1.47 points, inside the range of the data. We use the output gap lagged three quarters. The search is exploratory, and the p-values of the linearity tests do not account for it; the size of the AIC gain is the more informative number.

How to read it The linearity test rejects strongly: F = 4.73 for the 12 restrictions, p < 0.0001. In the sequence that chooses the form, the first-order test (H02) has the smallest p-value (below 0.0001, against 0.011 for H03 and 0.018 for H04), so the rule chooses the logistic form. The speed \(\gamma\) is 10.0 (standard error 7.5, so it is not precisely estimated, as expected when the transition is quick) and the location is \(c = 1.47\) output-gap points (standard error 0.16, t = 9.4). A \(\gamma\) of 10 means that the transition function rises from about 0.12 to 0.88 as the lagged output gap moves through about half a point around 1.47, which is roughly one standard deviation above the mean gap. So the switch is quick but not a step.
The coefficients in the two regimes

How to read it The linear part is the regime when the lagged output gap is low (G = 0) and the nonlinear part is what high gaps add. When the gap was low, the funds rate adjusts slowly (coefficient on its lag 0.963, standard error 0.021), does not respond to inflation (0.025, 0.041) and responds to the output gap with 0.268 (0.031). When the gap was high (G = 1), the lag coefficient falls to 0.381 (0.261), the response to inflation rises to 0.928 (0.376) and the response to the gap is 0.303 (0.137). The changes in the lag and inflation coefficients are significant at 5% (p = 0.030 and 0.017). The changes in the intercept and the output-gap coefficient are not (p = 0.52 and 0.81). The long-run response of the funds rate to inflation, the inflation coefficient divided by one minus the lag coefficient, is 0.68 in the low regime and 1.50 in the high regime. The second is above 1, the Taylor principle, so the rule is stabilising only after a boom. The first should be read with care, because it divides a small coefficient by a number near zero. The high regime rests on few observations, so its standard errors are wide.
Fit, residuals and the transition over time

How to read it The smooth-transition model lowers the sum of squared residuals from 144.3 to 107.7 and the residual standard deviation from 0.787 to 0.689. AIC falls from −109.6 to −167.0 and BIC from −95.7 to −132.4, so both criteria prefer it even after counting \(\gamma\) and \(c\) . The Ljung–Box test rejects no serial correlation (statistic 15.7, p = 0.003), so the dynamics are not fully captured with one lag; the AR(2) variant below gives the same \(\gamma\) and location, so the main result does not depend on it, but the standard errors should be treated with care. The first chart shows the transition function: it is zero for output gaps below about 0.9, rises between about 1.1 and 2.5 and is one above that. The second chart shows it over time. It is at or near zero most of the time and rises only in booms: the mid-1960s, the early 1970s, around 1979–1980, around 1990, in 2000 and in 2006–2007. It is zero throughout the 2010s.
Does the answer depend on the form, the lags, the delay and the range?

How to read it The baseline results hold across the variants that are well behaved. With two lags of the funds rate the speed is 10.5, the location is 1.50 and the AIC gain is 57.1. Widening the range for \(c\) to the 5th to 95th percentiles changes nothing, because the baseline location (1.47) is inside the range. The variants that change the answer are flagged in the table. A narrower range for \(c\) (15th to 85th and 20th to 80th) puts the location on the edge of the range (1.45 and 1.14), which shows the range is cutting off the best location. The exponential form, imposed by hand, also ends on the edge of its range (1.65) and its AIC gain is 32.4, well below the logistic 57.4. A delay of four puts \(c\) on the edge with \(\gamma\) above 100, and a delay of two gives a slower transition ( \(\gamma = 3.0\) ) but an AIC gain of only 17.0. The delay of three quarters, the logistic form and a location of about 1.5 points are what the data support.
Smooth or abrupt? Compare with the threshold regression

How to read it The threshold regression with the same specification and the same delay rejects linearity (sup-F = 72.9, bootstrap p = 0.018 with 499 draws, 5% critical value 59.0). It places the threshold at 1.38 (95% interval 1.22 to 1.43), with 38 of 237 observations above it. Its fit is almost the same as the smooth model: a sum of squared residuals of 109.4 against 107.7, and an AIC of −165.1 against −167.0. The data therefore cannot separate an abrupt switch from a quick smooth one, which agrees with the wide standard error of \(\gamma\) . Both place the switch at an output gap of about 1.4 to 1.5 points. Choose the threshold model if you want a simple statement (a rule that changes at a level), and the smooth-transition model if you want to show how the response changes through the range.

How to write it: results We find that the response of U.S. monetary policy to inflation depends on the state of the cycle. The federal funds rate is modelled with a logistic smooth-transition regression on its own lag, inflation and the output gap, with all coefficients moving with the output gap lagged three quarters. Teräsvirta's linearity test rejects strongly (F = 4.73, p < 0.0001) and the sequence of tests selects the logistic form. The transition is centred at an output gap of 1.47 points (standard error 0.16) with a speed of 10.0 (standard error 7.5). When the lagged gap is low, the rate adjusts slowly (coefficient on its lag 0.96) and does not respond to inflation (0.03). When the gap is high, adjustment is faster (0.38) and the coefficient on inflation is 0.93 (standard error 0.38), a long-run response of 1.5, above the Taylor-principle threshold of 1. The model lowers AIC by 57 points and BIC by 37 points relative to the linear rule. Residual serial correlation remains (Ljung–Box p = 0.003), and the high regime contains few observations, so these estimates are imprecise. The results are the same with two lags and for a wider range of the location, and a threshold regression with the same specification gives a similar fit and a threshold of 1.38.

Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification): a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

What does a structural shock do to the system? The reduced-form VAR is and the residuals are linked to the structural shocks \(\varepsilon_t\) (uncorrelated, unit variance) by \(u_t = B \varepsilon_t\) . The data give \(\Sigma = BB'\) , which does not pin down \(B\) : any rotation of \(B\) fits equally well, so identification needs \(n(n-1)/2\) extra restrictions. The impulse response of variable \(i\) to shock \(j\) at horizon \(h\) is then \(\Psi_h B\) , where \(\Psi_h\) are the moving-average coefficients of the VAR. Three schemes are common. Recursive (Cholesky): \(B\) is lower triangular, so a variable ordered earlier does not respond to later shocks within the period. Long-run restrictions: the cumulative effect of some shocks on some variables is zero, for example demand shocks have no permanent effect on output (Blanchard and Quah 1989). External instrument (proxy-SVAR): a series \(z_t\) correlated with one structural shock and uncorrelated with the others identifies that shock's column of \(B\) (Stock and Watson 2012, Mertens and Ravn 2013).
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

Three checks before you trust a structural VAR Can you defend the identifying assumption in words? The restrictions are not tested by the data (a recursive or long-run scheme is exactly identified). Write down the economic argument, and test how much the answer depends on it by changing the ordering or the scheme. Is the VAR well specified? Stationary or differenced variables, enough lags to leave the residuals white, and a stable system. Long-run identification also needs a stationary VAR. Is the instrument valid (proxy-SVAR)? Relevance is testable (the first-stage F statistic) and exogeneity is not, so the argument for exogeneity must come from how the instrument was built. How to write it: the model
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

We estimate a structural VAR for real GDP growth and the unemployment rate and identify supply and demand shocks with the long-run restriction of Blanchard and Quah (1989): only the supply shock has a permanent effect on the level of output. The VAR has four lags, a compromise between the Akaike criterion (eight lags) and the Schwarz and Hannan-Quinn criteria (two lags); two, six and eight lags are robustness checks. Confidence bands are 95% percentile intervals from a wild residual bootstrap with 500 replications, which is robust to heteroskedasticity. We check the result against a recursive identification with both orderings.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)
Load the data and check the variables

How to read it The sample has 240 quarters (1960Q1-2019Q4). Real GDP growth (annualised) averages 3.01% with a standard deviation of 3.25; the unemployment rate averages 5.97% with a standard deviation of 1.61. Both series are treated as stationary: the ADF test rejects a unit root for growth (p < 0.001) and for unemployment (p = 0.045, borderline), and the KPSS test does not reject stationarity for either (p = 0.059 and p = 0.10). Unemployment is very persistent, which is why the largest VAR root is close to one. Long-run identification needs a stationary VAR, so this check matters.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)
Choose the lags and check stability

How to read it The Akaike criterion keeps falling slowly up to eight lags (-1.120), but most of the gain comes by two lags (-1.087 against -1.118 at four). The Schwarz and Hannan-Quinn criteria both choose two lags. We use four lags as a compromise and test two, six and eight below. With eight lags the largest root of the VAR is 0.93, so the system is stable and the long-run restriction is well defined.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

How to read it The long-run impact matrix shows the identifying restriction: the entry for the effect of the unemployment ("demand") shock on GDP growth is exactly zero, so only the supply shock moves the level of output permanently. The supply shock raises the cumulated response of annualised growth by 3.97, which is about 1% of the level of output. The supply shock explains 87% of the forecast-error variance of GDP growth at one quarter and 80% at five years, and 5% of that of unemployment at one quarter, rising to 38% at five years. The demand shock explains 95% of the variance of unemployment at one quarter and 62% at five years, and 13% to 20% of that of GDP growth.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

How to read it A supply shock raises GDP growth by 2.69 points on impact (band 1.46 to 2.82), 0.42 after one year, and the effect dies out after two years, which leaves the level of output permanently higher. Unemployment falls by 0.30 points after four to eight quarters (band at four quarters -0.46 to 0.05, at eight quarters -0.47 to 0.00), a borderline-significant decline that fades by year five. The demand-side shock raises unemployment by 0.22 points on impact and 0.45 after one year, and lowers GDP growth by 1.02 points on impact (band -2.37 to 0.03), after which growth is above its baseline (0.17 at two years, band 0.02 to 0.41) as unemployment returns to normal. The unemployment response is back to zero within five years (band -0.05 to 0.17), as the identification requires for the demand shock.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

How to read it The recursive schemes give the same shapes but different impact effects, because each ordering assumes away one of the two contemporaneous responses. With growth ordered first, a growth shock lowers unemployment by 0.44 after one year and 0.39 after two; an unemployment shock has no effect on growth on impact by assumption. With unemployment ordered first, the unemployment shock raises unemployment by 0.50 after one year and lowers growth by 1.59 on impact. The long-run scheme (-1.02 on impact) lies between the two. The persistence of the unemployment response (a peak of 0.31 to 0.50 after about a year, mostly gone after five years) is similar in all three, so the conclusion about dynamics does not depend on the identification, while the impact effect of the unemployment shock on growth does.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)
Proxy-SVAR: check the instrument before the responses

How to read it The same instrument gives very different first stages depending on the policy indicator it is paired with. For the one-year Treasury yield the robust first-stage F is 4.4 (R-squared 0.026): the instrument is weak and the engine's warning applies, so the responses would be unreliable. For the federal funds rate the F is 17.4 (R-squared 0.049), above the rule-of-thumb value of 10. Choose the policy indicator and the sample for reasons stated in advance and report the F statistic for the choice you use, not for the best of several; exogeneity of the instrument cannot be tested. How to read it The shock is scaled to raise the federal funds rate by one percentage point on impact. The rate peaks at 2.31 points after twelve months (band 1.12 to 2.94) and returns to the baseline by month 36. Industrial production rises insignificantly (1.32 after twelve months, band -1.92 to 4.29), and prices are close to zero throughout (-0.11 on impact, 0.20 after 24 months, bands including zero). The credit spread falls by 0.71 after twelve months (band -1.27 to -0.17). The estimates are too imprecise to say anything about the real effect of monetary policy; they show the workflow, and they show how wide proxy-SVAR bands can be with a short sample and a weak-to-moderate instrument.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

How to read it The impact response of GDP growth is almost unchanged (2.62 to 2.69) with two, four, six or eight lags, and the response of unemployment after one year is between -0.25 and -0.35. The upper end of the 95% band is just below zero with four and eight lags and just above it with two and six, so the borderline significance of that response depends on the lag length; the 90% band excludes zero (-0.44 to -0.04). Changing the bootstrap seed moves the band limits in the second decimal place only.
Structural VAR (Cholesky, Long-Run and Proxy Identification)

How to write it: results A supply shock identified with the long-run restriction of Blanchard and Quah (1989) raises GDP growth by 2.69 percentage points (annualised) on impact and 0.42 points after four quarters, with a permanent effect on the level of output of about 1%. Unemployment falls by about 0.3 percentage points after one to two years, a response that is borderline significant at the 5% level (95% band -0.46 to 0.05 after four quarters, -0.47 to 0.00 after eight) and fades within five years. The supply shock explains 80% of the forecast-error variance of GDP growth and 38% of that of unemployment at a five-year horizon. A demand-side shock raises unemployment by 0.45 points after one year with no permanent effect on output. The shape of the responses is similar under recursive identifications with either ordering, which differ mainly in whether unemployment shocks move growth within the quarter (0 or -1.59 against -1.02 here). The results are stable across two to eight lags (impact on growth 2.62 to 2.69).

Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code and more.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable

Does the process switch between regimes when a variable crosses a level, and where is that level? In a threshold regression the coefficients depend on whether a threshold variable \(s_t\) lies below or above a threshold \(\gamma\) : When \(s_t = y_{t-d}\) and \(x_t\) holds lags of \(y_t\) , the model is the self-exciting threshold autoregression (SETAR); \(d\) is the delay. The regime is determined by the data, not by the calendar, which is the difference from a structural break (see the Bai–Perron guide ): the same regime can occur in 1965 and in 1985. The switch is abrupt. If you expect a gradual move between regimes, use the smooth-transition guide .
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable

The threshold \(\gamma\) is estimated as the value that minimises the sum of squared residuals, searched over observed values of \(s_t\) that leave at least a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of the sample in each regime. Because \(\gamma\) does not exist under the null of linearity, the usual F test is not valid. Hansen (1996) shows how to bootstrap its distribution, and the confidence interval for \(\gamma\) is the set of values whose likelihood-ratio statistic stays below 7.35 (Hansen 2000). Four checks before you trust a threshold Does the bootstrap reject linearity? Without rejection the threshold estimate is not reliable, whatever it looks like. Report the p-value. Is the threshold stable? Re-estimate with other lags, delays and trimming. A threshold that moves everywhere is not identified.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable

Do the regimes contain enough observations? A regime with a handful of observations gives imprecise coefficients and can be driven by a few episodes. Is the switch really abrupt? If the residuals look better under a gradual change, use the smooth-transition model. How to write it: the model We test for threshold nonlinearity in U.S. inflation with a self-exciting threshold autoregression (Tong 1978; Hansen 1996, 1997). Quarterly inflation, the GDP-deflator rate, follows an AR(2) whose intercept and coefficients may differ between two regimes defined by whether inflation \(d\) quarters earlier was above a threshold \(\gamma\) . The delay \(d\) is chosen from one to four quarters and the threshold is searched over values that leave at least 15% of the 236 observations in each regime. We test linearity with the sup-F statistic and a fixed-regressor bootstrap with 999 draws, which accounts for the search over \(\gamma\) and over \(d\) , and we report a confidence interval for \(\gamma\) from the likelihood-ratio statistic.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
Load the data and look at the series

How to read it The sample runs from 1960Q1 to 2019Q4 (240 quarters; 236 remain after allowing for two lags and a delay of up to four quarters). Inflation averages 3.19% with a standard deviation of 2.31, ranges from −0.53% to 12.14% and is skewed: the median is 2.42%, well below the mean, because of the 1970s. The series is highly persistent (first autocorrelation 0.90, ADF p = 0.19). That matters for a threshold model: a persistent series that spends a long spell at a high level can look like a threshold process, so the bootstrap test and the robustness checks below carry the weight.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable

How to read it The sup-F statistic is 25.9. The bootstrap p-value is 0.081 with 999 draws, with the delay searched from one to four quarters in the data and in every draw, and the 5% bootstrap critical value is 28.6. Linearity is therefore rejected at 10% but not at 5%: the evidence for a threshold is suggestive, not conclusive. The search chooses a delay of three quarters. The test of one threshold against two does not reject (statistic 10.0, p = 0.13), so the model has one threshold and two regimes. Note that the bootstrap already accounts for the search over \(\gamma\) and \(d\) ; testing at a delay picked after looking at the data would give a p-value that is too small.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
The threshold, its interval and the regimes

How to read it The threshold is 4.23% inflation, three quarters earlier, with a 95% interval from 4.01% to 5.51%. The lower regime holds 180 quarters and the upper regime 56 (24%). Below the threshold the AR coefficients are 0.51 (standard error 0.076) and 0.30 (0.062), they sum to 0.81, and the implied mean is 2.21%. Above it they are 0.88 (0.12) and −0.12 (0.14), sum 0.76, intercept 1.55 (0.46), and the implied mean is 6.56%. Persistence is similar in the two regimes; what differs is the level the series gravitates to, which is the intercept. The threshold model lowers the residual standard deviation from 0.990 to 0.945 and the sum of squared residuals from 228.3 to 205.2. AIC falls from −1.9 to −19.0 even after counting the extra coefficients and the threshold as parameters.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
Look at the likelihood and at the regimes over time

How to read it The likelihood-ratio statistic is far above the 5% critical value of 7.35 (between about 12 and 21) for almost every candidate threshold, and it falls below it only for values between 4.0% and 5.5%. That is the confidence interval: one well-defined region, with a sharp edge, as an abrupt switch implies. The second chart shows where the regimes sit. The upper regime contains 4 quarters in the 1960s, 34 in the 1970s, 16 in the 1980s, 3 in the 1990s and none since 2000. Fifty of the 56 high-regime quarters therefore belong to the Great Inflation. This is the main caution: the threshold may be picking up that episode, which the Bai–Perron guide dates with mean shifts in 1973Q2 and 1982Q4 and a high-inflation mean of 7.4% between them. The two readings agree on what happened. They differ on why: a threshold model says high inflation sustains itself, while a break model says the regime was a period.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
Does the answer depend on the lags, the delay and the trimming?

How to read it Six of the nine specifications put the threshold between 3.98% and 4.45%: the baseline (4.23%), AR(1) (3.98%), AR(4) (4.45%), a delay fixed at three (4.23%) and 20% and 25% trimming (4.23% and 4.01%). The evidence for it, however, depends on the lag order. The bootstrap p-value is 0.03 with one lag, 0.08 with two, 0.16 with three and 0.19 with four, because more lags absorb part of the nonlinearity. A delay fixed at one gives no threshold (p = 0.32, threshold 1.40%), so the delay matters. The p-values for a fixed delay (0.020 for a delay of three) are smaller than the baseline because they ignore the search over delays, so report the baseline. With 10% trimming the search picks a delay of four and a threshold of 5.75% (p = 0.076). Taken together: a threshold near 4% is the most stable finding, and it is moderately supported.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
Is a second threshold needed, and what if the threshold variable is another series?

How to read it A second threshold is not supported. With 10% trimming, so that smaller regimes are allowed, the sup-F test of one threshold against two has p = 0.79. The second experiment replaces the threshold variable with the unemployment rate (lagged one quarter), in a regression of inflation on its lag and unemployment. Linearity is not rejected (sup-F 5.8, p = 0.86). The estimated threshold of 5.2% (interval 4.3% to 7.6%) is then not meaningful, and the coefficients by regime should not be interpreted. This is the output you should expect when there is no threshold: a threshold estimate always exists, and only the bootstrap test says whether it is real.
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable

How to write it: results We find moderate evidence of threshold nonlinearity in U.S. inflation. The bootstrap sup-F test of linearity gives a statistic of 25.9 and a p-value of 0.081 (999 draws, with the delay searched over one to four quarters), so linearity is rejected at 10% but not at 5%. The estimated threshold is 4.23% inflation, three quarters earlier (95% interval 4.01% to 5.51%). When inflation was at or below this level (180 quarters), the AR(2) coefficients sum to 0.81 and the implied mean is 2.2%; above it (56 quarters) they sum to 0.76 and the implied mean is 6.6%. Fifty of the 56 high-regime quarters lie in the 1970s and 1980s, so the threshold may reflect the Great Inflation, which the Bai–Perron procedure dates with mean shifts in 1973Q2 and 1982Q4. The threshold near 4% is stable across lag orders, delays and trimming, but its statistical support weakens with three or four lags (p = 0.16 and 0.19) and we treat it as suggestive. We find no evidence of a second threshold (p = 0.79), nor of a threshold in the unemployment rate (p = 0.86).
Threshold Regression and SETAR: Regimes Defined by a Variable
