VAR in First Differences: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is: do stock prices and real activity help to predict each other? Finance theory says stock prices are forward-looking and should lead output; a feedback from output to prices is also possible. A vector autoregression (VAR) treats every variable as endogenous. Each variable is regressed on its own lags and the lags of the others, so you do not have to decide in advance which one is "the" dependent variable. The model selection tool found that the log S&P 500 and log industrial production are both I(1) and are not cointegrated . With no long-run relationship to preserve, the correct model is a VAR in first differences: The first difference of a log, multiplied by 100, is a percentage growth rate, so the VAR is in monthly stock returns and monthly industrial production growth.

Why not estimate the VAR in levels? With unit roots and no cointegration, a regression in levels is a spurious regression: the usual t- and F-tests are not valid. If the series were cointegrated, differencing would throw away the long-run relationship, and you would need the VECM guide instead. This is why the cointegration test comes before the model. How to write it: model section Augmented Dickey–Fuller tests indicate that the log S&P 500 index and log industrial production are integrated of order one, and the Johansen trace test finds no cointegrating relationship between them (trace statistic 4.74 against a 5% critical value of 15.49). We therefore model the joint dynamics of the two series with a vector autoregression in first differences, \(\Delta y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} A_i \Delta y_{t-i} + u_t\) , where \(\Delta y_t\) contains the monthly stock return and the monthly growth rate of industrial production, both in percent.
Load the data and take first differences

How to read it In levels the ADF p-values are far above 0.05: both series have a unit root. After differencing they are 0.000: the growth rates are stationary. The plots show the same thing. The levels trend and wander; the differences move around a constant mean. One observation is lost by differencing, leaving 419 months.

The lag order \(p\) is chosen with information criteria. Each one trades off fit against the number of parameters; the lowest value wins. How to read it The star marks the minimum of each column. AIC and FPE choose 4 lags; BIC and HQIC choose 3. The criteria often disagree, because BIC penalises extra parameters more heavily. A sound rule: start from the AIC choice, check that the residuals are free of serial correlation (Step 5), and use the BIC choice as a robustness check. Too few lags leave autocorrelation in the residuals, which invalidates the tests. A few too many lags only costs some precision.

How to read it There is one equation per variable. In the ipg equation, the second and third lags of the stock return are positive and highly significant: a rise in stock prices is followed by faster industrial production growth two to three months later. In the ret equation, the first two lags of industrial production growth are also significant. Individual VAR coefficients are hard to interpret because the lags interact. Do not build your results section on them. Papers report three summaries instead: Granger causality tests, impulse responses and variance decompositions, which follow below. Most papers put the coefficient table in an appendix. The correlation of the residuals (−0.08) is small. That will matter in Step 7.

A VAR is only usable if it is stable and its residuals are free of serial correlation. How to read it Stability. All eigenvalues of the companion matrix have modulus below 1 (the largest is 0.83), so the VAR is stable: shocks die out, and impulse responses are meaningful. A modulus at or above 1 would mean the system is not stationary, and you should check the differencing and the lag order. Serial correlation. The portmanteau test has the null of no residual autocorrelation. The p-values of 0.66 and 0.85 do not reject it, so four lags are enough. If this test rejected, you would add lags. Normality. Rejected, as is usual with financial data and extreme months such as October 2008. Estimates stay consistent; with over 400 observations the asymptotic tests remain usable. Report the result.

ARCH. Both equations show volatility clustering. This does not bias the coefficients but affects standard errors, which is a reason to treat borderline p-values with caution. How to write it: specification and diagnostics The lag length is set to four months, as selected by the Akaike information criterion; the Schwarz criterion selects three, and results with three lags are reported as a robustness check. The estimated VAR is stable, with all eigenvalues of the companion matrix inside the unit circle (largest modulus 0.83). A portmanteau test does not reject the null of no residual autocorrelation up to 12 lags (p = 0.66). Multivariate normality of the residuals is rejected, reflecting a small number of extreme observations, and the residuals show ARCH effects, as is common for monthly financial data.

Variable \(x\) Granger-causes \(y\) if past values of \(x\) improve the forecast of \(y\) beyond what the past of \(y\) alone provides. The null hypothesis is no Granger causality : all coefficients on the lags of \(x\) in the equation for \(y\) are zero. How to read it Both nulls are rejected at the 1% level, so predictability runs in both directions. The evidence is much stronger from stock returns to industrial production (the larger F-statistic), which fits the view that stock prices look ahead. "Granger causality" is about prediction, not cause . Stock prices may rise because investors expect output to grow; that does not mean higher prices cause the growth. Use the phrase "Granger-causes" or "helps to predict", never "causes".

An impulse response shows how each variable reacts over time to a one-time shock in one of them. Because the residuals of the two equations are correlated, the shocks must be separated first. The standard method is the Cholesky decomposition, which requires an ordering : the first variable can affect the second within the same month, but not the reverse. We order stock returns first. The justification is practical: the S&P 500 series is an average over the month, while industrial production for a month is published only in the middle of the next month, so stock prices cannot react to it within the month. How to read it Each panel shows the response of one variable (named second in the panel title) to a shock in another. The dashed lines are 95% confidence bands: a response is statistically different from zero only where the band excludes zero.

A stock-return shock of one standard deviation (3.4%) is followed by significantly higher industrial production growth two to three months later. The cumulative effect, which is the effect on the level of industrial production because the VAR is in growth rates, builds to about 0.6% after two years. An industrial-production shock (0.5%) raises stock returns over the next two months, with a cumulative effect of about 1.7%. All responses return to zero, as they must in a stable VAR. Because the model is in first differences, always say whether you are describing the response of the growth rate or the cumulative response of the level. Readers usually care about the level.

The forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD) answers a different question: of the unpredictable movements in each variable, what share is due to each shock? How to read it At a two-year horizon, stock-return shocks account for about 12% of the forecast error variance of industrial production growth, up from under 1% at one month. Industrial production shocks account for about 5% of the variance of stock returns. Each variable is mostly driven by its own shocks, which is normal; what matters is that the cross shares are not zero and that the share of stock shocks in output grows with the horizon. Statistically significant Granger causality can go with a small variance share. Report both: one says whether the link exists, the other how much it matters.

The three choices a referee will question are the ordering, the lag length and the sample. How to read it This table changes the conclusions, which is exactly what a robustness table is for. Ordering and lag length do not matter. Reversing the ordering, or using 3 or 8 lags, leaves the tests and the size of the responses almost unchanged. The ordering is harmless here because the residual correlation is only −0.08. The sample matters a great deal. Before 2008, stock returns still Granger-cause industrial production (p = 0.002), but the cumulative response is less than half as large (0.26% against 0.61%). The reverse channel, from industrial production to stock returns, disappears completely (p = 0.63).

After 2010 neither test rejects. With only 120 months the tests have low power, so this is weak evidence of no relationship, but it is certainly not evidence for one. The honest summary: stock returns lead industrial production, with an effect that the 2008–09 crisis roughly doubles; the feedback from production to returns is a crisis-period result only. A paper that reported only the full-sample numbers would overstate both findings. Always run the subsample check before you write the results section.

Section What goes in it From which step Data Sources, sample, transformations, unit-root and cointegration tests Step 2 and the selection tool Method The VAR equation, why first differences, lag selection, identification (ordering) Steps 1, 3 and 7 Results Granger causality table, impulse-response figure, variance decomposition table Steps 6 to 8 Robustness Diagnostics, alternative ordering, lag length, subsamples Steps 5 and 9 Appendix Full coefficient estimates Step 4 How to write it: results Table 3 reports Granger causality tests. In the full sample, the null that stock returns do not Granger-cause industrial production growth is rejected at the 1% level (F = 13.06, p < 0.01), as is the reverse null (F = 4.58, p < 0.01). Figure 2 shows the orthogonalised impulse responses. A one-standard-deviation shock to stock returns (3.4%) is followed by a statistically significant rise in industrial production growth two to three months later, and raises the level of industrial production by 0.6% after two years. Stock-return shocks account for 12% of the forecast error variance of industrial production growth at the 24-month horizon.

These full-sample results are influenced by the 2008–09 financial crisis. In the 1985–2007 subsample, stock returns continue to Granger-cause industrial production growth (p < 0.01), but the cumulative response falls to 0.3%, and there is no evidence of predictability running from industrial production to stock returns (p = 0.63). We conclude that stock prices are a leading indicator of real activity, while the apparent feedback from activity to stock prices reflects the crisis period. What a referee will ask Why this ordering? Give an economic or institutional reason, and show the reverse ordering. Why differences and not levels? Cite your unit-root and cointegration tests. Is the lag length arbitrary? Report the criteria and a different lag length.

Is this causal? Granger causality is predictive. Structural claims need identifying restrictions that you must defend. Is it stable over time? Show subsamples, especially around 2008. Only two variables? Omitted variables, such as interest rates, can create or hide Granger causality. Say so, or add them.
Vector Error-Correction Model: a step-by-step guide to writing the empirical paper, with Python code, real output and sample text.

The question is: are short and long interest rates tied together in the long run, and which one adjusts when they drift apart? The expectations hypothesis of the term structure says the long rate is an average of expected future short rates plus a premium, so the two should not move apart permanently. The model selection tool found that both yields are I(1) and cointegrated . A vector error-correction model (VECM) is a VAR in first differences with one extra term, the deviation from the long-run relationship in the previous period: Part Name What it tells you \(\beta' y_{t-1} + \rho\) error-correction term how far the system was from its long-run relationship last period

\(\beta\) cointegrating vector the long-run relationship between the variables \(\alpha\) adjustment (loading) coefficients how fast each variable moves to close the gap \(\Gamma_i\) short-run coefficients the short-run dynamics Why a VECM and not a VAR in differences? A VAR in differences uses only changes, so it ignores the information that the two rates are currently far apart or close together. When the variables are cointegrated, that gap predicts future changes, and leaving it out is a misspecification. The VECM is the model that keeps both the long-run relationship and the short-run dynamics. How to write it: model section Both yields are integrated of order one, and the Johansen procedure indicates one cointegrating relationship between them. We therefore estimate the vector error-correction model \(\Delta y_t = \alpha(\beta' y_{t-1} + \rho) + \sum_{i=1}^{k} \Gamma_i \Delta y_{t-i} + u_t\) , where \(y_t\) contains the 10-year and 1-year Treasury yields, \(\beta\) is the cointegrating vector describing their long-run relationship, and \(\alpha\) contains the adjustment coefficients that measure how quickly each yield responds to deviations from that relationship.
Load the data and look at the long-run relationship

How to read it Each yield has a unit root in levels (p-values of 0.81 and 0.53) and is stationary in first differences: both are I(1). But the difference between them is stationary (p below 0.01). That is cointegration in its simplest form: two series that wander, but wander together. The plot makes this visible. Both yields rose until the early 1980s and fell for decades afterwards; the spread kept returning to its mean of about 1 percentage point. Always plot your candidate long-run relationship before testing it formally.
Choose the lag order and the deterministic terms

Two specification choices come before the cointegration test. Lag order. k_ar_diff is the number of lagged differences in the VECM. It equals the lag order of the VAR in levels minus one. Deterministic terms. This choice matters more than students expect, because the critical values of the Johansen test depend on it. Option in statsmodels Meaning Use when "n" no constant almost never "ci" constant inside the cointegrating relation the series have no trend; the long-run relation has a non-zero mean. Interest rates, spreads, ratios. "co" constant outside the relation the series have linear trends (log GDP, log prices) "cili" trend inside the relation the long-run relation itself trends Interest rates have no deterministic trend, and their spread has a positive mean, so "ci" is the right choice here.
Choose the lag order and the deterministic terms

How to read it AIC chooses 7 lagged differences, HQIC 5 and BIC only 1. As in any VAR, the choice is settled by the residuals: Step 8 shows that with 1 lag the residuals are strongly autocorrelated, so the BIC choice is too short. We use 7 and check 5 as robustness.

The rank \(r\) is the number of independent long-run relationships. With two variables it can be 0 (no cointegration: use a VAR in differences), 1 (one long-run relation: use a VECM), or 2 (both series are actually stationary: use a VAR in levels). How to read it Read each test from the top. "Rank ≤ 0" is rejected (29.39 is above 15.49), so there is at least one cointegrating relation. "Rank ≤ 1" is not rejected (1.07 is below 3.84), so there is exactly one. The trace test and the maximum-eigenvalue test agree, which makes the conclusion solid. When they disagree, most authors follow the trace test and say so.

How to read the long-run relation The software reports the vector as \(\beta' y + \rho = 0\) . Moving everything except the first variable to the right-hand side changes the signs : a coefficient of −0.936 on the 1-year yield means the long-run relation is yield_10y = 1.31 + 0.936 × yield_1y In the long run, a 1-point rise in the 1-year yield goes with a 0.94-point rise in the 10-year yield, and the constant of 1.31 is the average term premium. Forgetting the sign change is the most common mistake in student papers that use a VECM.
Test restrictions on the long-run relation

Theory often predicts a specific value. The expectations hypothesis implies that the long-run coefficient is exactly 1, which would make the simple spread stationary. How to read it The estimate of 0.936 is not significantly different from 1 (p = 0.12). The data are consistent with a one-for-one long-run relationship, which agrees with the stationary spread found in Step 2. Testing the value that theory predicts turns a statistical result into an economic one.

The adjustment coefficients show which variable does the correcting . How to read it Sign. For the variable the vector is normalised on, the adjustment coefficient should be negative : when the 10-year yield is above its long-run value, it falls. Here it is −0.111 and significant, so the error-correction mechanism works. A positive or insignificant coefficient on every variable would mean there is no adjustment, which contradicts cointegration. Speed. The 10-year yield closes about 11% of any gap per quarter, so half of a deviation is gone after roughly 6 quarters. Weak exogeneity. The coefficient for the 1-year yield is small and insignificant (p = 0.65). The short rate does not respond to the gap: it is weakly exogenous . In economic terms, the short rate, which follows monetary policy, leads, and the long rate adjusts to it.

How to write it: long-run results The estimated cointegrating relationship is \(y^{10}_t = 1.31 + 0.936\, y^{1}_t\) , with a standard error of 0.041 on the slope. The hypothesis of a unit long-run coefficient cannot be rejected in the system estimate (p = 0.12), consistent with the expectations hypothesis and a stationary term spread, although dynamic OLS yields a smaller coefficient of 0.84. The adjustment coefficient in the 10-year yield equation is −0.111 (t = −2.78), implying that about 11% of a deviation from the long-run relationship is corrected each quarter, with a half-life of roughly six quarters. The adjustment coefficient in the 1-year yield equation is statistically insignificant (p = 0.65), so the short rate is weakly exogenous: the long rate adjusts to the short rate rather than the reverse.

How to read it Causality. In a VECM there are two channels. Long-run causality runs through the error-correction term (Step 7). Short-run Granger causality runs through the lagged differences, tested here. The 1-year yield Granger-causes the 10-year yield (p below 0.01); the reverse is not significant at 5%. Both channels point the same way: from the short rate to the long rate. Serial correlation. The portmanteau test does not reject (p = 0.67): 7 lags are enough. With the single lag that BIC preferred, the same test rejects strongly, which is why we did not use it. Normality. Rejected, because of the extreme interest-rate movements of 1979–82. The Johansen procedure is robust to non-normality, in particular to excess kurtosis, so this does not overturn the results. Report it.

How to read it VECM impulse responses differ from those of a stationary VAR in one important way: they do not return to zero . The variables are I(1), so a shock moves their levels permanently. What cointegration guarantees is that the two responses settle at levels that respect the long-run relationship, so the gap between them closes even though each yield ends up at a new level.

How to read it The long-run coefficient is stable in the Johansen estimates. It lies between 0.87 and 1.02 across lag lengths and subsamples, always within about two standard errors of 1. The adjustment is less stable. With 5 lags the 10-year adjustment coefficient is smaller and only significant at 10%, and weak exogeneity of the 1-year yield becomes borderline (p = 0.06). In 1990–2019 the adjustment coefficient is not significant at all (p = 0.18). Error correction was fast and clear before 1990 and is hard to detect afterwards, a period that includes seven years of short rates held near zero. Dynamic OLS disagrees on the size. It gives a long-run coefficient of 0.835 with a small standard error, which is significantly below 1. Single-equation and system estimators can differ in finite samples, and when they do the paper must say so.

What can be claimed: the two yields are cointegrated, the long-run coefficient is close to one, and the long rate does the adjusting. What cannot be claimed without qualification: that the coefficient is exactly one, or that the adjustment speed is constant over time.

The trace statistic rejects the null of no cointegration (29.39 against a 5% critical value of 15.49) but not the null of at most one cointegrating vector (1.07 against 3.84). What a referee will ask Why these deterministic terms? Justify the choice from the behaviour of the data; do not leave the software default unexplained. Is the rank robust to the lag length? Show the test for at least two lag lengths. Did you read the signs correctly? Write the long-run relation as an equation in the text. Is the adjustment coefficient negative and significant? If not, the error-correction story does not hold. Is the long-run relation stable? Report subsamples; long samples of interest rates span very different monetary regimes. Does a different estimator agree? Report DOLS or FMOLS next to the Johansen estimate.

Open Econometric Systems is a free tool on this site that runs 51 econometric models in your browser: you upload a CSV, choose the model and read the results, and nothing leaves your computer. Every model has a tutorial guide with real output and the Python code behind it.
Which model should I use for time series that are not stationary?

It depends on the unit-root tests. All variables stationary: OLS or local projections. All I(1) and not cointegrated: a VAR in first differences. All I(1) and cointegrated: a VECM. A mix of I(0) and I(1): ARDL, or NARDL if increases and decreases may differ. The Time-Series Guide has a decision tree and a questionnaire that picks the model from your answers.
When should I use a threshold regression and when a smooth-transition regression?

Use a threshold regression (TAR or SETAR) when behaviour changes abruptly once a variable crosses a level, and you want to estimate the level with a bootstrap test and confidence interval. Use a smooth-transition regression (LSTAR or ESTAR) when the change is gradual as a state variable moves through a range. With a very fast transition the two give nearly the same fit, which the smooth-transition guide shows on a Taylor rule.
How is a threshold different from a structural break?

A structural break is tied to a date: the parameters change at some point in time and stay changed. A threshold is tied to the level of a variable: the same regime can occur at several dates whenever the variable is above or below the threshold. The Bai-Perron guide covers breaks and the threshold guide covers thresholds. If the high regime sits in one period, as high inflation does in the 1970s, the two readings can look alike.
How do I estimate the effect of a monetary policy shock?

Use a structural VAR or local projections. The SVAR guide identifies shocks by a Cholesky ordering, long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah) or an external instrument (proxy-SVAR). The local-projections guide gives impulse responses horizon by horizon without a full system. For Bayesian versions see the Bayesian guide.

The Panel Data Guide covers pooled OLS, random and fixed effects, GMM, Driscoll-Kraay errors, mean-group and CCE estimators, first differences, pooled mean group, CS-ARDL, panel local projections and Hansen's panel threshold regression, with a decision tree to choose among them.
How do I estimate causal effects?
The Causal Inference Guide covers difference-in-differences and event studies, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and related designs, each with code and real output.
Is there a guide for Bayesian estimation or Markov-switching models?

Yes. The Bayesian Guide covers Bayesian VARs, factor-augmented and time-varying parameter VARs, stochastic volatility and more. The Markov-Switching Guide covers Markov-switching autoregressions, regressions and VARs.
Can I run the models on my own data?

Yes. Open Econometric Systems runs in your browser: choose a model, upload a CSV, map the columns and run it. The data stay on your computer. Each result can be reproduced with the Python code shown in the model's guide.
